titleStmt.title: Hippiatrica Berolinensia; or, The Berlin Hippiatrica

sourceDesc.p:
Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un helleniste) a partir du texte grec deja present dans le corpus zoomathia sous zoo80/2g (Hippiatrica Berolinensia, compilation byzantine de medecine veterinaire equine transmise sous le nom collectif de plusieurs auteurs anciens cites nommement dans le texte meme : Apsyrtus, Hierocles, Pelagonius, Theomnestus, Eumelus, Hippocrates, Anatolius, entre autres). Le decoupage en 3047 unites de traduction reprend fidelement, dans l'ordre du document, la structure de divisions du fichier source (types book/chapter/section/subsection et leurs numeros n, lesquels renvoient au systeme de numerotation comparative de l'edition critique moderne recoupant plusieurs temoins manuscrits et ne correspondent donc pas a une numerotation continue simple). Les paragraphes qui ne contenaient que de purs reperes d'apparat (numeros isoles, lettres seules du type "t"/"t1") ont ete silencieusement retires de l'extraction quand ils constituaient tout le contenu d'un paragraphe source ; lorsqu'un tel repere n'etait qu'un prefixe accole a du texte reel dans le meme paragraphe, il a ete omis de la traduction sans affecter le texte substantiel. Une poignee de reperes isoles qui subsistaient neanmoins comme entrees de traduction distinctes ont ete rendus explicitement par la mention entre crochets '[apparatus reference marker "..."]'. Les lacunes du manuscrit (signalees dans le texte source par des points de suspension ou des passages manifestement interrompus) sont rendues par la mention explicite "[lacuna]" plutot que comblees par conjecture. Le texte source zoo80/2g.xml contenait une erreur de balisage XML corrigee au moment de cette traduction : une balise fermante

manquante juste apres la recette "Aristos... pros ta kata neuron traumata" (a la frontiere des sections 84/84.1.1) avait pour consequence, en XML generique bien forme mais semantiquement incorrect, d'imbriquer tout le reste de l'ouvrage (chapitres 84 a 130, soit plus de 960 paragraphes reels) a l'interieur de ce seul paragraphe non ferme, le rendant invisible a l'extraction automatique standard. Cette erreur a ete localisee et corrigee dans le fichier source avant l'extraction finale ayant servi de base a la presente traduction, permettant de traduire l'integralite du texte disponible plutot que seulement les 2084 premiers paragraphes initialement detectes. Ce texte est une compilation pharmacologique et hippiatrique tres dense (mesures grecques/byzantines rendues en anglais courant, non converties : litra/"pound", ounce/oungia, cotyle/"cotyla", drachme/"drachm", statere/"stater"), melangeant recettes veterinaires, notes d'anatomie et de conformation du cheval (dentition, catalogue des races regionales), et un vaste formulaire pharmaceutique final de plusieurs centaines de recettes composees (emplatres, onguents, cataplasmes, collyres) largement partage avec d'autres temoins de la compilation hippiatrique. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un helleniste specialiste de medecine veterinaire antique avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte grec deja present dans le corpus sous zoo80/2g.

div.p: Hippiatrica Berolinensia

Having served in the units stationed on the river Ister, I came to know the ailments that befall horses, on which authorities also disagree. Having therefore set these in order, together with the remedies for them, I address this book to you, dearest Asclepiades, my fellow citizen and a very great physician. In it you should not look for fine style, but recognize the natural experience that comes from practice.

I speak first about the horse with fever, as will be recognized from these signs. I have set out these signs for you, so that from such things you may recognize with greater certainty the ailments that befall horses from such signs, and not be laughed at by those who know precisely, speaking without purpose or understanding. For this reason, then, every horse-doctor must know these things very well.

These are the signs: it holds its head drooping toward the ground, unable to raise it up, and its eyes are swollen and bloodshot and hard to open, and sometimes it weeps; its lips are slack, and its whole body likewise, and its tongue is dry, and its testicles are slack; it becomes hot all over its body, and its breathing is likewise hot and heavy, and it thrusts out its legs; led by its handler it cannot walk, nor driven either, but it steps forward little by little, its body swaying, and it leans to one side, and it cannot roll. Such, then, are the accompanying signs.

This happens either when the horse has become overstrained from exhaustion, from driving or from a hard run. It also occurs from excessive cold or heat, and sometimes too from the rawness of its fodder, which especially happens when it takes in some of the new grain or fodder, for these are hard to digest and slow to pass.

This is treated by drawing blood from the temples or the face, and by withholding all food on the first day, only water being given a little at a time, with a few gentle walks; in winter let it be covered, and let its standing-place be warm. When it seems to be doing better, it should be led out to pasture, if the season allows. If not, dry fodder should be offered gradually, a little at a time, sprinkled with honey-water, and the barley should be made into gruel, and this too should not be given in large amounts at first.

Often, too, a horse not suffering fever holds its head drooping and thrusts out its legs likewise, and sways when it lies down. But you will recognize this one too when barley or some other food is offered: for if it eats eagerly, it has no fever, but only fatigue. The one with fever, however, takes none of this, but is without appetite and downcast, seeking only drink.
Never bleed the neck veins of such a horse. For it happens that it becomes convulsed, throws itself down, and cannot be roused. For the ailment intensifies and thus becomes
fatal, if the refusal to eat persists. The horse with fever endures from the onset up to three days, but does not survive beyond that.

Those who, touching the ear and placing a hand on the side near the shoulder-joint, say the horse has fever, do not speak truly. For there is no proof of fever from this. One should not draw blood from a horse showing signs of mere fatigue. For by further purging its strength we will easily do it harm. But the horse with fever must necessarily be bled from the places mentioned, because its head is overcome by the illness and it is easily susceptible.
Hierocles' proem on the same subject.

But even if it were now proper for us to give ear to others, and to render service to those in need in the law-courts, and to devote our zeal to these pursuits, still your request should not go unhonored, most excellent Bassus. For a burden is indeed sweet, and toil easy to bear, says Euripides, when imposed by some friend, and especially by you, for whose sake I would choose, if I may venture to speak in jest, to desert for a time from the phalanx of those who plead in court. Come then, since this seems to you, as Pindar somewhere says, more pressing than leisure,

I shall follow your command and begin to say what ailments are wont to befall horses, and what remedies for each of them. Let Poseidon, god of horses, and Asclepius, savior of the human race, be called upon as helpers of this discourse,

who surely also cares for horses, if we are to make worthy mention of Chiron the Centaur and his pursuits on Pelion. They say, then, that you call a horse into the open field, if I may borrow the proverb from its proper starting-point, before this discourse's writing.

For my part, had it been someone else who had prompted me to this, I might perhaps have been compelled to write many books, going through the nature of horses, their mating and gestation, and further their rearing and the placement of pastures, which are wont to provide them the finest and most healthful grazing and diet, and before these, how one might judge the best horse and train it not to be hard to lead nor hard-mouthed and ticklish, but ready to accept the bit, and not bear its rider with difficulty, and obey the impulses of its riders in everything they wish - all this I would have gone through, had it been for someone else.

But since you are not unpracticed in learning, and have inherited from your forebears a devotion to horse-rearing, and hear of old Simon, who inscribed his methods of horsemanship at the Eleusinion among the Athenians and marked them in figures, and have read through the treatise on horsemanship written by Xenophon son of Gryllus, for this reason it is enough to indicate briefly the most essential points concerning the care of horses.
Those, then, who have more precisely composed treatments for human bodies say, I believe, that one must also take into account the complexion or size of each

of those being treated, since not all require one and the same help, but the very pale and those resembling Scythians, and, by Zeus, the fat, and those extremely dark, like Ethiopians, and the lean, seek a different manner of treatment according to the humor that is deficient or excessive in them. But those who have applied their zeal to the healing of horses have not gone into such refinement, nor for them must one distinguish black from chestnut, or the long-flanked from the round-bodied. Nor indeed do they think it worth troubling over breed, whether a horse be Arcadian or Cyrenaic, or from Iberia, or Cappadocian, or, by Zeus, Thessalian or Mauretanian, or even the Nisaean breed so prized by the King of the Persians.

Since this has been said beforehand, it seems to me not out of tune with the discourse on treatment to speak of the years to which they say a horse's lifespan extends. Aristophanes of Byzantium, then, epitomizing the works on the nature of animals from Aristotle the philosopher, says that a horse can live fifty years and more. And in the Georgics of the Quintilii we found that a horse served one of the cavalrymen continuously through his whole term of service, for twenty-five years in succession.

Tarantinus relates that when the Athenians were building the temple of Zeus near the Enneacrounos, they voted that all the yoke-teams from Attica should be driven into the city. For fear of this decree, one of the farmers led forth an old mule,

in its eightieth year. The people, in honor of its old age, appointed it leader of the teams in the building of the temple, and voted that it should walk ahead unyoked and unstruck, and that none of the grain- or barley-sellers should drive it from their stall or keep it from feeding. Aristotle says that the female is capable of conceiving and being pregnant up to thirty years.

But let our discourse of such matters halt here, lest, carried too far from our subject, we forget ourselves. Seeing that the most approved physicians foretell certain signs, by which one may recognize each ailment from its symptoms, I think it most necessary to adopt this same method of forewarning in the medicine of horses. For if men, who by their natural power of speech can indicate what troubles them, nonetheless required examination by signs from those who treat them, much more, surely, is understanding of these taught indications needed for those who cannot recount what has befallen them.
So, that we may begin from the greatest matters, let us first go through the subject of fever.
On fever.

If a horse is gripped by fever, the ailment will become evident through the following signs: it bows its head strongly toward the ground, so that it cannot raise it up, and its eyes are swollen and tearful, and it lifts its eyelid with difficulty. Further, you would see its jaws slack, and its testicles slack, and its whole body loose and hot,

its breathing coming up fiery and heavy, and it thrusts out its legs. If one drags it along, it is not able to walk, not even if one urges it on; it advances little by little, dragging its body, like men made tipsy and unsteady by too much drink; nor indeed can it roll.

It falls into this feverish state whenever it becomes overstrained from a run and hard driving, or also from excessive cold or heat, and sometimes too from rawness, when it takes in fresh, newly-harvested barley, which is hard to grind and hard to manage.

Treat it, then, in this way: draw blood from the temples and the face, and do not offer it food on the first day, but give only drink, a little at a time, and make it walk a little and gently, kept covered, the place too where it stands being warm. When it seems to be doing better, let it be led out to pasture, if it is the season for grass. If not, let fodder be offered gradually and a little at a time, and well-husked barley in moderate amount, not much at first.

There are also times when a horse not suffering fever bows its head from some fatigue, and likewise thrusts out its legs, and sways when it lies down. But you will recognize this one too by offering it barley or some other food. For if it eats eagerly, it has no fever. For the one gripped by fever does not wish to eat, being dejected and seeking only drink, and, having lain down on the ground, cannot rouse itself nor sleep.
They say that the feverish horse endures from the onset up to three days, but beyond that, unless it happens to get help, does not last.
Stratonicus says that even if it escapes this time, it will one day die of the same ailment.

It is agreed that one should not draw blood from those showing signs of mere fatigue, lest their strength be further purged. But the feverish horse must necessarily be bled, from the parts I have mentioned, because its head especially is weighed down and it is easily susceptible. Those, however, who think they can diagnose fever by touching the ear and the flank near the point of the shoulder seem to me not to attain the true understanding.

You will also be able to help the feverish horse by means of drenches. Grind ten bay-berries carefully, pour on a cyathus of honey and a cyathus of wine and an equal amount of water, then, having mixed it, pour it in through the mouth. Or grind celery seed and pour on two cyathi of wine, and grind again, then add three cyathi of water, and pour it in through the mouth.
If you see it beginning to fall asleep, lead it out for a walk of not more than ten stadia, then make it roll; then also add to its food, giving barley-gruel and radishes,
if they are available, and bay-shoots.
Prognosis and cure of fever.
Its eyes are tearful, and a mist lies over them. It breathes hot, and to the touch it is hot all over, and it hangs its head low, and a chill comes upon it, and it trembles and grinds its

teeth, and its testicles swell, and its mouth is full of thrush, and the withers-ridge is raised, soft, and hot, its eyes swell, and its lips are slacker. When, then, you sense beforehand that hour in which the chill comes upon it and the fever sets in, steam it, or wrap it in cloths, and give it warm raw-must to drink, and reduce its grain, so that it becomes lean.

If its belly becomes bound, take the tender shoots of mulberry, or, failing that, grind the root, boil it in water, then mix in a cup of honey, pour on three of the boiled water, then pour it into its nostrils, and, leading it to a bath, wash it, and rub it down blowing in wine and oil, then wrap it in cloths. And when it is about to sleep, offer it food a little at a time. Draw off about three cups of blood from its temples, and on another day from the legs above the knee, and let six cups flow off, and tend it as best you can.
Anatolius, on the same subject.

You will recognize the feverish horse from its bowels loosening and it relieving itself frequently. It should be treated, then, with a warm bath in summer, but in winter kept warm so that it does not take a chill. A small amount of vetch or wheat-flour should be given as food, and lukewarm water brought for drink, and it should be purged through the bowels, and blood drawn from the neck, or from the veins around the throat or chest, or from the leg, and its knees anointed with warm vinegar. When it seems to have recovered strength, wash it with warm water.

If it has fever from fatigue and grows thin, mix together a cup of goat's milk, enough starch, half a cup of oil, four eggs, and the juice of pounded purslane, and pour it in through the mouth for three days or more, until it recovers.

If it has fever from an inflammation of the tonsils or of the head, it should be kept warm, and its palate anointed with salt mixed with marjoram and oil and pitch together. Its feet and knees should be warmed with warm water, and the parts around its mouth rubbed with nightshade and ground wine-lees, and it should be fed on moss or green fodder without barley.
If it bleeds through the nostrils, one must pour in strained coriander juice.
Eumelus, or Chiron.

When fever comes on, draw blood from the tendon, then take a half-ounce each of cassia, myrrh, and frankincense, mix in sea-turtle blood and old wine, and pour it in through the nostrils for three days.
Or take a bundle of southernwood, enough dried figs, rue, celery, mint, carrot, boil them together, and for three days give the cold decoction to drink.
Agathotychus' drench for the same purpose.
One must drench the feverish horse with three eggs, two ounces of rose oil, one pound of light, fragrant white wine, and let it stand in a well-ventilated place, giving it no barley, only fodder.
Bring cold water to it repeatedly, and even if it does not wish to drink, open its mouth and rinse it out repeatedly.
When it settles down, after three days offer barley gradually.

One ounce of tragacanth, two ounces of chia-clary seed, two ounces of Syrian sumac, one ounce of white pepper, two pounds of boiled-must, three ounces of opopanax, two and a half ounces of celery seed, four ounces of trogline myrrh, nine ounces of germander, three ounces of chamomile, four ounces of male frankincense, two ounces of black pepper, half an ounce of gentian - pound all these together and anoint the whole animal.
Another, for fever and leanness.

If a horse has fever, or is lean, or is worn down by some inner ailment, take two ounces of manna, three ounces of frankincense, half a pound of Illyrian iris, one ounce of pepper, one ounce of bay-berries, one ounce of celery seed, pound them together and, mixed with boiled-must, drench it beforehand.
Another drench.

One pound of donkey's milk, two cyathi of oil, one gramma of saffron, two grammata of myrrh, a full spoonful of celery seed. Grind all these and mix with the milk and oil, and drench it. Give also wheat-flour with lukewarm water in winter, but if it is summer, drench it with barley-flour and cold water. If its flanks are drawn tight and the fever does not stop, it must necessarily be cauterized, and thus receive proper care.
Another.
Half a pound of goat's milk, enough starch, four eggs, one cyathus of oil, and the juice of the plant called partridge-wort, which the Ro-
-mans call 'urciolaris' - mix its juice with the other ingredients, and, drenching with this for six days, you will heal it more quickly.
An ointment for fever.

One pound of roses, one pound of old oil, one and a half pounds of vinegar, one and a half pounds of henna oil, half a pound of purslane and old walnuts, enough mint and rue - pound together and thus anoint.
Another drench.

A feverish horse must of necessity be bled, and then drenched thus: six ounces of gentian, four ounces of birthwort, two ounces of hyssop, two ounces of southernwood, two ounces of wormwood, two ounces of figs, six ounces of celery seed, one bundle of rue - put these into a pot and boil with water until reduced to a third, and when you see it turning black, know that the remedy has been properly boiled, and then take a half-pint of it and drench through a horn.
Another, simple drench.
Strain the juice of fenugreek cleanly, and boil together a bundle of celery and rue and melilot and hyssop, and, mixed together, give it through a horn.
A liniment against fatigue, for fever.

Four ounces of iris oil, one ounce of opopanax, four ounces of bay oil, four and a half ounces of unripe-grape oil, four ounces of castoreum, four ounces of hyssop, one pound and one ounce of tallow, six ounces of Pontic wormwood.
Another anodyne, for feverish horses.
Two ounces of southernwood, two ounces of soda-froth, two ounces of adarce, two ounces of fresh bay-berries - mix these and anoint all over.
On arthritis.
On arthritis, by Apsyrtus.

Sabinus, since you have asked what afflictions befall horses, and whence, I shall show you the gravest of the ailments that befall them, one from which the animal does not easily recover; the affliction is what most call 'malis' (glanders), some call it catarrh, and in Latin 'suppurium'.

In truth it is arthritis, of which these are the signs: thick discharges drip from the nostrils, foul-smelling, apple-yellow in color, and the head hangs heavy, and it snores, and it grows thin from being off its feed, and lameness arises through alternation on each side of the joints. And whatever part of the body it happens to lie upon becomes ulcerated, because there is an effusion beneath the hide, and the joints are full of the most acrid humor.

This happens because the animal does not possess, at the liver, the vessel called the gall-bladder, but instead has a certain slackened little sinew which receives this humor and from there makes its excretion, mixing it with the blood through the arteries fitted along the spine; then the humor, carried up to the spinal marrow, corrupts it and the brain as well. For the head draws its nourishment from the spinal marrow, and so the head is overpowered, and the tongue too, since it also belongs among the jointed members.

One would succeed in treating it by bloodletting, opening the veins in the face and those in the chest, and further by cutting into the pasterns, making use also of every kind of feed, and of a nasal drench of centaury and wormwood
and hog's-fennel boiled in wine. For bitterness is driven out by bitterness. These drenches have also been described by those before us.

These are our own discoveries: about an oxybaphon-measure of Egyptian colocynth seed, pounded and toasted, ground fine in about two cotylae of fragrant white wine, then strained through linen and drenched through the right nostril, and the pulp itself may also be used toasted. Best also is to cut fine the root of the wild cucumber, about half a mina, pour on two cotylae of water, soak overnight, then rub it up, strain, and mix in three drachms of pounded soda; then, taking hold of the tongue, drench through the mouth with half the remedy for seven days, and mix the remaining half into the drinking water.

Bleed it at the outset, but no longer once the affliction has become chronic; for once the strength has been diminished, the animal happens to die. Likewise give the drench at the outset, before the head becomes overpowered and it snorts through the nostrils; once that has occurred, one must give up hope.

Know this too: that from this disease a horse does not easily recover and be purged of it, but a mule not so easily, since, being of mixed-species stock, its arthritis is more entrenched. There is a remedy for this too: take an Egyptian stater's weight of white hellebore, and, cutting the hide of the chest and the underlying tunics, place two linen or hempen loops on either side of the incision, and thus
insert the hellebore, and tie off the loops, and leave it,
until they fall off of their own accord, and do not touch the place with the hand
nor bring it into water.
Give also a drachm of raw pounded soda through the nostril in a cotyla of wine, and let the wine be lukewarm.
Sprinkle the barley too with soda, and likewise the fodder, and offer it, and put soda into the drinking-water as well.
Those that are gelded do not easily fall into this affliction.
It happens, generally, in foals, when they are taken from the herd and brought to the stall, that an effusion of the arthritis sets in, and thus they perish in the winter.

It will be recognized even before the discharge appears through the nostrils, when the horse coughs in such a way as to suggest it had swallowed bones; and it is readily known that it is held by the arthritis, and one must give help as quickly as possible, as written above.

Useful also is this remedy, to administer when it is autumn: press out white grapes to make a quantity of two cotylae, and, mixing into this two heaping spoonfuls of pounded and sifted birthwort, drench likewise through the nostril daily, for up to seven days.
By the same author, on dry glanders, moist glanders,
arthritis, and subcutaneous glanders.
There are four kinds of glanders: the one is moist, another dry, another arthritic, and another subcutaneous.
Of these, some are easily treated, one is treated with difficulty, and one is untreatable.

Easily treated are the moist kind, whose signs are that a thin discharge like water flows through the nostrils, and the subcutaneous kind, from which mange results. Treated with difficulty is the arthritic kind, as written above. Untreatable is the dry kind, from which nothing at all flows through the nostrils, but the animal grows thin though eating and drinking, and does not digest its food, and its flanks are stretched taut, drum-like, and raised, and its hide hardens. For such a case there is no treatment, but it perishes, as has been said also by Eumelus of Thebes:
'Of dry glanders neither I nor anyone else is a physician.' I shall explain the cause: the lung ruptures at the right side, and the horse becomes pleuritic.

Remedies for this too, whenever one perceives the horse has been seized by glanders and is coughing: grind three obols' weight each of manna and frankincense in one cotyla of wine, and let it be drenched through the left nostril; let one also help by cutting radishes fine and mixing them into the barley and offering it.

This too was found by those before us: to fumigate the glanders, in horses and in other beasts of burden that have solid, undivided hooves, with marjoram, covering the head at the nostrils over a new pot holding embers, not more than three days running, but every other day for more days; and let the marjoram especially be the mountain kind.
When glanders occurs in a foal still newborn and nursing, one must take care of the nursing mare, feeding it well

with feed of every kind, and giving it soda to drink, so as to induce thirst, and offering radishes too. Those in the herds that develop glanders must be separated out; for the affliction is contagious, and they readily harm the rest.

Of the so-called glanders, which would be reckoned the gravest and most treacherous of ailments, there are four kinds: one is moist, another subcutaneous, another arthritic, and another dry. Of these, some are easily treated, one is treated with difficulty, and one is untreatable. The moist kind, from which a thin, watery discharge flows through the nostrils, is easily cured. So too the subcutaneous kind, from which mange results; the arthritic kind is treated with difficulty; and the dry kind, as they say, is untreatable.

If, then, an animal falls into the moist glanders, it coughs and discharges a moist humor through the nostrils, and does not take food, but grows weak, and collapses in body, and does not hold up its head or ears. Treat it thus: grind a drachm each of saffron, cassia, myrrh, and cinnamon, and with these put bay-berries and celery seed into a mortar, pour on half a cotyla of honey and a cotyla of fragrant wine, and pour it in through the left nostril. Drench also through the mouth with the broth of a pig's ham boiled together with its trotters,
about two cotylae of it, strained, and with honey poured in, and eggs mixed in, and beaten up. The same may also be drenched through the

left nostril to advantage. And so that the windpipe too may be smoothed, put mustard-seed into a mortar and grind it thoroughly, and, pouring on half a cotyla of wine, pour it in through the left nostril. Or, if you prefer otherwise, grind birthwort root, and, adding on half a cotyla of fragrant wine, drench through the nostril; or grind about three drachms of cyclamen root, and drench likewise in half a cotyla of wine; then lead it out to pasture.

If it is subcutaneous glanders, as Hieronymus the Libyan says, it breathes through the nostrils something foul-smelling and purulent, and it coughs, and grows thin, and breaks out, wherever on the body it happens, and pus-like matter comes out. For such cases one must offer feed of every kind to satiety, and drench through the mouth with the broth of barley-gruel strained from oats, boiled in it best of all a puppy, well cleaned and plucked of hair, or failing that a fowl, and bathe it in warm water.

If arthritis is troubling it, thick apple-yellow discharges drip from the nostrils, and it hangs its head heavy, and its body grows thin from not desiring food, and lameness arises on each side of the joints alternately. And if it lies down anywhere, the part on which it lies becomes ulcerated, because there is an effusion beneath the hide and the joints are beset with the most acrid humor. For since this animal has no vessel called the gall-bladder by the liver, the place that receives the humor of the bile, being slackened and having taken on the affliction, makes its excretion

more irregularly, and mixes it into the blood. So the humor, carried through the arteries fitted along the spine to the spinal marrow, corrupts it and the brain as well, which draws its supply and, as it were, nourishment from the spinal marrow; wherefore the head especially becomes heavy, and the tongue is affected.

One must treat it, then, by bloodletting from the veins in the face beneath the cheekbone and those in the chest, and further from those in the pasterns. Offer feed of every kind, and drench through the nostrils with wine in which centaury, wormwood, and hog's-fennel have been boiled; and make these other drenches too: toast and pound about an oxybaphon-measure of Egyptian colocynth seed, mix it in two cotylae of fragrant white wine, strain through linen, and pour it in through the right nostril.

You may also use the pulp of the colocynth, even unroasted, instead of the seed. Cut fine about half a mina of wild cucumber root, pour on two cotylae of water, and soak overnight; then rub it up and strain, mixing in three drachms of pounded soda, and, taking hold of the tongue, drench through the mouth with half the remedy for seven days, mixing the remaining half into the water you give it to drink. Let it be bled, however, at the outset, since, if the affliction becomes chronic, bloodletting is superfluous once the strength has been reduced, for the animal perishes. And likewise give the snorting through the nostrils attention at the outset and before
the head becomes strongly overpowered.

A horse, then, is saved from this affliction with difficulty, and a mule no more easily, since it too comes of a hybrid animal. Apsyrtus, accordingly, recommends this method of treatment: cutting the hide and tunics of the chest, insert two linen or hempen loops on either side of the incision, and thus insert an Egyptian stater's weight of white hellebore; then, tying off the loops, leave it until they fall off of their own accord, and do not touch the place with the hand, nor put it into water.

Give also a drachm and a half of raw pounded soda in a cotyla of lukewarm wine through the nostril, and let the barley and fodder be sprinkled with soda. Apsyrtus also thinks the soda should be put into the drinking-water.

Dry glanders is the most dangerous, and nearly untreatable. For nothing at all flows through the nostrils, but it lets its head droop, and grows thin (even while taking food) through indigestion, and its flanks are stretched taut, drum-like, and raised, and its hide hardens, and its whole body is drawn tight. Eumelus of Thebes, then, says that such a case is not to be treated, since the lung too undergoes rupture.

Let this remedy too be recorded, for when one perceives at the outset that the horse is about to be seized by glanders and is coughing slightly: grind three obols' weight each of manna and frankincense in one cotyla of fragrant wine, and let it be drenched through the nostril. It helps also

if you also cut radishes fine and mix them into the barley you offer. Give also a drachm and a half of pounded soda in a cotyla of wine through the nostril, and let the wine be lukewarm. Nor should this be overlooked, that the barley and fodder must be sprinkled with soda before being offered.

One must know that the drenches used for moist glanders are suitable also for the dry kind. Some also approve this remedy for glandered horses: pressing out white grapes and collecting two cotylae of wine from them, and pounding and sifting two spoonfuls of the thick birthwort, they drench through the nostrils for seven days; then, having purged it, they lead it out to pasture. If there are no grapes, one must use the remedies written above. It also seems to some to help to fumigate with marjoram through the nostrils, covering the head over a new pot holding embers, every other day, for several hours at a time. They say that gelded horses do not fall into this affliction.

Glanders is a hard-to-dispel settling of putrefied humors, taking its particular name from the part of the body in which it settles. There are two varieties of the disease: one is dry, the other moist. And the dry kind is hidden, the moist kind visible. For a phlegmy discharge, turned to a white color, flows through the nostrils; whence they also call the affliction 'malis' (from its color), naming it from its hue. The
discharge that flows from this affliction, whether through the nostrils or the palate, if odorless, is easily treated, but if foul-smelling

is treated with difficulty, for this reason: as long as the discharge is odorless, it is not from an ulcer but from a residue, which must be purged and cleared away with the remedies and methods about to be described:
A remedy for moist glanders
that is odorless, purgative and clearing, to be drenched both through the mouth and through the nostrils.

One must take three eggs and, having emptied out their insides, fill the shells again, two with honey and one with fish-sauce, and pour it back where their own liquid was poured out, then mix in a quarter-pint of old oil, or an equal amount of henna-oil, and the same of iris-oil; to these add three spoonfuls of the finest pepper, an equal amount of the finest kermes-grain, and an equal amount of Illyrian iris; beat all these together and drench, either through the mouth or through the nostrils, and hang the head up to a moderate height for about half an hour, and thus make

the animal trot. And when it has trotted, one must bind it with the strap of the halter, extending the head downward, drawing the tether from the forefeet to the pasterns, so that, as the animal nods its head, all the fluid runs off onto the ground while it snorts. When you have done this for three days, and the discharge no longer flows, you will treat it in this way: one spoonful of pounded and sifted gentian, one spoonful of

birthwort, one spoonful of bay-berries - mix these with an Italian pint of honey-water, and drench, until you heal it. This, then, is the diagnosis and treatment of moist, odorless glanders; let us now
take up also the foul-smelling kind.
On moist and foul-smelling glanders.
When putrefied humors generate the moist glanders,

that is, blood and phlegm, and manage to inflame the places where they settle, then the discharge that flows smells foul, and is treated with difficulty. Its treatment is this: mix four pints of honey-water with an oxybaphon of oil, and drench for three days. And when the discharge at last flows freely,
first boil cabbage and mallow and press them, then put into a mortar one cabbage, one mallow, three leeks, and one pound of old lard, and pound them together, and make suppository-like pellets

five or seven fingers long, and, taking a mouth-gag and holding down the tongue, give them to swallow; and when they have slid down, drench with spiced wine together with its lees. Doing this for three days, you will cure it. Drench also with old wine mixed with the fourfold remedy, and you will heal the animal, unless an ulcer has already formed. But if ulceration has occurred, use honey-water and the fourfold remedy alone. Having spoken of the varieties of glanders, odorless and foul-smelling, and their diagnosis and treatment, let us speak also of the dry kind:
On dry glanders.
The dry kind, too, arises from putrefied humors settling in the regions around the heart and lung, though not from

phlegm and blood, but from the two biles, and that is why it is dry. It will be recognized in this way: the animal grows suddenly thin, draws in its flanks, and its skin becomes stretched taut, which, when struck along the ribs, resounds like a drum; it will not take food, is unable to cough though eager to, and opens its mouth and is irritated toward coughing, yet does not cough, but stands as though it had swallowed little bones, wincing. If it shows all these signs, it is overpowered and near to death. For such a case it is superfluous to apply treatment. But for one not yet overpowered we shall give help, though with difficulty. Nevertheless, we shall set forth a remarkable remedy, by which we have often cured it. This will heal the animal, if only water still drips from the nostril. Its composition is this: press white grapes to make an Italian pint of must, and add in two spoonfuls of the finest sifted hog's-fennel, and an equal amount of birthwort; drench through the left nostril for seven days, and keep it on a lighter
diet. For thus the dry form of the disease will be cured.

Having spoken of glanders and its varieties, its diagnosis, treatments, and after-treatments, as we ourselves know from having treated it, by both theory and experience, let us also give, without any reserve, what is found among the ancients. What comes from abundance is never superfluous, but rather useful in treatments. Hippaeus, on glanders, who was a Theban - from the Greek Thebes of the seven gates - writes concerning arthritic glan-

ders - when a horse or beast of burden droops its head heavy and nods, drooping its ears, the horse or other beast of burden, and moist discharge flows through the nostrils, and it collapses all over in body, and the joints become callused, and the tail dries out, and the member protrudes, and it goes lame now on one foot, now on another. This, then, is its treatment: one ounce of cut wild-cucumber root, six ounces of soda, two ounces of cassia-fistula, three ounces of southernwood, two ounces of hog's-fennel, one ounce of myrrh, two ounces of aloe, two ounces of cardamom, three ounces of marjoram - pound and sift, and drench three spoonfuls of the remedy in one ounce of water. And anoint along the feet, drawing on also enough scraped verdigris.
Nepho's treatment for arthritic glanders.

If a horse or mule is afflicted with the arthritic disease, it shows these signs: it goes lame on alternate days, first on one foot then another, and the joints swell and gather fluid. You will treat it thus: draw blood from the pasterns until it runs dry. And cauterize the joints with straight cauteries, until water comes out. Then take a pound of preserved tunny, put it into a new pot, pour on four cotylae of old wine, and boil until reduced by half, mixing in enough oil, three drachms of opopanax, and four of rocket-seed, and drench half a cotyla of it each day. In winter you will keep the animal out in the open air, but in summer make use of swimming as well, and it will boil out over the whole body; and use

straight cauteries. And when the scabs have come away from the joints, use a wound-remedy such as this: put in equal parts verdigris, misy-stone, and copper ore, boil, and make a wax salve to anoint around.

Grind fine one ounce of black cumin, the kind that grows together with the grain, put it into half a cotyla of wine and oil, and, adding an equal amount of water, drench for three days. And if the disease is drawn down into the joints, one must cauterize without delay.

[lacuna] Though I could write of all those who have composed the cauterizing remedies, I have declined to lengthen the book; but having found two for the two varieties of the disease, the moist and the dry, I shall set these forth, and you will be satisfied with them, as they are proven remedies:
A drench for moist glanders.

Kermes-grain, Cnidian grain, costus, cyperus, opopanax, ginger, parsley, hyssop, southernwood, tragacanth, saffron, myrrh, aloe, camel-hay flower, melilot, spignel, cardamom, cardamon-seed, birthwort, and fine centaury - pound and sift an equal amount of each, bind together with Attic honey, and make pastilles, cooling them in the shade, each pastille weighing three drachms; and drench, in winter with old wine or spiced wine, in summer with chilled caraway-water, mixing in one ounce of rose-oil.
A drench for dry glanders.
Eight ounces of lettuce seed, eight ounces of purslane juice, one pound of rose-oil, three ounces of saffron, one ounce of poppy juice,

two ounces of cultivated cucumber seed, four ounces of wormwood juice - mix the liquids with the pounded and sifted dry ingredients, store in a leaden vessel, and when needed take three drachms of the remedy, three ounces of rose-oil, and an Italian pint of honey-water, and drench for three days; and once cured, lead it out to pasture by a river, or in a marsh, but not by the sea.
A drench for every kind of glanders.

One pound of birthwort, a quarter medimnos of dried figs, three ounces of marjoram. Pound these separately and carefully, boil in water over a gentle fire the whole night through, and, having strained out an Italian pint, add a quarter of honey, and drench through the mouth.
Another.
Put a land-lizard and a frog, both alive, into oil, and boil them in a pot until their flesh has dissolved into the oil; then strain it and drench the animal through the nostril.
Another, for the outset of the disease.
Mix together the finest fish-sauce, unripe-olive oil, and egg-white with soda-froth, stir it well, and drench through the nostrils.
By Tiberius, for the same affliction.
Give monkey dung mixed with old lard, in three pellets on the first day, seven pellets on the second, and likewise on the third; and after you have given it, let it be handled gently.
Another.
One drachm of myrrh, one drachm of saffron, one drachm of nard, six drachms of opopanax, six drachms of celery seed - grind all these fine, and pour on cotylae
two of sweet wine and one cyathus of white oil, and pour it into the left nostril.
Prognosis and cure of moist glanders.

Glanders also arises from the chaff-dust of straw, when it settles on the lung, or from fodder, when you offer it rotten. Signs of the disease: it discharges something foul-smelling through the nostrils, coughs, draws in its flanks, and refuses food. Use this treatment: dry and pound cyclamen, make it into a fine drachm's weight, and add half an obol's weight of opopanax and some bay-berries; pound both together and drench in wine.
A remedy for the same affliction.
Mix ivory filings with fine salt in fragrant white wine, and drench.
Hippocrates' composition of a pastille for every

kind of glanders: two ounces of bay-berries, five ounces of soda-froth, five ounces of unfired sulfur, three ounces of myrrh, six ounces of saffron-dregs, three ounces of Illyrian iris, and celery-seed and birthwort in equal parts. Put these into a mortar and grind until fine, mix in wine as well, and, having made pastilles, keep them; and when needed, drench with white wine.
On the elephant-disease (elephantiasis).
By Apsyrtus.

When it develops swellings in the neck, and veins stretched taut and bulging in the head and face and likewise raised up, nostrils distended, and what flows from them and from the mouth is frothy and blood-tinged, and it is also drawn taut from the flanks, and it snorts through

the nostrils, and though eager to eat it cannot, nor to drink, but takes only a little at a time, and breaks out all over the body, so that especially the extremities become ulcerated - the nostrils, lips, ears - and fall off of their own accord, and the tongue becomes constricted, which it also thrusts out, unnaturally white and misshapen, and it is unable to whinny - such a horse has the elephant-disease, and there is no remedy for it. It must not stand together with another, but be cast out far away.

[lacuna] ...to make use, along with the others, of this too: mix two cotylae of hot water with three spoonfuls of pounded soda and half a cotyla of good oil, and likewise drench through the nostril, until it appears to be doing well. It is said that one must dry and finely grate deer-rennet, and mix it in [lacuna] and give it to eat.
Another, by Hieron.

To recognize horses with the elephant-disease is not so much difficult as easy. For the dangerous irregularity of these cases is well known to everyone. Whenever, then, you see a horse swollen in the legs, holding its ears erect, the region about the loins harder and unable to bend, its neck stretched taut and unable to shake or bend it, and its gaze unsteady, then know that it is held by the aforesaid affliction.
Its treatment, then, is this: let it be stabled in a warm building, and let the veins of its neck be opened, and after the third day let blood be drawn from its shoulders. And if

need calls for it, from the thighs too after five days, so that, with the veins opened all over the body, the whole venom of the affliction may be dispersed together with the blood; for once the flow of blood has occurred, it does not soon perish. For the rest, give it its usual feed, and if it is unwilling to eat barley, give barley-meal with ground beans, and lukewarm water to drink; and after this, put in wine, oil, soda, bitumen, rue-seed, and bay-berries, and, having boiled them, rub down the whole body against the grain of the hair with the decoction, until you tire; then bandage the region about the loins with fleeces soaked in the same decoction.

Three ounces of wine, half a pint of oil, and wheat, barley, vetch, chickpeas, kidney-beans, and spurge, one pint each - boil all together into one, and, taking out the aforesaid solids, and reducing the decoction alone by a third, rub down the whole horse with it, and make use of the drench given below.

Half a pint of old wine, two ounces of frankincense, two ounces of costus, one ounce of goat's tallow. Grind these together, add half a pint of honey-water, and drench for three days; and on the fourth day with wine and oil, adding also one ounce of laser-resin, and likewise drench for another three days.

One ounce of soda, two ounces of castoreum, two ounces of bay-berries, two ounces of Pontic rhubarb, two and a half ounces of rue. Pound and sift these separately, then mix them together, and adding wine

one ounce and six ounces of oil, give it either through a horn or as you wish. Use this remedy daily until complete recovery. Cover it with blankets at all times, so that, if possible, the animal may sweat, since such an affliction is naturally dispelled by heat.
An emollient for the same affliction.

Four pounds of dried boxthorn-extract, four pounds of cypress-gall, four ounces of lard, one pound of roasted resin, one pound of pounded wormwood - pound and sift the dry ingredients and mix with the melted ones, and use. Give daily the drenches suited to the same affliction, either the five-ingredient powder or other draughts that are needed for the aforesaid disease.
Against plague.
By Pelagonius.

One must learn the treatments and draughts by which plagues are driven off. For horses often fall into plague, either from debility or from heat, or indeed also from cold and hunger, and sometimes too when they are driven to a run after a long period of ease, or when at the proper time they fail to urinate, or when they drink after sweating and much exertion. We know the treatments handed down and set forth by those before us, and we ourselves have also learned by experience.

The so-called five-ingredient antidote is made up of gentian, birthwort, bay-berries, myrrh, and ivory filings. These, pounded and sifted in equal weights, are combined, and the resulting powder is stored away. When, then, the animal falls into the aforesaid disease, take one spoonful of this,
heaping for a horse, and, stirring it into wine, pour it down the horse's throat each day, until it recovers.

This remedy too is very useful: grind and sift wild-cucumber roots, and mix six ounces of soda, itself well pounded, into five measures of wine, and drench the animal with it for five days. And besides this, sprinkle the water it is about to drink with ground wild-cucumber.
Another.

One pound of savin, that is, juniper-herb, three ounces of germander, two ounces of centaury, three ounces of birthwort - pound and sift together, and when needed, mix one heaping spoonful into an ounce of wine, and drench the animal.
Another, by Pisterius the Sicilian.

Pound and sift equal parts of dwarf-elder root and nettle root, pour in a quantity of fish-sauce equal to three eggs, and, straining this through linen, drench through the nostrils of the animal a measure equal to one egg, for three days.
Another dry remedy, by Pelagonius, against plague.

Take a stork chick not yet able to fly, but already feathered, put it alive into an earthenware pot, and, coating this with gypsum, place it in an oven; and once it is well baked, pound it in a mortar, make it into a powder, and store it in a glass jar; and when needed, pour a full spoonful mixed with wine down the throat, until it recovers. For this powder is a healthful one.
Another.
Pour a full cup of the finest fish-sauce into the nostrils of the animal,

the horse's, so that it falls asleep, and see that it stands in a cooler place. Then pound the leaves and roots of coriander and wild fig, and give them with enough honey and wine; and after this pour an oxybaphon-measure of leek juice down its throat, or give crushed vetch mixed with wine for three days, or likewise ground bean-flour with wine for three days. And so that the flour may be soaked the day before and ground fine together with the wine on the next, mix in with it also a little honey and an equal amount of butter, and remember to give these with lukewarm wine.
Another.

Pound about three ounces of wild-fig roots and soak them the day before in about four ounces of water, then stir and strain; then mix in sixteen ounces of well-ground Alexandrian soda, and give for seven days. And if the remedy proves insufficient, add water and pour it in through the mouth with a horn.
Another, against arthritic plague.

Bleed the animal from all the joints, then bind them round with wild-vine, and moreover anoint the joints themselves with liquid pitch, and make it walk about more continually, its feed of course being reduced; give, however, four ounces of ground and sifted barley with wild fig. For this too contributes considerably.
Another.
Having bled the animal, and soaked barley in water or urine, mix vinegar with cow dung and cumin and mustard, and apply to the joints.
Another.

Toast and pound about an oxybaphon-measure of Alexandrian colocynth seed, sift it and mix it in fragrant white wine, and, straining it and putting it into a horn, drench through the nostrils for five days.
Another.

Plagues must be forestalled with remedies. So mix roots of all-heal and eryngo, and also fennel seed, with wheat-flour, and leaven it with hot water. In addition, mix an equal quantity of cassia, myrrh, and frankincense with the blood of a sea-turtle, and give three ounces of old wine through the nostrils. Take two ounces of this remedy, make it up to three, and administer for three days.
Another.

Five ounces of carrot, ten ounces of agaric, three ounces of cassam, three ounces of nard, three ounces of ground-pine herb, six ounces of betony, one ounce of Illyrian iris, three ounces of rush leaf, one ounce of white pepper, ten ounces of southernwood, three ounces of horehound, three ounces of sandonicum - grind all these well, and, straining them into wine, give as a drench.
Another, for the same purpose, by Aemilius Spanus.

Bleed the animal from the feet, then mix four ounces of trogline myrrh, six ounces of saffron, four grammes of centaury, one ounce of Indian spikenard, three ounces of white pepper, five spoonfuls of celery seed, one ounce of poppy, one ounce of propolis, one pint of honey, and enough soda, and make it into pieces the size of a hazelnut, and, dissolving one in a pint of lukewarm water, give it to the ailing animal.
Another, by Litorius of Beneventum.

For a horse suffering from plague, one must first draw blood from the chest, then from the legs; and if necessity presses, from the temples too. It is also good to give it varied feed, that is, barley- and wheat-flour, and also bran, and a little fodder; and besides these to prepare a draught and pour it in through the nostrils, boiling centaury and wormwood in equal weight with enough wine.
Another.

If it begins to go lame in the forelegs, draw blood from the forearms; if in the hind legs, from the thighs; if it drags its flanks and holds its nostrils open, from both temples. Then boil a seven-day-old puppy thoroughly, and, mixing in the urine of an unspoiled child and a cotyla's worth of wine, drench.
Another.

When an animal begins to go lame in the forefeet, first anoint its whole body all over with wine-and-oil, then drench it beforehand with this remedy: four ounces of bear fat, six ounces of centaury, one ounce of the herb called turnip-wort, six ounces of wild thyme, three ounces of hyssop, one ounce of germander, one ounce of fragrant wormwood, one ounce of sharp trefoil, six ounces of wild rue root, three ounces of vervain, three ounces of betony. Boil all these in honeyed wine, and give through the mouth (adding to these also six ounces of wild thyme, three ounces of hyssop, one ounce of germander).
On the lung.
By Hierocles.
Whenever a horse suffers pain in the lung, the affliction is a very

chronic one, and the horse is especially weak in spring. Signs: its body collapses, and it coughs as if it seemed to have swallowed a bone, and it brings up mucus and snores, and drinks much, and seeks more food. Its treatment, then: pound saffron, myrrh, cassia, and cinnamon, grind them together with honey, and, adding wine, drench. One must anticipate it with treatment; for if the lung is allowed to fill with pus, it dies.
By Tiberius, for the same.

Take honey and pepper and a pine-cone still holding its resin, and boil them with wine, and thus drench through the mouth for three days. Feed it especially with more fodder, and allow it to roll about, observing the signs closely. For it happens also to turn into a different disease.
By Eumelus, for the same.

The signs of lung-disease are these: the legs and veins swell, and the testicles twitch more frequently. Fever also comes on in the body, which is detected when the hand is brought near the armpit. Draw blood from this one, then, from the tendon, and, mixing it in summer with vinegar and oil, in winter with wine, anoint the whole body with it. Give this same animal a drench too, mixing one ounce each of spikenard, saffron, myrrh, camel-hay, cassia-fistula, and white pepper, then adding an equal amount of ground vetch, and, grinding and sifting all together, bind with honey and store; and from this, when needed, dissolve an obol's weight in water,

and pour it in through the left nostril. And before giving the drench, wipe out the mouth with wormwood, soda, honey, and vinegar-water. And if it is not helped, apply the cautery to it as well, until it discharges pus.
By Cassius, for the same.

If a horse suffers pain in the lung, it emits breath through the mouth and nostrils, and distends its ribs with the breathing, and looks more distressed, and leaves its food half-chewed in the manger, and smells foul. It is drenched with a compound such as this: grind about two beans' weight of dried bay-berries and turpentine-resin, and enough honey, in vinegar, and pour it in through the nostril. For after this it will urinate blood-tinged and purulent matter, and after that give a drench of one ounce of alum and an equal amount of soda and honey-water, then afterward with honey-water alone, and offer it good fodder.
By Hippocrates, for the same.

A horse afflicted in the lung discharges moisture through the nostrils, breathes heavily through the mouth, and has its flanks drawn in. It is drenched thus: boil the most astringent tree-nuts in one cotyla of wine, and likewise of oil, and give through the mouth, and use smooth feed, mixing vetch into the barley; or boil a pig's brain in one cotyla of wine, and, mixing in half a cotyla of oil, drench with enough of it, and likewise with the aromatic remedy; or boil a cockerel until it falls apart, and, mixing in one pint of sweet wine, drench. Also bleed it, according to

the animal's strength. Give also dog's-tooth grass or lucerne, and sprinkle the drinking-water with flour, so as to keep the animal's strength well-nourished - [lacuna] - if the season permits. Or pound Illyrian iris with water, eggs, and oil, and drench.
On rupture of the lung.

Apsyrtus to Dionysius Tomeus, greetings. Since you keep horses, I want you to know that if rupture of the lung occurs, the neck grows thin, and the chest likewise, and it breathes heavily and coughs and snores and expectorates thick purulent matter, and it goes lame in the forelegs. It is cured slowly, and even once cured it does not endure strenuous exertion.

One must treat it thus: crush vetch and soak it in water a night and a day, and, after washing it, cool it and make it into fine flour, and, sifting it with fragrant dark wine and hot water in equal parts of each, give it to drink; and if it is unwilling to drink, hold its tongue and drench it. And let it not walk about much, but stand covered in a warm place. Warm the strained liquid of the crushed vetch and give it to drink, and mix soda into the rest of the drinking-water while it is warm. Suitable for this too is a raw mixture of fine barley-flour sprinkled with soda and given to eat.

By the same treatment one whose windpipe is strained is also cured, though it takes longer. Both these must be treated by blowing in oil and wine, and the whole rubbing-down must be done against the grain of the hair. It is also beneficial for one with ruptured lung to drench with
warmed sharp vinegar, or human urine mixed with twenty drachms' weight of melted pork fat, but not a woman's urine, when it is in its natural state.
[apparatus reference marker "6.4"]
By Eumelus, for the same.

In some cases it happens that the lungs rupture, either from being forced to run very far, or from continual coughing. Such animals, then, some suppose to have swallowed bones, because they take food and drink more greedily, and discharge pus. Drench it beforehand, then, thus: grind and mix equal weights of saffron, cassia, nard, myrrh, and cinnamon with a cotyla of dark wine, and give it. If these are not to be found, mix ground vetch with wine and hot water, and give enough of it.
[apparatus reference marker "6.5.t1"]
A preliminary drench for those with rupture of the lung
[apparatus reference marker "6.5.t2"]
who are enduring it, or who fall into lung-disease also from running.

Take one ounce each of spikenard, saffron, myrrh, costus, camel-hay, cassia-fistula, and white pepper, and enough vetch-flour, grind and sift all, bind with honey, and, when needed, dissolve it and pour it in through the left nostril. But before doing this, rinse the horse's mouth with wormwood, soda, honey, and vinegar-water.
[apparatus reference marker "7.t.1"]
On peripneumonia, that is, broken wind.
[apparatus reference marker "7.1.t"]
Cure of peripneumonia.
Take six ounces of sulfur, grind six ounces of myrrh, and, pouring on about half a cotyla of wine and about a cyathus of oil, pour it into the nostrils, and give the rest of the usual care. But if

it is not healed by these, cauterize it beneath the armpits toward the belly, holding the iron shallow so as not to reach the depth. And if pus flows, stop, and treat the burn with pitch, wax, and oil.
Slaughter a suckling piglet, with the ailing animal already standing ready close by, and immediately pour the seething blood into its throat.

From wheat leaven, from which bread would otherwise be made, make little balls with boiled must, and give to the animal for as many days as needed, until it recovers. And when giving it to drink, remember to mix flour into the water.
Peel Gallic garlic and pound it in a mortar, mix it with old lard, and make pastilles; then mix honey, boiled must, and eggs, and, dipping the pastilles in this mixture, give for three days.

Soak six ounces of ground bean-meal in three ounces of boiled must, and grind well in a mortar thirty-one peppercorns, and, mixing in one pound of goat's tallow, grind them together again, and drench through a horn for three days.

Following the chapter on coughing, I have written also on lung-disease; for it is especially from this strain that the lung ruptures. Rupture often occurs, too, from running or from jumping, when it clears a fence or a ditch. This often happens in the course of hunting-chases; and sometimes also

a horse or other beast of burden, having become very thirsty, gulps down its drink all at once with much heaving breath, and ruptures the lung, for this reason: the lung has the thinnest membrane of all the internal organs, and the whole of it is filled with its own proper breath.

The fluid within it, being frothy from its continual motion, is exceedingly thin. It has no sinew, flesh, or muscle in it at all, but is the softest of organs. For nature has propped it up against the ever-throbbing heart in such a way that it might never, by coming up against something resistant and being struck, become a cause of death to the animal. Such an organ, then, undergoes rupture under only slight strain. And when the rupture in the lung is at its outset, the affliction follows a course that must be treated. But when it goes unnoticed, it becomes suppurative and is called 'empyic.' One must, then, treat the fresh rupture one way, and the suppurative condition another.

We shall, then, set forth the signs and treatments of both, since we shall also point out to you one way in which lung-disease may be man-made, having ourselves witnessed it and treated it and kept it in memory. A soldier, thinking himself a lover of fine things, used to overfill his own horse with salt once a day, in this manner: having a hollow horn, he filled it with salt, and, raising the horse's head and opening its mouth, he poured the salt into its throat all at once, and hung the head up again, so that the salt would settle in. For this is what he told me when I asked him.
By doing this he made the horse consumptive, though it was a very well-bred and excellent animal. For the salt, being thinning in nature, all at once

poured in through the horn, when the horse's head was tilted back from the hanging, ran down into the lung, and the most acrid discharges, dripping down, ate deep into the membrane of the lung, and, having made an ulcer, wrapped the animal in consumption, and it grew thinner every day. Having recognized and understood, then, what had befallen it, and that it came from nothing other than the salt, I gave the weeping and lamenting man a horse, by no means well-bred, but healthy. And I took his horse, and, having treated it, had it again
as a competitor, so that it pleased the king and was kept by him.

I shall, then, set forth the diagnosis and the treatment. This is the diagnosis of ruptured lung: it breathes shallowly, and shows the region along the ribs with its mouth, groans in a stifled way, being in pain while breathing, is afraid to cough, and coughs as though it had swallowed a bone. One must, then, leave it in quiet, and bleed it at the projection by the hip-socket. For it grows suddenly thin in the rupture of the lung.

One must, then, drench for seven days with goat's milk together with barley-gruel juice, or better still if of oats. And if it is not the season for milk, boil a very fat pig's trotter, with goat-tallow along with it, and drench with the broths for seven days. Let it drink water made milk-like in consistency, in winter from wheat-flour, in summer barley-gruel; for thus the rupture will knit together.
But if it comes to be suppurative, these are its signs: it takes much water, it eats more than usual, and

the horse, coughing gently, often brings up pus, and sometimes even scabs themselves. You will drench such a horse with a drench such as this: purslane is a wild garden vegetable. Drench its juice with rose-oil for three or seven days, adding tragacanth soaked in sweet Cretan wine and goat's milk - or, if there is no milk, barley-gruel juice or of oats - especially when the suppurative discharge smells very foul through the nostrils. You will finish its treatment over seven days, drenching it with this: pound two ounces of costus and four ounces of cassia, sift through a fine sieve, and, adding raisins, drench with wine. Let it abstain from exercise, and take only a few walks, led by a handler.
On barley-surfeit and immoderate drinking.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Ammonius of Alexandria, greetings. You wrote asking me whence barley-surfeit comes upon horses, and what the treatment for it is; a question readily answered, since the name is derived directly from what occurs. When, coming from a journey or a run and still short of breath, a horse takes barley, it fails to digest it, and rawness spreads beneath the hide, and stretches out over the whole body, and it becomes cramped and does not go forward, nor can it bend its joints, and it passes urine only with difficulty, and throws itself down and is unwilling to rise, but eats lying down.
It is treated thus: draw blood, cutting the forward nostril-veins, from the inner side

or the outer, and let a sufficient amount run off; then, binding off the vessels with a ligature, douse them with warm vinegar-water in this quantity: mix a hundred ounces of water with twenty ounces of vinegar, and apply it with a sponge at the shoulder-joint, so that the flow runs down over the upper foreleg. Do this at both places. And on the following day likewise draw blood from the same places on the hind legs, and douse as described above.

Do not offer this horse barley for up to fourteen days. If there is green fodder, use that especially. Make it walk each day, leading it out into the sun, anointing it with vinegar and oil, so that the hide becomes supple. Do not mix in wine (for, being cooling, it binds things further together), and rub against the grain of the hair on the lower parts; for the affliction seems to work its way out through the feet. That is why it also sheds its hooves, in which the frogs become soft and bleed; these one must scrape from underneath and trim around.
When it seems to be improving in its walking, lead it to a rolling-place and let it roll. But do not let it roll at the outset, so as not to close up the pores.

It happens also, often, in the course of a journey, or when coming to drink, that the horse gulps down its drink greedily, and it becomes bound up in the same way. In this case too you will use the same treatment. Such a case recovers quickly, and its hooves do not shed. For the barley-surfeited horse it is also said to help to give soda to drink, and to grind the herb scorpion-tail, also called helio-

trope (heliotrope), and pour it in through both nostrils; for thus the hooves shed more quickly. But a horse that survives this affliction does not retain the same strength for use for the rest of its life. And if, when a horse is being bled, you wish to stop the blood, burn and pound alum and bind it on, and it will stop.

It is useful to go through barley-surfeit more fully. When, coming from a journey or a run, and still panting, a horse eats barley, it fails to digest it, and the rawness, having gone in beneath the hide, spreads over the whole body. It becomes cramped, then, and does not go forward, nor can it bend its joints, and it passes urine only by force, and it sweats at the thighs and ribs, and the feed, given while it is still short of breath, is drawn along with its breathing, and it is unwilling to rise, but eats lying down.

It will be treated thus: cut a vein at the forward pasterns, on the inner or outer side, and, letting enough run off, bind off the vessels with a ligature, and douse it with vinegar-water, mixing ten choes of water with two choes of vinegar; apply it with a sponge at the shoulder-joint, so that the flow runs down over the upper foreleg. Do this on both legs. And on the following day, likewise draw blood from the same places on the hind legs, and douse as described above. Do not offer barley for up to fourteen days.
If there is green fodder, use that especially. Let it be made

to walk daily, and let it be rubbed against the grain of the hair on the lower parts; for the affliction seems to withdraw through the feet. That is why it also sheds its hooves, in which the frogs are wont to become soft; these one must scrape from underneath and chip around. When, indeed, it improves through walking, let it roll and shake itself. But at the outset it does not help to let it roll, lest the pores be sealed and become blocked.

Some say that, if one perceives at once that the horse has become barley-surfeited, one should throw a handful of salt into a pint of sharp vinegar and drench it through the mouth. If, however, something similar happens to it in the course of a journey, from having gulped down its drink greedily, and it seems bound up, the same treatment must then be used. For its hooves do not shed, and it recovers more quickly. You will recognize this affliction by the horse shivering, and by the skin of the palate swelling gently.

It also pleases some to give the barley-surfeited horse soda to drink. And if you wish it to shed its hooves more quickly, grind the herb called heliotrope in wine and drench through both nostrils. Know, however, that a horse surviving this affliction does not retain the same strength for use for the rest of its life.

If it has eaten much wheat and is put into a bad state, one must open the veins in the chest by the shoulders and those in the forelegs. But those in the neck must not be opened, since they are jugular and carotid veins, and the spinal marrow is nourished from these.
Some have prescribed not to give it drink,

but to give an enema instead, thus: mix wheat-bran and an eighth part of soda and half a cotyla of oil with water, to make two choes, and pour it in through the anus, and make it walk. Try also to empty out the dung with the hand anointed with oil, then make it run briskly uphill. For this too will contribute to its cure.
Prognosis and cure for the same affliction.

These are the signs of barley-surfeit: the eyes are not in good condition, the mouth is full of sores, the palate-ridge, that is, its raised line, is prominent, it breathes hot, the veins are full of blood, and a filminess also comes over the eyes.

One must, then, observe all these signs, examining the fattened horse, and, if one wishes, stationing it so as to see each of the signs one by one. And first draw blood from it at the palate, counting to the third or fourth ridge from the left side, about three cotylae. Also draw blood from the forelegs, on the inner side above the knee, and let about three cotylae run off.

And do not feed it barley or chaff on this day, but cut fine tender grass and soak it in water. Let it drink not more than one chous of this water, so that it does not chill. And on the next day let it have not more than two choenices of barley, and let more grass be given, and one chous of drink each time; and on the third day, one and a half times all these amounts; and on the remaining days, its usual measure. But if the affliction inclines toward the hind parts,
having opened a vein on both legs below the groin,
draw off about six cotylae. This same treatment applies also to the
Another, for the same.

Of henbane, if it is summer, when it has green leaves, take about ten or fifteen leaves and grind them well in a mortar with Italian wine, and drench with half of it, and immediately walk it about, and it will be healed at once. But if it is winter, when green leaves are not to be found, take as much of its seed as three fingers can hold, grind it likewise, and use with Italian wine.
On phlebotomy (bloodletting).
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Toranius Varro, greetings.
Since you ask which are the veins in horses that must be opened, through which afflictions will easily be carried off, I thought it necessary to show you.
One must first draw blood from the palate, by which alone, and first of all, it is possible to keep the animals in health.

If it is overfull in body and too heavy with flesh, or scratches itself so as to rub against the mangers and walls, and gnashes its teeth at itself, or shakes its head, or droops its ears, or yawns frequently, and thrusts its forelegs forward alternately, or seems to have oilier eyes and carries rheum, or sleeps too much over the manger, or passes blood in its dung or urine - in this horse one must cut the third or fourth vein-ridge in the palate.
Punctures near the canine tooth are hard to stop once the blood is flowing.

Likewise you will recognize a feverish horse by its head drooping down toward the ground. In this case draw blood from the temples and the face. But from those with opisthotonos, called by some 'tetanic,' one must not draw blood. For the sinewy tissue becomes dried out further by the drawing of blood. Not only does this affect it, but, since the affliction also brings on loss of appetite, the horse is harmed by being bled.
It happens to this horse, from the strain of running and much driving, to be unable to stand, yet, though willing, unable to lie down, and to walk only on the tips of its inflamed feet.
One must bleed this horse from the pastern veins, alternately from the front and hind legs.
Barley-surfeit is called a hard-to-cure affliction, in which there is a wringing-out of the joints, and it is long-lasting. In this case too one must open the pastern veins likewise.

The affliction happens when feed is given while the horse is still panting: it is drawn along with its breathing, it holds its nostrils wide open, and sweat forms between the thighs and along the false ribs.
Having eaten wheat, contrary to its nature, it will show the same accompanying signs. One must bleed this horse from the veins in the chest by the shoulders and those in the forelegs.
But the veins in the neck must not be opened, since they are jugular and carotid veins, and, further, the spinal marrow is nourished by them.
Some say that in cases of madness one should draw blood from these places, but we prefer to draw it from the legs and forelegs, for this is closer to the seat of the affliction and safer.
If it has struck its foot, or caused a sprain, or
a bruise, if the occurrence is recent, one must cut into the veins in
the coronet, on the inner or outer side, but not that at the
hoof-wall. For beneath that vessel lies a sinewy ligament of the
coffin-bone, as those before us have also said. But we do not
favor puncturing these places.
If mange occurs over the whole body, or in
any part whatsoever, or lichen-sores or eruptions, in these cases too
one must open the veins in the pasterns and forelegs.
For all that suffer from surfeit and indigestion
it is best to bleed from the elbows and forelegs. For, the animal's
nature being hot, it is quickly inflamed by the indigestion of its
food, and for this reason fever readily comes
upon it. One must, then, know that bleeding
horses that are healthy is approved neither by Apsyrtus nor by Eu-
melus. If, however, a horse is accustomed to it, it is better to draw blood from the
palate, by which the animals will be kept safer.
One must pay attention in bloodlettings, lest the vessels of the animal be
very thin and hard to see. For it happens sometimes that
in the parts called the flanks by the knees and in the
shoulders inflammation arises from the bloodletting and causes
lameness.
It will be treated thus: dousing it with warm water
three or four times a day, and anointing it with Cimolian earth mixed with
vinegar, and making it walk about gradually. Therefore one should try not to
pierce the veins clean through, nor to ulcerate them, and this will not then occur. One must be especially attentive when blood is drawn from the neck or mouth. For these veins are more dangerous.
[apparatus reference marker "t.1"]
Whether phlebotomy is best for horses.

Apsyrtus to Achaicus of Nicaea, greetings. Since you have been earnest about the art of healing and ask whether phlebotomy is best for horses, I say that it is not the best. It has also been said by Eumelus the horse-doctor that one must especially avoid accustoming horses to having blood drawn, though he did not add the reason. For by causing the outflow of blood we induce heat, and make them sick. But if they are already accustomed to it, one must draw blood in the manner we have described in the letter to Publius Varro.
By the same, that it is not advantageous to cut the veins on the inside of the thighs.

The veins on the inside of the thighs are inexpedient for phlebotomy. For, when bled, they cause sympathetic soreness and pain in the groin. The one performing the phlebotomy will recognize this the next day, and in the days following, by the horse limping and stepping only with difficulty. And if one cuts higher up, near the testicles, the so-called 'snake-vein,' it brings death. When some ailment occurs in the hindquarters and requires the drawing of blood, one must draw it below the hocks, near the so-called ankle-bones, on the inner or outer side, or from the pasterns. Punctures in the coronet of the foot are also inadvisable; for they bring on not only the callus called
'marble,' but the hoof too is implicated. For a blood-red mark forms in it from the puncture, and because of this it sometimes goes lame.

Apsyrtus to Sextus Numenius, greetings. I want you to know that if a horse is worn out and fatigued from a journey, one must not draw blood from it. For it is not the veins that are fatigued, but the sinews. If, then, you puncture the veins, the sinews dry out further. For the veins, being fiery, keep the sinews supple. One must, then, blow in wine and oil on the shoulders and legs, and rub down with soft hands, and let it stand not on a hard surface, but where dung or other soft bedding lies beneath. And if it becomes overly strained from the fatigue, do not give it barley even for its evening feed. The same has been declared by Eumelus too.

But this escaped him: that while the horse is on its journey, the humors are separate and not yet mixed with the blood. If, then, you bleed it immediately, you will see only the flow of blood, and, without any benefit, you will harm the animal.
