For its constitution dries out further as its heat is driven back, and it becomes further bound up. One must, then, draw blood the next day or the day after. For it is then that the humors run further into the veins, seeking an outlet. The one performing the bleeding will recognize this.
By the same, that one must not withhold drink for a long time from a horse that has been bled.
Never, having bled one of the solid-hoofed
animals, withhold its drink for a longer time. For if you fail to water it once it has grown thirsty, it will easily suffer a rupture.

When it happens that slackness occurs in the knees and shanks, and the pasterns become low-set, one must recognize that the fibula is displaced in them, and the horse is lame. Those horses that have the parts below the knees, called the shanks, thick and fleshy, easily strike their feet together while standing, and are the so-called 'stumblers.' These one must bleed monthly from the pasterns.
That one must not draw blood from gelded horses.
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Demetrius Pappus, horse-doctor, greetings. Since you come eagerly to horse-keeping, I wish you to
know that, for all horses that have been gelded, one must not draw blood from them. For it happens that they become weaker in strength for use, and, when bled, inflammations arise at the puncture.

It is best to know when one must draw blood from horses, and in which seasons, and how, and from how many veins, and to distinguish their natures and conditions. For some are in good condition, others lean, others sickly, and the blood is not the same nor alike in all afflictions, but differs in color according to each affliction. For the blood of horses in good condition is well-tempered, abundant, and tawny. Draw blood, then, so that no affliction may set in. But the blood of those growing weak is mottled and frothy, while that of the barley-surfeited is dark and viscous. One must, then, first make the horse graze on green fodder for six days, in a rooted meadow, wherever the grass happens to be tender, and it will thereafter gather fresh blood into its veins, and will be the more robust. Draw blood in the second hour of the day.

Since we have gone through the discussion on this, let us now begin how one must draw blood from a horse. One must apply a neck-band, wrapping the place - that is, the neck - and drawing it tight, until the veins stand up; but do not sink the lancet in deep, since you will not be able to stop the blood easily, if you pierce clean through the artery
itself. And if you wish to draw blood from the temples, wrap a neck-band around the head near the ears, until the veins stand up, and cut, as has been said, not deeply.

Apsyrtus to Apion of Alexandria, greetings. It happens that in the parts called the flanks, by the knees, and in the shoulders, inflammation arises from phlebotomy and causes lameness. It is treated thus: dousing continually with warm water three or four times a day, anoint with Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar, and let it walk about a little, and it will be well. Try not to pierce the veins clean through, nor to ulcerate them, and this will not occur. It happens in those horses whose vessels are hidden and not clearly marked, but thin and hard to find. That is why one must feel around carefully in such cases.
By Pelagonius, for a vein pouring out blood beyond measure from the lancet.

Apply the horse's own dung to the bleeding veins. And if the blood continues to flow, soak a fitting tuft of wool in oil and apply it to the vein, or make a small wooden peg and place it upon the bleeding vein, and use it as a most excellent and ready-to-hand remedy.
A poultice with quicklime, against inflammations from phlebotomy.
If a flux and inflammation occur from phlebotomy at the foreleg, it is fitting to spread equal parts of quicklime, copper ore, honey, and birthwort onto linen and bind it on,
or to dry and pound wild hemp and use it with honey.
By Pelagonius, against every kind of inflammation.

Mix Cretan Cimolian earth with Spanish oil and vinegar, and add four ounces of frankincense-powder, and, mixing in ground bulbs and snails, apply to the inflamed places. And if it is winter, use the remedy warm; if summer, cold.
On leukoma (white film) of the eyes.
By Apsyrtus.

If a flux settles in the eye, or glaucoma occurs, or a white speck, or a film, or an abrasion, or a blow, so that the eye becomes whitened, in these cases one must cut the vein in the face called the one beneath the cheekbone, which drains from the eye. Those who, when these things have occurred, cut the vein at the temple instead bring evils upon the eye. But once glaucoma has occurred, even bleeding is a wasted effort, for it is untreatable. From this arises what is called 'hyaloma,' resembling a white pebble.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If the eye becomes whitened from a blow or an abrasion, one must scrape cuttlefish-bone, grind it with myrrh and honey, and anoint underneath; or grind rock-salt or Indian salt with saffron and boiled honey, and anoint underneath; or mix white-lead with Attic honey, and anoint underneath; or grind the flower of wild carrot and anemone, and drop it in twice a day. And if it is ulcerated, grind myrrh and camel-hay flower as fine as possible, pour on honey, and anoint underneath. And if leukomata (white films) occur,

one must draw blood from the temples, and rather from the veins in the face beneath the cheekbone, as Apsyrtus approves, and, having doused with cold water, anoint underneath, grinding the pulp of an onion with soda-froth, and dissolving it in oil, best of all wild-olive oil, or, failing that, the oldest oil available.
Another, for the same.

One ounce each of balsam, myrrh, saffron, cadmia, and rue, two and a half ounces of spikenard, two ounces of white pepper, half an ounce of Attic honey, half an ounce of asparagus root, two grammes of old wine, five ounces of sea-sponge-stone, mixed in rainwater or river-water and finely ground beforehand - use this.
Another, for leukoma of the eye.
Gather and dry soda-froth with myrrh and the finest honey, and fennel, pound and sift and mix them, and use.
Another.
Grind a drachm of myrrh, three ounces of saffron, and an oxybaphon of honey until fine, and use against leukomata.
Another.
Mix two ounces of boxthorn-extract, two ounces of galbanum, six ounces of white pepper, an equal amount of male frankincense, one gramme of burnt copper, and enough honey, and use.
Against leukomata in mules.
Chew ivy thoroughly, and blow the juice into the eye, and it will be healed.
By Eumelus, for the same.
You will treat leukomata by taking blood from the temples, and by mixing onion juice with soda and applying it.
Another.
Burn black beans, and, mixing them with an equal amount of honey, anoint underneath.
Another, for a recent leukoma.
Apply rose-oil with honey, egg, and soft wool. But first take blood from the vein beneath the eyes.
A remedy for the same.
Boil together three pints of Aminaean wine, one pint of the finest fish-sauce, and three ounces of honey, and use.
Another.
Burn swallows' heads and grind them fine with honey, and use.
For those that have already developed leukomata.
Burn dry barley-leaven and grind it fine, bind it with fennel juice, soda, and honey, and anoint with this.
Another ointment for the same, by Theomnestus.

Mix two ounces of white pepper, or four of black, four ounces of ammoniac gum, two drachms of myrrh, three drachms of saffron, and enough balm-of-Gilead sap, and make a liquid ointment; apply it, and you will not let the leukoma form.
Another.
Take the herb ironwort, which some call 'achalion,' others 'marsh-mallow,' and grind its seed, and blow it in, holding the eye firmly shut; then rinse it with cold rainwater.
Another.
Burn clean linen and toast salt, put them together with honey, blend, and anoint underneath.
Against leukomata.
Mix cyclamen juice with Attic honey, and anoint well.
Another.
Grind goose-fat with rose-oil, and cuttlefish-bone with unsmoked honey, and anoint.
An eye-salve against leukomata.
Cuttlefish-bone and fennel juice, saffron and myrrh
and Syrian nard in equal parts, mix with honey, grind fine, and use. Bind up linen and a small sack, burn them, and, grinding the ash fine, blow it in.
A dry eye-salve, against cataract.
Pound two ounces of soda, and add five grains of white pepper, or ten of black, and grind a little fleawort together with them, and use.
Another.
Mix equal parts of honey and old oil, and use.
Another.

One and a half ounces of Attic salt, an equal amount of scraped cuttlefish-bone, and crocodile dung. Grind these together, adding in saffron and a little leaf-spikenard, and also a little iris-root; grind these too and sift through an eye-sieve; bind together and store in a glass jar, and anoint with it when needed. And if it ever dissolves or becomes moist, mix in a little ground gum. This works well both when reconstituted and when dissolved in water and applied in that form.
An eye-salve against leukomata.

One ounce of honey, one ounce of male frankincense, one ounce of leaf-spikenard, one ounce of trogline myrrh, one ounce of white pepper, one ounce of saffron, one ounce of liver-colored aloe, two ounces of ammoniac incense, one ounce of ammoniac salt, one ounce of pure storax, one ounce of split alum, one ounce of Greek soda. Grind these carefully fine, and use against every kind of leukoma.
Another.
Put equal parts of ammoniac gum and fennel into a mortar, and grind for three days; and on the fourth, pour on river-water, or
spring-water, and grind twice a day for eight days, pouring on six ounces of honey.
Another, against pain in the eyes.
Pound equal parts each of wax or resin, ammoniac gum, and soda-froth, and use.
Preparation of an eye-remedy.
Two drachms of spikenard, one drachm of saffron, two drachms of starch, and enough Attic honey.
For an ulcerated eye.
Grind myrrh, saffron, and camel-hay flower as finely as possible, pour on honey, and anoint.
Against ophthalmia.

Ophthalmia is wont to arise from a seething of the blood and overfeeding. One must treat such a case by drawing blood from the temples, and by dropping honey and milk into its eyes for three days. And if they run with flux, take honey and liver-colored aloe, and anoint it, and this will check the flux that has settled there, and it will be well.
Another eye-remedy.

Clean deer-marrow well, so that no small bone remains within it, grind it in a marble mortar, and add to it a drachm of ground saffron; store it in a wooden or horn vessel, and use it against ulcers of the eyes.

Burn the heads of green reeds carefully, and add three obols' weight of the sweetest myrrh and an equal amount of Syrian nard; grind all together into one, and store in a bronze box, and use against leukomata.
Grind a leek fine and press it out, and put the
juice into a bronze vessel, and use it as an anointment.
By Anatolius, for the same.
If the eye is inflamed, mix one drachm each of frankincense, starch, and lamb's marrow, one ounce of rose-oil, and egg-white all together, and anoint.
Another.

Grind Thurian salt, and blow it into the nostrils. And if it will not open its eye, turn back its eyelids, scarify with a small lancet, then blow in wine, then draw blood from its temples, and it will be well.
Another, against leukomata.

Mix enough fennel juice, an equal amount of juice from the tender leaves of rock-ivy, the milk of a bitch or a she-ass, the blood of a tame dove, and dew from a cabbage-leaf, with Attic honey, and use.
By Eumelus, against scars in the eyes.

While still fasting, chew salt and spit it onto the eye, and you will thin the scar. Or scrape cuttlefish-bone and use it. Or mix pounded wild-carrot seed and plantain juice with Attic honey, and use.
For a bruised eye, and for
[fluxes:] douse the eye with cold water; and you will cure the fluxes by boiling salt in good wine, adding ground myrrh and mixing in Attic honey; anoint, and afterward douse again with cold water.
For wounds in the eyes.
You will treat wounds in the eyes thus: take one ounce each of saffron, white pepper, ammoniac salt, poppy-juice, and garlic, and, grinding each fine, bind them with honey and
anoint with it. Dried and ground human dung is also effective, or wild-artichoke root mixed with salt and sprinkled onto the eye.
An ointment against incipient cataracts.
Attic honey, hyena's or fox's gall in an amount equal to the honey, an equal amount of balm-of-Gilead sap, and half as much pepper. Grind these, gather them into a glass or tin jar, and anoint.
Against pterygia (wing-like growths on the eye).

Pterygia are certain upper-lying discharges of thick humors, blood and phlegm collecting about the head, brought upon the eyes - certain membrane-like bodies whose roots appear when pressed, and which, taking hold of the pupil, rob it of light, veiling it like a star behind a cloud. I shall set forth for these a swift and easily obtained cure: one must, drawing the eye taut on both sides so as even to wrinkle the face, lift up with a surgical hook, without a barb, the membranous pterygium as it appears on the surface, and cut around it in a circle with a scalpel.

Do not be afraid to do this, since the membrane is of the nature of the cornea. Once it is cut, sponge it with vinegar-water. And if the horse is greatly distressed, restrain it with a tether; and on the third day finish the treatment with this remedy: one ounce of Cimolian earth, six ounces of bellows-soot, two drachms of iris, and enough honey; bind together and anoint, until you complete the cure.
Against bloodshot eyes and staphylomata (grape-like protrusions).
Make egg-white, rose-oil, and white-lead into the thickness of a paste, and anoint. But first draw blood from

the temples. And if the persistent flux produces a pterygium or a staphyloma, pause the anointing for two days, and blow in wine and rinse the eye through the narrow passage adjoining the nostrils. For this passage leads through to the eye. And after this, anoint again with the remedy just described. For this remedy, both reconstituted and applied as an anointment - in summer with cold water, in winter with lukewarm honeyed wine - is beneficial.
By Pelagonius, against blows to the eyes:
an eye-salve.
Grind one ounce of trogline myrrh and one obol's weight of saffron, and boil them in honey-water; add three more ounces of honey, and use.
A natural remedy against cataract.

Take down a swallow's nest, so that absolutely nothing of it is lost, put it into a vessel, and, adding water, stir it and strain it; give the strained liquid to the thirsty animal to drink, or drench it through a horn.
Another remedy against leukomata, stronger than the others:

one ounce each of balsam, myrrh, saffron, cadmia, and rue, two and a half ounces of spikenard, two ounces of white pepper, six ounces of Attic honey, six ounces of asparagus root, two grammes of old wine, five ounces of sea-sponge-stone, and two ounces of rainwater or river-water.
Against cataract of the eyes.
Before all else, let the horse be stabled in a warmer place, and let it abstain from barley, being fed only on bran and chaff. Take half a pint of wheat-flour, one pint of honey-water,

one pint of frankincense-powder, one ounce of resin, two eggs, and enough wine; boil them, and, anointing the whole face, bind it up, and let it remain overnight with the remedy on. In the morning, remove it, and offer the aforesaid feed. On the fourth day, anoint the eyes with Attic honey.
Against scars in the eyes.
Two ounces of balsam, two ounces of pepper, one ounce of marrow from sheep's trotters, enough Gallic garlic, a bundle of fennel, and one egg-yolk.
For a wound of the eye.
Grind together myrrh, saffron, and camel-hay flower, add honey, and anoint.
Four grammes of opopanax, two ounces of dried violets, six ounces of spikenard, six ounces each of cassia, myrrh, and oil, six grammes of pepper, and five grammes of wine.

Mix the juice of white acanthus with old wine in equal weight. It is better if you burn the acanthus to ash, and add Attic honey and oil, and use against every affliction of the eye. Or mix an equal weight of white pepper with the ash of white acanthus and honey, and anoint the eye with a feather.

Take equal weights of verdigris and salt, and add enough vinegar. Or one ounce of oil, one ounce of sea-sponge-stone, half an ounce of saffron, one ounce of white pepper, one ounce of long pepper, one ounce of savin (that is, juniper-herb), one ounce of frankincense-powder, one ounce of myrrh -
grind each of these and sift through a fine sieve, and use with six ounces of honey.
If a horse injures its eye.

Put wool soaked in rose-oil and egg into the eye; and on the next day douse it with the warm juice of boiled fenugreek, and, having soaked a sponge full, apply and bind it, and again apply wool with the aforesaid mixture. And when it is doing better, apply the eye-salve.
Against carcinomata (cancerous growths) in the eyes.
Mix ground vetch, rose-oil, and egg with Attic honey, and anoint the wound.
Against scars in the eyes.
Burn the hide of an old skin and make it into a powder, and apply it to the eyes.
Against inflammations in the eyes.
If an eye suddenly becomes inflamed, soak a sponge in vinegar, apply it around the eye, and bind it on.
Apsyrtus' composition of eye-salves for leukomata.

Two ounces of male frankincense, two ounces of trogline myrrh, one ounce of Cyrenaic saffron, two ounces of fennel juice, one ounce of unsmoked honey, two ounces of rose petals, one ounce each of white pepper, long pepper, and saffron-dregs, two ounces of ivy juice, one cotyla of Italian wine, and enough balm-of-Gilead sap.
On incision of the eyes.

Apsyrtus to Hippocrates, horse-doctor, greetings. Since the equine race is naturally prone to suffer harm in its sight, it is necessary, as a horse-keeper, that you know the remedies. If an incision occurs in it and it discharges thick rheum, one must know

that the eye is running. It is treated thus: grind sheep's thigh-marrow, anoint with it and hold it in place with the hand, pressing gently, twice a day. It is best if the marrow is fresh. And if there is no marrow, grind goose-fat or the fat of domestic fowl, and anoint underneath. Marrow mixed and ground together with goose-fat is also fitting.

Once the perforation has filled in and the incision has scarred over, so that rheum no longer discharges, anoint with this composition: one obol's weight of copper sulfate, two of myrrh, one drachm of saffron, a stater's weight of the aforesaid sheep's marrow; grind these together, pour on Attic honey, and use it, wiping the scar clean. Let the marrow be ground beforehand.

And if it ever happens that the eye becomes clouded from a blow or from some other cause or from an abrasion, or a film runs over it, it is best to bleed it, cutting the vein in the face beneath the cheekbone, and on the next day to anoint with the former remedy.

But this composition is more effective for this: grind as fine as possible one obol's weight of verdigris, one obol of myrrh, and two obols of Alexandrian soda-froth, and, grinding it together with Attic honey, use it. And for the incision itself, use the remedy composed with marrow.
This too is beneficial: grind vetch and sift it through linen, and, mixing it with Attic or Cretan honey and grinding it together, anoint the outer area around the incision with it.
A useful and immediate remedy for whatever occurs is to blow in
wine, holding the eye open. And if inflammation occurs,

use this remedy: knead barley-meal in wine, apply as a poultice, and bind it on. And when it runs with flux and the flux does not stop, one must cauterize around the eye, holding the sight itself covered with a sponge; for the cautery-iron will run beneath it. This is best for those running with flux: wash and grind litharge and henbane-juice, equal amounts of each, and a third part of poppy-juice, and an amount of verdigris equal to the poppy-juice; grind them one at a time, then together again, and, dissolving them in thick sweet wine, anoint the eye.

If an eye is incised and thick rheum discharges, and there is fear that the eye may run empty, it is treated thus: grind sheep's thigh-marrow and anoint with it, and hold it in place with the hand for a time, twice a day. It is good if the marrow is fresh. And if you have no marrow, grind goose-fat, or that of domestic fowl, and anoint underneath. Marrow mixed with goose-fat is also beneficial. And when the wound has filled in and the incision has scarred over, so that rheum no longer discharges,

anoint with the remedy written below: one obol's weight of copper sulfate, two obols of myrrh, one drachm of saffron, a stater's weight of sheep's marrow; grind the marrow beforehand, then grind them all together, and, pouring on Attic honey, use it and wipe the scar clean.
And if the eye ever becomes clouded from a scar or another cause or an abrasion, or a film runs over it, shear

the vein in the face beneath the cheekbone, and on the next day anoint, as described above. Some grind verdigris, myrrh, and Alexandrian soda-froth, and, grinding them together with Attic honey, use them. A useful remedy, indeed, at the very moment it occurs, is to blow in wine, holding the eye open. And if inflammation occurs, mix barley-meal with wine, apply as a poultice, and bind it on. And when the flux does not stop as it runs,

wipe away what runs beneath with a sponge, cleansing it thoroughly. This too is useful for those with flux: grind and wash litharge and henbane-juice, equal amounts of each, and a third part of poppy-juice, and likewise verdigris and sulfur, grinding them one at a time, then together, and, dissolving them in a rather thick sweet wine, anoint.

The affliction of pterygia is not easily cured. For certain white membrane-like growths, as it were, form on the eyelids, and blind the animal. Slip your finger beneath, then, unclasp it and cut it out, then anoint the cut area with salt and oil, and for six days anoint with sheep's marrow from what is called the 'little bride' (a particular cut of marrow). You will find various compositions of eye-salves written in my second book.
On the one-eyed and pale-muzzled horse.

Apsyrtus to Flammarountius Homerus, greetings. Horses that see unequally with their two eyes do not see the same with both. For just as one lame in one leg or one foot limps and falls behind in walking, so too these horses fall behind in sight. They are also bad-tempered and skittish because of this unequal-sightedness.
The Parthians, however, prize them as most noble.
And it is thought that this trait first arose among them.
And those that are dappled in color are also thought to have first arisen among them,
and this is why the ancients also called them 'Parthians.'
Know this too: that among horses, those that are pale-muzzled and
pale-faced, and those marked so around the eyes,
these live longer, from birth to old age, than
the rest.
On breeding (mating).
Apsyrtus to Carissanius Fronto, greetings. Since you are earnest
in horse-breeding and ask from which kind of stock, and
of what quality, one should form the breeding stock, it is necessary for you to know this too:
of those having some leukoma in their sight, not from a
blow, but arising spontaneously, one must not take these for breeding.
For the offspring, once born and having come to the same age, is disabled
in the same way. But this does not happen to a mare's offspring born from such a sire,
since she has an annual purgation. But to
the male offspring born of her the same thing will happen likewise. Those horses
that are difficult to prepare for mounting, and sluggish, one must
also set these aside, being inferior at the task. And one must not take
one-testicled horses, since they are for the most part infertile,
or produce offspring like themselves. And those that have swellings
on their testicles, which are called 'krissokabones' (hernia-marked), are unfit.
For the stallion must be sound, free from any defect.
By the same, on what sort the
donkey (jack) should be.

It is useful for those producing crossbreeding between horse and donkey to know that the mounting donkey must be large in build, and ample in bodily girth, having a large head, not horse-like, likewise its face, and large jaws and lips on it, eyes not small nor sunken, large nostrils, ears not small nor bent-down, a broad neck, not short, likewise a broad and fleshy chest, well-muscled, sturdy enough to withstand kicks given in anger, large shoulder-blades, and the parts below these, and above the knees, thick and fleshy and strong and, as much as possible, well set apart. For it must, in mounting, be able to easily embrace the mare being covered.

Let it have a large back, and a broad spine along it, not humped or hollow, and let the line along it be narrow, and not crooked. Let it not be low-shouldered, and let it have withers rather high and even, and along it a marked tail-bone, broad, full, and elongated, and not too narrow or constricted; and a belly not too swollen, small flanks, broad ribs, large and even hips, neither ill-flanked nor sharp-rumped. A tapering tail is more handsome. Let its thighs not be large but rather fleshy, and not turned outward, but well set apart; for it will be steadier in mounting. Such donkeys are also stronger than those with thighs held close together.
Let its testicles be even and not large, and its knees

not large, and rounded, and let the legs and shanks below them be not large or bony, but rather fleshy and sinewy, not knock-kneed, nor having differently-colored stripes. Let its pasterns be neither too high nor too low, and let it not walk dog-like (splay-footed). Let it have feet neither splayed nor flattened, a thick hoof-wall, a hollow sole underneath, and a small frog. And let its voice be not hoarse, but clear and ringing; for this too contributes to the mare being struck with awe and made compliant.

In color, the handsome ones are the bright and the purplish-hued, and white in the face and not grey. Handsomest of all are the black ones, provided they do not have a grey belly but one of the same color throughout. And if it happens to have the inside of its mouth black, and its tongue too, it is evidently going to sire offspring like itself. Do not take the white-dappled ones, which they call 'marones,' nor use them for breeding stock; for the offspring produced from these are, for the most part, unattractive in color.
Another: so that a hernia-afflicted stallion may cover mares often.
Burn a deer's tail, grind it with wine, and anoint the testicles and genitals. And when you wish to stop, anoint with oil.
By Anatolius, on the age of horses suitable for breeding.

One must select noble horses, both males and females, in the manner we shall describe. Let the stallion taken for breeding be five years old, and let him cease from breeding at fifteen. The same span is set

for females as well. We shall determine age not from the teeth alone, for this would not be an accurate test; the teeth do not clearly reveal the age. Some judge also from the jaws: if the skin, when lifted easily from the rest of the body by hand and let go again, springs back readily, they declare it young. But if, once the skin is lifted, it settles back onto the flesh slowly, they affirm it to be old.
By the same, on the season for breeding.

The season for breeding is from the spring equinox to the summer solstice. One must beware of covering a mare that is lean and dirty. For the stallion seems to be roused more quickly by such mares, as though delighting in her filth. When we bring the stallion up to mount the mare, we shear her tail. Some have also made a practice of making stallions amorous toward the mares, adorning them with an adornment made of their own hair and other beautiful trappings, and whatever else is enticing to desire, and, making the mare run alongside the stallion as though racing, they seem to arouse the stallion to desire for the one so displayed. One must separate the males from the females five months beforehand, and beforehand feed them for a little while on toasted wheat and vetch, and on fine wheat-meal sufficiently soaked in water; for they become more vigorous for breeding by this. And if the mare does not accept the stallion, grind soda and the dung of small birds with turpentine-
resin, and anoint the mare's private parts; but much better still, anoint her all around with squill, for the mare becomes more receptive to breeding.

And if, once covered, she does not accept the stallion again, one must wait twenty days and then let him in again. And if even so she does not tolerate it, separate her thereafter, trusting that she is pregnant.
By the same, on donkeys suitable for breeding.

We shall select for breeding those donkeys we have raised together with the horses. Some, doing well, also tame the wild ones, and their offspring is the finest, since they are not penned up, but left free-ranging. It is better for mares to be covered by donkeys than for she-donkeys to be covered by horses. And some, doing an even finer thing, place donkey foals under mares to suckle. For they will be reared on better milk, and, having been raised together, will have a more affectionate disposition toward mares from their upbringing, so as to mount them eagerly.
Let the period of nursing be two years, just as for horses. Let donkeys be used for breeding from three to ten years of age. [lacuna]

for the offspring will be of the same kind. Some do an even finer thing: they cover the mounting donkey or horse or other animal with a cloth of whatever color they wish the offspring to be born. For whatever color the cloth is with which the mounting animal is covered, such will the offspring be too.
By Pelagonius, on the hernia-afflicted stallion.
If you wish to know whether a hernia-afflicted stallion is useful and will be

proven for breeding, take, with two fingers, some of his semen, and draw it out with a small tuft of wool; and if it holds together and does not break apart, it proves the hernia-afflicted stallion useful. For this is affirmed by Hipparchus. But if the semen, when drawn out, breaks apart immediately at the touch and does not cling like birdlime, the seed will be useless, and such a hernia-afflicted stallion is not to be accepted.

The temperaments of horses are commendable when they are found to be roused up from a gentle state, and again when they become gentle from an aroused state. Such horses prove useful for this kind of service, and are also fit for labors.
By Apsyrtus, on destruction of the embryo (abortion).

Apsyrtus to Verus Marcellus, greetings. It is useful for you to know the methods of destroying embryos. For often it is not advantageous for the mare to carry to term, if an ill-bred stallion has covered her, or if she has conceived while we are training her for some race. One must insert the hand through the genitals and reach into the womb. And if the foal is already hairy, take hold of its mouth, strangle it, and crush its head. But if the membrane is still soft, tear it open. It is destroyed by a drug in this way: take the fattest pine-torch available, cut it as fine as possible, and pour on eight cotylae of sweet wine, and boil it until reduced by a third, and drench with this, dividing it over three days. And let her be trotted, though not strenuously. It is also said that one may grind bryony roots in wine and do the same. Some pound hartwort instead, and drench it with the wine.
On prolapse of the womb in a mare.

Thanks be to the one who discovered the remedy for the womb in mares. He says one must help thus, if the womb falls out: one must lay the mare down, so that she lies on her back with her head tilted down, and douse the womb with much hot water, and prick it with a fine needle; then, having boiled together equal parts of dry wine and olive-lees, and half as much oil, along with pomegranate rinds, push it back inside; then take a fresh bladder and insert it, and make it lie inside inflated, and tie it off, so that it holds the air, and bind the genitals three times at intervals, so that the bladder stays inside while the urine is still passed.

Pour in also burnt bay-leaves with dry dark wine, and, after leaving off for twelve days, pull the stitch out, and prick the bladder. And once the air has escaped, remove it, and feed the mare well, keeping her quiet. For it is beneficial for her to become more fleshy.
On pregnancy and destruction of the embryo.
By Hierocles.

So as not to seem ignorant of any of these matters, we shall say a few words on pregnancy and destruction of the embryo. From conception, then, a mare carries for eleven months and ten days. And if it happens that she foals sooner - that is, at nine months and twenty days - the foal is usually still reared and reaches maturity. But one must separate it from the herd, since it will not be a fine specimen.
If, indeed, when she is about to foal, her udder relaxes and the teat on the right side, this signifies that she will bear a male.

But if she has conceived from a horse that is not of good stock and not useful for racing, one must insert the hand through the genitals into the womb, and, if the foal is already hairy, take hold of its mouth, strangle it, and crush its head. But if it is still soft and hairless, destroy it thus with a drug. The drug is this: take the fattest pine-torch available, cut it as fine as possible, pour on eight cotylae of fragrant wine, and, having boiled it down to a third, drench with it over three days, dividing it. Then let her be trotted, though not strenuously. It is also said that one may grind bryony root in wine and drench with it. If, however, one does not wish pregnant mares to miscarry, one must take care that they do not perceive the smell of a lamp being extinguished; for miscarriage is wont to result from this.

We shall give pregnant mares the appropriate care, as it were relieving them of their burden, and not allowing them to carry loads, letting them graze quietly, and offering them lighter feed - fresh-cut green fodder (for this is sweetest), soaked barley, and the like - watering them twice a day, stabling them in a warm stable in winter and cooling them in summer, and strewing beneath their feet round pieces of wood suitably arranged, so that they may have softness in their bedding, yet firmness under their feet for the sake of their hooves, and so that their urine may run off easily.

The mangers must be somewhat high, so that the feed-bags hang from them and the mares take their feed with their heads raised. This is especially to be observed with foals. For we accustom them to hold their necks high, which is especially a mark of beauty in a horse. One must not startle them with a variety of unfamiliar pastures and waters; for they miscarry from such unfamiliar disturbances.

To mares that have foaled we shall offer lucerne, and apply the aforesaid care much more diligently. After about two or three months, the mare must be exercised, so that her milk becomes better in quality, and the foal, following alongside, is exercised in running.
And if the foals have soft hooves, we shall exercise them in rough terrain, strewing pebbles too beneath their feet; for thus the hooves would harden.
It is good to treat their soft hoof thus: mix old pig-fat and goat-fat, unfired sulfur, and garlic, and anoint their hooves and frogs.
If a broodmare foals slowly, hold her nostrils gently shut with felt, and she will foal at once.
Boil down one small bundle of fennel in water, and, warming eight cyathi of this water together with eight cyathi of old wine and two cyathi of oil, pour it in through the nostrils.
If you wish a broodmare to conceive, push nettles into the horse's mouth.
If a broodmare, having foaled once or twice, ceases to bear foals,
do as follows, so that she may conceive.

Grind carefully and cleanly one oxybaphon-measure of anise, twelve drachms of myrrh, and four drachms of saffron, and, shaping them into the form of large acorns, insert them one at a time into the mare's genitals, up as far as the womb. Beforehand, douse the genitals with heated seawater and about one cotyla of oil, and rub the loins, the genitals, and the inner thighs with unguent twice a day, until she conceives. And every five or seven days, boil together three cotylae of milk, a quarter-measure of rose-oil, one drachm of horse-parsnip, five grains of pepper, and two drachms of myrrh, and drench the womb with it lukewarm, inserting a long small tube. And boil barley-flour in water and give it to her to drink, until she foals.
On conception in a barren mare.

If you wish to make a barren mare conceive, pound a bundle of leeks in a mortar, add one cyathus of wine and twelve speckled blister-beetles, and, mixing water with these, rinse the womb with it for two days; and on the third day release the mare. Let her be covered, and bathe her twice after the covering.
Another.
Take soda, sparrow-dung, and turpentine-resin, grind them together into one, and insert some of this into the mare's genitals.
On parotis (swelling by the ear).
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Degmius Plasticus, greetings. Since you are earnest about horses, it is necessary for you to know this too. It happens

that a horse develops a swelling at the junction of the head and neck, near the ear, with a hardness; it is called 'parotis.' One must treat it thus: soak a sponge in hot vinegar and bind it on twice a day until it comes to a head, and then cut along the flow of the swelling, excising, myrtle-leaf-fashion, as much as is needed, and, drawing off the fluid, wipe the area clean with fine salt; and on the next day foment the place with hot water and cleanse it thoroughly. And once it is clean, spread on ground-vetch mixed with honey, and it will be well. One must not insert a finger, for the place readily turns into a fistula.

And when it occurs at the so-called throat, or beneath the gullet, or at the so-called isthmus, and the horse cannot eat or swallow, and the tongue swells and falls sideways to the outside, and turns livid, and it drools, it is treated in the same way; this is called 'paristhmia' (quinsy). And if it ever happens that the rupture occurs on the inside, and pus is discharged through the mouth, rinse it with vinegar-water through the ear and the nose, and drench by inserting a mouth-gag and a plunger, anointing generously with honey, and insert it and rub the area.

You will recognize parotis when a hard swelling, the size of a nut, occurs at the junction of the head and neck. Soak a sponge in hot vinegar, then, and bind it on twice a day until it comes to a head, and then cut along the flow
as much as is needed, and, having let out the fluid, wipe it around with fine salt.

And on the following day, foment the place with hot water, and, having cleansed it, sprinkle on ground-vetch flour, anointing with honey. One must not insert a finger, for this place readily turns into a fistula.

If it happens that an animal has parotis-swellings or scrofulous swellings, which some call, in more particular terms, 'glandulae,' it discharges purulent humor through the mouth. One must, then, treat it by applying barley-flour with vinegar. And if this does not help, cut the skin and remove entirely, with an iron instrument, the so-called 'glandulae' themselves, without touching them with the hand. And if it is not cured this way, cauterize the places, until the gathered humor is carried off. Treat the cauterized areas in the manner described above. It proves best of all, at the outset of the affliction, when the animal is undergoing inflammation from such a disease, to hang a lead ball from the halter beneath the jaw, so that the area of the throat is, in every way, exercised by being struck by the lead. Wild-cucumber root, mixed with barley-flour and the sharpest vinegar and applied as a poultice, has the same curative power.

If it has swollen knots and parotis-swellings, apply poultices, so that the affliction comes to a head and opens. Then, once opened, apply lint dressings with oil and vinegar to the wounds, until they are cleansed.
And when the wounds have healed, make from dried pomegranate-rinds
a dry powder, sprinkle it on, and you will complete the cure.
Against parotis-swellings and scrofula.

Mix twenty-eight drachms of wax, twenty-six drachms of turpentine-resin, one drachm of honey, four drachms of galbanum, fourteen drachms of ammoniac gum, and, in summer, six cyathi of oil, in winter eight cyathi, and you will effect the cure.
Another, on parotis.
Poultice the parotis-swellings with wheat-flour, resin, vinegar, and lard, mixing them all together. And once they have come to a head, cut them off.
On an ulcer in the ear.
By Apsyrtus.

When an ulcer occurs in the ear, or an abscess in its fold, it happens to contain a purulent fluid, or one resembling a honey-cyst. One must cut it lengthwise, following its natural line. It is treated with honey and alum. It is inevitable that the ear will become drooping afterward.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If an ulcer or an abscess occurs in the ear, with a purulent fluid gathered, or one resembling a honey-cyst, let it be cut lengthwise, as is customary, and treated with honey and alum. And if the ulcer is internal, rinse it with oil and unmixed wine; then pound leeks, and, pouring oil onto their juice, and soaking it in, pour it into the ear, having first rinsed with lukewarm water. Also dissolve centaury in wine, and pour it into the ear likewise.
Another, against earache.
One must treat the pain of the ear, lest the animal fall into madness. And before all else, cleanse its ears, lest something lodged within cause harm or pain. And, having

cleansed it with a soft sponge, put honey, soda, and strained water into the ear, having first wiped it dry. And let a small sponge remain in the ear for one night; and on the next day, douse it with hot water and soda, until it heals.
If water gets into the ear.
Pour equal parts of old oil and soda into the ear, and apply wool. By this method, if there are wounds too, they will be healed.
On paristhmia (quinsy).
By Hierocles.

Paristhmia (quinsy) occurs when a swelling arises at the so-called throat and the gullet, at which time especially the whole tongue also falls sideways inward, turning livid, and the horse drools, so that it cannot eat or swallow.

The cure is the same as for parotis. If, however, it happens that the discharge occurs internally, and pus is carried out through the mouth, let it be rinsed with vinegar-water through the nostrils, and, inserting a mouth-gag, and anointing the plunger with honey, insert it and rub the area.
Another.

If paristhmia occurs, along with inflammation around the ears, you will treat it by dousing the place with hot water, and applying a poultice of barley-meal; and when it gathers to a point, cut around it with a scalpel, and tend to it. And if it does not respond, you will cure it by cauterizing.
Another, by Eumelus, against pain of the jaws and
inflammations.
Foment with hot vinegar and old lard. And if the pain persists, cauterize. The same remedy is also beneficial when applied against inflammations.
By Apsyrtus, on stones forming in the jaws.

Apsyrtus to Damnatus Tomeus, greetings. Since you keep horses, I want you to know that stones that form in the jaws must be operated on, for, if left alone, they grow larger. One must therefore restrain the horse and make an incision, then take hold of and remove the stone, carefully observing the incision, lest any part of the stone remain behind and grow again, requiring a second operation.
On cynanche (canine quinsy / severe throat inflammation).

Apsyrtus to Historicus, horse-doctor, greetings. When cynanche occurs in a horse, it will readily die. These are its signs: a stiffening occurs at the temples, and the tongue falls out and swells, likewise the head, and the eyes swell, and the gullet and the windpipe become blocked, and it can neither eat nor drink.

It is treated by anointing the head, or the temples, and the tongue, with bull's gall, and by dousing further with hot water, and by drenching through the nostrils with wine and oil; and let the oil be old, but if there is none, use what there is. It is also said one may boil figs, and drench likewise with soda together with the decoction.

It is also fitting to dissolve bdellium-gum and anoint it with this. And once there is relief, and it begins to seek food, give it green fodder; better still, let it graze. And if there is none, sprinkle dry fodder with soda, and offer barley likewise. Disadvantageous, however, is
the drawing of blood from other places; it is fitting only from the palate. And once it is doing well, purge it with wild-cucumber and soda.

Cynanche is among the treacherous and most dangerous diseases; these are its signs: the head swells, and the eyes and the lips, and the tongue falls out swollen, and the throat and windpipe become blocked, so that the horse can neither eat nor drink.

Let it be treated by anointing the head at the temples and the tongue with bull's gall, and dousing further with hot water, and drenching through the nostrils with wine and old oil. It is also fitting to dissolve bdellium-gum and anoint with it. And once there is relief and it seeks food, offer it green fodder; better still, let it graze. If, however, it is not green, sprinkle the dry fodder with soda, and likewise dust the barley with wheat-flour, and give it to drink. Draw blood only from the palate. As it improves, purge it with wild-cucumber and soda. Some, among them Stratonicus, advise, after the dousing, to apply a poultice of flour boiled together in mixed wine.
Another.
Rub the tongue with soda, oil, and honey, then apply a poultice of flour kneaded with wine.
Another.
Mix pig dung with honey, and anoint all around. Let the honey be enough to cover the dung.
On the excision of scrofulous glands (khoirades).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Damas of Laodicea, horse-doctor, greetings. For the scrofulous swellings that occur in horses, many have prescribed many remedies that are impossible or useless; for some say to poultice with a raw mixture, or a boiled one, that is, with barley-flour and resin. Others boil it in vinegar; others do the same with wheat-flour and wine, and, dipping a sponge in hot vinegar, bind it on. Others say one must incise, and apply pounded wild-fig, or spurge, or wild-cucumber root. Worst of all is what they do when they anoint with a caustic. For it happens that the swelling becomes unable to suppurate and break open, and hardening sets in instead, the hide being drawn tighter, and it will not allow the place to be touched by hand, and the whole head becomes heavy, and swelling appears in the face, the veins in it also becoming raised likewise, and the muzzle swells.

The best treatment for these is excision, as practiced among the Alexandrians. One must excise thus: lay the horse down, and, restraining the feet and holding the head, and taking hold of the swelling with flesh-forceps, cut around the hide with a scalpel in a circular fashion, as much as is sufficient, through which it will be removed. Likewise, pull back the tunics with the flesh-forceps and cut around them. Having laid the swelling bare, slip the small spatula beneath the tunics, and undercut the hide; then, boldly inserting the finger, first pull it away from the upper part near the jaw, and lift it out with the finger all around as far as the gullet, on

each side. It is better if one keeps it intact; but if not, remove it piece by piece, leaving nothing of it behind. For if anything is left behind, even if small, it will grow large, and one will need to operate again. One must guard the veins and distinguish them carefully. And if bleeding occurs while operating, do not be alarmed, for it carries no danger.

Having raised the horse, treat it thus: soak plucked wool-tufts in the sharpest vinegar and salt, and insert them into the incision, and the blood will stop. And if it does not bleed, mix oil with the vinegar, but not the salt, and untie it on the third day. Then, having doused it with hot water, likewise pack it with the same wool-tufts soaked in wine and oil, once a day for up to four days, and douse the swellings and the incision with hot water further. Once they are astringed, use wool-tufts with honey. And when it becomes clean and has filled in,

leave it undressed, and anoint with the fatty ointment, and it will be well. Keep the horse without water before it is operated on, and no bleeding will occur. And on the first day, do not give barley, but only fodder. For the jaw-muscles, when set in motion, bring on a more vigorous inflammation.

It is necessary that these be removed while the horse is still in its colthood, whether it is shedding its first teeth or about to get its second set. For they seem to appear at that time. It happens that, when the arthritic form of glanders occurs, a settling takes place in the head. For the humor runs down into the veins lying
beneath them, and they swell, and the nostrils become filled
and blocked, through which it breathes, and the tongue becomes constricted,
and it dies from loss of appetite. But in gelded horses this
swelling does not occur, nor does the humor run down,
but even those glands present from birth dry up instead.
It has been devised, among the Sarmatians, while the foals are still newborn,
to compress them and geld them in this way, so that this does not happen. And of these,
it is said that their birth-teeth remain, and no others
grow in.
It happens to foals in the herds, five
and six months old, that their glands swell up and
become inflamed, and they are unable to pull at grass or take
the teat. One must incise these, as has been written, and remove
the gland, and wipe it clean with fine salt, and release it into
the herd; and treat the one that has suppurated, and release
it, and on the third day anoint underneath with boiled olive-lees or pitch-oil, so that
no maggot forms.
Hieronymus says one must treat the glandular swellings thus:
douse with hot water, then apply a poultice of barley-flour
boiled in water with soda, twice a day. And when it becomes taut
insert the knife, cut, and divide
the tunic, then, having pounded fig-leaves, or spurge, or horehound
with salt and wine, soak and apply it, until the
ulcer becomes clean. And, having pounded the roots of wild
cucumber, use them likewise, until it fills with flesh, then with fine
ground vetch, until it is healed, or use iris-oil with honey.
Others say one must incise instead, and insert pounded wild-fig leaves, or wild-cucumber root.

Apsyrtus, however, rejects this method: for hardening sets in, and, as the hide is drawn tight, the animal suffers pain, and will not allow the place to be touched by hand, and the whole head becomes heavy, and the face and nostrils swell as the veins become raised. He says, then, that this is the best treatment: lay the animal down, restrain the feet, and, holding the head, and taking hold of the swelling itself with flesh-forceps, cut around the hide with the scalpel in a circular fashion, as much as

is sufficient, through which the gland will be readily removed. Likewise, pull back the tunics with the flesh-forceps and cut around them, and, having laid the swelling bare, and undercut the hide beneath with the small spatula, insert the finger firmly, first pulling it away from the upper part, and lift it out with the finger all around as far as the gullet, on each side. It is better if it comes out whole; if not, piece by piece, until nothing of it is left. For if a small part is left behind, it will become large, so that one is forced to operate again. One must guard the veins and distinguish them precisely.

And if bleeding occurs, soak a plucked rag or small wool-tufts in the sharpest vinegar and place them into the incision, and it will be checked. And if it does not bleed, mix oil with the vinegar and salt, and, having applied it, untie it on the third day; then, having doused it with

hot water, make plucked-rag dressings soaked in lukewarm wine, and apply them once a day for up to four days, and douse the swellings and the incision further with hot water. And once they are astringed, soak the plucked-rag dressings in honey and apply them. And once it has filled in, becoming clean, anoint with the fatty ointment.

On the first day, do not offer barley. In the gelded horse, the glandular swellings do not arise; but if they were already present, they dry up. And if glandular swellings burden a five-month-old foal, so that it cannot graze because of the inflammation, one must incise, as has been written above, and, having removed the gland, wipe it clean with fine salt, and release it into the herd; and on the third day anoint underneath with boiled olive-lees or pitch-oil, so that no maggot forms.
By Theomnestus, on glandular swellings and paristhmia.

If the glandular swelling is at the isthmus of the throat, beneath the gullet, do not operate, but apply a poultice, scraping the place, with substances able to bring it to a head: first a raw mixture, old pig-lard, boiled marsh-mallow, and ground garlic. And if the place has not broken open, apply cauterizing points, so as to burn through only the hide, so that the swelling may drain, and use this drawing remedy: one pound of Gallic soap, two pounds of old lard, enough wax and pitch, old oil, fat dried figs, and two ounces of oak-mistletoe.
By Hippocrates, for the same.
The affliction of glandular swellings for the most part arises from
a change of water, being about the size of a nut. Apply a firm cautery to such a case. And if it coughs, and, once strain has set in, brings up foul-smelling breath, drench with softening remedies,
so that the cough is not aggravated. For the windpipe, once irritated, is wont to be harmed. Boil down cedar-resin, then, and strain it through a cloth,
and anoint and drench with it. Finally, use the aromatic draught, drenching with wine, oil, eggs, and honey. But first draw blood from the neck as well.
A composition against glandular swellings.
One pound of figs, six ounces of soda, six ounces of galbanum, six ounces of propolis, two ounces of pitch.
Another.

If glandular swellings or growths occur under the jaw, foment it first; then, mixing figs and soda, pounded together into one with lard or barley-flour, and boiled in honey-water and oil, apply as a poultice. And if it is not cured, incise, and cauterize the incision.
An emollient against broken joints and glandular swellings
and boils.

Six ounces of Illyrian iris, one ounce of wax, six ounces of iris-oil, three ounces of ammoniac gum, four ounces of silphium; mix with wax melted in iris-oil, and use. And if you wish to make the emollient into an anodyne, mix two ounces each of galbanum, opopanax, wax, silphium, and ammoniac gum, one ounce of roasted resin, one ounce of pine-resin, and two ounces of Colophonian resin, and treat with it.
Another dispersing remedy.
Burn sea-whelk shells and boil them together with honey, and apply as a poultice.
On polyp in the nose.

A polyp is an unnatural growth that forms in the nostrils, resembling in substance the flesh of the sea polyp, having its origin in thick, sticky humors. The treatment is common to both the polyp and to ozaena (fetid nasal ulceration). When the polyp affliction occurs in the nostril of a horse, the animal is troubled. For the nostril becomes blocked, and pus with a putrid smell issues from it, and it breathes with difficulty, and wastes away in its whole body, and is always dejected, and cannot whinny. The polyp is, in size, comparable to a mulberry, or smaller in girth.

It is treated, when it appears externally, or part of it does, by excision and by sprinkling on raw copper ore. The same is also fitting mixed with vinegar to a thick consistency, applied rather frequently, or boiled olive-lees mixed with birthwort. But when it is deeper inside and elevated, there is no treatment for it. It is said by some that one should also rub it with lead. This condition occurs more often in the regions of Sarmatia.

A polyp occurs in the nostril, comparable in girth to a mulberry, and it greatly troubles the animal. For the nostrils become blocked, and foul-smelling pus is discharged from them, and it breathes with difficulty, and grows thin and is continually dejected, unable even to whinny. When, then, the whole polyp, or part of it, appears
one excises it and sprinkles raw copper ore all around. Copper ore mixed with vinegar to a thick consistency, applied rather frequently, is also fitting, or boiled olive-lees mixed with birthwort.

When, however, it is deeper inside and elevated, it is difficult to treat. Some say one should rub it with lead instead. This disease is most prevalent in the regions of Sarmatia. Some say one should bind three long needles together and, tilting back the head, first prick the polyp with them until all of it comes out, then rinse at once with wine and oil, and likewise on the following days, and it recovers.
Another, for the same.
Six ounces of frankincense, and equal parts of soda, poppy-juice, and rue, mixed in one pint of dry wine, and drench.
On coughing.

Apsyrtus to Secundus, horse-doctor, greetings. I want you to know that for those troubled by coughing it is fitting first to purge the whole body with wild-cucumber and soda, then to grind four of the thicker rinds of squill, and, dissolving a bean's-weight of Cyrenaic silphium-juice in white wine and old oil, to hold the tongue and pour it in through the mouth. One must also fumigate it over coals with a compound such as this: equal parts of Cyprian garlic and onion, one drachm's weight of realgar, and an equal amount of bitumen; grind all these together thoroughly, divide into three parts, and fumigate with one part a day, covering the head

and binding round the eyes. And after the fumigation, melt deer-fat or sheep-fat and wax in sweet wine, and, holding the tongue, drench with it. Or grind horehound with oil and salt, dissolve it in wine, and drench likewise. There are many other remedies too, but these are the best of all.

If coughing troubles it, one must first purge the whole body with wild-cucumber and soda, then grind four of the thicker rinds of squill, and, dissolving a bean's-weight of Cyrenaic silphium-juice in white wine and old oil, hold the tongue and drench through the mouth; and fumigate it over coals with a preparation such as this: equal parts of Cyprian garlic and onion, ground together with realgar and made fine; divide into three parts, and fumigate with one part a day, covering the head and binding round the

eyes. And after the fumigation, melt deer-fat or sheep-fat and wax in sweet wine, and, holding the tongue, drench with it. Or grind horehound with oil and salt, dissolve it in wine, and drench likewise. Or soak tragacanth in warm water with boiled must and old oil, and drench. Or boil crushed vetch and strain off the water, and, grinding it with pork fat, give it to drink. Or mix dripping lye, soda, oil, egg, and honey, and drench. Or soak equal parts of tender cabbage-leaves, garlic, and pork fat in cedar-resin, five
lumps, and drench; or use one ounce of genuine myrrh, and give no water until the third hour.
Give lard with liquid pitch to drink at bedtime, on three days, the third, fifth, and seventh.
One ounce of pepper, one ounce of gentian, one ounce of birthwort, one ounce of myrrh, two ounces of bay-berries, one ounce of resin, six ounces of silphium-juice, six ounces of opopanax.
Having emptied an egg completely, put inside it cedar-resin and split orpiment, pounded together with garlic and pig-lard, and, sealing it inside the egg, give it three times.
Grind the seed of Christ's-thorn and give it to drink.

A recent cough is cured by the flour of ground and hulled lentils, or likewise of ground and cleaned bitter-vetch, given in one pint of hot water through a horn. Let the ailing animals be fed on green fodder or on the tender shoots of trees, until they return to natural health.

A recent cough occurs from ulceration and roughness of the windpipe. You will check this by grinding soda and pouring it in through the nostrils together with one pint of wine; also anoint the whole body with wine-and-oil. Or pound and sift four ounces of frankincense, one ounce of myrrh, and one ounce of saffron, in three cotylae of wine and half a cotyla of oil, and pour in through the nostrils about half a cotyla of it, over many days. Or an equal amount of pounded dill and iris
and four drachms of ground rue, mixed in three cotylae of wine, and pour it in.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

Coughs occur especially in foals, when they first take the bit. For, being made to gape unaccustomedly out of necessity, their chests are chilled. And in summer too, gaping and taking in dust, their lung-passages become blocked, and coughs arise in them. In mature horses this happens rarely, either from chilling or from blockage. It also occurs when a horse drinks muddy water, or takes in barley together with dust, or, from a journey in summer, when it takes in much dust. The so-called 'wild' cough often ruptures the palate and brings up blood.
It coughs violently at the time when, from the strain, it also passes wind and urine. This happens especially to racehorses.

When, then, it suffers from cold, one must use remedies that relax and warm. When from dust, remedies that clear and smooth. When it coughs violently, using both of these, I have cured some cases, but with others I have not succeeded. And, being greatly troubled over a racehorse afflicted in this way, and almost bursting from its coughing, I devised a remedy that also cured those ruptured by coughing. It is fitting also when applied against every kind of cough. And if you apply it three times at most, you will effect a cure. And, in general, in composing
this remedy, do not wish to have any other for driving off a cough. For, having tried very many, this alone I
found always to prevail over the disease.

Its composition is this: half a pint each of white raisins, good honey, and bay-berries, two ounces of marjoram, one ounce of marjoram-oregano, five pounds of old unsalted pig-lard, and nine large heads of garlic; pound the dry ingredients and melt the meltable ones, and mix them; make pastilles, and, dividing the remedy into three parts, give it to the animal over three days. But when you are about to give it, soak the pastilles first in more honey, and use it in this way.

Soak five eggs, shells and all, in sharp vinegar overnight, and by morning you will find them softened, so as to be soft, like those laid prematurely, the outer shell no longer resisting the touch, but containing the fluid like a bladder. Then, opening the animal's mouth and holding the tongue, push these whole down through the throat, one at a time, raising the head high, until each of the eggs is swallowed. After these, drench with fenugreek juice or barley-gruel mixed with honey; using these for three days, you will effect the cure.

Pound garlic and old pig-lard, each separately and then together, then mix in boiled cabbage and leeks, and make five hand-sized pellets. And, opening the animal's mouth and holding the tongue, soak the pellets - elongated in shape - in pitch-oil, and give them one at a time in dark wine,
and with the fourfold remedy composed of myrrh and bay-berries, round birthwort, and gentian in equal parts.
A composition for a drench, for the same.

Boil pig's trotters with one pint of barley-gruel, until they become tender, and, straining, drench with it. And if it persists in coughing, boil one pound of goat-fat with one pint of barley-gruel, and do the same, or one pound of sheep-fat with one pint of shellfish-broth. Use each of the above for three days. Or boil together one pound of pig-fat and three pints of sweet wine, and drench.
A windpipe-remedy against coughing.
Four ounces each of myrrh, saffron, cinnamon, cassia, spikenard, bay-berries, and sweet-flag, three ounces of white pepper, and six of turpentine-resin.
Another.

Four ounces of Indian boxthorn-extract, four ounces of spikenard, five ounces each of myrrh, storax, saffron, white pepper, cardamom-clusters, and long pepper, one ounce of cinnamon, one ounce of all-heal, two ounces of sweet-flag, two ounces of honey, one ounce of celery seed, two ounces of bay-cassia, three ounces each of male frankincense, aromatic reed, and Celtic nard, one pound of dried roses, one pint each of anise and parsley, one pound of saffron-dregs, and four ounces of Lemnian earth.
Another, for the same.
Mix four pints of honey with goat's or cow's milk, and drench.
Another, against coughing and broken wind.
One pound and four ounces of cinnamon, four ounces of castoreum, and stor-
By Anatolius, for the same.

For a horse just beginning to cough, mix barley-flour with ground vetch or beans, and give it to drink in wine. And if the affliction intensifies, pour in through the mouth two cotylae of honey, or enough liquid pitch.
Another.

For a beast of burden coughing severely and chronically, dissolve and soften one ounce of birdlime, and, adding four ounces of oil and one Italian pint of wine, give it through the mouth for three days.
By Hippocrates, for the same.

Cut tragacanth as fine as possible and wash it, and, mixing it with barley and vetch, give it to eat. Or soak the same tragacanth in one cotyla of honeyed wine for three days, and, adding oil, drench. Or boil rue root in one cotyla of water, rinse with it, and drench with the same amount. Sprinkle the barley too with the juice of pounded tamarisk. And if it brings up purulent matter through the mouth or the nostrils, soak pork fat in children's urine for three days, and, adding one cotyla each of wine and oil, boil together and drench. Or boil bay-berries, pound them with barley-meal and old lard, soak them in sweet wine, mix, and feed as morsels daily. Or boil the herb mugwort in water and one cotyla of oil, and drench. Mallow too, boiled in sweet wine and
oil, has the same effect.

Boil a hand-sized bundle of horehound, one pint of white wine, soaked fenugreek, and one ounce of dried figs, or dates in proportion, down to a third, and give for three days. Also anoint the body of ailing horses, down to the hooves.
Another.
Boil down bran and press it out well through a linen cloth, strain it, and, mixing in unripe-olive oil, give it, taking care that no husk of the bran remains behind.
Another.
Make barley-cakes from pig-fat, and, coating them on the outside with butter and honey, give them through the mouth.
Another.
Add enough Aminaean wine to cabbage juice, and drench.
Another, by Gregorius.
Two pints of barley, seven leeks, five cabbages, half a cotyla of honey, sheep-fat, four ounces of pure oil, and celery.

Boil leeks with the herb called ironwort, pound them, and make pastilles the size of eggs, and, dipping them in rose-oil mixed with boiled must and honey, give for three days. Nothing prevents also drenching, on these same three days, with the juice of the same herb together with the decoction of the other ingredients.
Dissolve a lump of laser-resin, about the size of a small hazelnut, in wine, and give this through a horn on one day only.
There is a cough that arises from the lung, which happens from excessive sweating.

One must treat this thus: four ounces of costus, one small bundle of hyssop, three ounces of all-heal root, four ounces of trogline myrrh, one ounce of male horehound, three ounces of centaury; pound and sift all together, and, boiling with half a pint of honey, make pastilles from this and give to the ailing animal.
Against coughing and broken wind.

Pound Gallic garlic and the herb ironwort, which the Romans call 'perdicium,' and, mixing them with old lard, make pastilles from these, and, dipping them in honey and butter, give to the animal for three days.
Against the cough that arises from the lung.

One bundle of hyssop, five ounces of laser-resin, two ounces of Cretan carrot, two ounces of the herb savin, which the Romans call 'Sabina,' three ounces of dittany, six ounces of castoreum, one ounce of poppy-juice, one ounce of cress, one ounce of frankincense-manna, one ounce of trogline myrrh; mix in honey-vinegar, and administer to the animal.
Against a cough arising from the throat.

Two ounces of myrrh, one pint of toasted linseed, half an ounce of cress, one pint of raisins, one pint of pine-nuts, two pounds of honey; grind all these carefully, make pastilles the size of a nut, and give three each day to the animal, for five or seven days.
Another.
Slaughter a fowl and immediately split its back, take its belly, just as it is with the dung inside, and, wrapping it in honey,
give it to the animal down the throat while it is still warm.
Against a severe cough.

Boil cypress balls thoroughly, pound them in a mortar, and, adding the leaves of the herb ironwort, which the Romans call 'paritaria,' and Gallic garlic and lard, make pastilles; give these for three days, putting them into oil and wine, and mixing in boiled must and eggs. And if you do not wish to boil the cypress balls, pound cypress leaves instead, and, making a powder, use it with the aforesaid ingredients.
Another.

Before all else, one must purge the body of the animal with wild-cucumber ground together with Alexandrian soda, and old wine mixed in, and drench through a horn. And after three days, apply this remedy: pound four parts of the thicker part of squill, and, adding a bean's-weight of laser-resin, one pint of old wine, and one pound of old oil, drench through a horn.
A fumigation for coughing horses.

Grind one ounce of realgar, one ounce of bitumen, and equal parts of garlic and onion, make three portions, and fumigate the animal with one of these each day, covering the head and binding round the eyes. And after the fumigation, mix and dissolve deer-fat or sheep-fat in enough sweet wine, and, adding a little ground honeycomb and warming it, drench through a horn.
Preparation of pastilles for the same.
One and a half ounces of Macedonian parsley, six ounces of carrot, myrrh

one ounce, one ounce of spikenard, one ounce each of saffron, pepper, sweet-flag, ammoniac-gum drops, and cassia; pound and sift, and, mixing with water and honey, make pastilles, and give them dipped in boiled must; soak the tragacanth the day before in honey-water.
A preliminary drench for the same affliction.
One ounce each of tragacanth, cumin, spikenard, myrrh, and pepper, one pound of clary-sage seed; mix with two pints of boiled must, and drench through a horn.
Another.
Grind soot cleanly, and, putting a heaping spoonful of it into a horn, mix in old wine, and drench for three days.
Against a chronic cough and quinsy.

Three ounces of red storax, two ounces each of trogline myrrh, opopanax, Illyrian iris, and galbanum, four ounces of turpentine-resin, one ounce of harmonious henbane, half an ounce of poppy-juice; pound together and mix with wine, and drench.
Another.

One pound of Attic honey, one and a half pounds of lard, twelve dried figs, a whole burnt pine-cone; mix in the juice of boiled cabbage, and, adding half a pint of good fish-sauce, make small balls and give to the coughing animal.
Another.
Grind ivy leaves and those of the white poplar - not just any kind - and, mixing them with old white wine, drench through the nostrils.
Another.
Mix sharp-rush seed into the fodder offered to the animal.
Another.
Grind the tender leaves of rue, and with old

wine pour it in through the nostrils, and sprinkle the fodder it eats with wild-cucumber juice. It is better still to mix the dried seed and roots of the wild cucumber itself with barley, and offer it this way.
Another.
Mix unfired sulfur and enough savin with honey and wine, and drench through the left nostril; or pound all-heal root and, adding half a pint of wine and three cyathi of oil, do the same.
Another.

Mix four grammes of savin, one gramme of myrrh, two grammes of saffron, one and a half pints of wine, and half a pint of oil; give half a pint in the morning and half a pint after the midday meal, through the nostrils; or ground radishes with half a pint of wine.
Another.
Grind cleanly a third of a gramme of mulberry root and half a gramme of heliotrope, and administer with half a pint of warm wine through the mouth.
Another.
Add hulled and finely ground lentils to an equal quantity of hot water, and pour it down the throat for three days.
Against a chronic cough.
Mix three cyathi of leek juice with half a pint of oil, and give through the mouth for many days.
Another.
Burn a piece of elm-wood, take the ash and strain it into water, and, mixing in an equal measure of oil and three eggs, give it.
Against a chronic cough.
Put a denarius-weight of horehound juice, twenty-two figs, and one and a half pounds of Attic or Sicilian honey into a pot, and boil

until reduced by half. And after this, add one ounce of trogline myrrh, one and a half ounces of cassia, one and a half ounces of cinnamon, one ounce of male frankincense, two ounces of birthwort, and one ounce of all-heal root; once it is well boiled together, put it into a wooden or leaden vessel, store it, and use it when needed, giving two spoonfuls.
Another.
Toast and grind lentils, and grind linseed and fenugreek, sift them, and, mixing one spoonful of each, and enough Gallic garlic, drench with wine.
Another, useful also for humans.

Mix a four-denarius weight of camel-hay flower, four denarii each of opopanax, spikenard, myrrh, poppy-juice, Sicilian saffron, spikenard leaves, and costus, and a two-denarius weight of Attic honey, and give it.
Another preliminary drench.

Six ounces of southernwood, an equal amount of Cretan hyssop, one obol of poppy-juice, two ounces of costus, two ounces of spikenard, one ounce of all-heal root, six and a half ounces of burnt pastille, one ounce of cinnamon, two ounces of myrrh, two ounces each of male frankincense, white pepper, and camel-hay flower, one ounce of black pepper, two ounces of cassia, half an ounce of cardamom, half an ounce of castoreum, five pounds of the finest honey, two ounces of saffron.
Another.

Boil the herb called dock carefully, make small balls, and to these add Spanish oil, putting in also vinegar, cumin, and salt in moderation; give to the animal, on the first day three balls, on the second four, on the third five, and you will know the benefit of the remedy.
Another.

Having often attended horses and mules, so as to treat them with remedies, and having made no less use of preliminary drenches, and still, with the disease persisting, I only with difficulty came to recognize this remedy as useful and beneficial above all others against coughing, to be given through a horn for three or five days: boil one pint of toasted bean-meal, and, after boiling, grind it in a mortar, and, adding three ounces of butter and two ounces of goat-fat, melt them in a new pot in warm ash, and mix with the bean-meal.

And after this, boil fenugreek in a bronze pot with water, and pour off its first boiling, and, adding another four pints of water, mix into the same pot twenty dried figs and two ounces of licorice, and boil it down so that of the four pints, three remain. And, mixing this decoction with the aforesaid ingredients - that is, the ground bean-meal, the butter, and the goat-fat - grind it together. And if it is still found too thick, add as much of the boiled liquid as is needed to make it fluid enough to pass through a horn, and drench.
On the neck of a beast of burden that has become raised/swollen.
By Hierocles.

If the neck of a beast of burden becomes chafed and raised, it is good to use the treatment we found in the writings of Cleomenes the Libyan: grind equal parts of tamarisk and squill, mix in equal parts of melted pig-fat and wax, and add sulfur, litharge, frankincense-manna, and frankincense
in equal amount, and white-lead, and cedar-resin. Having pounded all the dry ingredients,
pour in the cedar-resin, and, mixing it all together, anoint generously with the fatty ointment.
Or grind equal parts each of white-lead and litharge,
pour on rose-oil, and, making it the thickness of a wax salve, use it.
And if it has a swelling from a whip or some other such cause,
grind sulfur and boil it with vinegar, and anoint the affected place.
On dislocation of the neck.
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Orion of Alexandria, greetings. You wrote
to me asking by what method one should restore a dislocation of the neck in
horses to its natural condition. I want you to know, then,
that it is not truly a dislocation, but a displacement. In these cases some, using
bandages with splints and cords, accomplish nothing
good. This is our own discovery: with the horse standing,
one must push back the displaced, humped part of the neck
into place; then, having made tamarisk-wood loops, apply them
to the place under the hide, boring counter-loops with the lancet
[on the opposite side]. And make the knot the so-called 'wolf' knot,
and thus draw the loops together and bind them,
and soak the place with vinegar and oil twice a day,
until they fall off, and douse it with hot water and
treat the wounds with the fatty ointment, and it will be well. Let the
binding-cord be of linen or hemp, of the thickness of a bow-
string.
By Hierocles, on dislocation of the neck.
The name of this affliction is 'dislocation of the neck.'
Apsyrtus says it is not truly a dislocation, but a displacement;
he criticizes, then, the bandages that use splints.

He says that, with the horse standing, one must push the displaced, humped part of the neck back into its proper position, then, having made tamarisk-wood loops, insert them at the place under the hide, boring counter-loops with the lancet.

And make the type of binding the so-called 'wolf' knot, and, thus drawing the loops together, tie them off, and soak the place with vinegar and oil twice a day, until they fall off, and douse it with hot water, and treat the wounds with the so-called fatty ointment.
Let the binding-cord be of linen or hemp, having the thickness of a bow-string.

It happens to a horse or other beast of burden to suffer displacement of the neck, when it is first tied and fastened to a tree, and, becoming distressed, wrenches itself about, or when misbehaving in the yoke, or when the harnessing is thrown off as a vehicle overturns;
and one side of its neck becomes hollow, the other humped.

We shall treat such a horse by laying the hollower side of the neck upon the ground and the humped side uppermost, and, pressing down firmly, we push it back into place, until the vertebrae of the displacement return to their natural position; then, having made three tamarisk-wood loops, bore through the neck at the humped part with the lancet at equal intervals, and pass them beneath the skin, and bind them off through the hide with a

tightly twisted hempen cord, of the thickness of a sinew-string. Make the knot the so-called 'wolf' knot, and bind it off, and soak it with vinegar-and-oil three times a day, and with this draw the loops together, until they fall off, and douse with hot water and treat. For thus it will no longer be twisted out of place.

Mix sheep dung with old wine and oil, and, warming it, rub down the neck with it repeatedly, many times, and put lukewarm honey-water into its drinking water. And if a hardness persists at the same place, dissolve, over a gentle fire, one pound each of pig-fat and goat-fat, six drachms of Corinthian resin, a quarter-portion of goose-fat, and half a cotyla of henna-oil, and keep this for anointing.
