Mix honey and oil, and pour it in through the nostrils.
Two ounces of lard, one pound of wax, two ounces of alum, two ounces of garlic heads; grind them all together and boil, and use.

When a saddle-gall occurs in a horse or some other beast of burden - which happens especially to pack-carrying animals, and is precarious and dangerous - large swellings arise around the place, containing humor, and they crust over. Such swellings are treated by cutting around and into them. They are bloodless, gassy swellings, and into the incisions is put astringent

pomegranate-rind, and barley-meal on top. On the following day, one must pound cypress and mix it with the barley-meal, and, kneading it with vinegar, apply it as a poultice, having first scraped away with the hand what was applied before.

Do not apply water, and likewise insert the pomegranate-rind again; and on the third day do the same. And when it seems to be under control, wash it with water, and, pounding cabbage-leaves and mixing in barley-flour, sprinkle it on, and it will be well.

Saddle-galls are wont to occur in beasts of burden, especially in pack-carriers. This brings danger to them, and especially the 'female' kind. For there is also a 'male' kind of the swelling that occurs at the place, large and containing humor and crusting over. One must, then, incise the swellings, which are gassy growths, containing no blood.

One must put astringent pomegranate-rind into the incisions, and barley-meal on top. On the following day, pound cypress and mix it with the barley-meal, and, kneading it with vinegar, apply as a poultice, having scraped away with the hand what was applied before.

One must not apply water, but insert the pomegranate-rind again. And when the treatment progresses well, wash it with water, and, mixing barley-flour with cabbage-leaves, apply as a poultice, and it will be clean. Or mix leeks with vetch-flour, and apply as a poultice until it is healed.

To some it seems best, after the excision, to soak it with vinegar, and to fill the incisions with the edible part of the pomegranate. On the following day, apply a poultice of barley-meal and lentils from the marshes, first soaked in vinegar,
then, once the swellings have subsided, rub around and wash around, and treat with the wound-remedy.
On an injured shoulder.
By Hierocles.

If a shoulder is injured or bruised, let it be treated, as Hieronymus says, thus: draw blood from the chest, and douse it, in summer with cold water, in winter with hot, and do not move it, until it settles. Some say the best dousing is if you boil elm-leaves in water down to a third, and douse with that.
By Theomnestus, cure for a bruised shoulder.
Mix equal parts of bitumen, resin-dust, ammoniac incense, galbanum, unfired sulfur, and bdellium-gum, and anoint the affected place.
By Apsyrtus, on dislocation of the shoulder and hip-socket.
Apsyrtus to Apelles of Laodicea, horse-doctor, greetings.

Those who say they have treated a true dislocation in the shoulders, and 'pegs' in the hind parts, do not understand what actually occurs. For a true dislocation is when the sinew holding the knuckle-joint - what we call the 'peg' - from the shoulder-blade or hip-socket, tears loose. For these there is no treatment whatsoever. For, when put back into place, they do not stay, but slip out again, having no attachment. It is treatable, however, when there is a stretching of the sinew and a loosening of the shoulder, and, walking, the horse drags its hoof, or the joint, displaced from above, gives way as it walks.
The treatment is this: one must push the joint of the shoulder back into its natural position, and insert loops

of tamarisk-wood, counter to each other, and soak it with vinegar-and-oil, first dousing with hot water, until the loops fall off, and then treat the wounds with the fatty ointment. And once it is healed, cauterize it over the joint with a round criss-crossed pattern, and it will be well.

But those in the hind parts are hard to remedy, and remain lame, and the hip wastes away and dries out, and the horse drags and wears down the hoof. This happens when, while trotting, it slips and, falling, is wrenched, in what they call being 'frog-legged.' And sometimes too it collides in the field with another horse while riding, and thus a stretching of the sinew and a wrenching of the shoulder occurs, and this happens readily to pack-carrying horses. It also happens when, kicking against a wall, a stone, wood, or something similar, or startled for some reason, it wrenches the fetlock, which occurs spontaneously and returns to its natural position on its own. One must immediately, of necessity, bleed it from the pastern, and bind it, just as for fractures, for up to fourteen days, and, once it is stabilized, cauterize it, weaving in a woolen cord. And if it is not bled, the humor and blood run down beneath, the place having become separated, and the fetlock becomes unnaturally misshapen in girth, and it goes more lame.

If, in the course of driving or a journey, a horse or some other beast of burden breaks or dislocates its shoulder and goes lame, if it comes out of its natural position, treat it by drawing blood from that very shoulder, and receive the blood into a vessel, and mix

into it oil and three eggs, boiled must, and well-ground raw bulbs, and fifty small snails, and anoint well while warm, and use the adhesive plaster, which will be set forth at the end of this treatise.

And if it is a true dislocation, cool the shoulder and settle it, and proceed in this way. But if you see that the shoulder, or another joint, has been permanently disabled, make the animal lie down, and strike the affected place with a rod, so that the hide becomes loosened. And then, three fingers' breadth below the callus, cut with a lancet enough to admit a small reed, and insert the reed, another person blowing breath through it and pushing with the hand in a circle up to the hide, and prick that part of it frequently with a lancet, and apply a poultice of white salt and vinegar, and rub it in together with the blood, and anoint it as it lies there. Let there be a quarter ounce of the salt and half an ounce of the vinegar. On the third day, douse it with much hot water, and for six days, daily, until it no longer goes lame. Once it is healed, one must put it back to work gradually. Anoint it with the strengthening emollient of loosened oil, the one made with bdellium-gum. This treatment succeeds especially in summer.
If lameness occurs at the joints of the shoulders and forelegs, these are the signs: it does not bring the leg forward, nor does it draw in the foreleg, but drags the leg,

and, going downhill, it stumbles badly. Treat it, then, by anointing with wine and oil, and drawing blood from the forelegs and washing it for seven days; then anoint for one day with children's exercise-oil scrapings mixed with wine and vinegar.

If the pain in the shoulder is chronic, one must use Apsyrtus' method. It is this: with the horse lying down, one must strike the shoulder with a rod, or with a thin sandal-sole, wrapping a soft rag around the sole. And if the hide separates when struck, one must bore beside the hide with the lancet, near the joint of the shoulder, toward the middle of the shoulder-blade's tail-end (Hieronymus says four fingers' breadth from the point of the shoulder), and thus, pushing the scalpel through, undercut it; then, inserting a small reed, blow into it vigorously, and drive the inflation around with the hand in a circle about the shoulder as far as the elbow-joint, and prick the hide with the lancet, and, sprinkling on fine salt and vinegar, rub it in together with the blood, and anoint it as it lies there. Let the quantity of salt be a small dish, and of the vinegar three half-cotylae.

On the third day, douse it with hot water, and thereafter daily, and use also an anointment, dissolved in oil, made up with the emollient of bdellium-gum. If not available, rub with wine and oil, keeping the puncture-marks open, until it no longer goes lame. Once it is healed, put it back to work gradually and reasonably. This treatment is fitting in summer, since in winter it succeeds
with difficulty, and sometimes even does harm.
When, indeed, this occurs in both shoulders,
they call it 'synomiasis' (double-shoulder affliction), though it is treated in the same
way. And at the point of the shoulder, by the armpit, it happens
that a swelling arises spontaneously, which some say arises from
indigestion. If recent, then, it is treated by anointing
with a caustic. And when it has become fatty and hardened, once excised
it is treated like the rest.
Of the ulcers that occur in the spine and in the double shoulders, the best
treatment, as Apsyrtus says, is by the cautery.
For those cut around lose flesh and lose skin, and are hard
to scar over, so that a deep-seated putrefaction sometimes results.
And once this reaches the sinewy tissue, the horse, once fallen, cannot
rise again, but perishes.
If a horse's shoulder is dislocated, or that of some other beast of burden,
throw it down onto the ground, so that the dislocated shoulder is uppermost,
and, having bound its foot and stretched it out to a tree, place a small tuft of wool
on the chest [lacuna] and, having pierced the skin of the shoulder, up to
four days, insert fig-wood setons, then soak them thoroughly in wine and
oil, wrapping wool around the setons, and after
four days remove it, then, drawing out the setons, soak them
again in the same materials.
A poultice for pain of the double shoulders.
Wolfsbane, or white hellebore, and burnt
eggshell, and colocynth-pulp, and three cherry-stones, and wild cucumber; pound all these together, and sprinkle it on.

First douse it with much hot water, then blow warm air into it, and rub it with wine and warm oil; and on the next day draw blood from the shoulders, not much, but about six cotylae, so as not to bring on a greater weakness. And likewise, as before, douse with water and rub. If, then, it becomes healed from this treatment alone, well and good; if not, take a lancet, and cut the skin clean through near the point of the shoulder, leaving a gap of two fingers' breadth from the point.

Then, inserting a small reed, blow into it, and drive the skin over the joint of the shoulders, so that you separate it evenly on all sides. Then, taking out the reed, pack the incision with greasy wool, then douse further with hot water, taking care that none of the water leaks away. Then, if pus forms, take care not to let it be sealed off for two days, and on the third day take out the wool, and let it seal off. Give the rest of the treatment as has been written. If this does not work, cauterize it on the shoulders with round cauteries.

If it feels pain in the double shoulders from excessive running or a burden, or holds its shoulders as if bound together, and feels pain in the neck when going downhill, let it be doused with hot water, and let it be rolled. Make it a plaster of a choenix of barley-flour, enough sharp vinegar, a stater's weight of frankincense-manna, and two eggs,
beaten together into one, and anoint the shoulders and the neck.
And if the treatment does not succeed, cauterize with straight cauteries, then anoint with salt and oil, and again with exercise-oil scrapings, for seven days.
And when the scabs fall off, use the vetch-remedy, as is customary.
By Apsyrtus, on echedermia (chronic hide-tightness) and chronic shoulder pain.
Apsyrtus to Epiphanius, horse-doctor, greetings. Since you are earnest about the use of horses, it is necessary for you to know:

'Echedermia' is the name in horses for when there is chronic pain in the shoulder. It is treated thus: with the horse lying down, one must strike the shoulder with a rod, or a stick wrapped with woolen rag, to make the hide separate; then thus bore beside the hide with the lancet, near the joint of the shoulder, toward the middle of the tail-end, and then push the scalpel through and undercut it; then insert a small reed and blow into it vigorously, and drive
the inflation with the hands around the shoulder as far as the elbow-joint,

and prick the hide with the lancet, taking hold of the hide where it has been inflated, and make as many punctures as are sufficient, not too sparse, and sprinkle on fine salt and vinegar; let it be rubbed in together with the blood, and anointed while it still lies there. Let the quantity of salt be a small dish, and the vinegar three half-cotylae.

On the third day, one must douse it with much hot water, and on the following days, daily, use an anointment, dissolving in oil the emollient made with bdellium-gum; and if this is not available, rub with wine and oil,

keeping the horse's puncture-marks open, until the hide settles back down. Use the anointments and the fomentation, until it no longer goes lame. Once it is healed, put it back to work gradually. Perform this treatment in summer; in winter it succeeds with difficulty, and sometimes even does harm.
When, indeed, this occurs in both shoulders, it is called 'synomiasis,' and is treated in the same way.
Cure for the point of the shoulder.

For those with pus-filled points of the shoulder, cauterize the sides, and cut open all the abscesses, and tilt the horse, so that the pus drains off and has room and can breathe out, and so that the cauterized area, having received too small an incision, does not scar over prematurely. And when you have cauterized and incised, give the same care as has been said concerning cauterized horses.
By Pelagonius, treatment of the shoulder-blade.
If a horse's shoulder-blade is injured, one must bleed it from the veins in the middle of the shins, and mix frankincense-powder with the very blood that flows out,

and anoint the painful part. And so that the animal does not lose too much blood, apply some of its own dung to the veins, and bind it with a rag. On the next day, again release blood from the same places, and proceed in the same manner. Let the animal abstain from barley and be content with a little fodder, and, after the third day up to the sixth, pour about three cyathi of leek juice with half a pound of oil down the throat through a horn. And after the sixth day, make it move about. And when it has
walked about, let it swim. And thus, progressing gradually, with firmer feed being offered, it will be healed.
Another for the same affliction, good and simple.
Soda-froth, wine, oil, boiled must, lard, and bulbs -
pound all these together, and rub the shoulder-blades with this.
Another: if it suffers lightly in the shoulder-blades.

If a horse suffers lightly in the shoulder-blades, rub it down with wine-and-oil. And if it suffers more severely, pierce its body, beginning from the mane, between the skin and the cartilage, eight fingers' breadth, so as not to touch the flesh itself, and, having blown in air, insert it, and gently strike the shoulder-blades with a thin rod, and rub with salt and oil on that same day. On the following day, make a poultice-paste, whose preparation is this: two pints of fine wheat-meal or wheat- or barley-flour, the whites of two eggs only, one and a half ounces of frankincense, knead with vinegar, and rub the shoulder-blades with it by hand, and for many days douse them with hot water, so that they become well moistened, and each time apply some of the paste, first washing the place with wine.
Another.

Half a pound of bay-berries, one pound of old wine, enough soda; pound and sift the soda and the bay-berries, and, mixing them all in one vessel, first douse the shoulder-blades with hot water, and anoint in the sun with this remedy. And if the shoulder-blade is dislocated, put it back in place, and use the same treatment. And if this does not succeed, apply the cautery.
Another.
One pound of bay-berries, three ounces of unfired sulfur, two pints of liquid pitch; pound all, mix with wine and oil, and rub it in this way.
By Tiberius, against slackness of the shoulder-blade.
Two pounds of dry pitch, two pounds of Colophonian resin, two ounces of turpentine-resin, two ounces of galbanum; mix them together, and use.

Apsyrtus to Marcus, horse-doctor, greetings. I want you to know that on the shoulder, at the so-called elbow, near the flank or beneath the girth, swellings happen to arise spontaneously. Those before us said they arise from indigestion; I do not agree with them. If recent, and gas-filled, they are treated by anointing with a caustic. And when it has become fatty and has hardened, it is excised and treated, like the rest of the ulcers that occur on the spine, which are called 'cysts.' The best treatment is by cautery, and likewise for those on

the double shoulders; for those cut around lose skin and remain hard to scar over. And when a deep-seated putrefaction occurs in them and reaches the underlying sinew, the horse, once fallen, cannot rise again, but perishes.
By Pelagonius, on dislocation of a vertebra.
First rinse with soap, then, putting oil into rainwater, and stirring in egg-white, make a plaster, and use it.
Another.
Burn dry fig-tree branches, and, taking their clean ash, sift it, and after this put it into a mortar together with
the ash, and mix in enough wine, an equal amount of oil, and the whites of two eggs, and, stirring it all together, use it when needed.
Against broken vertebrae or backs.

Boil together with oil one pound of wax, four ounces of roasted resin, two ounces of verdigris, and use. And so that mules' necks do not suffer a rupture, do this: boil two pounds of fresh pig-fat and two pints of vinegar down to a third, and, straining it, use.
Against pain of a vertebra.

One must draw blood, and use warm anointments, that is, mix wax, oil, old lard, soda, liquid pitch, bitumen, and bay-berries in wine, and rub the whole body; and, if need calls for it, take it into a bath and bathe it. After this treatment, drench it beforehand thus: mix enough ginger, parsley, cumin, poppy-juice, and bay-berries with good wine and honey, and give it warm.
Against pains of the vertebrae and spasms of the sinews in them.

Cauterize the vertebra cleanly on both sides, and after this anoint with lard, and after seven days rinse with hot water, and, after it has cooled, anoint with warming ointments, and bind it round with a hide together with wool.
By Hierocles, against an ulcer on the spine and the side.
If the ulcer is superficial and the part is bare of hair, burn a dog's head, and sprinkle on the ash; for besides curing it, it will also grow hair back. And if it is deep, or has a callus,
bind vetch-flour with honey, and, having filled a wick with it, apply it and pack it in, and it draws out the callus and heals the scar.
Another, for the spine.

Ulpius Phoebus, the prefect's man: put fig leaves into an oven, until they dry, to the point where they can be pounded; pound and sift them, and apply as a plaster. For this same remedy cleans and heals the scar.
Another.
Grind fresh spurge together with its root, and sift it, and apply as a plaster; and if the wound is small, pound in enough salt with it.

Six ounces of resin-dust, six ounces of pine-resin, three ounces of bull's-hide glue, six ounces of frankincense-manna, one pint of fine wheat-flour, and enough old wine; put them into a small pan and boil, and anoint against the grain of the hair.
Another, against the shoulder.

One ounce of balm-of-Gilead sap, one ounce of saffron, two ounces of Cyrenaic silphium-juice, one ounce of numicium, one ounce of antimony, four ounces of cinnamon, one ounce each of male frankincense, Syrian nard, trogline myrrh, white pepper, opopanax, and pine-resin, one pound of Attic honey; mix these and use.
Theomnestus' cauterizing and strengthening emollient

A cauterizing and strengthening emollient, not only for beasts of burden being treated for ulcers on the spine or the double shoulders, or at a joint, or over the kidneys, when they remain unstrengthened after treatment. For with only a slight cause it returns them again to the same condition. One must also be mindful

of the preceding treatment. The strengthening remedy for all such cases, then, is the one set out below: one pound each of dregs-of-oil, roasted resin, Judaean bitumen, pitch, wax, and verdigris, six ounces of ammoniac incense, four ounces of frankincense, nine ounces of galbanum, two ounces of opopanax; melt the meltable ingredients, and, stirring with a spatula, anoint while still warm. And if it becomes too hard, add pounded old lard, and thus make it softer, and use it. Add ammoniac incense too. It also works well without the verdigris. When it is hot weather, so that the ointment does not dissolve, add four ounces of ship-scrapings and old caulking-tow, and use this marvelous remedy.

[Another strengthening remedy.] Not faulting the weakness of the previous one do we write this second remedy, but we shall set forth one from our abundance, one more easily obtained and possible for poorer people to prepare: six ounces each of Judaean bitumen and split alum, one pound of old lard, three ounces of litharge, one ounce of galbanum, one ounce of opopanax, one pint of squill-vinegar, and half a pint of oil; boil them, and anoint well.

Knead barley-meal with wine and oil, and plaster it all around the wounded place. And if it forms proud flesh ('lung-tissue'), cut this away with iron, and apply horse dung with oil, vinegar, and roasted salt.
If a horse feels pain in the spine, bleed it, and
treat it with these warm ointments: mix bay-berries, sulfur, oil, lard, and soda with cedar-resin and wine, and rub the horse's whole body with it, having stood it in the sun or in the warmest place.
Another: if it develops wounds on the back.
Grind oyster-shells, and, making a powder from them, sprinkle it on the affected place; or sprinkle on one pound of burnt crabs.
Another, for the back.
Mix one ounce of iron-slag and one ounce of copper verdigris, and make a powder; and, first having rinsed the horse's back with wine, sprinkle on some of this powder.
Another: if it has a wound on the back.
Grind Syrian galls, and, mixing them with honey, apply to the wound.
Against a wound on the back arising from a rider's inexperience:

take a bundle of onions - that is, of the withered leaves that happened to hang from them - and put them into hot water and boil them, and apply them, still hot, over the animal's inflammation, and bind it with a bandage; or, if you wish, put the saddle itself on the horse, so that it remains this way for one day and night.
On orthopnea (labored upright breathing).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Secundus, horse-doctor, greetings. When orthopnea occurs, these are the signs: while walking, the horse falls behind, and breathes heavily throughout, and cannot walk uphill, but leans to one side, so as even to fall. And once fallen, it does not stretch itself out or lie flat, but rather wishes

to rise again. It is treated thus: one must grind very fine two drachms of frankincense and one drachm of sulfur, and, dissolving them in fragrant white wine and honey, drench through the nostrils. Or mix pitch-serum and fine roasted soda with honey and wine, and pour it in, until the labored breathing stops. And let it not be exposed to cold, nor take exercise. Put soda into its drinking-water too, and sprinkle its fodder with it; and if it does not stop with these, use the purgative.

These are the signs of orthopnea: it breathes with difficulty, and its nostrils are swollen wide, and it is drawn in from the flanks. One must, then, offer it warming feed, as Cleomenes the Libyan says: soaked vetch, chickpeas, oats, barley, and mix flour into its drinking-water, and drench it with a little tragacanth and unfired sulfur in sweet wine.
Slaughter a puppy, and pour the blood, still warm, in through the mouth, sprinkling on two spoonfuls of ground Ethiopian cumin, for nine days.

Bruise comfrey, which they call 'horse-tail,' and press out its juice to two cotylae, and add two spoonfuls of Ethiopian cumin, and, dissolving it in a cotyla of wine, drench; and grind frankincense and sulfur, and, dissolving them in honey and wine, pour it in through the left nostril.
On dyspnea (difficult breathing).
These are the signs of a horse suffering from dyspnea: it has a yellowish right eye, and from each nostril it emits a foul

smell, it drags its flanks, and small knots form under its jaws. Observe, then, its gait: and if it tends more toward the right side, it is not easily cured. But if the affliction is recent, use this method: draw its blood for three days, then drench it beforehand thus: one pint of old wine, half a pint of bay-oil, one ounce of saffron, one pound of rose-oil, half a pint of mastic-oil, one ounce of trogline myrrh, three pints of honey-water; put all these into a new bronze vessel, and, boiling a cockerel together with them, reduce it by a third, and give half a pint of it with honey-water and one egg, through the nostrils, for six days. Of this preliminary drench, if you wish, also apply some to the head, and bandage it down to the foot, and you will effect a cure.
Another, by Mago.

If a horse is gripped by severe dyspnea, its flanks hang down, and it has either both eyes, or the right one, discolored, and its jaw likewise inflamed, and its gait is not straight. This affliction, at the outset, is easily treated, though with much care. Examine its posture carefully, then: and if it is bent toward the right side, it will be cured; if toward the left, it will live only with great difficulty. Nevertheless, one must apply these remedies: open the horse's twelve veins, in such a way that over three days you open four veins each day; after this give this preliminary drench:

One ounce each of saffron, trogline myrrh, spikenard, and white pepper, three pints of honey-water, one pint of old oil, half a pound of rose-oil, half a pint of lentils; put all these into a new vessel, and boil together with a puppy about ten days old, adding honey or honey-water and one egg, and drench for many consecutive days.
Another, by Pelagonius.

One pint of Cretan boiled must, one ounce each of Illyrian iris, pepper, saffron, trogline myrrh, frankincense-powder, and tragacanth, and enough raisins. Mix all these and give, and afterward massage its throat with honey, butter, lard, and salt.
Another.

This too the Greeks called 'orthopnea.' It is recognized when the animal holds its ears erect, and discharges a purulent fluid, and continually draws in its flanks, and holds its eyes wide open. Its treatment is this: take blood from the vertebra, and, mixing it with vinegar and oil, anoint the animal. Let it also abstain from food as much as possible, or use warming feeds, vetch or chickpeas or wheat-flour in winter, barley in summer. Put in tragacanth, boiled must, and bitumen, and add also
dog's blood, and as much ground cumin as you can hold with three fingers, and, adding wine, give it. Or egg-white with honey and ground pine-nuts, for twenty days or more, until the lung is healed.
And if this does not help, apply black hellebore root to the

chest, or to the roots of the ears, or to the nostrils, through which the whole disease will be expelled. Give also pastilles with honey-water and bitter almonds and wild-cucumber root, bound with honey. Or grind about three obols' weight of mulberry root, and pour it into the nostrils with warm wine. And for animals with difficult breathing, first wipe the head with one cyathus of oil and one pint of wine, by which means a cure is promised even for otherwise helpless afflictions.
Another.

Dyspnea arises from excessive sweating, and from fatigue and panting. And the horse gripped by this affliction discharges through the nostrils a humor tinged with pus. Most useful against this affliction is this preliminary drench: one and a half pints of Cretan boiled must, three ounces of costus, two ounces each of hyssop-flower, cassia-fistula, and tragacanth, three ounces of southernwood, two ounces of dry male frankincense; pound all these carefully, and, mixing them with the boiled must, drench through the throat.
By Tiberius, for the same.

These are the signs of dyspnea: the horse's flanks heave violently, its nostrils flare, and distress comes upon it, troubled by the affliction. Treat it, then, thus: soak eggs in vinegar - three on the first day, five on the second, and seven on the third - and give them in its mouth, squeezing out through their shells.
Against gangrenous sores in the jaw.
By Apsyrtus. An affliction occurs at the bit-ring of the jaw. Roast copper ore in the fire, then, until it becomes glowing, and grind it with honey, so as to
make it fine; put it into a box, and use it against gangrenous sores and spreading ulcers in the mouth, and everywhere else.

If a gangrenous sore occurs, open it up and expose it, and cauterize it, taking care not to touch the tendon. And if it is on the spine, quickly incise the tunic, and cauterize. And if it is on the flank, cut down to the bone, taking careful precaution. Then apply a poultice of cypress, finely pounded, mixed with an equal amount of barley-meal, and, kneading it with vinegar, first anoint the place with oil. Do not wash around the ulcer, however, for three days. On the fourth day, wash around it, without bringing the hand close. Or pound cabbage-leaves, and, adding barley-meal, knead with water and apply as a poultice.
Or pound wild and cultivated leeks, and, adding barley-flour and grinding, apply as a poultice.

And when the scabs fall off, and the gangrenous sore becomes exposed, first anoint with the wound-remedy, then apply pounded birthwort or raw pitch onto the gangrenous sore, or alkanet, or ground copper ore, or mullein leaves, or ironwort. You have, against gangrenous sores, further compositions in my second book, among the preparations of remedies.
Another.
Pound a sour pomegranate and sprinkle it on with barley-meal, and, kneading it with vinegar, anoint. Or pound cypress, and, soaking it in barley-meal and vinegar, sprinkle it on.
Another.
Pound and sift dwarf-olive, and likewise pound and sift an equal amount of round birthwort, and, kneading them with water, bind it on.
On the horse-doctor.

Apsyrtus to Agathocles, greetings. It is useful for you, as a horse-keeper, to know the signs of the cardiac ailment and the remedies against it. These are the signs: the horse becomes lean and draws in its belly, and is downcast in look and distressed, and its testicles swell, and likewise it suffers and swells below the knee. It is recognized from these signs, and is treated thus:

One must pour in warming remedies through the nostrils, or, holding the tongue, through the mouth: pepper with wine and oil, and squill likewise, or bay-berries, or frankincense, or birthwort, or myrrh, or thyme, or use other suitable warming remedies. Offer dry feed, and none of the green kind, and rub with wine and oil. Let it be covered over the belly, especially the chest, and rub with sulfur mixed with oil, and give it too. And the stable must be kept clean, and something fragrant placed in it: myrtle, bay, or the like.

And when, in addition to the signs described, this occurs, that it is unable to walk, and, when forced to, veers off toward the walls, and collides with whatever it meets, and is downcast, as has been said, and sweats at the belly and the shoulders, so that trembling and spasm occur in it, and it falls suddenly and does not lie flat, but lies upon its belly, in great pain, and cannot bear it, and, wishing to rise,

is unable to, except with force, and has its testicles drawn up, and its member protruding, and passes urine only a little at a time - one must know that in such a horse the bile has fallen into the arteries and has been carried to the heart, and it cannot live.
By Hierocles, for the same.

You will recognize a horse with the cardiac ailment by these signs: it draws in its belly and flanks, and is downcast, and sweats especially at the head. Warming remedies help it, poured in through the nostrils and the mouth: pepper with wine and oil, or squill, or frankincense, or birthwort, or bay-berries, or myrrh, or thyme, or one of the other warming remedies. Let dry feed be offered, and let it be rubbed with wine-and-oil, covered over the belly, especially the chest, and rubbed with sulfur mixed with oil. Let the stable, indeed, also be clean, and let there be placed in
it something of the more fragrant kind: myrtle, or bay, or the like.

When, however, it is severely overcome by the cardiac affliction, it is unable to walk. And if forced to walk, it is carried into the walls, and collides with what it meets, and sweats at the belly, and trembles especially in the shoulders, and there is spasm in it, and it falls suddenly, and, wishing to rise, cannot except by force, and draws up its testicles, so that it also passes urine only a little at a time. In such a horse the bile has already fallen into the arteries and to the heart, and it could not live.
By Theomnestus, or Cassius, for the same.

If a flux settles onto the heart of a horse, or some other pain, spasm follows, and it falls onto its knees, and its body suffers, and especially the head. If, then, it shows these signs, drench with this: a bean's-weight of silphium, four ounces of honey, three ounces of soda, two pints of warmed water, mixed with one pint of vinegar, and drench together. And, having wrapped it up, walk it about, and let it be drenched over three days, and let it be fed on green fodder, or dog's-tooth grass, or lucerne. And if it does not recover, draw blood from its forelegs, on the inside of the knees, and from the hind legs likewise, and you will heal it. This has been tested and proven.
By Pelagonius, for the same.

We recognize and diagnose the cardiac ailment, if it repeatedly knocks its head against the ground, or bites its own flanks very often, and if it sweats simply while standing still. One must treat it thus, if it can tolerate a swelling: grind together a bean's-weight of mustard and laser-resin, two oxybaphon-measures of honey, two cyathi of hot water, and four cyathi of vinegar, into one, and drench it beforehand. And walk it about, and offer green feed. And after health has been restored, one must open the veins at the tendons, and draw blood from the hind parts, so that health may remain lasting.
By Eumelus, against pain of the heart.
Pain of the heart is diagnosed when the horse weeps from the right eye, and breathes more heavily, and falls onto its knees. Let blood be drawn from this horse, as has been said above.

Let it be drenched through the left nostril thus: mix about an oxybaphon-measure of fennel seed, an equal amount of anise, and one cotyla of white wine, and drench for three days. And if it persists, take blood from the legs, and after this

mix a bean's-weight of laser-root, an equal amount of soda, two oxybaphon-measures of honey, and four cotylae of hot water in one cotyla of vinegar, and drench. Or mix squill, a little birthwort, frankincense, myrrh, and thyme in wine, and pour it in through the nostrils. Let the animal be covered with blankets, and let the stable be clean, and let it be fumigated with either myrrh or bay-leaves, and let it abstain from barley.
On nephritis (kidney disease).
By Apsyrtus.

Nephritis is the name for that of which these are the signs: it drags its hind legs and staggers, and, while walking, veers about into the walls. We shall cauterize this horse, then, at the junction of the hips and the bladder with straight points, no more than twenty-four, half on each side of the spine, making three rows, spaced three fingers' breadth apart from each other.
By Hierocles, for the same.

These are the signs of nephritis: the testicles are drawn up, and it does not put weight on its hind feet, and it urinates dark, blood-tinged, thick fluid. It is treated thus: foment the hips and the loins, and anoint with wax-salve, and cover with blankets, and offer diuretic remedies, fennel and celery. Give also green lucerne and white chickpeas in wine, then
let it be drenched with about two spoonfuls of celery, an equal amount of carrot, two parts of dill, and three obols' weight of myrrh, ground in a cotyla of sweet wine, and let it take gentle walks.

Let it also be given an enema of lukewarm water, not less than a chous, and bed it down softly, until you see the urine clear, and the testicles no longer drawn up, and the hind feet overstepping the fore-tracks by less than six fingers' breadth.

Cleomenes of Lindus says one must burn mullein root and grind it in wine, and, mixing in an equal amount of water, give an enema through the anus. Others prescribe offering wheat-flour, good fodder, as much bread as you wish, and chickpeas, and taking light walks.

These are the signs of nephritis: the suspensory ligaments are swollen, the flank staggers, it is light-footed, its eyes are raised (unsteady), and it cannot walk, because of the swelling of the kidneys lying beneath. Use, then, this treatment: draw blood from the groin, then curtail its feed, and use this drench: take two ounces of frankincense, a quarter-measure of crushed vetch, and, grinding the two together with honey, pour it in through the nostrils for a sufficient number of days, and give it more frequent walks.
Then use this drench too: take an unborn puppy, boil it thoroughly with barley-gruel, and, straining it, pour it in through the mouth with honey, for a sufficient number of days, and it recovers.
Prognosis and cure for the kidney-afflicted horse.
If a horse or other beast of burden falls into this ailment,

it has these signs: it does not gape at all, and cannot stand still on its hind legs, but shifts them about. Further, in its gait, it falls behind the forelegs, and circles with its hind legs, sometimes with both, sometimes with only one, and the fetlocks become thick and slower.
The treatment of this disease is this: heat water, and douse it generously along the spine, as much as it can take. [lacuna]
If a horse suffers this pain, its flanks and testicles throb, and it urinates only with difficulty, and it treads more heavily on its hind feet than its forefeet, and it whinnies more frequently.
Treat it, then, thus: boil asphodel root together in good wine and grind it, immerse the belly in lukewarm water, and warm the kidneys thoroughly with warmer ointments.

If a horse suffers pain in the kidneys, it shows signs in its urine, and drags its hind parts. Let it be drenched with about one cotyla of sheep's milk, for three days; or with one cotyla of boiled deer-marrow, and an equal amount of oil; or with the aromatic remedy together with wine, oil, honey, and eggs.
Use also a fomentation of wine-and-oil and soda-froth, and apply a cloth over the back with a hot fomentation. This affliction arises from strenuous running.
A remedy against kidney ailment.

Four ounces of pepper, four ounces of parsley, four ounces of trogline myrrh, one ounce of spikenard, one ounce of celery seed, one ounce of castoreum, two ounces of poppy-juice, four ounces of anise, four ounces of cassia. Pound
and sift these, and give a heaping spoonful mixed with spiced wine.
Another.

A horse is seized by nephritis either when it is overloaded with a great weight, or leaps over a pit, and its hind legs happen to sink in. It also arises from severe cold. You will treat it, then, by dousing the loins with hot water, and afterward using a caustic.
A preliminary drench for the kidney-afflicted.
Burn and grind eleven fresh cypress-galls, and add three ounces of toasted and ground soda, three ounces of good oil, four pints of old wine, and, mixing them together, give for four days.
Another: if it suffers pain for a longer time.
Open the veins of the hooves, and, taking the blood that flows out, mix it with lard and oil, and apply it over the kidneys. And if necessity requires, use an emollient too.
An anodyne for kidney ailment.

Ten pounds of oil, ten ounces of spurge-sap, four ounces of dried thistle-root, four pounds of henna-oil, four ounces of unfired sulfur, three ounces of pepper, three ounces of soapwort, two ounces of pellitory, four ounces of wild raisin, four ounces of thapsia-juice, dried wild-cucumber roots; pound and sift all the dry ingredients, and, soaking them in the oil, make it the thickness of honey, and pour it into a glass vessel, and use.
On the loins.
If a horse suffers pain in the loins, these are the signs: it twists its hindquarters about, and, in twisting the hindquarters, staggers, and drags its hind legs. One must cure it

thus: beginning with straight cauteries from the elbow to the knees, cauterize on each side, pressing the cautery in, so that the whole heated part sinks in. For the place is thick with flesh. And then, grinding salt fine, sprinkle it on lightly,
then, after wiping it clean with hot water, blow in wine and oil, and burn clean barley-bread and grind it, and on the very
cauterized place sprinkle it on, and do not move the horse until a sufficient number of days have passed since the cauterization, and give as much feed as possible.
An ointment for the same.
Mix equal parts of vinegar, bitumen, unfired sulfur, and opopanax, and use.
Against pain of the loins.
Grind cabbage, and, adding half a pint of wine, apply it with cold water.
Another.
Grind cypress leaves fine to make a half-pint measure, add one pound of barley-meal, and, kneading it with vinegar, apply to the aching part.
Another.
Boil two ounces of dry resin until it dissolves, and add barley-flour and goat-fat, until you make it thick, and apply it hot to the aching part, and do this frequently.
Cure for the hip.

If a horse suffers pain in the hip, it moves its hind legs as though bound together. Draw off, then, about four cotylae of blood from each of its groins, and douse it with much hot water, and, blowing in wine and oil, rub it down. If it becomes healed this way, well and good; if not, cauterize it in a round pattern, a third on each hip, and tend to it as has been written.
Another.

If a horse suffers pain in the hip from opisthotonos, or from some other cause, raise the tail and examine the veins, and, if the vein running along the tail is prominent, open it, and the horse recovers.
Another.

When a horse is gripped by this affliction, it breathes more rapidly, and has pain around the loins and the spine. One must, then, use this treatment: draw blood from the thighs and from the hoof, use a plaster and a fomentation, and keep it in a warm place.
An anodyne for sciatica.
One pound of Colophonian resin, half a pound each of turpentine-resin and old oil, one and a half ounces of opopanax, two ounces of galbanum.
Another, for the same.
One pound of spurge-sap, one and a half pounds of adarce, one and a half pounds of sea-sponge-stone, three pounds of wax, four pounds of bay-berries, one pound of pepper, two pounds of henna-oil.
On a hip that has suffered rupture.

It pants frequently, and groans, and has its belly distended with gas. Palpate the loins, then, and mark the painful places, and, having hobbled the horse, cauterize it, and a fluid will follow, like the yolk of a spoiled egg. Grind fine salt, then, and, soaking it in pitch, apply it to the cauterized place.
On abdominal pain (colic).
By Hierocles.

When a horse suffers abdominal pain, one must pay especially close attention to the signs. For some, treating it as though gripped by dysuria, cause the animal to rupture. The belly requires relief instead.
It sweats, then, at the ribs, the flanks, and the testicles,
and the belly is drawn up, and it strikes the ground with its feet, and turns toward the affected side on either side, as if pointing to the aching place, and sometimes it trembles all over its body.

But these signs also occur in a horse suffering from dysuria, though it does not show the other signs by which the dysuric horse is recognized, which we shall discuss next. For now, our task is to say how the horse with abdominal pain is treated.

Cut the veins in the chest, and draw enough blood, and, having anointed and inserted the hand through the anus, remove the nearby blockages, and, inserting about an oxybaphon-measure of fine salt, irritate it so as to make it pass dung, and it will be free of pain.

It is also useful to douse it with much hot water along the back and hips, and to drench it with a decoction of beet mixed with two cotylae of sweet wine, through the left nostril. Or boil figs in four cotylae of wine, and, mixing in one ounce of ground soda, drench; or likewise boil hoary-leaved sage in one and a half cotylae of wine.

Let it walk about, trotting gently, though not vigorously, and let it not eat barley for three days. And on the day the affliction occurred, let it not even be given water. Let it eat fodder, especially green, and barley after those days, gradually.
It is good also to learn the cause of the pain: when, having stopped from a long run and eaten barley, it fails to digest it, but most of it remains unprocessed, it writhes all the more. Or if,

a small spider like a tarantula, which they call a 'bouprestis' (blister-beetle), gets into the fodder and it eats it. For it swells up from this, so as even to throw itself onto the ground from the pain. It is helped, then, by drenching it through the left nostril with ground cabbage-leaves and four cotylae of wine and one cotyla of oil, or with wormwood boiled in wine. Let the belly also be anointed with sulfur ground in oil, made liquid, and let the barley, moistened with beet-water, be offered. The same also helps those with intestinal worms.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

A horse suffers abdominal pain if it does not digest its feed, but expels whole barley grains, or even if some of these remain still in the belly. For it drinks more because of the indigestion, and the barley swells further from the moisture, and it becomes bloated and writhes, and, if it does not pass dung soon, it is in danger. One must, then, use enemas, injecting oil-and-water through the anus, and, with the hand itself anointed with oil, carefully clear out its dung, and also insert a scammony pastille, the size of an egg, into the anus, and the belly will be relieved. Its other signs are similar to those of the dysuric horse; but it particularly bites itself and tears at its belly, distressed by the discomfort. One must drench it through the left nostril with cabbage juice mixed with wine-and-oil; let the quantity be one pint of wine, a quarter-pint of oil, and an equal amount of cabbage juice.
It often happens also from several other causes

that abdominal pain occurs: when it eats a blister-beetle in the fodder (this is a grub resembling a tarantula), or when it eats a spider, or the so-called 'wolf-spider,' which is often born in fodder. It also happens from bad water and from unfamiliar surroundings. And when this affliction is recent, the drench is fitting. It also suffers abdominal pain from intestinal worms.

When, then, it suffers pain and continually rolls about, one must drench it with one ounce of ground dry fleawort, half an ounce of opopanax, and one ounce of deer-antler filings, mixed in honey-water. Let the water contain a decoction of mint and tender bay-shoots. And if dysuria arises from this affliction, drench with one drachm of opopanax dissolved in oil and sweet Cretan wine.

Add a little soda to the water it drinks and the fodder it eats, and, mixing cabbage juice with one cotyla of sweet wine, drench through the left nostril, and you will cure it; or chamomile ground together with wine and oil, drenched through a horn.

Pain of the belly is naturally born when worms, biting, feed upon the neighboring parts. The animal is continually tormented, and rolls about, and the belly swells up, and it turns its face or mouth toward the belly very often. Use, then, the treatment written above, and add, if you wish, also centaury or wild-cucumber root.
Another: an enema against pains of the belly.
Mix equal parts of soda and oil with green beet, and the broth of a boiled goat's head and a cockerel, and barley-gruel juice, and, making up a quantity of two cotylae, give the animal an enema.
And when the pain arises, foment; or pound and dry celery seed and germander, and, grinding them with myrrh in fragrant white wine, drench.
By Pelagonius, against pains and aches of the belly.
Grind two grammes of all-heal root and one gramme of birthwort in fragrant wine, and drench; or one oxybaphon-measure of rue-seed with old wine.
Another.

Grind nightshade and cress seed in wine and oil, and, warming it, give it. Or mix myrrh-oil with one pint of old wine and a little salt, and, putting a red-hot iron into this very preparation, and thus warming it, give it. Or thoroughly rub the animal's palate with human dung.
Another.

Grind hare's dung with nine spoonfuls of honey and fifteen peppercorns in a mortar, and drench through a horn together with cabbage juice. Or burn three pig's ankle-bones that human teeth have not yet touched, and, grinding them in about half a pint of wine and oil, drench.
On a painful liver.
By Apsyrtus.
A horse in pain turns around frequently, looking at the painful place as though pointing it out, and groans, and has its mouth quite dry, and its tongue rough and swollen, and,
when it falls, turns itself around, not lying on that side, and, rolling about, is in pain, and rises again frequently.

It is treated with a few walks, covered with several layers of bedding for lying down, and rubbing with wine and oil, and a drink not cold, mixed with soda, though not every day. Hoary-leaved sage boiled in wine and drenched through the mouth or the right nostril is also beneficial. One must also do the same by boiling Illyrian iris in water mixed with wine, to a quantity of two cotylae. Best of all is to grind the herb polemonium with wine and drench likewise, which is similar to the broad-leaved

catmint, but greyer still and more bitter, having a heavy smell, and it grows in moist meadows. Or one must boil fleabane, called by some 'knyza,' and drench it with wine and oil. Let the barley to be offered be soaked in hot water. Polemonium, pounded and applied as a poultice in the same way, is also fitting for humans. Fleabane too will have the same effect, with oil added.
Another, by Cassius, in the writings of Theomnestus.

If a horse suffers pain in the liver, it groans while coughing, and its eyes become poor-looking, and, though eating more voraciously, it does not accept drink. For a horse suffering thus, then, this drench will be fitting: mix together one pound of honey, half a pound of soda, one cotyla of white wine, and two cotylae of water,

and drench through the right nostril for five days. And if it does not recover, draw blood from its forelegs, and cauterize its third rib from the armpit with a rod, and, on both bends, skip one rib. Let the cautery-rod be four fingers' breadth at each bend.

A horse suffering pain in the liver shows these signs: its right flank swells, and it breathes harshly, and it falls behind in running, and, while walking, moves its hind legs more slowly, and avoids lying down. It will be dieted especially on healthful, moister feed, and given lighter walks, abstaining from exercise. Give it feed a little at a time, and prepare the softest bedding, and anoint it generously, and give it water boiled together with southernwood. For it is treated more through its drinks than through drenches.

If a horse suffers pain in the liver from running, and its flanks become ulcerated, a rupture occurs in the lung, and its body collapses, and it does not take food, and blood rushes up in its veins. You will treat it, then, by drawing blood from the neck, and drenching with a drachm each of myrrh and frankincense in one cotyla of wine. Anoint also with wine-and-oil, and give a drink of fine wheat-meal dissolved in water, and food, if it desires it. And if the affliction persists, draw blood from both armpits as well. This happens to some horses when they run rather strenuously over pebbly and
rough, stone-paved ground. To these horses too drench an oxybaphon-measure of cumin with wine-and-oil.
Another.

An oxybaphon-measure each of honey and soda, two oxybaphon-measures of cumin; dissolve together in wine, and, pouring on two cotylae of oil and water, pour it into the nostril. And if it does not become healed, draw blood from the forelegs below the knees. And if it still does not become healed this way, cauterize along the third rib below the armpit, midway between the ribs, with rods, leaving a gap of four fingers' breadth between each cauterization.
Another.
Warm marsh-frogs together with wine, and drench through the mouth for three days.
A preliminary drench for the liver.

Strain very finely the tiniest pine-nuts, one ounce of saffron, and an equal amount of Ethiopian cumin, and give in wine. Or use polemonium growing in the marshes, which resembles catmint, having a bitter quality. Or wild marjoram with ground pepper, and give in wine. Or grind butter, honey, opopanax, and myrrh in equal weight, and, mixing with wine, drench through the nostrils.
On dysuria, abdominal pain, strangury, and ischuria (urinary retention).

By Apsyrtus. Master Aelianus, it has been made known to me that you have asked why most horse-doctors, not properly distinguishing certain afflictions that occur in horses, apply opposite remedies. For they help a horse suffering abdominal pain as though it were suffering from dysuria,

and the animal suffers a rupture. It happens that, in abdominal pain, these signs appear: it sweats at the ribs, testicles, and flanks, and the belly is drawn up, and it strikes the ground with its feet, and turns to each side, as if pointing to the aching place, and sometimes trembling comes over its whole body. These signs also occur in the dysuric horse, which will be recognized, in addition to these, when it runs and lashes itself under the thighs with its tail, and, rolling about, sinks down at the hips, thrusts out its member, and passes urine only drop by drop, giving the impression that it is about to urinate. These, then, are the accompanying signs.

The dysuric horse is treated with drenches: boil a bundle of leeks together with their leaves, use the juice, and, pressing out about two cotylae, mix in a cotyla of fragrant wine and an oxybaphon of oil, and drench through the right nostril. And let it walk about and trot, and it will urinate without hindrance. Likewise, boil wormwood in about a cotyla of wine and drench; likewise grind about the size of a little finger's head of opopanax in the same measure of wine, and proceed as written above. Or grind two cyathi of edible radish seed, pour on wine, and use as described above. Or likewise pound a cyathus of celery seed - better still, if there is horse-parsley - and boil it and give in the wine, and likewise drench with alexanders roots. This too works: peel and bruise long onions, which are more pungent,
and insert about five of them into the anus, and let it walk about and trot; and it will urinate. Dousing with hot water over the hips is also helpful.

Some are not truthful in such matters, saying that one must correct the bladder, and they insert the hand through the anus and the rectum. But they cannot reach the bladder, having the hand in the intestine, and it (the bladder) lies against what is called the sacrum, in its fixed position, from which it never deviates. The hand, inserted, produces an itching in the urinary passage, and sometimes it urinates as a result. And as far as the anus, touching does no harm; but pushing further in, they do no good, but great harm;
for, from the manual rubbing of the intestine, great inflammation results, and the animal cannot bear the pain, and for the most part it dies, either immediately or shortly after.

For these are the three most acute afflictions in the horse and in other solid-hoofed beasts of burden: the bladder-ailment, and twisting of the intestine, which is called 'ileus,' and the cardiac ailment. The other afflictions the animal can endure for a good many days. And these also kill horses quickly, if help is not given at once: barley-surfeit, choking, and abdominal pain. For the horse suffering pain in the belly, one must give help thus: cut the veins in the chest, and draw off enough blood. One must also anoint the hand and insert it into the anus, and remove the nearby blockages, and
insert about an oxybaphon-measure of fine salt and honey. For this induces the urge to pass dung, and thus it will be free of pain.

Likewise, one must douse this horse too with much hot water along the back and hips. Use a drench of decocted beet with two cotylae of sweet wine, mixing in one cotyla through the left nostril; and boil figs in four cotylae of water, and, grinding them and mixing in about an ounce of soda, drench; likewise boil hoary-leaved sage in one cotyla of wine and do the same. Let it trot and walk at a gentle pace. Use a restriction of barley, giving none at all for up to three days; and on the day the affliction occurred, give no drink at all. If there is green fodder, use that especially. Offer barley gradually, once the days have passed.

It is best also to know the causes for which the afflictions of dysuria arise, which have not been written down by anyone. Dysuria most often occurs when, journeying or trotting for a whole day, the horse fails to urinate along the way. One must, therefore, make it deviate from the path and encourage it to urinate. For it happens that the passage from the genital organ to the urinary tract becomes inflamed, and the urine comes out only by force, for which reason it suffers pain and distress. And sometimes, from standing still and not being exercised, it generates very acrid humors, which, carried to the bladder, cause a biting sensation along the urinary passage, and for this reason it suffers strangury. Often, too, in winter, this arises from excessive cold. One must, therefore, for such

a horse, keep a fire burning nearby, and it will urinate. Know this too: that if a mule eats oleander, its bladder suffers a greater rupture, because the internal arteries called 'spinal,' which lie before the bladder, become paralyzed and chilled, and for this reason it ruptures and the animal dies. But this cannot happen to a horse, because its bodily constitution is warmer, and it digests its food quickly.

It happens that the belly suffers pain from indigestion, that is, when it passes whole undigested barley grains in its dung, or when even more of these remain within. For, filled up with drink, it suffers pain in the belly and writhes. Or when, in the fodder offered, a feather of soapwort happens to fall in while it is eating, this too brings on bloating and colic. There also occurs what they call a 'bouprestis' (blister-beetle), resembling a tarantula, which is born in fodder. If it takes this in while grazing, it will likewise swell up and be in danger. It also happens from bad water and unfamiliar surroundings.

Sometimes, too, if it has grubs or intestinal worms, it suffers pain in the belly for this reason. And from worms it is not so much in danger, since they are in the intestines and easily pass out; but from grubs it is, because of the roughness of the belly, since they are not easily purged out. You will recognize such a horse when it happens to throw itself down and bite the ground from the pain.
One must use this remedy: grind cabbage-leaves very fine, and, pouring on about four cotylae of wine and one of oil, drench through the left nostril,

and, grinding sulfur with oil, anoint the belly with it. Wormwood too is fitting for this, boiled in wine. It also helps to offer barley coated with oil, especially to the horse with intestinal worms. This too helps the dysuric horse: dissolve about an oxybaphon-measure of pellitory in a cotyla of wine, and drench.
Dissolve a bean's-weight of Syrian sap and a drachm's weight of roasted soda in wine, and drench, as written above.

Coax it and lead it to urinate, to a place where beasts have made a wet patch from their urine; and if it comes upon this, it will urinate very quickly. And if there is none nearby, one must lead it into mud, and it will urinate likewise.

This too has been found in the Georgics of Mago the Carthaginian. For he says that, scraping the underside of the dysuric horse's forefeet from the hoof-wall, one must grind the scrapings of the very hoof in about a cotyla of wine, and drench through the nostril, and it will urinate.

I have also learned this among the Sarmatians: one must stand the horse and drape a cloth over it from the neck to the hips, and fumigate castoreum on coals beneath the belly and the testicles, then, taking away the vessel in which it is fumigated, make the animal move about, and it will urinate very quickly. One must also make a suppository of salt and boiled honey, the size of an egg, and insert it into the anus. For this helps both the horse suffering abdominal pain and swollen, and the dysuric one; for it will make it urinate.

There are three kinds of urinary pain, and the name applied depends on which occurs. It is called 'dysuria' when the horse urinates with difficulty; 'strangury,' when it passes urine drop by drop; and 'ischuria,' when it cannot urinate at all. Of these, the first two are helped, as has been written. But the one that cannot urinate at all is not easily helped, and is in danger. And when sharp, acrid diuretics are administered, the affliction is aggravated, the passage becoming irritated. For such a horse, one must apply fomentations of hot water with a sponge around the so-called region, and use sweet drenches, mixed in hot water, equal parts of each, not more than two cotylae. Do the same with honey-water too, and drench likewise through the left nostril.

It is also fitting for such a horse to drench with a decoction of beet and mallow together with sweet wine, and to give green fodder; and if there is none, sprinkle the dry fodder with honey-water, and likewise offer the rest of the feed sprinkled as well. For, with such things offered, relief comes to the irritation, and the member is not raised. One must also sprinkle the barley, making it into a gruel, with honey-water, and give it thus. And if it should ever happen that a mare suffers dysuria, one must bring up to her a stallion as lustful as possible, and, being aroused, she will urinate very quickly. To sum up, this is my exposition and treatment of these afflictions for you.
Another, on preventing a beast of burden from developing strangury when crossing a
river.

When it happens, in winter, that beasts of burden on a journey come to a river with a great, deep current, so that their backs are submerged, one must unyoke them and make them urinate, and only then bring them in. For if this is not done, it readily happens that, in some of the waters, ischuria and colic occur.
By Hierocles, for the same.

There are three kinds of dysuria: dysuria proper, when it urinates with difficulty; strangury, when drop by drop; and the third, when it does not urinate at all. And the affliction arises when, journeying and running for a whole day, it fails to urinate. For then the passage leading from the bladder to the urethra becomes inflamed, and does not readily let the urine pass, from which the pain intensifies. And from standing for some time without exercise, acrid humors, carried to the bladder, corrode the passages of urination.

Sometimes strangury also arises from excessive cold in winter. For such a horse, then, a fire burning nearby helps. And a horse is not harmed by eating oleander in the same way as a donkey or mule, since its blood has a warmer constitution. You would see these same signs both in this horse and in one suffering abdominal pain. For the horse gripped by dysuria wants to run, and swishes its tail beneath its thighs, and, rolling about, sinks down onto its haunches, thrusting out its member little by little, giving the appearance of being about to urinate.
It is treated, then, thus: boil a bundle of leeks together with their
leaves, and pressing out the juice to about two cotylae,

and, mixing in a cotyla of fragrant wine and an oxybaphon of oil, drench through the right nostril. Then let it walk about gently, trotting, and it will urinate. Likewise boil wormwood in a cotyla of wine and drench. Or grind a finger's-breadth measure of opopanax in the aforesaid measure of wine, and drench. Or pound a cyathus of celery seed, and do likewise with a cotyla of fragrant wine. Better still, if you boil alexanders and give it, along with the roots of horse-fennel.
This too works: peel and bruise about five pungent long onions, and insert them into the anus. Then let it walk about, trotting, and it will urinate. Dousing the hips with hot water also helps.
Or thus: grind white or black chickpeas and boil them, then, pouring on water and adding two small bundles of wild thyme, and making up three cotylae, pour it in through the mouth.

Apsyrtus does not approve of those who insert their hands through the anus as though to correct the bladder; for as far as the anus, they do no harm, but pushing further in, they sometimes do some harm, since a severe inflammation arises in the intestine, so that the animal cannot bear the pain, and dies immediately or shortly after.

For there are three most acute afflictions in horses and other solid-hoofed animals: the bladder-ailment, and twisting of the intestines, which is called 'ileus,' and the cardiac ailment. The other afflictions persist for days. And barley-surfeit, choking, and abdominal

pain also are wont to kill a horse quickly, if help is not given swiftly. This too is useful for the dysuric horse: dissolve about an oxybaphon-measure of pepper in a cotyla of wine and drench, leading it into mud, or better, to where other beasts have urinated, and encourage it to urinate. Or boil ivy leaves in two cotylae of sweet white wine, and,
adding white soda, and, warming it and pouring it in through the left nostril, make it walk about.

Mago of Carthage says, in his Georgics, that, scraping the underside of the horse's forefeet from the hoof-wall, one must grind these very scrapings of the hoof in wine, and drench through the nostril, for it will urinate. This too is good, which the Sarmatians use: covering the horse from the neck to the hips with a cloth, they fumigate castoreum on coals beneath the belly and the testicles; then they make it walk about, and it urinates. And when it does not urinate at all, one must apply fomentations of hot water, and drench with sweet wine mixed in hot water, not more than two cotylae, and likewise drench with honey-water through the left nostril. Above all, drench with a decoction of beet and mallow together with sweet wine, and give green fodder; and if there is none, sprinkle the dry fodder with honey-water, and likewise the rest of the feed, making the barley into a gruel. For these will relax the animal. And when a mare is brought up to it, sometimes, being aroused, it urinates. One must, indeed, trust Ari-
stotle, who says that only the horse is subject to the affliction of dysuria.
Another.

Boil small bundles of cabbage with their leaves in a pint of water, then squeeze out the leaves and discard them, and, mixing the water in which the cabbage was boiled with half a pint of wine and one oxybaphon of oil, drench through the right nostril, and it will urinate.
Another.
Boil wormwood with one pound of wine, and drench through the nostril.
Another.
Mix a piece of opopanax the size of the last joint of the little finger with wine, and drench.
Another.
Grind radish seed, and give through the nostril.
Another.

Peel five long onions, being rather pungent, and insert them into the horse's anus, and make it walk about. It also helps, after this, to douse the animal's loins with hot water. Some are mistaken who say one must insert the hand into the intestine and twist its passage about; for they do the greatest harm by scratching it with their nails. If it urinates slowly, give it dog's dung mixed with salt, ammoniac gum, and wine.
Another.
Mix two peeled and ground garlic heads with wine, and drench, then make the horse run.
Another.
Grind the root of dwarf-elder, which the Greeks call 'chamaiakte,' with old wine, and press it out and strain it through linen,
and pour this in through both nostrils. Give also water to drink together with pennyroyal.
Another.

Boil the herb savin, and, from this itself while hot, douse the horse's genitals. And if it still urinates slowly, put a living bedbug into its ear, and crush another over the genitals, where it urinates from, and it will pass urine immediately.
Another.
Boil leeks and press out about one pint of the juice, and, mixing it with old wine and an oxybaphon of oil, drench through the nostril, and make it move about. Do this for three days.
Another.
Pour into the nostrils mud formed from the urine of any horse, mixed with wine and strained. And mud formed from such urine, even if it has dried, has the same effect when mixed with wine.
Another.
Grind celery root with somewhat sweet wine or honey-water, and drench through the mouth.
Another.

Two ounces of cassia, two ounces of costus, one ounce of spikenard, one ounce of cyperus, six ounces of Cretan hyssop, six ounces of Pontic wormwood, one ounce of myrrh; boil these in water, and drench for three days. This also works against expelling venomous creatures, against tetanus, coughing, and for stimulating the whole body. On the fourth day give oil, so that it may cleanse thoroughly.
Another.
Grind a spider, and drench with wine.
Another, against strangury.
Take four ounces of pig dung, one pint of wine, and, mixing them into one and straining, give it to drink, and it will urinate immediately.
Another.

One ounce of celandine, three ounces of lizard dung, six ounces of persea juice, three ounces of balm-of-Gilead sap, three ounces of aloe, four ounces of Attic honey, three ounces of male frankincense, three ounces of burnt quicklime, three ounces of white pepper, four ounces of reptile fat, two ounces of sheep's-trotter marrow, three ounces of goose-fat, three ounces of dove's blood; grind all these in a mortar, and give.
A preliminary drench for the same.

Grind three obols' weight of sweet-flag and an oxybaphon-measure of carrot seed with two cotylae of sweet wine, and pour it in through the nostril, and after this, by the customary encouragement, prompt the animal to urinate in a softer spot. The root of sweet-flag has the same effect, or its seed, ground and given with wine, or about an oxybaphon-measure of cultivated cucumber, and a bedbug put into the ear - into the left ear for a male, the right for a female. Pounded asparagus root, boiled in old wine and poured into the nostrils, also cures it;

or wheat-flour with sheep-fat, adding water and boiling it down to about two pints, and pour in through the mouth. Or mix four pints of cumin seed with old wine, and give through a horn for three days. Or about six cyathi of leek juice, and three cyathi of squill-vinegar, and an equal amount of honey, mixed, and give through a horn into the mouth; or opopanax,
five pints, mixed with wine and honey, for five days. Let it be fed on barley well soaked in water, and on cut fodder.
If the bladder becomes blocked, mix fennel juice and parsley and anise, and eggs and somewhat sweet wine with warmed water, and pour it into the bladder-passage, and it will open.
Another.
Grind the herb horsetail with wine, and drench; or anoint the belly with mud made from old urine.
Another, against those suffering strangury.
Mix one drachm each of roasted soda and Cyrenaic silphium-juice, and two dates, and, boiling well, give the decoction.
On tetanus and opisthotonos.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Numenius, son of Hephaestion, of Callipolis, greetings. I wish you, as a horse-keeper, to know that those who speak, among the diseases of horses, of 'tetanic' and 'opisthotonic' cases, have wished to wrap up what occurs under too many, over-elaborate names. Opisthotonos is that in which the horse has its neck held stretched out, and likewise its head, its ears erect and unable to bend, its eyes sunken, and the folds of skin near the nostrils are drawn back and laid bare, and its jaw-muscles are fettered, and its mouth cannot gape open, and its tongue is held fast, and it can neither eat nor drink alike. Its tail is drawn in, and its spine is stiff, and it cannot

turn, and, while walking, is unable to overstep with its hind legs, but drags its stretched-out hooves, nor does it bend its forelegs either, and it is drawn taut all over toward the rear, and it cannot shake itself, or only with difficulty, and it cannot walk uphill, but falls backward. It also happens to it, since the sinews in its back are stretched, that the bladder is sympathetically affected, and it excretes urine only by force.
And once fallen, it is unable to rise again on its hind legs, but sits up on its forelegs like a dog, whence it is also called 'opisthotonos' (backward-stretched).

It does not easily recover in winter, but one giving aid in summer might perhaps succeed. As they say, anoint it with pig-fat, and turpentine-resin, and wax, and ground pepper mixed with oil. Others, boiling vetch, douse the head with the water, and do the same with barley-water. Some dig a pit in dung and bury such a horse in it, or do the same in hot sand.

This too is said: pound ten peppercorns, an equal amount of parched barley, a drachm of soda, and a bean's-weight of Cyrenaic silphium-juice, each separately, and then together, and, mixing in half a cotyla of oil, drench with one cotyla of fragrant wine through the nostrils, twice a day. Also drench with fresh ox-blood, or, if this is not available, whatever kind can be found. Or dissolve three drachms of frankincense and an equal amount of salt in wine, and pour it in. This remedy improves

with age. They also say one must keep it moist, anointing with wine, oil, and soda, and rubbing it a great deal, and, sprinkling greasy fleeces with this, bind them on, and give wine mixed with soda in its drinking-water. These things, then, have been said by those great men before us.

We have also used these remedies: sixteen staters' weight of pig-fat, and an equal amount of bear-fat and goat-fat, four staters of turpentine-resin, eight staters of goose-fat, half a cotyla of cedar-oil, four cotylae of pure oil; melt these together, and knead into them wheat-flour pre-boiled in water, and eight staters each of soda and salt, and anoint with this warm. Also drench through the nostrils with pig-fat, honey, and oil, melted together. One must first melt the fat, and pour in the melted honey separately, and the oil, and, boiling it again together with wine, give it.

We have also used the emollient composed with bdellium-gum, dissolving it in oil over coals - better with henna-oil - with which one must anoint the head, the neck, and every part of the body, using massage, and, covering it with blankets, and bridling it, lead it to a sunny spot, exercising it at a canter, with someone mounted upon it, so as to make it sweat very much, and wipe off and rub down all the moisture against the grain of the hair, and, using this remedy, anoint it daily, and release it to pasture, until the affliction yields.

And use feed of every kind besides, especially mixing chickpeas into the barley, so that the jaw-muscles are kept in motion, but do not give beans, for the horse loses strength once it touches them; and give the drinking-water mixed with wine, and sprinkle in soda. Make the anointing of the remedy more generous, and, in winter, keep it standing in a warm, covered place. In mixing the wine with the oil, I have found the anointing to be inadvisable; for wine, being cooling, binds things further together. It is also beneficial to anoint it with pitch-oil, and exercise it likewise. Let the pitch not be much, however; for the pores become constricted, and it fails to sweat. In such cases one must not use bloodletting, and let no one say that those before us used it. For this escaped them: when the vessels at the temples are cut and bled, the sinewy tissue of the jaw-muscles dries out further, and is not kept in motion, and the horse remains without food. And those who use cauteries for such cases bring on exhaustion; for even if such a horse survives, it is less capable of service for the rest of its life.

Let us show, then, why and from what cause opisthotonos arises, which has not been written by anyone. When a horse becomes nail-pricked in the forefoot and is driven while lame and sweats, it falls into this affliction. And if, from a journey, it becomes sweaty in winter cold and stands out in the open on a stone pavement, this too causes it; and if, sweaty from a journey, it stands on frozen ground,

and goes without food, so that its jaw-muscles are not kept in motion that night, this too will befall it. And if it comes with a wrenched shoulder, and is laid up for a longer time, and, while being treated, sweats, the same affliction results. And if it is ever wounded, from whatever cause, at the groin, near that region, it too readily becomes opisthotonic. And, so that we may not seem to be rejecting the pronouncements of the great men before us, let tetanus too be counted among the signs described above. By Hierocles, for the same.
By Hierocles, for the same.

A horse is opisthotonic, or tetanic, when it has its neck stretched out, its head and ears erect, its eyes sunken, and the folds beside its nostrils are drawn back, and its jaw-muscles and mouth are compressed, and its tongue held fast, and it can neither eat nor drink. Likewise its spine is taut and stiff, and it is unable to turn, and, while walking, is unable to overstep with its hind legs, but drags its stretched-out hooves, nor does it bend its forelegs either, and it is drawn taut all over toward the rear, and does not shake itself, except with difficulty. This happens because the sinews are stretched taut; the bladder is also sympathetically affected, so that the urine is excreted only by force. And, once fallen, it cannot rise on its hind legs, but sits up like a dog. In winter, then, it is difficult to be saved from this affliction, but in summer, if
you should wish it, you might save it, by anointing it with pig-fat and turpentine-resin and ground pepper, dissolving these in oil. Some, boiling vetch, douse the head with the water.

Hieronymus, indeed, prescribes this: add oil to wax, resin, frankincense-manna, sulfur, and soda, and, melting it in a pot, judging the quantity so that it all fits, rub it in thoroughly, and foment the head with boiled vetch, or, failing that, barley; and cover the body with unwashed fleeces. Offer feed continuously, so that the jaw keeps constantly in motion, and give also raw chickpeas.

Apsyrtus approves these treatments: sixteen staters of pig-fat, four staters of turpentine-resin, eight staters of goose-fat, half a cotyla of cedar-oil, four cotylae of common oil; mix and boil these, and add to them flour pre-boiled in water, and eight staters each of soda and salt, and anoint with this warm; and drench through the nostrils with fat melted beforehand, then pouring in melted honey separately, and oil boiled together with wine, and give it.

As the treatment proceeds, we shall also use the emollient composed with bdellium-gum, dissolving it in plain oil over coals, or better with henna-oil.
