Then, having rubbed down the head, the neck, and every part of the body, one must cover it with blankets; then, having bridled it, have someone mount it and make it run in a sunny spot,

until it sweats sufficiently. Then, wiping off all the moisture, rub it down against the grain of the hair, and, anointing it again with the same remedy, let it graze; and let this be done daily, until the affliction yields. Offer also the rest of its feed of every kind, especially mixing chickpeas into the barley, so that the jaw-muscles are kept in motion - [lacuna] - and use these, applying and sprinkling them on. In winter let it stand covered in the warmest place. And let not too much resin be mixed in at that time, lest the pores become blocked and cut off the sweating.

The same Apsyrtus does not approve, in this affliction, of cutting the vein; for the sinewy tissue is dried out further by this. But he also says that it is not beneficial to use cauteries at times, and, even if the animal survives, it becomes much less capable for service. This affliction arises, for the most part, from causes such as these: when a horse, on a journey, stumbles on its forefoot, and is driven on lame and sweats. Or when, sweaty from a journey, it stands in the cold, out in the open, on a stone pavement. Or if, sweaty from a journey, it stands without food that night, so that its jaw-muscles are not kept in motion. Or if it is ever wounded, from whatever cause, in the groin, opisthotonos results.

Some have also used this method of help, when they perceive it at the outset of the affliction: bringing it into a bathhouse and making it sweat, they wipe it down inside with dry linens. And, taking it out a little while,

and bringing it in again, they wipe it down likewise; then, anointing it inside with a warm ointment of vinegar, soda, boiled must, eggs, and oil, and covering it with warm blankets, they lead it to the stable, and thereafter use the other remedies we have mentioned. And if you wish to make the stable warm, bring in coals well pre-kindled. For if smoke arises, it further afflicts the animal and destroys it. Best of all is also to give the fat of a freshly skinned goat, so that the fat is still warm.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

Tetanus arises in horses and other beasts of burden from nothing other than cold, when the solid parts suffer and undergo sinewy sympathetic affection. It is called 'tetanus' from the whole body being stretched taut, especially from the head, ears, and neck. It lives only so long as the heart is not chilled; once chilled, it will die.

I came to know this myself, when I spent [lacuna] days at Carnuntum in Pannonia, attending the emperor, and living with him as a friend. Suddenly, then, he was hastened away because of a wedding, and from Carnuntum, at the beginning of the month of February, he journeyed intensely toward Italy, so as to combine two or three overnight stops into one. When we had passed through the whole of Noricum, and then set foot upon the Alps called Julian, a great snowstorm suddenly broke about the first hour, as we were ascending the Alps. Then even the soldiers, upon their

horses, froze and perished, and remained stretched taut upon their horses. This was the sign that they had died: for, when the lips were drawn back, the teeth showed, and it happened that the horse was still alive. The horse carried the soldier's corpse and kept following along; the corpse still held both weapon and rein, and remained stretched, in a sense grown fast to the horse, so that it was a task for the living to bring it down. And if the horse too had died along with him, it stood frozen and remained standing. Many men, and horses, and mules suffered this fate.
Only those who were sent ahead of the emperor to the cities as day-runners neither died themselves, nor did their horses. The reason was clear: continuous motion warmed the cold and kept them alive.

And when, having come down, we stopped at our first town, having straightway plenty of firewood - for my host was most excellent, and provided smokeless wood - I stood my own horse alone in a small stable, and burned the wood around it in a circle, smokeless, though it was nearly dead. About the hour a cock crows, then, it began to stir. Having in my flask some spiced wine with lees, and since it could neither eat nor move its jaws, I soaked clean
bread in it and, as it lay there, drenched it a third time.

I had also prepared, for myself, an anodyne from simple remedies, for use in such wintry conditions, which, dissolving in henna-oil, I anointed onto the horse. It immediately began to sweat, and move, and eat. I shall now set forth its power and its composition.

With this you will treat every case of tetanus in horses and other beasts of burden, and drive off every effect of frost, and heal those that have been frozen, and restore to their natural state those that have become half-withered.
And, in general, no remedy warmer than this has ever been recorded by any physician or horse-doctor, nor will it be. It is this:

Two ounces of spurge-sap, four ounces of castoreum, six ounces of adarce, three ounces of bdellium-gum, one pound of pepper, two ounces of fox-fat, four ounces of opopanax, three ounces of laser-sap, six ounces of ammoniac incense, one ounce of old pig-fat, six ounces of dove-dung, two ounces of galbanum, five ounces of soda, three ounces of soda-froth, one pound of ladanum, one ounce of pellitory, three ounces of bay-berries, eight ounces of cardamom, six ounces of rue-seed, four ounces of chaste-tree seed, two ounces of parsley, five ounces of dried iris, three ounces of hyssop, three ounces of balsam-fruit, one pound of balm-of-Gilead sap, one pint of iris-oil, two pints of nard-oil, one pint of bay-oil, three pints of henna-oil, four pints of very old oil, one pint of pitch-smoke oil, one pound of turpentine-resin. Melt all the meltable ingredients separately, then put them together with the rest, and,

boiling it moderately, and straining into a vessel, use the remedy with wine, even in other cases of sinewy chilling and nerve-affliction. The longer it ages, the stronger it becomes. And if with time it becomes hard, dissolve it with henna-oil to the thickness of unguent, and use it. This also purges a congested head when given through the nostrils in a stronger dose.
By Hippocrates, for the same.

Three drachms of cassia, two drachms of trogline myrrh, one drachm of tragacanth; grind these fine, and put three drachms into each dose, together with egg-whites, one cotyla of oil, an equal amount of old wine, and two cotylae of honey, and drench for three days. Before it takes feed, give one cotyla of toasted vetch, or crushed vetch likewise.
Another.

If a horse is troubled by opisthotonos, it sits up like a dog, and its hind legs do not follow its forelegs. Bleed this horse, then, from the groin, and foment with hot water, then, mixing them, anoint with wine-and-oil and bay-berries. Let a fleece soaked in the same fomentation be placed on its head or its loins. Drench with three ounces of myrrh, one drachm of saffron, four cotylae of oil, and one pint of wine.
Another.
Add wax, ammoniac gum, Colophonian resin, galbanum, bdellium-gum, opopanax, lard, unfired sulfur, and enough deer-marrow, and drench.
Another.
If a horse becomes over-strained, it trembles all over its body, and, rising up, moves backward, then, standing

upright, trembles entirely and sweats. It is cured thus: one must open the veins in the chest, then those around the anus, and bathe it with much hot water, then anoint the body with wax-salve, and bed it down in a dark place, and make it rest in the stable. And when relief from its groaning comes, give it fodder to eat, sprinkling it with soda, and make it abstain from barley, until it is safely recovered.
Prognosis and cure of tetanus.

If a horse is gripped by tetanus, its head becomes fixed on the neck, and does not turn, except with difficulty, and the spinal veins are drawn taut, as in cases of gout, and the ears are thrown to the side, and the mouth is dry and without moisture, and the lips too. Warm, then, a cyathus of unmixed wine, and an equal amount of the remedy used against gout, and pour it into whichever nostril the breath is drawn through more strongly. And once you have poured it in, let it trot at once. And give it nothing that day except flour to drink, morning and evening, both breakfast and dinner.
Prognosis and cure of opisthotonos.

First, the horse's ears are held erect and taut, and its eye has a twisted appearance, and it cannot turn within a small space, but bends and turns its whole body about, and it does not carry its feet in a straight line, and its neck is stiff. If, then, its mouth closes shut first, it will perish from starvation. If, then, you get ahead of this, cauterize it, beginning from the eyes, burning around them in a circle, and on the neck three long lines, and on the flank
likewise, and on the spine long lines, and on the loins near the anus three on each side. Anoint

the wounds with sweet things, and foment with vinegar, and give the drench for seven days; and on the eighth day wash the sores with hot water, and treat with boxthorn-extract; make dressings of greasy wool, soaking them in honey.
Another, by Pelagonius, against opisthotonic horses.

The most diligent horse-keeper must, above all, guard against this affliction. For many have said differing things about opisthotonos, not knowing from what cause the affliction arises, nor even able to understand what its signs actually are. We, having sought with much labor and at great length the marks of such a disease, have found them. They are these: the neck stretched taut, unable to be arched; likewise the head; the ears standing stiff, unable to be bent; small eyes; the bones of the face showing; the skin taut

and hardened; the lips parched. Its mouth, too, is shut fast, unable either to open or gape, and it will not take food or drink; the tail, having become hardened, remains erect and unbending; it cannot look sideways; it sets down its steps in disorder; it thrusts its hind feet ahead of the forefeet so far as to scrape its hooves; it cannot bend its forefeet, and all its limbs are drawn taut in the hindquarters. It shakes itself either never, or only with difficulty, and, when forced forward, is drawn back into
itself. Such a horse urinates only with difficulty, and, once it has rolled about,
when it wishes to rise, rises with difficulty on its hind legs, and settles down onto its haunches, from which also the name 'opisthotonos' is derived.

You will treat such an affliction with difficulty in winter, but in summer, if you are willing, with the proper care, you will succeed. And first you will use these ointments: bind together pig-fat, turpentine-resin, and ground wax with oil, and use. Many, too, boiling vetch, douse the head with the water, and do the same with barley. Some also bury the ailing animal in dung, or in hot sand. They also make this preliminary drench: ten peppercorns, one ounce of soda, a bean's-weight of Cyrenaic silphium-juice; grind all these separately, then mix them, adding oil and two pints of the finest wine, and drench beforehand each day. Many also say this contributes, which has also come to us through experience:

Sixteen grammes of pig-fat, sixteen grammes of goat-fat, four grammes of turpentine-resin, six pints of cedar-oil, four pints of common oil; mix all these into water in which soda and salt have first been boiled. With this, as a warm remedy, we anoint the weakened animal, and through the nostrils we administer this treatment:
boiling enough pig-fat together with common oil and honey, and mixing them
together, we use it continually. Or, dissolving an emollient over live coals with common oil and henna-oil, we anoint from this the head, the neck, and the whole body.

After this treatment, cover it with blankets, and make it stand in the warm sun, and, having a rider mount it, exercise it at a canter, or at what is called the 'three-beat' gait, until it sweats, and wipe off the sweat with a linen cloth, and anoint its body with the aforesaid remedy, and thereafter let it graze, until it perceives the benefit of the treatment.
And thereafter offer it its usual feed too, mixing enough chickpeas into the barley, and wine into its drink.
In winter let it be stabled in a warm place, and let it be given warmer preliminary drenches.

It also contributes to be anointed with liquid pitch, and to be exercised in the manner described, in such a way, however, that the skin is not harmed by the pitch once sweat comes on. In the crisis of this affliction, bloodletting is useless.
Many also use cauteries; but even if the horse survives the cautery, it will be found useless from weakness, for it will not be able to endure travel.

I shall show, then, from what causes such a disease is brought on: when it walks on a rough road, and, journeying, goes lame in the forefoot from some cause, and is forced to keep walking and sweats, the symptoms of the aforementioned weakness necessarily follow.
And in winter, when, either from a long journey or from exercise, it stands out in the open, in the cold, or in a
colder or more damp place. And if, having suffered an injury to a joint, it lies down upon it after treatment for it, it will fall into this affliction.
By the same, for the same.

Before all else, one must cauterize; and the warmer preliminary drenches also contribute: laser-resin, or cumin, or garlic, or bay-berries; whichever of these is given daily with wine restores the animal to health.
If it occurs in the hindquarters, these will be the signs: it tangles its legs, and will have its shoulders and the vertebra up to the head cold, tearful eyes, and a cold tail.

One must use these remedies: cauterize the vertebra and the loins as far as the legs; after this, shut it into the warmest stable, and place live, smokeless coals there, so that more warmth may come to the place. Then, within the very same room, anoint with oil and salt for seven days. And when the scabs of the cauterized wounds fall off, wash with human urine, and douse with lukewarm water, and, instead of feed, offer leaves of the cultivated fig-tree with plenty of barley and wheat soaked in water. Let its drink be rather lukewarm.

If the aforesaid things are not to be found, knead wheat-flour with lukewarm water, and give it while it is fasting. Offer the drink in moderation, so that it thirsts all the more. It is better still if it also develops fever, since with the onset of fevers such an affliction is dissolved.

Afterward give whole beans; and if these cannot be found, at least barley-gruel. And if none of these helps, and necessity presses, then, finally, cauterize around the ears and the neck with alternating cauteries.
An ointment for the same.

Two pounds of bay-berries, one pound of liquid pitch, one ounce of all-heal root, six ounces of frankincense-powder, two pints of old wine; mix all these, and anoint in warm sunlight. And if this helps nothing, cauterize the head, and bind it round with a hide together with wool.
On diarrhea.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Ammonius, horse-doctor of Alexandria, greetings. I wrote to you before, more quickly, about barley-surfeit, but it is necessary for you to know about diarrhea too, which, when it becomes chronic in a horse, endangers the animal. One must treat it thus: sprinkle the barley with vinegar, and mix in wheat-chaff, or a small amount of tanner's sumac, or grind buckthorn leaves with barley-meal, and make morsels and give them. Or toast and grind cardamom-seed, and, dissolving it in a little water, drench through the mouth, in a small amount; give not much dry feed, nor much drink. Put into the water a little pounded mastic, or a small amount of tender bramble-shoots, so that it is not over-astringed; let it walk about a little.

Auxanon the horse-doctor said one must add Syrian sumac, and, toasting the barley, sprinkle it with vinegar little by little, as it is being toasted. For, he says, if you sprinkle it after toasting, the horse will not eat it because of the smell.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If diarrhea becomes chronic, it destroys the animal. Sprinkle the barley, then, with vinegar, mixing in wheat-chaff, and a small amount of tanner's sumac. Toast and grind cardamom-seed, and, dissolving it in a little water, drench through the mouth, in a small amount; give not much dry feed, nor much drink. Put into the water a little pounded mastic, or a small amount of bramble-shoots, so that it is not over-astringed. Let it walk about a little.
For the same: a cure.

If a horse or other beast of burden is troubled by diarrhea, take a choenix of barley-meal and a choenix of wheat, and toast and pound an equal amount of grape-pips, sift through a fine sieve, then mix them together, and, soaking them in two choes of clean water, give it to drink. And if it is unwilling, put it into a syringe and pour it into the mouth. Do not give barley, but chaff.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

You will treat the horse suffering from diarrhea by soaking the barley in vinegar, and mixing tanner's sumac into it, and offering it thus. You will also help it by grinding buckthorn leaves and kneading them with wheat-flour in water, and making pellets and giving them with vinegar-water. It is also fitting to pound tender mastic and bramble-shoots and put them into the water it drinks.
By Hippocrates, for the same.
Drench with sharp-dock seed together with dry wine. Or boil buckthorn leaves with dry wine, and do the same. Give also every kind of remedy that can astringe, and wheat
flour and barley-meal, giving them with wine, and you will help it.
Another: prognosis and cure.

When a horse is suffering from diarrhea, its belly discharges, and sweat comes upon it, and it breathes with difficulty. It is treated thus: grind very fine about a quarter-choenix of black myrtle-berries, add about two cotylae of garden purslane, and an equal amount of sweet wine, dissolving the myrtle-berries in these, and pour it in through the mouth. And if it is unwilling to drink, give it through a starch-paste, and offer toasted barley.
Hippocrates' drench for the same.

One pound of rose-and-pine resin, one ounce of tanner's sumac, an equal amount of Alexandrian galls, six ounces each of wormwood, southernwood, hyssop, and rue; mix these together, and drench with myrtle-wine.
Another.
Mix half an ounce of silphium with one pint of well-tempered wine, and drench.

Apsyrtus to Valens, decurion, greetings. You wrote to me asking what remedies there are against the twisting of the intestine. I want you to know, then, that those who push the hand further in do the very worst thing.

For, thinking that they can undo it with the hand - which is impossible - they instead produce inflammation and gas. It is helped by walking and by cantering, and one does not hinder it from rolling about; for it sometimes happens to become undone this way. They also drench through the mouth and nostrils with Cyrenaic silphium-juice together with sweet wine.

This happens to the large intestine, which is called the 'single intestine' (some call it the 'colon'), because it has no attachment to the rest of the intestines, but rolls about on its own; that is why it also produces a sound and a rumbling noise while walking and running. It shows these signs: while walking, it takes small steps with its forelegs, and brings its hind legs up close to them, and bends itself together in pain. The nature of the intestines is not the same in all horses. For some have intestines twenty-two feet long, and the thin ones sixty-two feet (some say fifty-two), and these are so from the time they are fully formed, while a younger horse has proportionally less by its age.

It happens that a twisting of the intestine occurs, and the animal is in danger. This is the sign: when it takes small steps with its forelegs, and brings its hind legs up close to them, unable to bend itself from the pain. This affliction occurs around the single intestine, which is called the colon, because it is not attached to the other intestines at either end, but rolls about on its own. That is why a noise is produced while running. Those, then, who push the hand in, as though to set it back in order, are mistaken. For they cannot accomplish this, and they produce inflammation and gas.

Let it be helped by walking and cantering, then let it roll about. For it sometimes happens to become undone this way. Let it be drenched through the mouth and nostrils with Cyrenaic silphium-juice together with
sweet wine. And once the intestine is torn, death follows quickly.
For it brings up its food and water through the nostrils, and, suddenly falling to the ground, dies.
A composition against pain of the intestines.

One pound of catmint, an equal amount of celery, six ounces each of bull-fat, rue, thyme, marjoram, pennyroyal, and Gallic silphium; boil these together until reduced by a third, and give as much as possible, so that it drinks.
Another.

If its intestines are in pain, you will treat it thus: wrap sufficient warm things around its belly and bind them tight, and make it move about. Also draw a sufficient amount of blood from the hind fetlocks, and bring it into a warm place, and douse it with hot water. Give also water boiled with wheat-flour to drink, adding two ounces of soda and one ounce of oil. Or take a grape-cluster from a vine and boil it with water and six ounces of oil, and put it into its mouth.
Another.

Four ounces of myrrh, one ounce of white pepper, one ounce of opopanax, two ounces of turpentine-resin, one pound of wax; put the pitch and the wax into a new pot, and melt them with vinegar; grind opopanax and storax, and pour them in, and, taking the pot off the fire, add galbanum and turpentine-resin, and softened bdellium-gum and bitumen, and use it together with ground ammoniac gum too.
On chordapsus (intestinal cramp/twisting).
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Asclepiades, son of Meidias, of Clazomenae, greetings. Since you keep horses, I wish you to know, regarding those who bring

up their feed again through the mouth and nostrils - the affliction being called 'chordapsus' - what remedies must be used: insert the hand and remove what has wedged the passages shut, and rinse through the nostril with water and soda, or with a decoction of beet with soda and oil. And bathe it with hot water along the back and hips, but do not bring it into cold water. Give it green fodder to eat, or boiled barley, and barley-flour, or ground spelt sprinkled with soda.

Make also an enema: cumin, marsh-mallow root or leaves, fenugreek, centaury, wild-cucumber root, cyclamen juice, soda, turpentine-resin, wormwood; boil the herbs, and to their decoction add the rest, and, mixing in rue-oil and butter, use it with a wider tube.
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Poseidonius of Tomis, greetings. Since you keep horses, I wish you to know, when the animal has an effusion,

it develops dropsy. You will recognize it by its having a large belly, swollen legs and testicles, and the elbows, or so-called 'knees,' of the forelegs swollen, a dry spine, and likewise the hips and flanks, and the 'lyres' (ribs) on each side of the back show bone-like ridges, and the veins in the head are indistinct, and those in the face, and likewise those under the tongue. When the swelling is touched by the hand, it yields and takes an impression. And when it lies down upon its belly, it does not remain so, but stretches itself out and lies flat, and, when rubbed, it sheds its hair.

It is treated with walks, increased gradually, little by little, mostly in the sun, covered with woolen blankets that induce sweat, and one must rub the whole body against the grain of the hair. Give as feed radishes and their leaves, and celery, and whatever is purgative and diuretic, and green fodder, if it is the season; if not, dry fodder, sprinkled with soda. Let the feed be especially lucerne, or offer fine chickpeas soaked in water a night and a day and then drained.

And if the affliction does not yield, one must puncture from the navel, or from the so-called 'pricking-line,' three fingers' breadth from the part toward the flank, and insert a small reed, through which the fluid drains off. And when it has drained off, it must be closed with clamps and treated as a wound.
Let the incision not be large, so that the omentum does not follow along with it. And once the wound has healed, make it run more, so that sweating may occur further.
Restrain it from drinking too much, so that the flanks do not become distended.

An effusion and dropsy sometimes occur in an animal, of which these are the signs: it has a large belly, and swollen legs (and apple-colored eyes, as some say), and swollen testicles, and the knees of the forelegs dry, and likewise the elbows, spine, and hip, and the bones of the ribs show, and the veins in the head and face are indistinct, and further those under the tongue too. When touched with the hand, the body yields and gives way under the fingers, and the hairs fall out when rubbed, and, when it lies down on
its belly, it stretches itself out and lies flat. These, then, are the signs.
Let it be treated thus: let it walk about in the sun, gradually, covered with a thick blanket, and let its whole

body be rubbed against the grain of the hair, and let it eat radishes and their leaves, and celery, and elm leaves, and whatever is purgative and diuretic, and green fodder; and if there is none, let it eat dry fodder sprinkled with soda, especially lucerne, or offer small chickpeas soaked for a day and a night, with the water drained off. And if the affliction does not yield, puncture it near the navel, four fingers' breadth
toward the tail, and insert a small bronze reed with side-holes, through which the fluid drains off. And when it has drained off, let it be closed with clamps and treated as a wound.

Let the incision not be large, so that the omentum does not follow along with it. And once the skin has scarred over, make it run more, so that sweating may occur further, and restrain it from drinking, so that the flanks do not become distended all at once.

And if it happens that the omentum does follow along, tie it off with linen thread right at the skin, and leave it bound, until it releases on its own. And if you recognize the affliction at its onset, it will suffice to use the other remedies without cutting near the navel.
Another, for the same.

If it has dropsy beneath the skin, hobble it and lay it down, and, three fingers' breadth from the navel, cut the skin open carefully. And when the fluid has been washed out, then treat the wound with sufficient remedies, cauterizing all around in a circle, keeping the cauteries apart from one another, so as never to touch the intestine, and, tilting it onto its side, let it drain off, and prick it with a fine needle.
Another.

If the animal is dropsical, it will be treated thus: give it a drink of three cyathi of mustard-seed, one cotyla of milk, and three cyathi of oil. And if this helps nothing, put two ounces each of wild-asparagus root, fennel, and celery into a small pot, and boil them together with eleven pints of old oil, so that they are reduced to one pint, and drench. Or grind six ounces of all-heal root, and give it to drink.
By Hierocles, for the same.
Boil dog's-tooth grass, and give it to fasting dropsical horses to drink. Or burn bull's dung and
mix in carrot seed, and, grinding it in water, drench.
By Pelagonius, on dropsy and tympanites (bloating).

It happens that a horse is quite often troubled by dropsy, and, this affliction becoming chronic, suffers from it. It is not recognized by everyone, however, and many are, for the most part, deceived in this regard. For they suppose horses with dropsy to have either an excess of flesh or a disturbance of wind. And indeed, in the case of spleen-afflicted horses, they mistakenly suppose the swelling of the belly to be a natural growth.

The signs of dropsy are these: the belly is inflamed with a hardness, the legs appear swollen, and such a horse, when driven, is unable to turn about, but, once warmed, is constricted in its breath, and walks with greater difficulty.
The spleen-afflicted horse, however, has its belly swelling imperceptibly, and, when exercised, sneezes continually, and moves its head this way and that from the pains.

In tympanitic horses there are other signs: the belly swells, the mane and the vertebra stand erect, and, for the most part, during the distension and inflammation of the intestines, it is torn apart in the passage of the dung.

For these, the remedies we point out prove beneficial: from the navel, toward the chest, two fingers' breadth in a straight line, not toward the flank, puncture, and insert a small reed, through which the humor may be dispersed, or the water that causes the dropsy. You ought to draw off about a four-pint quantity of the humor; and if it still swells, take out more. The animal must be kept

bandaged for as long as it took to become exhausted. Use diuretic preliminary drenches, and rub it down frequently, until sweat comes upon it too. Let its feed be green fodder, or soaked chickpeas, and let it drink from a river, since running water has been well aerated; or let it be anointed with the soaking-liquid of chickpeas, and, as it walks about, make its legs be bound with Calabrian wrappings. Some say it also contributes for such horses to walk about frequently near perfume-workshops, since the variety of scents imperceptibly benefits the lung.
A most suitable preliminary drench for such horses is also parsley ground with wine, or pomegranate pounded with wine. And let it eat as much celery as it can.
A preliminary drench against dropsy.

Make pastilles from honey and butter in a mortar with one cyathus of fine oil, and drench through the mouth with one and a half pints of wine. Or boil two ounces of wild-asparagus root with one and a half pints of old wine, until reduced by a third, and give through a horn; or grind half an ounce of all-heal root with wine, and drench. It also contributes for it to drink only a little, so that it thirsts more.
Against tympanitic horses, by Tiberius.

For tympanitic horses you will proceed thus: boil colocynth-shoots, and drench through the mouth. It is also necessary to drench radish juice through the nostrils, if the fruit is in season. It is better still if you use the seed of the aforesaid plants.
Another.

It is fitting for a tympanitic horse to have hot ash mixed with lard, spread onto a rag or linen cloth, applied to the belly, that is, the navel. It must be held in place by several men, lest, struggling against itself, it suffer injury. For the rest, one must grind all-heal root together with Gallic hartwort, mixed with wine and oil, warm it, and give it through a horn.
Another.

Put wild thyme, cumin seed, an oxybaphon of honey, a bean's-weight of laser-resin, and one cotyla of vinegar into three pints of water, and, grinding it, pour it in through the mouth. Let it abstain from feed during the night. And if this does not help, cauterize the left side, near the last rib, a length of about four fingers' breadth, not more than a finger's depth. Treat the cauterized place, as has been said.
On dysentery.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Chaireas Arion, horse-doctor of Alexandria, greetings. When a horse suffers from dysentery, an eversion and prolapse of the intestine near the anus occurs. One must treat this by cutting around it, and taking care not to cut anything of the sphincter itself. For otherwise it can no longer turn back inward, but remains open, and the intestine lying next to the anus falls out; and once this happens, the horse cannot live. After operating, one must drench with pomegranate-rinds boiled in vinegar-water, a cotyla's quantity, through the mouth, or, pounding and sifting a gall-nut, and
kneading it in vinegar-water, and making pellets, insert them through the
mouth, and offer ivy-leaves mixed into the barley. Let them be cut fine with a knife or something similar. This happens to a horse, but not as often as to a donkey or mule.

When a horse suffers from dysentery, an eversion and prolapse of the anus occurs. One must treat this, as Apsyrtus says, by cutting around the outer, as it were superfluous, part, and taking care not to cut anything of the sphincter. For otherwise the anus can no longer turn back inward, but remains open, and from this it dies. After it has been operated on, one must drench with pomegranate-rinds boiled in vinegar-water, through the mouth, or, pounding and sifting galls and kneading them with vinegar-water, and making them into a pellet, insert it through the mouth, and offer ivy-leaves mixed into the barley.
Let them be cut fine with a small knife or something similar. One must know that this happens less often to a horse, and most of all to a donkey and mule.
Another: a pastille against colic, dysentery, cramping, liver ailment, dysuria, spider-bites, and rabid-bites.

One ounce of saffron, two ounces of myrrh, four ounces of southernwood-flower, one ounce of parsley, four ounces of cultivated rue, two ounces of pellitory, two ounces of hyssop, one ounce of cassia. Pound and sift these, and bind with sharp vinegar, until the paste is worked through, and thus shape gramme-weight pastilles. Cool them in the shade, and, with the juice of

barley-gruel, grinding them, give to those with colic and dysentery. For those with cramping, dysuria, and liver ailment, give with two cotylae of hot water; for those stung by scorpions, bitten by spiders, or bitten by rabid animals, with unmixed wine.
On the spleen.

Apsyrtus to Euemeros, horse-doctor, greetings. You will recognize the spleen-afflicted horse by its having a large belly on the left side, harder than usual, and by breathing more heavily. It is treated with more frequent walks and gradual runs, so that sweating occurs, and by drenching through the left nostril with the pressed pulp of ben-nut, ground with vinegar-water, or with tamarisk-fruit pounded with vinegar-water, or with dwarf-olive ground with wine; let the whole quantity be a cotyla. Do this for several days. For this affliction is hard to cure. When giving it to drink, put soda into the water, and sprinkle its fodder and barley too. Some, however, put alum into the drink instead of soda. It is said by some that one should cauterize it; but this does not please us. For, the place being door-like (a natural cavity), the cautery-iron would run beneath it.
By Hierocles, for the same.

You will recognize the spleen-afflicted horse by its belly swelling on the left side and being harder, and by breathing more often, and eating much. One must treat it with more frequent walks and gradual runs, so that sweat is induced. And drench through the left nostril with ben-nut,
pressed and ground with vinegar-water, or with dwarf-olive ground with wine; let the whole be a cotyla. Do this too for several days. For this affliction is hard to cure.
When giving it to drink, put soda into the water, and sprinkle its fodder and barley too. Some, however, put alum into the drink instead of soda. Apsyrtus rejects the treatment by cauterization.
By Eumelus, against pain of the spleen.

Dissolve an oxybaphon of cumin seed, an equal amount of honey, a bean's-weight of laser-resin, and one cotyla of vinegar in three pints of water, from the evening before, and pour it in through the mouth, and let it abstain from feed during the night. And if this does not help, cauterize the left side, near the last cartilage, a length of about four fingers' breadth, not more than a finger's depth. Treat the sores from the cautery as has been said above.
Another, by Theomnestus, against spleen-afflicted horses, even if they have become hardened (indurated).

Boil the bark of caper root with eight and a half pints of water and one pint of vinegar, until it is reduced to a very small amount, and give it while the horse is fasting (with an empty stomach for good digestion).
Another.

Let it be bled from the shoulders, and abstain from barley, so that its body becomes leaner. Make also this preliminary drench: mix ground garlic, soda, and horehound with wormwood and dry wine, and drench through a horn, and make it walk about. In the morning let it be warmed with sponges and lukewarm water, and rubbed down with pressed hands. And if
the swelling of the belly persists, one must cauterize, after three days, measuring three fingers' breadth on each side, and taking great care not to burn a vein.
Prognosis and cure of the spleen.

If the affliction is around the spleen, the belly becomes large, and the horse groans greatly, and is in pain. If you wish to help it, take a glowing-hot cautery, and, keeping a palm's breadth away from the flank-ball, cauterize on both sides; the place is where we would give a heel-kick. Let the first burn, then, be at the aforesaid place, and apply a second, about three fingers' breadth away from the first. And when you have cauterized, as described, treat the sore with the aforesaid remedy.
On teredones (boring worms).
By Apsyrtus.

The class of teredones are worms that arise in the intestines and the belly, which, being passed with the dung, become entangled in the eversion of the sphincter, and cling there. These are the signs: it rubs its tail and anus against the manger and the walls. One must, then, insert the hand, and remove them, and sprinkle in ash from the hearth, when it passes dung. There is no danger in this.
It happens also that worms arise in the belly of deer, and, as they chew the cud, are brought up, and become
entangled in the gullet and remain there. And it does not stay in one place, but runs about. This animal has devised such a remedy for itself: it eats creeping creatures, and is cured in this way.
By Hierocles, for the same.

So-called teredones arise in the intestines and the belly. These are worms which, passed out with the dung, become entangled at the eversion of the anus. Its signs are rubbing the anus and tail against the manger and the walls. Let it be helped, then, by someone inserting the hand and removing them, and sprinkling in ash from the hearth, or fine salt.
Another. By Eumelus, for the same.

If it has teredones, that is, fine worms, it shivers all over its body, and has itching. Boil down thistle-root in water by a third, and, mixing in two ounces of opopanax and half a pint of wine, pour it in through the left nostril.
Another, by Theomnestus.

Teredones and 'wild-creatures' are white worms bred in the belly and intestines. Horses troubled by them show these signs: they rub their tail and sphincter against the walls. Their treatment is this: remove the visible ones with the hand, anointed with oil; then, once the animal is cleared, drench it with opopanax mixed with wine-and-oil. Then, pounding marjoram and fleawort, mix them with salt, and spread it onto a cake, and make it eat this. We forbid giving salt after using a horn (i.e., right after drenching).
Another, by Pelagonius.

It draws itself together with its whole body, and shivers frequently. Take, then, thistle-root, boil it and reduce it by a third, and, mixing this with two ounces of opopanax and one pint of wine, pour it in through the left nostril.
Another: prognosis and cure of teredones.
Suddenly rising, it runs, or sits, or, having lain down, gapes.
Take Cyprian garlic, or, failing that, a drachm's weight of earthworm-dung, and, grinding it in about a cotyla of vinegar, pour it into the nostrils.
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Statilius Stephanus, physician, greetings. You wrote to me asking how one must help horses that discharge blood through the anus and in their urine.
These are treated by drawing blood from the palate, and by a drench through the mouth of asphodel root ground with two cotylae of sweet white wine; and let the drench be liquid.
After this, boil clean wheat-flour with pig-fat and pomegranate-rind in water for a long time, so that the decoction is not thick, and pour it likewise into the mouth.
Take it about with vigorous walks and trots, and make the belly moister, giving it soda to drink and sprinkling the barley and fodder with it, and let it not become chilled.
And when it (blood) is being discharged through the nostrils, horses are helped by having the head doused with cold water containing a little salt. Let the water be as cold as possible.
By Hierocles, for the same.
Those horses that discharge blood through the anus and the urethra evidently need no other signs for recognition of the affliction, since they show, by the blood itself, what they suffer.
For these, the cure is this: let blood be drawn from the palate, and let it be drenched

with asphodel root ground with two cotylae of sweet wine; let the drench be liquid. After this, let clean wheat-flour with pig-fat, and pomegranate-rind boiled well in water, be drenched through the mouth, the drench not being thick. One must give it

vigorous walking, and sprinkle the barley and fodder with soda too, and take care that they do not become chilled. And when blood is discharged through the nostrils, one must douse the head with cold water containing a little salt. Use the coldest water available.
Another, by Anatolius, against those that pass blood in their urine.

Drench through the mouth, for three days, with cleaned boiled crushed vetch, mixed with deer-fat and a little wine. Or mix one cotyla of goat's milk, starch equal to the quantity of three eggs, and three ounces of oil, and drench through a horn.
By Pelagonius, against those that pass blood in their urine, or bring it up through the nostrils, or vomit it, or lose too much blood from phlebotomy.

Pelagonius to his own Arzygius, greetings. An excess of blood often harms even healthy horses. For it is clear that its overabundance bursts out from whatever place happens to give way; and, so that this may not befall horses, we shall be on our guard. Often, too, the urine of an overworked horse is found to contain blood; but this occurs in weaker horses, either from a long journey, or from a heavy burden, or from excessive fat. One must, then, treat it
thus: take blood from the belly (the ventral veins), and drench it beforehand with goat's milk, and starch, and three eggs, and the juice of the herb partridge-wort.
Do this in the case of horses that are excessively fat. But treat the lean ones without bloodletting; for the drawing of blood does not benefit them.
[apparatus reference marker "t"]
A preliminary drench against such afflictions.

You will use these preliminary drenches against such afflictions: half an ounce of tragacanth soaked in wine, four grammes of poppy-juice, an equal amount of storax, twelve pine-nuts; grind all these, and, making them the size of a Pontic nut, pour it in with one pint of wine through a horn, for seven days. This is also beneficial for humans, if you give a bean's-weight of it in an egg.
[apparatus reference marker "t"]
Another.
Pour leek juice with honeyed wine and egg down the throat, mixing in also a little myrrh-oil.
[apparatus reference marker "t"]
Another.

First take blood from the palate, then grind asphodel root in two pints of sweet wine, and take wheat-flour and sift it carefully, then boil Syrian sumac in water for a long time, and, mixing these together, pour it in through the mouth. Let it not walk about much. Before all else, wet its belly with water and soda, and likewise soak the barley.
[apparatus reference marker "t"]
Another.

If it discharges blood through the nostrils, this is dangerous. One must check it by blowing into the nostrils the juice of fresh coriander - [lacuna] - douse its head with the coldest water, mixing a little salt into the water.
Another, against those that vomit blood.
Boil wormwood and spikenard in a new bronze pot with water, and drench beforehand.
On obstruction (impaction).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Historicus, horse-doctor, greetings. When an obstruction occurs, these are the signs: it holds its tail stretched out, its nostrils distended, and strikes the ground with its foot, and sniffs at its dung, and sweats at the armpits, and trembling about the shoulders sometimes occurs, and, as though about to urinate, it relaxes its member, and rolls about. This happens when the intestine at the outlet from the belly becomes twisted, and what lies within it cannot pass out easily. It is treated by drenching with two cotylae of wine and oil, and by using more walking and green fodder, and by giving it soda to drink. Do not prevent it from rolling about. Such a horse survives only with difficulty.
By Hierocles, for the same.

An obstruction occurs when the intestine at the belly becomes twisted, and what lies within it has no way out, and it holds its groin-passage stretched taut, and its nostrils distended, and strikes the ground with its foot, and turns toward its belly, and sniffs at its dung, and sweats appear at the armpits, and trembling sometimes about the shoulders, and it shows signs of being about to urinate, and wishes to roll about. It is treated by drenching with two cotylae of wine and oil, and by using more walking. Or grind opopanax

together with celery in white wine, and, pouring on a quarter-measure of wine, drench through the left nostril. Let green fodder be given, and let it not be prevented from rolling about from the first day. Let it be drenched also with wheat-flour in lukewarm water.
Some, before the drench, approve of anointing the hand and inserting it through the anus to remove the nearby dung; and, when this is done, it urinates.
On hemorrhage (blood-flux at the back).

Apsyrtus to Aruntius of Corinth, greetings. You wrote to me asking whence it happens that horses and other beasts of burden bleed from the back. It happens when the season turns from dry to green fodder, in the spring, that the humor of the blood separates out and runs down beneath the hide of the back, and makes its exit through the surface, along the hair-line, which they call 'haimorrhois' (a bleeding). And once this occurs, the animal is purged and becomes robust. For this reason, one must not bleed such a horse from any place; for it

would be drawn back again from the outlet into the veins, and cause disease. One must, then, fatten it with feed, and especially with green fodder. For it then seems to make the flow and the discharge more abundant. In the care of such a horse, rubbing is inexpedient, since it closes up the pores. For if ever, once the effusion has occurred, an outlet does not follow, as described above, mange results.
By Hierocles, for the same.
We say that hemorrhage often happens from the

back in beasts of burden, when spring sets in. For the humor of the blood, gathering, runs down beneath the hide of the back, and makes its exit through the surface, along the hair-line, and some call this 'haimorrhois.' It is a purging of the animal, and it becomes more robust. For this reason one must not bleed it at all, from any place, for this. Otherwise, disease will arise in it. One must, then,

soothe it with feed, especially green fodder. For it seems then to make the flow and discharge more abundant. Wherefore let it be cared for, but not rubbed, so that the pores are not narrowed. And if a blockage occurs and no further blood is given off, but it is checked spontaneously, mange is wont to result quickly.
On colic (griping pain). Prognosis and cure.

A horse suffering from colic, first, paws with its foot and falls down, and rolls about, and, when standing, turns about, and turns its head to each flank, and sweats. Anointing the hand with oil, then, insert it into the anus - [lacuna]. Then, grinding especially centaury, about as much as three fingers can hold, and pouring on and warming a cyathus of wine and oil, pour it in, then let it be trotted. If not, use opopanax, or myrrh, or celery seed, or the moss from the Indians, or celandine, whichever of these you have. If not, having urinated, pour it in, and, rubbing with wine and oil and blowing in air, bathe it with warm water, and give it a raw solution to drink.
By Hierocles.
The remedy against colic is simple: break an egg
against its teeth, let it loosen, like lard, and you will cure it; or grind soda and, warming it with wine, drench.
Another, by Hippocrates.

A horse suffering from colic is recognized thus: it throws itself down here and there onto the ground repeatedly, and rises again, and drags its belly along the ground, and is convulsed and groans, and sweats at the testicles, and seems as though it were weeping, and stretches its tail, and moves from place to place, and breathes hot air, and its mouth is shut fast, and it has a quite dry, rough tongue, and its ears are drooping, and it nods off.
It is treated with a warm bath, and, being warmed with blankets, drenched through the mouth or the nostrils with five drachms of myrrh mixed in six cotylae of old wine.
After the drench, lead it out to run, not letting much time pass, nor making the run too strenuous.
Offer as feed a sufficient amount of celery, if it is available; give also warm water to drink, and, once the belly has emptied, make it trot again, so that it sweats.
Or drench cress-seed ground with water, through the left nostril, and wrap it in blankets, and give as feed the herb called lucerne.
Then grind scrapings of the front hooves in four cotylae of water, and drench; or use ground earth from a shrew's burrow.
Another, by Anatolius.
You will cure a horse with colic by bathing it with hot water, and

covering it with cloths; then strain together five drachms of myrrh, six cotylae of old wine, and three cotylae of oil, and drench for three days. Also rinse the belly with hot seawater, in which myrtle-berries have been boiled. Or drench with hoary-leaved sage and southernwood, or bitter almonds and dry dark wine mixed together, or pomegranate-rind with water.
Or grind soda and, warming it with wine, do the same.
Another.
Break four eggs into its mouth, and make the animal swallow them, shells and all.
Another: if the colic becomes severe and the belly does not move.
When the horse tucks its tail between its legs and bends over onto its own belly, drench it beforehand with wild-rue seed and half a pint of wine.
Another.
Grind ten onions, or nine grammes of dried figs, one gramme of soda, four grammes of dove-dung; mix all these, and, making two or three suppository-pellets, insert them into its anus.
Another.
Put warm myrrh-oil with oil and a little honey down the throat, and, if necessity requires, insert the hand through the anus and remove the dung.
Another.

One heaping spoonful of clean cumin, half a spoonful of rue-seed, a bean's-weight of opopanax, half a bean's-weight of laser-resin, one Italian pint of old wine, and enough unripe-olive oil; give to the animal for three days. Let it not eat barley.

A horse with colic is recognized thus: it rolls about continually, and its belly is distended with gas, and, once lying down, it groans and turns this way and that, and its intestines rumble. Treat it, then, thus: foment it and knead it by hand, blowing in wine and warm oil all over, and drench with storax and wine and oil and birthwort, or leek juice with wine and oil. Give it an enema of wine-and-oil, and, anointing the hand with oil, insert it into the anus and remove the nearby dung. Also gently rub the bladder area, and give it vetch or oats to eat, mixed with the vetch, and give it warm water to drink.
On kenopresis (empty-bloating).

By Apsyrtus. To Quintus Lollius Maryllius, greetings. It is useful for you, as a horse-keeper, to know the signs of kenopresis, and why it occurs. It arises for this reason: when the horse is overcome by dry feed, which, though it is itself digested, brings on difficult breathing and bloating; and from this, the flanks become stretched taut, and, when it passes dung, its belly is harder, and it discharges only a little, and the anus is distended with gas. It is called 'kenopresis,' but by some 'wind in the lyre' (ribcage); these have found that one must bore through the middle bone of the 'lyre' with a fine drill; others say one must give it an enema, pressing out wild-cucumber root juice into three cotylae, and mixing an equal amount of wine, and using it with a cotyla of oil.
We have also used these remedies:

a handful of dove-dung or that of domestic fowl, dissolved in wine and soda, we have given as an enema. And we have soaked its feed in wine and given it, and also put wine into its drinking-water, and we have advised that it not be over-exerted. Let it walk about a little, and let it be rubbed with wine and oil against the grain of the hair, not roughly. Bloodletting is also fitting, done at the root of the tail, four fingers' breadth from the anus.

Others become bloated with wind, whose nostrils are spread wide open, and they breathe with difficulty, and, while breathing, their belly and ribs collapse; these too are overcome by dry feed. They are treated by inducing thirst, and by being given green fodder.
Another, for the same, by Hierocles.

Kenopresis occurs when the horse is overcome by dry feed, which harms it and causes difficult breathing, and swells the flanks especially, and the belly is held distended, being harder, and it passes only a little dung, the anus being distended with gas. Some have called this affliction 'wind in the lyre.' It is fitting, then, to pound wild-cucumber root, and make its juice up to three cotylae, and an equal amount of fragrant wine, and a cotyla of oil, and eight drachms of soda; mix and bind these, and give as an enema.
Apsyrtus, however, approves these: dissolve a handful of dove-dung or domestic-fowl dung in wine and soda, and give as an enema, and sometimes sprinkle the feed with soda, and put it into

the drinking-water too. Let it walk about a little, and let it be rubbed with oil and wine against the grain of the hair. And if necessary, open a vein too. You will open it, as Apsyrtus says, at the root of the tail, four fingers' breadth from the anus. There is also another, simpler kind of bloating, when the horse spreads its nostrils wide, but, while breathing, its belly and ribs collapse.
These must be kept from drinking too much, offering them green fodder instead.
On a wound (incision) of the chest.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Antipater, horse-doctor of Alexandria, greetings. If it ever happens that a wound occurs in the small chest from iron, or from some other cause, treat it thus: apply not-thin linen or hempen loops on either side of the wound, into the hide, as many as are sufficient, and, making dressings of wool soaked in wine and oil, insert them, and thus bind it, drawing it together with the loops. And, untying it on the third day, douse it with as much hot water as possible, and do the same daily, dousing further for four more days. And when these have passed, untie the loops, and sprinkle on vetch-meal, soaking it in water, cold in winter and warm in summer. And once it is thoroughly cleansed, anoint it with the fatty ointment, and it will be well.

Sometimes it happens that gas-swellings arise throughout the horse's whole body beneath the hide, so that one might suppose there to be an internal inflammation. Therefore one must, in the chest, cut into the

hide, at three places apart from each other, in a circumference twice the size of a thumb-nail, and thus the gas-swellings will pass through, and there will be no danger. But if a wound occurs clean through at that place, do not treat it. For the horse cannot live, since the heart lies nearby and would suffer chilling.

If it ever happens that a wound occurs in the small chest from iron, or from some other cause, let it be treated thus: insert not-thin loops on either side of the wound, taking hold of the hide, as many as are sufficient, and, making dressings of wool soaked in wine-and-oil, insert them, and bind it thus, drawing it together with the loops. And, untying it on the third day, douse it with hot water, and do the same daily, dousing further for four more days. And when these have passed, untie the loops, and apply a poultice of vetch-meal, soaking it in hot water, until it is thoroughly cleansed.

Then anoint it with the fatty ointment, and it will be well. If, however, the wound at that place occurs clean through, the horse could not live, since the heart lies nearby and would receive chilling through the wound.
On prolapse of the penis.

Apsyrtus to Numenius of Alexandria, greetings. If a prolapsed penis cannot be restored again into its place, some prescribe making the horse swim against the current in a river, or in the sea. Others, laying it down and hoisting up its legs, rub it further with wax-salve mixed with pig-fat and

fine soda, and douse it with much cold water, and thus restore it into its place; it is better still if the water is seawater; if not, sprinkle salt into the water. We have also used this: with the horse standing, we lightly prick with a fine needle the skin around the shaft, and sprinkle sharp vinegar onto the pricks, and thus it returns to its natural position. Nettles rubbed on do the same thing. Pricking the anus and the perineal area with the needle also restores it to its place.

If a prolapsed penis cannot be restored to its position, let the horse be made to swim against the current in a river, or in the sea. Some, laying it down and hoisting up its legs, rub it further with wax mixed with goat-fat, and fine soda, and douse it with much cold water; it is better still if the water is seawater; if not, they put salt into the water.
Mix frankincense, egg, and cumin with wine, and drench. Or mix pig dung with vinegar and strain it, or grind two grammes of all-heal root with wine, and do the same.
Or mix wild-rue root with cabbage juice, and apply as a drench. This also works against colic.
Another.

Mix oil with wine, and pour it onto the loins. And if this does not help, make a very fine suppository from boiled honey and salt, and insert it into the opening from which the urine passes. Or insert a live fly, or a crumb of frankincense, or a suppository of bitumen, or a piece of garlic, in the same way as we have described.
On inflammation and swelling of the testicles.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Memnon, horse-doctor, greetings. It is necessary for you, as a horse-keeper, to know that they treat inflammations of the testicles arising from a wound, or from the bite of some beast, or when horses fight fiercely with one another, thus: bruise wild-cucumber root, and boil it in water and salt, and foment with a sponge soaked in it, and grind white-lead, oil, goat-fat, and egg-white, and anoint, and they heal it. And when the inflammation arises from some other cause, and not from a wound, one must help thus: douse further with hot water twice a day, and, sprinkling salt into the water, anoint with Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar, or likewise with potter's clay, or with fresh wormwood pounded to a juice, or with hemlock growing in dung-heaps, or with nightshade juice. Likewise, ground white-lead mixed with water is also fitting for anointing.
By Hierocles, for the same.
If the testicles swell, let them be doused with hot water,

a little soda mixed in, and let them be anointed with an application of vinegar. And if it does not respond to this treatment, let blood be drawn from the legs near the testicles. And if it still does not stop this way, let it be cauterized down the middle, taking care not to touch the testicles themselves.

Anoint inflammations of the testicles with potter's clay kneaded with vinegar, or with nightshade boiled with vinegar. Bleed it from the groin, and give it cold water to drink. And if it does not stop, foment with warm children's urine, placing beneath it heated millstone-pebbles, until the thighs sweat from the stones. Douse also with hot water, and anoint with iris-oil, and make it walk about.
Grind Cretan clay with cow-dung, cumin, and vinegar-water, and anoint until it is cured.
Against those discharging pus from the genitals.
Boil a cockerel and a puppy together with water, then strain the water, and, adding a drachm of ground bitumen, drench beforehand for nine days.

Apsyrtus to Dius, horse-doctor, fellow-citizen, greetings. You wrote to me about intestinal hernia. If, then, this happens to a horse - which is especially wont to occur in older animals - one must press together the scrotum, that is, the so-called 'pouch,' and, according to where the weight has settled, insert a loop and bind it firmly, and soak it with vinegar and soda. And if the loop rots away, one must wash
the thighs and the sore with cold water, and treat it with a gentle remedy.
Let the place also be supported with a truss, and it will be healed.

If intestinal hernia occurs, which happens especially in older horses, involving the large intestine, one must press together the scrotum, that is, the so-called 'pouch,' and, according to where the weight has settled, insert a loop and bind it as firmly as possible, and soak it with vinegar and soda. And if the loop rots away, douse the thighs and the sore with cold water, and treat with a gentle remedy. Let the place also be supported with a truss, and it will be healed.
On rheumatism (flux) in the knee.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Sisenna, centurion, greetings. Since you are earnest about horses, it is necessary for you to know this too: that fluxes settling into the knees, which in Latin are called 'phlemina,' must not be incised. For the knee becomes wrinkled from the scar. Those who use cauteries do worse still; for they bring on the flux even more, by sealing up the place.

It is treated thus: pull sea-sponge-balls (cast up by the sea) apart into fine shreds, and mix in Cimolian earth, and, soaking them in water for five days, apply as a poultice and bind for up to two days. On the third day, untie it and do the same again; for this draws out the humor. Or mix ash from a forge, spread out over the furnace, with boiled honey, and spread it onto a rag and bind it on. Or
mix barley-flour with water and do the same. Or pound wild-fig and bind it on, and lead the horse into cold water. And the dry
emollient too is beneficial for these cases. Use these remedies for as long as the humor is still liquid.
And when it congeals and passes into the inner part of the knee, a hard knot (strangulation) forms. One must treat this,
as has been said, with the dry emollient, until it descends and becomes a swelling by the pastern. Best of all for this is also the lard-based

emollient. There is also this kind of flux: when the horse has swollen, large legs, especially the hind ones, which, if bled, only bring on a greater excess. It is beneficial to use walks and gentle runs, and to lead it into cold water.

A flux settles in the knee. In Latin they call it 'phlimelium.' One must not incise this, for the hoof becomes wrinkled thereby, nor cauterize it either; for they only bring on the flow of the flux more, by sealing up the place. It is treated thus: pull apart sea-sponge-balls (cast up by the sea) into fine shreds; one must mix in Cimolian earth, and soak them in water for five days, then apply as a poultice and bind for two days, and on the third day untie it and do the same again, for the humor will be drawn out. Or

mix ash from a forge, spread out over the furnace, with boiled honey, and spread it onto a rag and bind it on. Or mix barley-flour with water and do the same. Or pound wild-fig and, mixing it likewise, bind it on. The dry

emollient too is beneficial. Use these remedies for as long as the humor is still liquid; and when it congeals and passes into the inner part and becomes a hard knot, one must treat it, as described above, with the dry emollient, until it descends and becomes a swelling by the pastern. Useful for these cases too is the lard-based emollient, and it is beneficial to use walks and gentle runs, and it is advantageous to lead the horse into cold water.
How inflammations in the knees may be dispersed.
Mix three ounces each of oleander, bitumen, soda, and old lard, and, making a remedy, use it.
This affliction occurs in winter, but in summer it is restored and healed. Such horses do not readily fall into the affliction of

Apsyrtus to Apollonias, horse-doctor, greetings. Fluxes settle into the feet, which some call 'seirai' (cords), others 'cheiramata' (chapped sores); from this the feet are said to 'suffer seiriasis' (in Latin called 'suffragina'). It is treated thus: draw blood from the feet themselves, cutting the vein at the pastern, on the outer or likewise the inner side, but not at the root of the hoof. Scrape from underneath and pare, so that the affected material falls away from there, and wipe clean with wine, and grind the juice of tawny acacia with water, and, making it the thickness of honey, anoint. Or grind pig-fat with liquid pitch, and do the same. Let it walk about, but do not lead it into water.

the arthritic form of glanders; nor do gelded horses become subject to fluxes either. Beneficial and immediate remedies are these: knead vetch-flour with wine or honey, and apply as a poultice, and bind it on. Do the same likewise with crushed vetch, kneading pig dung with wine. Boil and grind pomegranate-rind with wine, and apply as a poultice, and bind it on. The gall-nut too is beneficial,
when pounded and applied as a poultice. This too is useful: boil olive-lees and dry wine, and foment; or boil asphodel root in water and do the same, or grind salt, oil, and honey together.

There are three kinds of flux in the feet. One is the one described above. Another raises the hoof upward; in this case one must especially scrape from underneath, so that the hoof does not suffer chafing. The third is when the hoof cracks apart. This happens when the horse is advanced in age. Also subject to fluxes are those in whose mouth saliva collects, especially in older horses, when they take the barley, so as even to moisten it; and these live longer. It also happens to younger horses, but not so much or as continually as to older ones.
Another: prognosis and cure of flux.

First, the knees swell, and it goes lame and cannot put weight on them, but, when you press with the hand, it stands up straight. If, then, it is in the hind legs, cauterize it with round cauteries, on the inside with five burns at the hock, and on the outside with broad ones on both sides. And if it is in the
forelegs, below the knee, cauterize it in the woven-cord pattern, and tend to it as with the other cauterizations.

A horse has fluxes that settle into the feet, which some call 'seirai' (cords), others 'cheiramata' (chapped places); hence they say the horse 'suffers seiriasis,' as Apsyrtus also says. It is treated thus: let blood be drawn from the feet, cutting the vein at the pastern, on the outer side or the inner; but take care not to cut at the root of the hoof. Let it be scraped from below and pared. Let it be wiped clean with wine, then, grinding the juice of tawny acacia with water and making it the thickness of honey, anoint it. Do the same also with liquid pitch and pig-fat. And lead it about walking, but do not lead it into water.

This affliction occurs in winter, but in summer it settles down and heals. Gelded horses, however, do not readily become subject to fluxes, nor do they fall into the arthritic form of glanders-disease. Apsyrtus gives these immediate remedies too: knead vetch-flour with wine and honey, and apply as a poultice and bind it on. Crushed-vetch flour and pig dung do the same. (One may recognize the flux, when the horse has swollen, large legs, especially the hind ones, which, if bled, bring on a greater excess.)
Knead pomegranate-rind with wine and boil it in water, and apply as a poultice. The gall-nut, pounded and applied as a poultice, is also beneficial. Useful too is
this: boil olive-lees and dry wine, and foment with it. Or boil asphodel root in water and do the same, or grind salt, oil, and honey together.

There are three kinds of this affliction. One is the one described above; another raises the hoof upward, in which case one must especially scrape away the lower part, so that the hoof does not suffer chafing. The third is when the hoof cracks apart. This happens in horses advanced in age.

Also subject to fluxes are those from whose mouth saliva drips, so that, when they take the barley, they moisten it. This happens especially and more continually to older horses, who also live longer. It happens to younger ones too, but not so continually.
Another: by Eumelus, against fluxes in the legs.

Such afflictions must be treated by cauterizing with a heated iron. You will heal the wounds from the cautery by soaking a sponge in vinegar and laser-resin and applying it, and, on the following day, inserting a pessary that draws out the mucus-like discharge. The composition of the pessary is this: mix ammoniac gum with an equal amount of very sharp vinegar, grind it, and dry it in the sun, and make pessaries.
Another: for treating fresh fluxes without iron

Two pounds of roasted-barley groats, six ounces of galbanum, four pounds of turpentine-resin, four cyathi of the richer frankincense-meal, six ounces of soda, one pint of salt; mix and grind these, and, adding vinegar, bring it to a boil, and, spreading it hot onto a rag, in the manner of an
emollient-poultice, apply it to the knees for three days. Warming it daily, refresh it, and apply it thus.
Or mix one pound of Judaean bitumen, one pound of mustard-seed, and one pound of oleander with lard, and spread it as a poultice onto the knees.
Or apply wild mint root, vetch, and old lard, ground together with sharp vinegar.
Or mix six ounces of Alexandrian mustard, six ounces of cress, six ounces of African dried figs, two ounces of salt, one pound of old lard, and enough vinegar; use all together.
Grind salt with honey and use it.

Mix a caustic in cold water, and cleanse the wound with it, then apply a sponge soaked in vinegar for four days. On the fifth day, knead barley-flour with water, and apply it, until the wound forms a scar; and from then on, pound pomegranate-rind with lycium, and apply it to the open place.

One ounce of warm ash, one ounce of quicklime, kneaded with wine and honey; taking care that it does not dry out first, anoint the wound with it thus. Continue treating it this way, if the hard knots are fresh; but if they are old, cauterize it skillfully and treat it, as with the rest. This condition arises from exertion, when a horse is driven hard on dry ground or over stony ground, or travels bearing a heavy load on its back.
Strain and mix three ounces each of oleander, bitumen, soda, and lard, and, making a remedy from these, anoint it.
Another, against pain of the sinews and watery swellings (hydatids).

Abscesses arising from a gathering (of humor) must be opened with iron, then treated thus: three ounces each of bull-fat, galbanum, bdellium, white pepper, and ammoniac gum, four ounces of frankincense-meal, one ounce of bay-berries; mix these and make a remedy, by which every wound is wont to be treated.

You will also treat it thus: knead ash of cyclamen root with vetch-flour, honey, and vinegar, and apply to the wound. And if the wounds are deeper, mix red ochre with honey, and fill the wound with small dressings soaked in it, then apply a cloth or sponge with vinegar-water over it. Many also apply crushed gall-nuts, or horehound juice mixed with soot.
Another: to treat 'phlemina' (knee-flux) without iron.

Four grammes each of mustard and Alexandrian salt, one ounce of cress, two grammes of vinegar, one and a half pounds of old lard; grind all these, and spread them onto a linen cloth, and apply for three days. And after this, untie it and wipe it with a sponge sprinkled with Cyrenaic laser-resin, and thus you will open the scabs.
Another: if the fetlocks (ankles) become inflamed.
Burn hay-chaff and apply it with cold vinegar-water, until the inflammation is quenched. And after this, grind garlic, and apply it to the fetlocks. This is most highly approved.
Another, against slackened joints and watery swellings (hydatids).

For the horse: aloe, myrrh, frankincense-manna, and Brittany pitch - grind all these together, and add wheat-flour, mixing in also egg-white; then take it up and apply it to the joints, binding it carefully with paper, and, after some days, untie it, and treat again, applying the same remedy.
Another, for treating inflamed hollows of the knee (hamstrings).
Melt equal weights of wax, bitumen, and unfired sulfur over the fire, and, while they are still hot, anoint the hollow of the knee. Apply also bran with vinegar.
Another.

If a horse has thickened sinews or hard knots at its joints or feet, it is necessary to cauterize such places. And if the arrangement of the joints has also slipped out of place, then, of necessity, it is fitting also to draw off blood, and to rub the limbs themselves gently. You will also use this treatment: take up vinegar-oil in wool, and apply it to the joints for four days. Let this treatment be applied daily in this way. After this, the joints must be strengthened with a warm remedy. The preparation of the remedy is this: one pound of cleaned mustard, three ounces of galbanum, three ounces of deer-marrow, and enough vinegar.
Another.

If a flux settles into the feet of the horse, its knees swell, and it goes lame. If, then, it is in the hind legs, cauterize it with round cauteries, on the inside at the hock with five burns, and on the outside with broad ones on both sides. And if it is in
the forelegs, below the knee, cauterize it in the woven-cord pattern, and tend it as with the other cauterizations.
Against thickening of the sinews.
Mix fenugreek with pounded African figs and wine, store it, and untie it after three days.
Another.

If inflammation occurs about the legs or knees from a long journey or much running, it helps to douse the inflamed parts with cold water, or to lead the horse into a river or stream and make it pace about there; then apply a sponge with laser-resin, vinegar, mistletoe-glue, boiled-down wine, and lard.

Apsyrtus to Julius Faustus, decurion, greetings. It is useful for you, as a stock-breeder, to know this: that there occurs in the feet, especially the forefeet, at the growth-point of the hoof, which they call the 'crown,' hard swellings ('marmara') with hardened, callused knots. In these the horses continue to go lame, in winter because of the mud, in summer because of the dryness, and they wear down and grind their feet, and are continually overheated. This happens when, from travel and rough roads, overheating occurs, and the humors

run down into the ligament binding the pastern-joint. This happens likewise to those affected around the fetlocks and the sinews, because the veins in the 'dog' (pastern-cushion) become inflamed. In such cases one must not use bloodletting from those places. For, being pricked, they bring on more callus and inflammation instead.

It is more beneficial in use to have the emollient compounded for sprains. This affliction happens only to the mule; it is not common in the donkey, and the horse does not develop 'marmarosis' (hard knee-swelling), but rather podagra (gout-like lameness).
By Hierocles, for the same.

Experienced practitioners call a certain affliction 'marmaros' (hard swelling). It occurs especially in the forefeet, [lacuna] of the hoof, which is called the 'crown.' There are hard knots, so that the horse goes completely lame - in winter because of the mud, in summer because of the dryness - and it wears down its feet continually. This happens when, from travel and rough roads, overheating occurs, and the humors run together into the ligament of the sinews at the pastern-joint. This happens likewise to those affected around the fetlocks and the sinews. In such cases, then, one must not treat by drawing off

blood. For, when such places are pricked, callus and inflammation are brought on all the more. It is better, then, to use the emollient compounded for sprains. This happens to the mule, and rarely to the donkey; the horse does not fall subject to this affliction.
Another.
Grind together one pound each of African figs, quicklime, and old lard, and three cyathi of hyssop-flower, and apply.
On podagra (gout / foot-pain).
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Artemas of Tomis, greetings. It is useful for you, as a horse-keeper, to know that, if a horse falls into podagra, it can neither stand nor walk about, but lies down like a horse

foundered on barley, and has no appetite for anything offered to it, and its mouth is hot and quite dry, and its palate is swollen, and its testicles twitch alternately, one at a time, and its member hangs down and is drawn up, and its feet, in standing, gather up dung from the heat, as also happens when it paws the ground.

It is treated by preventing it from lying down, and by driving it about gently under shelter until it sweats, and by rubbing the body, and by drawing a small amount of blood from the palate, and again, after seven days, from the hind legs below the hocks near the pastern-joints, likewise not in great flow, and also from the forelegs. Give it warm water to drink mixed with soda and clean wheat-flour. There is also this remedy: dissolve a handful of iris root and an oxybaphon of frankincense-manna in wine, and pour it through the nostrils, a cotyla's worth daily for up to three days; and pound elm-bark in a mortar, and, rinsing it in wine, pour it in likewise.
This too is excellent: boil beets in water, and, mixing three cyathi of oil into three cotylae of the pressed-out decoction, pour it in likewise, and exercise the horse.

We have used all these remedies. But we are most pleased to make use of purging in this case. For, when the whole body is well disposed, it will result that the fluxes into the feet are lessened. After the purging, dissolve an oxybaphon of iris-root in sweet, fragrant wine, up to a cotyla's worth, and pour it into the
nostrils, and offer green fodder; and if there is none, sprinkle the dry fodder with soda - green fodder is better. And if the affliction does not stop, cut out the testicles, and it becomes healthy.

Podagra is wont to trouble a horse. It can then neither stand nor walk, but lies down like horses foundered on barley, and has no appetite for feed, and its mouth is hot and quite dry, and its palate is swollen, and its testicles twitch alternately, one at a time, and its member hangs down and is drawn up, and its feet, in standing, gather up dung from the heat, and the veins run down from the back along the mane.

One must treat it by not allowing it to lie down, but by driving it about gently until it sweats, and rubbing the body, and drawing not much blood from the palate; and after seven days, likewise draw not much blood from the hind legs below the hocks near the pastern-joints, and from the forelegs in the same way. Give it warm water to drink mixed with soda and clean wheat-flour. Some think this also useful: dissolve a handful of iris-root and an oxybaphon of frankincense-manna in wine, and pour it into the nostrils, a cotyla's worth daily for up to three days; and pound elm-bark in a mortar, and, rinsing it in wine, pour it in. Or, as some do, boil beets and pour it in with three cyathi of oil.
Apsyrtus is most pleased to recommend making use of purging,

for, when the whole body is well disposed, no abnormal fluxes into the feet will occur. After the purging, dissolve an oxybaphon of iris-root in sweet, fragrant wine, up to a cotyla's worth, and pour it into the nostrils.
