Offer green fodder; and if there is none, sprinkle the dry fodder with soda. And if the affliction does not stop, cut out its testicles, and it will become healthy.
Composition of a fatigue-relieving liniment ('akopon'), for the same affliction.

One pound each of turpentine-resin, pine-resin, bay-oil, wax, soda, bull-fat, ammoniac gum-drops, myrtle-oil, and iris-oil; six pints of common oil; two pints of old wine; one ounce each of castoreum, adarce, storax-oil, and pepper; three ounces each of deer-marrow and cyperus; four ounces each of wild thyme, peach-leaves, linseed, and sage; two ounces each of opopanax, galbanum, unfired sulfur, marjoram, bdellium, and frankincense-manna; six ounces of henna-oil. Mix these together and use it.
By Eumelus, for the same.
Grind half an Attic cotyla of bull's blood, ten drachms of frankincense, and one drachm of Spanish salt, and, adding one cotyla of wine and warming it, pour it in through the left nostril.
On loss (destruction) of hair.
By Apsyrtus.

When there occurs a loss of hair at the tapering end of the tail, one must wipe it clean with urine, and thoroughly wash away the scurf, and soak it with wine and oil. It is also said that one should anoint the place with the fat of a dog or a fox, for it is exceedingly beneficial. Best of all is

to boil marsh-mallow root, and to soak and wash the place with the decoction, wiping it gently clean first; for it will make the hairs long and thick. This works also on humans, both men and women; for if their hair is sparse, it will become thick.

If loss of hair occurs at the tapering end of the tail, let the horse be wiped clean with urine, and, once well washed, let it be soaked with wine, then anointed with pig-fat or fox-fat. Best of all is to boil marsh-mallow root and soak it with the decoction, wiping it clean first; for it will make the hairs long and thick.

And if the mane becomes ulcerated, shear the horse, and wipe it clean with roasted soda, and blow unmixed wine onto it, then, wiping it with urine, anoint it with the wound-salve for five days, and on the sixth day with water and the soft remedy. And even if the tail suppurates, you will nevertheless cure it, and it will be healed.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

If the hairs of the tail fall out and it becomes unsightly, we shall treat it, first wiping the shaft clean with urine, then with mallow and cabbage juice and marsh-mallow decoction, and thus soaking it each time with wine-and-oil. Others, anointing with fox-fat after the wiping, grow the hair back.
Another, by Hippocrates.
If you wish to make the hairs of the mane and tail grow, first wash with children's urine, then grind quicklime-lye, white-lead, and litharge, and, kneading them with water and boiling it, use it.
Another, by Pelagonius.
Burn paper or papyrus, and mix it with butter, and anoint; for it is useful.

And if you wish to make these grow faster, burn a tortoise over vine-twigs, and, making a dry powder from it, put it into a new pot. Mix in also three ounces of raw alum, and, moreover, grind enough deer-marrow with wine, add it to the pot, and anoint with it for many days. And thus you will make them grow.
Another.
Make a dry powder from burnt lupine-seeds, or likewise from roasted broad-beans, and sprinkle it onto the place.
Another.
Pound spikenard together with raisins, boil it in vinegar, and, while the remedy is still hot, rub the bald patch of the body with it.
Another, on slackness and movement of the tail.

If the horse holds its tail-switch very much in motion (constantly swishing), draw the tip of the tail up along the spine, and cut off about half of it, taking care not to sever a joint. And once the wound has healed, it will have a strong, upright tail-switch. For horses with the aforesaid fault are, for the most part, considered useless.
Against flux of the tail (loss of hair from the tail through discharge).
Boil fenugreek seed and enough linseed in wine, and wash the tail with it daily, and you will cure it more quickly.
Another, for growing hair.
Burn a dog's head, and, first anointing the place with butter, sprinkle it on.
By Tiberius, against sores of pack-animals, so that the hair grows back the same color.

Grind about two pints of barley and knead it, adding also a little soda-froth and salt, and, shaping loaves, put them into an oven, until they become charcoal; then pound and grind them, and, kneading with oil, anoint the sores all around. Do this for twenty days, and the hair will grow back the same color.
Another.

Burn and grind packing-bark (this is the bark used inside pack-saddles, placed against beasts of burden), and, on black animals, mix it in and anoint with oil; on chestnut animals, grind the packing-bark and mix in bear-fat with burnt ochre, and use it thus. And if the animal is white, add white-lead instead of ochre, and anoint. Treat the scar beforehand, before the hairs come back, so that, being still fresh, it will take the ointment well.
For growing hair while on a journey.
Burn the plant 'blachnon' (wild mint), and, making a dry powder from it and mixing it with wine, anoint.
For a scar, so that it may bring forth hair.
Make soot from burnt hay, and rub it in.
By Pelagonius, if you wish to turn white hair black.
One gramme of writing-ink (calligraphic black), four grammes of oleander juice, enough goat-fat; mix and grind these, and anoint.
If you wish to turn hair white.
Take a denarius'-weight of wild-cucumber root, two denarii'-weight of soda, half a pint of honey, and an equal amount of oil; mix these, and rub the part you wish to whiten.
On horses that twitch (convulse).
By Tiberius.
[lacuna] ...carefully, drench through the mouth for three days.
Some have named an affliction 'hippotilos' (horse-twitch) from what occurs;
for the horse twitches, and a collapse of strength follows from this, and its legs become bound together (locked). This kind of affliction is indeed dangerous.
It is treated thus: make the horse thirsty, then, pouring about an oxybaphon of hyssop into the water, give it to drink.
And if it survives, first draw blood from the legs and knees, and, putting it into cold water, let it stand there for half an hour,
then dry and pound blackberry-leaves, and put them into the drink.

You will also help by means of drenches: stir edible pomegranate, barley-groats, and about a cotyla of fragrant wine together, making the whole, with an equal amount of water added, up to about a cotyla, and pour it in through the mouth.
On the shin-bone (kerkis, the splint-bone of the foreleg).
By Hierocles.

If the shin-bone is fractured, use this treatment: an equal amount each of fenugreek seed, linseed, and barley-flour, ground as finely as possible; boil these in mixed wine, until they thicken and become sticky;
then, having doused it with hot water, apply as a poultice for seven days.

And if it does not respond to this treatment, apply an emollient, until it settles. And if it still does not yield to treatment, cauterize it, in the manner they call 'woven-cord' style, down to the hide, not making the burn any deeper, because the area is bare of flesh and full of sinew.
On herpes (creeping sore).
By Hierocles.

A certain white membrane-like film forms beneath the hide, so that the place where the creeping sore lies becomes moist. Cut around it in a circle, then, taking in also some of the healthy tissue around it, apply edible pomegranate. Let it be poulticed with barley-groats and lentils from marshes, and let the place first be soaked with vinegar beforehand. Some, after the excision, first cleanse it with squill and cabbage pounded with oil.
After this, wiping it vigorously clean, they sprinkle on vetch-flour.
Another: cure of herpes (creeping sore).

Take sun-dried raisins, remove the seeds, and grind the flesh thoroughly, and use it thus, until it is healed. Boiling asphodel root in wine and grinding it, and applying it as a poultice, is also good.
On hystrichides (bristle-like hairs).
By Hierocles.

Hairs resembling pig-bristles form in the tail; rubbing the tail against the wall, then, causes a sore. Pluck out the hairs cleanly, then, dissolving gum in vinegar, anoint the place, having first wiped it clean with soda.
'The measure is best,' said one of the wise men in his maxims; obeying this, we must put an end here to the first book.
By Hierocles, Book Two of Horse-Treatments.

Hesiod says that the beginning is half of the whole, urging, I think, by this too, that one take up the best pursuits, since, for those who have begun, the task is already half accomplished. Though the portion beyond the half is not great, still, one must complete what remains, for the
fulfillment of the whole. And I think that I myself have shown this to be true, not least of all, in my treatise on the treatment of horses.

For, having begun to write the first book, and not expecting to complete it easily, I extend, in a manner altogether like the responsion of lyric poets, this second book as a counterpart, having taken care to leave nothing lacking in the composition. For, just as it was fitting to set a sufficient measure to the first book, guarding against the satiety that comes from excessive length, so it was likewise proper not to leave the work unfinished, especially since it is composed concerning serious matters.

For this animal, I think, the horse, may reasonably be considered the most beautiful and altogether most prized of animals to men: lightening his master's toils on a journey, making a procession appear more solemn and admired when in a parade, and, in the struggles of war, sharing the danger and taking part in the deeds, so as to catch fleeing enemies, and to save friends in need of rescue.

For this reason it has reasonably been honored thus among men, so that, at Olympia and Delphi and everywhere in the games, prizes for speed are set before horses just as before men. And among the gods it has been deemed worthy of such regard, that it is not only yoked to their divine chariots, but has even been set among the choir of the stars in heaven.
It might perhaps seem to someone not without relevance to the purpose of this treatise, to make mention also, in part, of the things recorded by the philosopher

Aristotle: that the horse has not tallow but soft fat, and a three-lobed lung with no gall-bladder attached to it, for the gall lies beside the intestine, abundant and foul-smelling; and further, besides these, that in horses and mules a bone has been found in the heart.

And yet many were ignorant of such things, as was Mikon of old, who thought that the horse also has hairs on its lower eyelid, which the Greeks call eyelashes; Simon, at any rate, takes him to task, blaming him for this ignorance.

Since it is not my purpose here to speak of the nature of the animal, but to set forth the treatments for each of its afflictions, I pass over these things - and also, by Zeus, those things which Aristotle records so admiringly, testifying to the animal's intelligence together with its self-restraint, and how it would not mate with its own mother: he says, at any rate, that a certain horse-breeder brought one of the horses to its mother, having carefully covered her and taken pains that it not be discovered. And the horse, having been led by ignorance to desire her, did mate with her; but, coming somehow to realize it afterward, it flung itself down over a sheer cliff, unable to bear living on after such an impious deed. But these matters require other treatises; we, for our part, shall keep to the task before us.
On an ulcerated mouth.

If a horse's mouth becomes ulcerated, and also the throat and windpipe, take dry pomegranate-rind, pound it and sift it through a fine sieve, and sprinkle it into the mouth, having tied the tongue outside for half an hour, so that the astringency may take full effect. Then, untying it and drawing the

tongue outside the mouth, rinse it with unmixed wine. And if you do not have this, dry olive-leaves, pound them and sift them through a fine sieve and sprinkle them in, first tying the tongue for half an hour, then rinse with water, until it is healed.
On aphtha (mouth-sores/thrush).
By Hierocles.

If the horse develops aphtha - for so they call this affliction - it gives off a smell and brings up froth, and the mouth becomes inflamed. Pound and sift edible pomegranate, then, and anoint the mouth with it, first tying the tongue for half an hour, then, untying it, rinse with water. Do this until it is healed.
Another.

This affliction is wont to arise in horses from green fodder, in their mouths, especially in the season of spring. It is one kind, but has two variants: sometimes a foul-smelling condition arises in the mouth without ulceration, sending out fiery froth; sometimes it comes with a bloody ulceration in the throat itself and the mouth. I shall set out here the treatment for each of these:
Treatment of aphtha without ulceration.

You will treat the foul-smelling, frothy, and inflamed aphtha thus: pound dry edible pomegranates as fine as possible, then, having drawn out the animal's tongue and tied it to the halter-strap with a bandage, sprinkle it into the animal's mouth, and, rubbing it in a little, suspend the tongue thus for half an hour, and then rinse it with water. Do this for seven days, and you will cure the animal. Let the disappearance of the foul smell be your sign that the treatment is working.
Another: treatment of aphtha with ulceration.

When aphtha occurs unnoticed, it ulcerates the throat, the pharynx, and the windpipe; you will treat this thus: likewise binding the tongue with a fig-bark bandage and tying it outside, and anointing the ulcerated parts with honey, and leaving it for half an hour, so that, by licking the sores with the tongue itself, it strips away the scabs from them; and thus, again seizing the tongue, and having ready finely ground dry pomegranate and, likewise ground, dry olive-leaves, mixing an equal amount of each, sprinkle it onto the ulcerated parts, and, just as with the previous affliction, suspend it for half an hour, so that it may be thoroughly astringed, then rinse with wine. Do this daily for nine days.
On those exhausted from a journey or a run, and on those suffering a drawing pain in the flanks.
By Apsyrtus.
Apsyrtus to Marcus Aemilius, decurion, greetings.

I wish you, as a horse-keeper, to know that it is beneficial to use this treatment for those exhausted from a journey or a run: mix fine barley-groats with fragrant wine, and, making little balls, give them by holding the tongue. And if the horse suffers a drawing pain in the flanks, let it be drenched through the nostrils with a three-obol weight of saffron in a cotyla of water, and also through the mouth.
Another: prognosis and cure of exhaustion (kopos).

First, the horse cannot stand, but stands trembling, holding its head and ears drooped low; its eyes are sunken, and its neck is drawn tight and hard. And if you disturb it, it raises its head and lets it drop again. One must, then,
first lay the horse in a place that is not hard, but soft,
where there is dung, having wrapped it in blankets. Then, taking wine and oil
and warming them, blow it in and rub it down; then, in
hot water, bathe it copiously, and, having scraped it clean, anoint it and rub it down,
and wrap it in blankets, and stand it under shelter.
Another, for those whose breath is labored (strained) from
a journey.
For those whose breath is labored from a journey
or a run, use wine mixed with water, an equal amount of
each, making the mixture up to a quantity of two cotylae, and daily
pour it in through the mouth for up to seven days. And if it
suffers a drawing pain in the flanks and is over-tense, do not give it
wine, but mix a three-obol weight of saffron into a cotyla of water, and,
rubbing it in, pour it through the left nostril. It happens,
once the purging has occurred, both in the horse and in beasts of burden,
that a collapse of strength occurs, while the internal organs
suffer nothing in sympathy. But the flow of blood, once a collapse
occurs, brings weakness to the body; wherefore one must use
food of every kind, and in greater quantity.
Another remedy for the same.
For those suffering a drawing pain in the flanks, or having some other
weakness in the lung, or wasting away, you will use
such a composition as this: two staters of saffron, twelve staters of pounded
and sifted Illyrian iris, six staters of
pepper, half a cotyla of honey, half a choenix of raisins with the
seeds removed, an equal amount of clean pine-nuts as the raisins;
from this, drench two spoonfuls in a half-cotyla of wine and a quarter-cotyla of oil, through the mouth.

Sometimes a horse, either from ravenous hunger or from weakness, becomes almost completely limp in its limbs, and the afflictions differ, but the signs of the illness very often turn out similar, and mislead those who wish to treat it. For indeed we find in animals signs of a different disorder than the one we suppose. For when we wish to know whether a horse has fever, we observe its head carried low near the ground, and its breathing more continual. But these signs belong not only to a horse with fever, but also to one enduring pains. And again, there are signs thought to belong to a horse with opisthotonos (tetanic spasm), which occur in those animals that have become weakened from too much sun or from exertion, unable to stand, but collapsing with their legs drawn together in one place. Do not, then, suppose it to be simply a pain of the belly, or colic, and treat it as such, but rather apply to the affliction the treatment that actually suits it. Many, then, are the signs common to related afflictions, and many belong to conditions not clearly distinguished from one another; these you will easily recognize, if you attend to them more carefully.
Treatment.
It pleased Celsus that animals suffering in this way be kept from drink, so as to make them extremely thirsty, and, after such a burning thirst, he prescribes making them stand in cold water

for one hour; this, he strongly affirms, helps powerfully. Florus prescribes chopping elm-leaves with wine and drenching through a horn. We, however, know to give wheat-flour with water, or to drench three eggs with pennyroyal, vinegar-water, and oil.
On an ulcerated windpipe.
Another, on a ruptured windpipe.

If the windpipe is ruptured, the horse breathes heavily and wheezes and coughs, and something purulent is discharged through the nostrils, and it goes lame in the forefeet [and its testicles twitch frequently, and its flanks are drawn in, its legs grow numb and tremble, its veins are either extremely dry or overfull of blood, its mouth has aphtha-sores, and it will not allow the hand to touch its flesh]. One must, then, soak vetch for two days and nights, and strain it off, once it is thoroughly soaked. And when it has become as dry as possible, chop it fine, and, sifting it, put it into a drink of two parts sweet dark wine, and
five parts water, mixed together. For it will become healthy and fat, being helped in this way, within sixty days.
Another, by Pelagonius: preparation of a remedy for the windpipe.

Four ounces of cave-myrrh, three ounces each of saffron and camel-thorn flower, five ounces of cinnamon, five ounces of white pepper, four ounces of black pepper, half an ounce of cassia, five ounces of Colophonian resin,
four ounces of birthwort, three ounces of sweet-flag, three ounces of bay-berries.
Another.

Ten ounces of myrrh, three ounces of pepper, one pound of roasted linseed, one pint of raisins, one pint of pine-nuts; boil the meltable ingredients, then add the dry ones, mixing in honey. For the dose, make balls the size of a walnut, and, giving them through the mouth for eight days, you will complete the cure.
Another.

Three ounces of myrrh, one and a half ounces of cinnamon, three ounces of saffron, four and a half ounces of male frankincense, four ounces each of Syrian nard, turpentine-resin, white pepper, and ammoniac gum, two ounces of nard, one pound of tragacanth, one pound of first-quality honey; grind all these and mix with wine, and pour it in through the nostrils.
On those overheated from a journey.
By Hierocles.
If a horse becomes overheated from a journey or a run, make cakes of old pig-fat, and, soaking them in old fragrant wine, give three of them through the mouth.
Another.

If a horse suffers from heatstroke: one pint of goat's milk, two ounces of tragacanth, two ounces of Gallic hartwort, two ounces of pine-nuts, two ounces of carrot, one bundle of hyssop, two ounces of chopped horehound. From all these, drench one pound daily with wine-and-oil.
Another.

Boil barley-gruel juice, goat-fat, and sheep's trotters with coriander and old dill, then, grinding fresh coriander well and mixing it with the gruel-juice, as with the rest, and straining it, give it for three days.
Another.
Let cabbage-leaves, chopped with celery and mixed into a pint of wine, be given to the horse through the left nostril.
Another.
Grind parsley-seed, carrot-seed, Gallic hartwort-seed, southernwood, and camel-thorn in equal parts, and drench with honey-water.
On those burned by lime (quicklime/caustic).
By Apsyrtus.

If it ever happens that a horse is burned by quicklime, or by what some call 'konia' (lye/potash), in whatever part of the body, or steps into a dung-heap that is spontaneously smoldering and its legs are burned, or the injury happens some other way: it is treated with cold water in summer, and warm in winter, and anointing it with the fatty ointment, if you wish, mixed with lard, or with the quicklime itself mixed with oil. Do not lead it into the sea, until it has scarred over.
Another, by Hierocles.

If it happens that a horse is burned by quicklime or lye, in whatever part of the body, or also by smoldering dung, or some other way: in summer let it be doused with cold water, in winter with warm. And let it be anointed with the fatty ointment, if you wish, mixed with fat, or with the quicklime itself mixed with oil. Do not lead it into the sea, until it has scarred over.
On those with an internal strain/rupture.
By Apsyrtus.

Those who have strained something internal have eyes that are hollow compared to before, sunken and downcast, and their flanks are drawn up, and, though eating and drinking, they waste away. When walking, they take small steps,

and, when standing, they bring their hind feet close together toward the forefeet. Such horses linger on for a while, as long as they are not passing blood in their urine or dung. But if either of these occurs, they die more quickly. If the intestine is torn apart, or divided into two, these are the signs: food and water pass out through the nostrils from the intestines, and the horse collapses suddenly, and dies quickly.

A remedy for the same. Twelve staters of pounded and sifted Illyrian iris, six staters of pepper, one and a half cotylae of honey, half a choenix of seedless raisins; mix these together, and, making a compound, drench with it, putting in six ounces with one cotyla of wine and four cotylae of oil, through the mouth, for all internal pains.

Another, on something internal having ruptured, which is dangerous. Since it is unclear to the non-expert what exactly has ruptured, it is necessary to explain by what signs one who does not know may recognize it. If, then, the belly or some intestine is ruptured, this is the sign: it passes dung through the nostrils and sweats. And if it is the bladder, it discharges fluid immediately through the anus. And if something of the lung is ruptured, it discharges blood through the nostrils. And if the liver is affected, the genitals swell, and the belly, and the thighs. And if it is the spleen, it grows weak and refuses food. And if it is the kidneys, it passes blood in its urine.
If, then, the belly or intestine or bladder is ruptured, you will accomplish nothing by helping. But if the lung is affected, take two choenixes of white

vetch and one oxybaphon of salt, knead with water and shape into a loaf, and, once dried, burn it, and grind it thoroughly, and sprinkle it into the drink when watering the horse. Also drench through the mouth thus: saffron, myrrh, Syrian nard, cassia, starch, fine birthwort, celandine-juice, dog's-tooth grass, and oil; grind all the dry ingredients and combine them with the liquid ones, add an oxybaphon of honey and one cotyla of first-quality wine,

and pour it in through the nostril; or likewise use the barley-gruel juice extensively in the same way. And if the liver is affected, give it pomegranate-juice, and add wheat-flour to the drink in winter, barley-flour in summer, and drench it with a decoction of old dried figs. And for the kidneys, keep the animal in stillness, and anoint it gently with wax-oil salve, and let it rest, until it is cured.
Another.

There is a certain plant that grows on walls and rocks, which the sons of physicians call 'polygonon' (knotgrass), laymen call 'symphyton' (comfrey/bone-knit), the Macedonians call 'osteokollon' (bone-glue), and prophets call it 'pallantion.' They say that, when boiled together with divided pieces of meat, it unites them; hence it is also called 'symphytos' (grown-together) and 'osteokollos' (bone-gluing), taking its name from what it does. This plant is always green and living and leafless, and has branches hanging down like a cord, resembling a thinner and longer rope. It is not so much good for binding as rope is, but, because of its many joints, it very easily comes apart at the joints under the pull of the hand of those who take hold of it. It does not
spare growing even leafless upon trees, without root, the plant.

Taking this while fresh, they boil it down with wine, until it is reduced by a third, and the Spaniards drench their mares and horses with it. They also use it as a preventive medicine against illness, and, if they suspect anything internal to have ruptured, they help with this.
Another, against all internal afflictions.
Put equal weights of butter, opopanax, myrrh, and honey, and, grinding them together with wine, pour it in through the left nostril.
If the intestines protrude from a wound.

Soak a vulture's feather in oil, and put it into the mouth, until, touching the gullet, it induces vomiting. And if this draws in the internal organs, then stitch the place, drawing together the edges of each side, and treat the wound with the usual wound-remedies.
For prolapse of the internal organs.

Bind up again the skin that has been split into two parts, and cut away the excess, and treat with the wound-remedy. It also helps for the horse to be covered, so that it sweats. Let it abstain from walking about and especially from drinking. And let its feed be elm-leaves, fresh mint, and clover.

Drench it thus: grind white cress-seed with frankincense-root and six grains of pepper, and three cyathi of Cretan carrot-seed, mixing with old wine and honey, and drench through the mouth for seven days. Or boil asparagus root or seed with water, until reduced by a third, and, for

four days, pour in half a pint through the nostrils each day. And after this, give two ounces each of opopanax, sagapenum, honey, and butter with half a pint of old wine through the mouth, for three days. Cyrenaic bark found in the feed or drink is wont to harm animals most of the time. You will treat this thus: grind honey and wild mint together, and, warming them in wine, pour it in through the nostrils.
On a horse suffering from bulimia (ravenous hunger/faintness).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Herakleion, military tribune, greetings. One must help a horse suffering from bulimia thus: soak the soft part of bread in wine, and, rubbing it in, drench it through the mouth. This is for use on the road. But when it happens at home, knead three cyathi of fine wheat-flour and dissolve it in wine, and drench likewise. Or grind pine-nuts thoroughly and give them with wine.
By Hierocles, for the same.

They help a horse with bulimia in this way: they soak the soft part of bread in wine, give it, and, rubbing it in, drench with it. They also do this likewise with pine-nuts, giving the same measure in wine.
Another.

Sometimes horses collapse from being unable to bear hunger. It is easily possible to help these without great loss. For when the horse begins to be endangered by such hunger, soak a portion of clean bread in wine, and grind it in the wine itself, so as to make a paste from it, and, drenching it through a horn, you will help it. But do this either at the onset of the hunger, or
on the road, where the necessary things cannot be found. And if such a condition persists, mix three cyathi of fine wheat-flour with wine, and give it through a horn.
If the animal endures hunger, and the things suitable for treatment are lacking, knead earth in wine, and put it into its throat, or, making little balls from it, give them through the mouth.
On those wasting away from an unclear cause.

Apsyrtus to Fronto Valerius, greetings. You wrote to me asking what remedy one must use for horses wasting away from an unclear cause. These are helped by being drenched with wine and oil and a three-obol weight of myrrh. Or grind twenty grains of white pepper and give them. Or boil rue in wine and drench, or do the same with sage, or likewise with hoary-leaved sage-mullein. In every case let the amount be a cotyla of fragrant wine and a cyathus of old oil. This affliction is not, in fact, unclear, but is due to chilling. Those before us called it unclear. Such a horse, when it is not eating, and shivers in its body, and has its hairs standing on end, is drenched with fresh pig's blood mixed with an equal amount of wine, through the mouth. It is also said by some that one should dissolve onions and the seed of rocket in wine and drench through the mouth. Or make an infusion of the wormwood plant and give it in the drink, and mix soda into the rest of its water. It is also beneficial to offer these fresh wheat-fodder, if it is the season.

For those becoming thin from an unclear cause, one must use a drench of wine and oil with a three-obol weight of myrrh. Or grind twenty grains of white pepper, or boil rue in wine, and drench. Let the amount everywhere be a cotyla of fragrant wine and a cyathus of oil. Apsyrtus says the cause is not unclear, but arises from chilling. If, however, it does not eat, but also has its hairs standing on end, drench through the mouth with fresh pig's blood mixed with wine, an equal amount of each. Some, dissolving onions and rocket-seed in wine, drench through the mouth.
It is also good to soak the wormwood plant in wine and give it, and to offer the whole drink in this form. And offer fresh wheat-fodder, if the season allows.

For the horse that is thin from continual exhaustion, and wasted for this reason, you will help thus: crush white vetch, about a choenix's worth, soaking it with four cotylae of fragrant white wine, and, letting it stand for one day, give a third of the choenix daily, before watering the horse, for thirty days, and offer roasted barley alongside. Let the crushed vetch not be too finely ground.
Another, for the same, by Eumelus.

If thinness occurs in animals without any accompanying disorder, they will be restored with grain and roasted barley. And often wine, mixed into the water they drink, will also help, until they recover their natural strength. The bodies of such animals need a great deal of rubbing, so that, through

it, they may gain a greater appetite for food. They must also be kept standing in a dry place; for this benefits both the body and their hooves. Let vetch also be mixed into their feed. And let straw be strewn beneath them when they sleep.

You will use this remedy against hidden afflictions, which is a discovery of the Armenians, but has been proven to me through much experience: two staters of saffron, twelve staters of pounded Illyrian iris, six staters of pepper, half a cotyla of honey, half a choenix of seedless raisins, an equal amount of clean pine-nuts as the raisins; mix these together with half a cotyla of fragrant wine and a quarter-cotyla of oil, and drench the animal with about two spoonfuls of this.

Three modii of barley, six pints of broad beans, eight pints of chickpeas, six pints of wheat, four pints of kidney-beans, three pints of fenugreek, and one pint each of raisins and pine-nuts; taking these, make one modius from all of them together, and soak it in clean water one day before use, and, pouring off the water, let it dry a little, and from this give the horse half a medimnus in the morning, and the rest in the evening, and do this daily with careful attention. And if it is very thin, keep it shut up for thirty consecutive days in a warm stable, so that it eats and drinks indoors. And if less thin, let it be fed this way for twenty days. And if, from this careful regimen, it becomes
too fat, one must bleed it from the belly, so that, having become too fat, it does not fall into danger of death.
Another.
Boil a suckling pig with barley-gruel, until its flesh dissolves, and from this pour it in through a horn for three days.
Another.
Boil together a small bundle of rue, two ounces of myrrh, fifteen bay-berries, three ounces of Ethiopian cumin, half a cotyla of good oil, with one pint of old dark wine, and drench for three days.
Another.
Give roasted grain mixed with water and honey, about a modius's worth, daily, for twenty days.
Another.

Offer boiled, sweet lupine-seeds - sweet enough that even a human could eat them - to the animal to satiety, giving a modius daily. And if the lupines are not sweet, they will cause colic in the animal.
Another.
Roast chestnuts in an oven, pound them in a mortar, mix them with barley ground not too finely, and give them to the animal; you will cure it.
A preliminary drench for the same.

For whatever animal has thinness and an irregular condition, it is treated thus: mix half an ounce of unfired sulfur, one soft-boiled egg, and an obol's weight of myrrh with wine, and put it into its throat. This is also beneficial against coughing and pains of the belly.
Another, on thinness.
If the skin of some animal becomes very dry, and it shows no improvement from feed, which is wont to happen from

great exertion, you will treat it thus: first anoint the whole body with rue-oil, and after this give the following preliminary drench: one ounce each of carrot, tragacanth, wild rue, and wild mint, an equal amount of celery, melilot, and Pontic wormwood; mix and grind all these together, and, boiling them with wine and water, give as a preliminary drench.
On mange (psora).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Hegesagoras, most excellent physician, greetings. It is necessary for you, as a horse-keeper, to know this: mange arising in horses must not be treated right away, but left alone, until it has all turned outward. For it is an outpouring of a hard humor beneath the skin, which, if you treat too quickly, you will block its outlet; for, since the applied remedies are astringent, the humor is necessarily forced back inward, and this results in harm. When, then, it seems to be at its height, treat it then, drawing blood from the pastern-veins and the forelegs, and likewise from the hind legs, and anoint it, grinding bitumen thoroughly with a portion of sulfur and liquid pitch and children's scraped-off bath-oil.
Best of all is to mix in butter; and if there is none, then grind everything together with bath-oil-scrapings, and, making it the thickness of honey, use it.

And this too: boil very sharp vinegar, children's bath-oil-scrapings, and cedar-tar together, and, making a sponge-on-a-stick applicator, anoint it while hot. And if there is no cedar-tar, anoint with pitch, but not much; wipe it clean beforehand with old urine, mixing in warm water, and whatever astringents are suitable.
This too works: grind equal parts of sulfur and bitumen,
pour cold oil on it, and anoint; and let the horse stand in the sun, and, at night, out in the open air, if it is summer.
This too is excellent: melt equal parts of pig-fat, pitch, and wax, and grind in sulfur and mix it, and, pouring on hot oil, anoint with it.
Purging by means of soda and wild cucumber is also fitting.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If mange arises, one must not treat it immediately, but let it be, until it has all turned outward. For it is an effusion of a hard humor beneath the skin, which, if you treat too quickly, you will block its outlet. For, since the applied remedies are astringent, the harmful matter is of necessity forced to turn inward. When, then, it seems to be at its height, draw blood from the pastern-veins and forelegs, likewise from the hind legs, and anoint it, grinding bitumen and sulfur thoroughly with a portion of liquid pitch and butter; and if there is no butter, children's bath-oil-scrapings. Grind everything together, then, and, making it the thickness of honey, anoint. Or otherwise: boil sharp vinegar, children's bath-oil-scrapings, and cedar-tar together, and anoint hot, binding a sponge to a stick. And if there is no cedar-tar, anoint with more pitch. Wipe it clean beforehand with old urine, mixing it with warm water.

Or otherwise: pour cold oil onto ground sulfur and bitumen, and anoint. And let it stand in the sun, and in summer also out in the open air at night. Or grind pitch together with old oil and wax, mixing in fine sulfur, and use it. This too is excellent: melt equal parts of pig-fat, pitch, and wax,
and grind in sulfur and mix it, and, pouring on hot oil, anoint. Purging by means of wild cucumber and soda is also beneficial.
In what is called 'starvation-mange' (limopsora), scurf also appears. Help it by boiling lupine-seeds and dousing the animal with their water.
Prognosis and cure of mange.

First, the body becomes bare of hair and turns white and is drawn tight, and scales are scraped off, and the horse walks taking short, frequent steps because of this tightness. Wash it clean, then, with lye, and, rinsing with hot water, anoint the scaly parts with the remedy. And when, from being anointed, it shivers, bring it into a warm room, and keep a fire burning nearby, and watch over it, so that it does not roll about, nor stand in mud or dung. Then, after some time, wash it off and rub it down, blowing in wine and oil. And if it is doing well enough, leave it. But if not, anoint it with the remedy. Give the best possible care to its food and drink.
Another.
Burn willow-bark, and take the drippings, and, mixing them with water, anoint. Or anoint with what is called soap-drippings.
Another.
Roast wild mint and grind it with salt, and, soaking it in old oil, anoint.
Another.
Unfired sulfur, turpentine-resin, a little quicklime; grind the sulfur and the quicklime, and bind them with the resin, and, making a plaster, use it.
Another.
Two pounds of bitumen, two pounds of unfired sulfur, two pounds of soda, two pounds of pine-resin, four pounds of wax,
two pints of cedar-tar, ten pints of liquid pitch, twelve pints of oil, three pints of vinegar, two pints of old olive-lees oil, four pints of lard; mix all these and use it.
Another.

Mix one pint of sharp vinegar, one pint of pitch-oil, and one pound of soda, and anoint the horse, having first washed it clean, of course, mixing in also one pint of lees-oil and one ounce of unfired sulfur.
Another.

Six ounces of Italian cedar-oil, an equal amount of unfired sulfur, three ounces of sandarach, five ounces each of vetch-meal, gall-nut, and unripe-olive oil, half a pint of bay-oil, enough sharp vinegar, dog's dung; mix all these and boil them, and put them into common oil, then, making a sponge-on-a-stick applicator, anoint the mangy place.
Another.

Mix dark wine with an equal amount of water, add in gall-nuts too, and use it. And if it does not stop, give it dog's dung with dry wine. Or pound the plant 'kynoprason' (dog's-leek) and boil it with oil, and anoint.
Another.

Two ounces each of soda and unfired sulfur, two ounces of soda-froth, two pints of liquid pitch, one pint of oil, half an ounce of sandarach, an equal amount of vinegar, twenty-five bay-berries; mix and grind all these, then, warming it, anoint it in with your hands.
By Eumelus, for the same.

Slaughter a toad, boil it in a bronze pot with wine and water, and anoint with its broth, that is, its liquid. Or rub in, along the grain of the hair, pitch with honey, unfired sulfur, old olive-lees oil, and sheep dung. Or bitumen and

cedar-tar with two ounces each of frankincense-meal, birthwort, and soda. Or boil six ounces of liquid pitch and two pints of oil with one and a half pints of vinegar, and do the same, having first scraped and roughened the skin with a curry-comb or a potsherd. Or burn reeds, taking them before they turn fully to ash, and pound and sift them through a fine sieve, and, mixing in oil, anoint along the grain of the hair. Or boil wild-cucumber root in water, and, after boiling, add wine and cow-dung, make it like a poultice, and use it. On the following day, lead the animal out into the warm sun, wash it with lukewarm water and soda-froth, then rub it down with old lard. The hair grows back smooth, if you burn hay and anoint with its ash.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

Mange in horses and in other beasts of burden is nothing other than a corruption of bilious humor and blood, which, from heat, has boiled up from the depths and made its way outward to the surface. And it is easily curable and without danger for the skilled practitioner, since the nature of the heat itself assists him. But for one who treats it unskillfully, the remedies applied often bring on death. Apsyrtus, indeed, calls this affliction, from its location, a hard 'sub-dermal' swelling. I do not disagree in naming the kind of affliction differently. One must treat it in no other way than by cooperating with nature, using remedies that draw out, that loosen, that first scarify - and not those that scar it over. Let there be, then, one remedy at the onset of the affliction, another at its height, and another in its decline.
And when it is at its
onset, one must bleed from the neck and the groin on one
day, but afterward from the groin alone, so that, by drawing
the humor downward, you do not make it hard to pass through; but not
from the neck, so that, isolated there, it does not settle upon the region around the heart.
For the matter flows in toward the constricted places, at the sites of the incisions.
After bleeding it in this way, anoint it with pitch and myrrh-oil and
lye and soda and verdigris, so that it may come quickly to the
surface. And when it has all ulcerated, boil barley-flour in
water-and-oil, and anoint with the remedy while it is lukewarm. And when
it reaches the third day, wash it off with hot water or myrrh-oil, and scarify
until it bleeds; then, wiping it dry with a hair-cloth or rags, anoint it
with liquid pitch, olive-lees, unctuous oil, and unfired sulfur.
And, bleeding it from the neck, drench it with wild cucumber and
soda, ground in equal parts, in wine or honey-water. Let the
full-grown horse take three Italian pints, the younger two, and the foal one.
By Hierocles, for the same: preparation of a plaster.
One ounce of resin, two ounces of wax, one ounce of powdered lime, and quicklime, or
barley-gruel - one and a half ounces; mix these together, and, making a plaster,
apply it.
By Pelagonius, for the same.
Take the plant called oleander, and another plant,
'perdikion' growing on walls, that is, ironwort, and, making
three little bundles of them, boil them in sharp vinegar and juice-oil...
boil them in sharp vinegar and juice-oil with soda-froth, and after boiling, add
enough unfired sulfur, and, anointing it and putting it out in the sun once a
day, you will cure it.
Another.

Six pints of oil, six pints of cedar-tar, six pints of liquid pitch, six drachms of sulfur, an equal amount of misy (copper ore), two drachms of bitumen, three drachms of wax, three drachms of split alum, resin and soda in equal amounts, six drachms of wild raisin (staphis agria), two pints of vinegar; boil these together and anoint with it.
Another.

One gramme of old urine-sediment, six ounces of pig dung, half a pint of olive-lees, three ounces of sulfur, three cyathi of liquid pitch; boil these together, and, while still hot, anoint once a day.
By Tiberius, for the same.
If mange occurs in a horse or in some other beast of burden, treat it thus: take marsh-frogs, very sharp vinegar, oil, and soda-froth; mix these in due proportion of each, and, boiling them, anoint.
Another.
Take southernwood, and burnt reed-bark, and add enough marsh-mallow, and, working it up with water, anoint.
Another, by Dioscorides.
Boil olive-lees down to a honey-like consistency, and mix in a decoction of lupine-seeds and the plant chamaeleon and pig-fat, and anoint; you will cure it.
Another.

Stand the horse in the hottest sun, and scrape it with a curry-comb to such a degree that a flow of blood results. And then take wild ivy-root and sulfur and liquid pitch and alum, and, mixing all these and warming them, anoint the mange.
Mange, often, if it does not receive help, brings about

death. One must, then, first wash the mange with warm human urine, then with water, and after this, when the sun is hottest, rub it with mastic-oil or cedar-oil, or mix nettle-seed with vinegar and brine, and rub it in. And if the affliction is found to be more severe, mix bitumen with sulfur and liquid pitch and old lard in equal weight, and boil it down. But first scrape the mange with iron or a scalpel down to the living flesh, and thus use the aforesaid remedies.
On inflammation of bones.

By Hierocles. You will help inflammations of the bones arising from a wound, or from a bite, whether from some wild animal or from horses biting one another, thus: boil wild-cucumber root in sea-water, or spring-water containing salt, and, after dousing, sponge the place, then grind white-lead, oil, goat-fat, and egg-white, and anoint. And if it is inflamed from some other cause and not from a wound, douse it with hot water twice a day, and anoint their shoulders with Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar, or with potter's clay, or with fresh wormwood pounded to a juice, or
with hemlock growing in dung-heaps, or with fresh nightshade
juice, likewise. And wormwood alone, mixed with water and anointed on, is also fitting.
A plaster against inflammations.
Four pounds of soda-froth, one pound each of burnt copper, Judaean bitumen, frankincense-manna, oleander, blue vitriol, litharge-scum, and verdigris, enough lard; pound all these and,
spreading them onto a thick linen cloth, apply to the painful places.
By Anatolius, for the same.
You will treat any inflammation by applying a poultice of salt and oil, or of hoary-leaved sage-mullein or of great mullein,
burnt and mixed with wine.
Soak three pounds each of dried figs and cypress-tips tied in bundles, and vinegar,
and, pressing out the juice, add one pound of soda,
six ounces of ammoniac gum, and one ounce each of opopanax and aloe.
Grind these all together, mix them, and apply as a poultice, soaking
the bandages beforehand in the leftover vinegar from the figs, and
let it stay bound for three days, and you will cure it. And if the horse has the wrinkle-like sores called
'ozainai' (foul-smelling fistulous sores), add three ounces of pomegranate-rind, alum,
misy, chalcitis, soreus, blue vitriol, and verdigris, one ounce of each,
and grind them all together into one, so as to make a plaster; having first wiped
the animal clean with urine, apply as a poultice, and bind it for three
days, then make it walk about, moved gently, and let it swim. Then
wipe it clean again with urine, and apply the same remedy as a poultice
for the same number of days, and you will cure it.
One pound of Megarian bulbs, five eggs, two pounds of African snails,
one pound of frankincense-manna, six ounces each of aloe, burnt copper,
and coriander-flower; grind all these together
in a mortar and anoint.
Against the spreading of inflammations.
One pound each of male-fern root, reed-root, Gallic garlic,

marsh-mallow, African fig, cypress-balls, wax, iris, and burnt cuttlefish-bone; pound all these together in a mortar and, binding them onto the animal's knees, you will cure it without iron (surgery).
Another.
Six pounds of wax, three ounces each of deer-fat, galbanum, wallflower, white pepper, ammoniac gum, turpentine-resin, and gentian; mix and grind each kind together, and use it.
On wounds in hollow (body-cavity) places.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Publius Cocceius Justus, centurion, greetings. You wrote to me asking how one must treat those wounded in the body-cavities. It must be treated thus: one must stitch up the peritoneum, in the same manner as physicians do in a human, with a not-thin twisted woolen thread, and draw the ends out, and then clamp the fat and the hide together with a waxed hempen suture-clasp, and treat with the wound-remedy. And if inflammation occurs, anoint with Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar. And when the seventh day comes, undo the abdominal stitching and remove the thread. And if the intestine has prolapsed, it must be pushed back in with a sponge soaked in hot water and squeezed out; for direct pressure from the hands causes inflammation. And if the intestine is wounded or has become distended with gas, one must give up hope.

And if the omentum (caul-fat) has prolapsed, one must trim it off with scissors and not push it back in. And if it is wounded, but no prolapse occurs, and the horse holds its foreleg forward, and is downcast or gloomy-looking, and strains repeatedly through the anus,
one must recognize that something internal has been wounded, and that it cannot live.

And if some part of the deep flesh is wounded, one must apply tent-dressings soaked in vinegar and oil, and place clamps, to which the dressings will be bound; let these be of wool. Do this for up to three days. And then undo the clasps, and douse with hot water, and apply vetch-flour as a poultice.
Wounds that occur below the knees are slow to scar over, because that area lacks flesh and lacks fatty skin.
And for a horse wounded in the hind legs, below, at the groin, or near the genital region, opisthotonos (tetanic spasm) easily results, and it dies.
By Hierocles, for the same.
One must treat those wounded in the body-cavities thus:
stitch it with an abdominal needle and a not-thin twisted woolen thread, then one must draw the ends out, and then clamp the fat and the hide together with a waxed hempen suture-clasp.
One must treat the inflammation by anointing it with Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar.
And when the seventh day arrives, undo the abdominal stitching, and remove the threads.
And if the intestine prolapses, it must be pushed back in with a sponge soaked in hot water and squeezed out; for direct pressure from the hands is wont to cause inflammation.
And if the intestine is wounded or distended with gas, one must give up hope.
And if the omentum has prolapsed, it is fitting to trim it off with scissors, or push it back inside.
And if, however, the horse is wounded, and no prolapse occurs, but it holds its foreleg forward, and looks gloomy, and strains, plucking out something

blood-like, one must recognize that something internal has been wounded, and that it is unlikely to be saved. And if some part of the deep flesh is wounded, one must apply tent-dressings, holding them in place with clasps, soaking the dressings in oil and binding them, then undoing the clasps, and dousing with hot water, and then applying vetch-flour as a poultice. And a horse wounded in the hind legs, below, at the groins, easily falls into opisthotonos and perishes.
On a horse that has fallen down a cliff or into a ditch.
By Apsyrtus.

If it ever happens that a horse falls from some height, or falls into a large ditch - which happens in military camps - and none of its joints or legs is hurt, but there is suspicion that something internal has been injured, use this drench: dissolve twice a bean's-weight of Cyrenaic laser-sap in vinegar-water, in equal parts up to two cotylae each, and give it through the nostrils. Or dissolve lye from the hearth in four cotylae of water, straining it through a linen cloth (let the lye be from oak or holm-oak), or dissolve one ounce of the juice of tawny acacia in two cotylae of wine. Or pound edible pomegranate and give it with two cotylae of wine through the mouth. And if, after falling, it passes dung or plucks out bloody fluid, drenching is superfluous, for it cannot live.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If it ever happens that a horse falls from a height, or falls into a deep place, and none of its joints is hurt, yet it is suspected that something internal has been injured: dissolve twice a cyathus'-measure of Cyrenaic

laser-sap in two cotylae of water, and drench through the nostrils. Or one must dissolve lye from the hearth in four cotylae of wine, and strain it through a linen cloth; let the lye be from oak or holm-oak. Or dissolve one ounce of the juice of tawny acacia or of edible pomegranate in three cotylae of wine, and give it through the mouth. And if, having fallen, it immediately plucks out bloody fluid, drenching is superfluous, since it cannot live.
Another, for the same.

One pint each of vetch-flour, fenugreek-flour, and lupine-flour; grind these and sift them finely, add one pint of Italian wine and half a pint of honey, and, kneading them together, make one loaf, and give it for six days.
On a horse that has been kicked.
By Apsyrtus.

When it happens, as horses fight one another, that both kick each other with their hind legs into the flank, a rupture of the peritoneum occurs at the suspensory ligament of the testicles, and the intestines fall into the scrotal sac, or 'pouch' as it is called, and the horse cannot live. These are the signs: the scrotal sac swells, and, while walking, it stops still, and does not eat, nor can it stand, but throws itself down, and rolls about, throwing its head back toward its spine. It survives one or two days, but on the third day it dies. The intestines do not fall in on the same day, but on the following day.
Another, for the same.
Make a brine, and mix it with oil, and drench, also mixing in sea-water and enough wine.
By Hierocles, for the same.

A horse kicked by another horse in the flank, with the peritoneum violently ruptured at the suspensory ligament of the testicles, is in danger. For, while walking, it stops still and does not eat, and, unable to stand, throws itself down and rolls about, throwing its head back toward its spine. It dies on the third day; for it is then that its intestines fall into the so-called 'pouch,' and not on the same day. And if a horse is bitten by another, one must soak the bite-wounds with vinegar-and-brine. Bite-wounds occurring on the sinews easily cause lameness. It is treated, however, with marsh-mallow, as written above.
On fractures.
Apsyrtus to Fronto of Ephesus, horse-doctor, greetings.

As many fractures as occur below the knee, in the hind or fore legs, are treated thus: one must set the fracture back into alignment, and bind it so, first placing dirty wool wrapped in linen bandages soaked in vinegar and oil, as many as are sufficient, evenly, not twisted, loosely spaced and not overlapping, and likewise throw on soaked wool and secure it. And add three splints, and bind it on each side with the knot called the 'wolf-knot,' and keep the horse standing upright for forty days, during the first twenty of which one must undo it three times and bind it again, and soak it daily with vinegar-oil, and after this undo it, then bind it again, likewise applying the splints too. And when the forty days have passed, if
it has set firm and the horse is walking, undo it and use the fat-based emollient, and let it walk about gradually.

But fractures occurring above the knee - do not touch these; for they do not heal. And if the thigh is broken, give up hope. If the shoulder is broken, there is no treatment; for opisthotonos results. And if it ever happens that a fracture occurs along with a wound, and the hide is cut through, do not touch it, nor bind the parts beneath; for putrefaction creeps in. And if a rib is broken, the horse becomes healthy again. Never apply cauterization to a fracture that has already formed a callus; for, as the scabs are thrown off, the callus is undone, and you will have to treat it
all over again.

If a fracture occurs below the knee in the forelegs, it is treated thus: having set the joint back into alignment, then wrapping dirty wool around it, bind it with knots soaked in vinegar and oil, exactly even and joined together. And, applying likewise soaked wool, and adding splints, as is customary, bind it on each side with the knot called the 'wolf-knot,' and keep it standing upright for forty days, during the first twenty of which undo it three times, and bind it again, soaking it daily with vinegar-oil, and adding the splints after twenty days. And when the forty days have passed, if the callus has set firm, use the fat-based emollient, and let it walk about gradually.
But if the break occurs above the knee, or the thigh is broken, it is hard to treat. And if it happens that the fracture occurs along with a wound and a cut, it is likewise
risky. But if a horse's rib is broken, the cure is easy.

Never apply cauterization to a fracture that has formed a callus. For, once the callus is undone, the place becomes hard to treat. One must know, indeed, that the shin-bone of a hind leg, once broken, does not knit together, since it has no marrow but blood, especially in the donkey and the mule.
Another, for the same.

When a leg is broken, and the hide is stripped off, and the joint is dislocated, wrap the hide back around it and set the joint, and anoint it with the remedy, not too hot, and bind it, and, suspending the animal, anoint the surrounding area with wine-and-oil. This is the remedy: twenty weights of pitch, ten pounds each of opopanax, turpentine-resin, oak-mistletoe glue, and wax, five pounds of bitumen, six pounds each of ammoniac incense, pine-resin, and galbanum, four pounds each of frankincense-manna and bdellium, two pounds of myrrh,

melt the bitumen, resin, pitch, and wax together, and, warming the ammoniac gum by the fire and flattening it, add it in. Grind the myrrh and bdellium and mix them in last, then put the opopanax into the pot, and the mistletoe-glue, then the galbanum, and last, spreading the ground ingredients onto a linen cloth, use it.
Another, by Hippocrates, on a fracture of the skull.

When a fracture of the skull occurs, if the bone or the membrane (meninx) is cut through, the eyes become bloodshot and full of blood, and the horse coughs, and its legs become swollen. Such a horse cannot be saved.
A plaster by Hierocles, for the same.
One pound each of litharge and vinegar, one and a half pounds of oil,
three ounces of ammoniac gum, two ounces of wax, two ounces of resin, three ounces of
turpentine, six ounces each of bitumen, pitch, and verdigris; boil the vinegar and the
oil and the litharge. Then, when they are about to
thicken together, add the pitch, until it too is thoroughly dissolved. And,
taking the pot from the fire, add the bitumen, without
stirring it. And when it too has dissolved, add also the rest,
and boil. Then, once it has thickened, strain it into a mortar.
The plaster called 'barbara' (the barbarian plaster),
effective against fractures.
One pound each of sharp vinegar, common oil, and litharge,
six ounces of dry pitch, six ounces of wax, four ounces of Judaean bitumen,
two ounces of ammoniac gum; grind the litharge with the oil,
and boil it for a long time. And when it has boiled sufficiently, add the meltable ingredients:
first the ground pitch, and when it has dissolved,
take the pot from the fire, and add also the
bitumen, and let it dissolve. Then, putting it back on the fire,
when it boils up, add also the rest.
A yellow plaster, for the same.
One pound of dry pitch, two ounces of wax, one ounce of frankincense-
manna, four ounces of ammoniac incense, one ounce of dry resin,
one ounce of galbanum, two cotylae of vinegar. Boil the pitch and
the vinegar, add the ammoniac, spreading it out over the fire, or
pounding and sifting it. It is better to let it melt in the vinegar and
empty it into the pot. Then add the resin, the frankincense-manna,
and the galbanum.
Another.
One pint of old oil, one pound each of lard and litharge; boil these together, until bubbles rise up, and anoint with the remedy while it is lukewarm.
On wet and dry cholera (a severe digestive ailment).
Apsyrtus to Julius Fronto, centurion, greetings.
You wrote to me asking what the signs of dry cholera are; they are these:

The horse becomes hot all over its body, especially in the belly, and, when it passes dung, discharges it with force (hence it is also called 'dry'), and it avoids lying down, and is in great pain, and its mouth is hot and quite dry.
This happens, when the bile does not find easy passage through the duct leading to the bladder, and does not get discharged through urination, but remains retained, and occurs during travel or a run.

It is treated by giving an enema of soda and oil with water, and by having a rest from work and standing at ease. Let it eat soft green fodder; and if there is none, sprinkle the dry fodder with soda, or offer it with sweet wine or honey-water, and boil mallow in hot water with sweet wine, and drench it through the nostrils.
Do not offer barley, until it is purged, but give it the soaked infusion of barley with soda to drink, and use not much rubbing.
Let the enema-syringe be a small skin bag, with a little reed tube bound in and waxed, which is inserted at the sphincter; one must first remove by hand the dung lying nearby.

The wet form, when it occurs, will be recognized by these signs: the eyes become apple-yellow and glistening, the nostrils are held wide apart, it sweats at the ears and flanks, and its mouth is hot, and the veins under the tongue are likewise apple-yellow, and, shaking itself, it groans. Sometimes it also goes lame in one of its legs, which is swollen. It urinates pale and bilious fluid. And, once lying down and stretching itself out, it groans. It is said to be helped by drenching with vinegar-water, equal parts, up to two cotylae each. We ourselves have used these remedies too: grinding cumin and thyme in equal parts, mixing them with wine and honey up to a cotyla's measure, and the same amount of water, we drench through the mouth, and we draw blood from the pastern-veins. Some prescribe bathing the horse; others use the warmth from a fire and smoke.

If it is afflicted with wet cholera, the belly becomes loose, and colic-pains arise, and, standing in its stall, it pushes its chest against the wall, and rises with difficulty, and kicks, and shivers, and passes thick, dark urine. Grind wild cabbage-leaves, then, and boil them in two cotylae of old wine and half a cotyla of honey, and drench through the mouth. Opopanax and pepper, ground with old wine and drenched, do the same. Let it be given its usual feed, though a little less than usual.
Dry cholera is treated thus: wild cabbage,
likewise, and soda, ground in wine, and, once the drench has been given, let it be doused further with cold water at the navel.
Another.

Stratonicus prescribes an oxybaphon of honey and an oxybaphon of fennel-seed, and a weight of melilot, ground in a cotyla of wine and six pints of water, poured in through the mouth. And if the belly becomes constipated, insert an enema-syringe and expel the wind, or, having a boy insert his hand through the anus, clear out the dung. Give it lukewarm water to drink, adding soda little by little, and give it soft fodder.
Another.

Pound and grind a quarter-mina of viper's-bugloss root, and pour it in with wine. Or pour in ivy-leaves mixed with dark wine, or pound pomegranate-rind and wild olive and, moistening them with wine, apply to the mouth, so that it swallows them. And if it does not stop with these, prick the veins above the nostrils, and draw blood.
Another, on wet cholera.
Give roasted wheat and wheat-flour, and, grinding the herb called 'herakleia' and dissolving it in wine, pour it into the mouth with milk and wine.
Another.

If cholera troubles the animal, and it cannot sleep, grind wild myrtle and mix it with wine, and drench it into both nostrils, and do not feed it barley, and give it less water - hot water in which crushed barley has been mixed - and less of its usual feed, until it becomes cheerful again. Provide it also with a softer bedding for lying down and standing.
Grind dark ivy with wine, and drench.
By Eumelus, against oppressive/burdensome bile.

Oppressive bile is recognized by inflammation about the belly. One must, then, insert the hand and draw out the dung, and after this mix wild marjoram, wild raisin, and fine salt with boiled honey, and, making pessaries, insert them. This both purges the belly and draws off the bile. Some insert three ounces of ground myrrh with wine into the throat, and anoint the anus with liquid pitch. Others flush the belly with sea-water. Others do the same with fresh brine.
Chop leek-heads and boil them together with green barley, and give the juice, lukewarm, to drink.

Bile is naturally produced in both a wet and a dry form, and it especially afflicts the donkey and mule kinds. The signs of the dry form are these: the horse convulses over its whole body, and strikes the manger with its hooves, as though startled, and its eyes are so disturbed that it cannot look a person in the face, and it strains to pull the halter toward itself, and rolls about more frequently. This happens when the region around the heart is filled with bile. Take blood, then, from the sinew and the temples, and rub the animal down with it,
and pour in four pints of wine through the nostrils, so that, through such a fullness, it may readily be able to vomit; for through this the belly is loosened too. But if

this does not happen, evacuate the belly somewhat, or grind one drachm of black hellebore and an equal amount of linseed, and, mixing it with two cotylae of wine, give it through the mouth. And if linseed cannot be found, give two drachms of scammony instead, and afterward soak wormwood and centaury in honey-water. Pour it in through the nostrils. Wash the whole body with cold water. Or grind frankincense-manna and myrrh together in equal parts, and pour it in through the mouth.
Or grind a shrew together with these, and, with one cotyla of white wine, warming it, pour it in through the left nostril.
Another, on the wet form.

The signs of wet bile are these: lying down, it cannot easily rise; and, once roused, it trembles and collapses. This happens if it eats fresh barley that has been neither soaked nor crushed, or, having moved too vigorously, drinks cold water.

Treat it thus: grind three ounces of gall-nut, one ounce of pine, an equal amount of tanner's sumac, and an equal amount of red apple-bark, and, adding one cotyla of wine, and warming it, pour it in through the left nostril, and force it to walk about.
Another.
The signs of choleric horses are these: they go lame on each foot in turn, their skin is drawn tight, their veins are full of blood, and much heat afflicts them.
One must treat it in this manner: let blood be taken from the neck, and, on the following day, let the vein be reopened with a scalpel, and, if the blood is bad and livid, let it flow
until the blood runs clean, and let honey-water be poured in through the mouth.
Let it be fed with green fodder and flour, with dark wine added. Let the skin be loosened by rolling about and by rubbing down.
Some, grinding ivy-leaves and mixing them with wine, and warming it, poured it in through the nostril.
On carcinoma (a cancerous/malignant growth).
Another.
If an animal has a carcinoma, one must cut around it, and after this cauterize down to the living flesh, and apply ground blister-beetles with alum and henna-oil.
Another, by Hippocrates, for the same.

With sour lees, pound together chopped pine-bark, burnt pumice, hemlock-seed, and wild-cucumber root, and apply as a poultice with cold water and vinegar, and afterward rinse with wine. Use this remedy: burn white lees
with ground litharge and blue vitriol, and, taking quicklime-lye for this, apply it very dry. Anoint the surrounding area with oil. And if it hardens, anoint with vetch and honey.
Another: against carcinomas in the eyes.

If the animal is in danger of death, treat it thus: apply ground vetch with rose-oil and egg, and, once the wound is cleansed, anoint it with Attic honey, so that, once the wound has scarred over, it may be healed.
On melikerides (honey-like cysts).
By Hierocles.

Hieronymus advises cauterizing the melikerides and the blister-swellings with straight cauteries, until you have burned through the skin, sparing the inner membrane, and squeezing out the fluid, so that none is left within. Treat the burns with wax, oil, and lard melted together. And, if there is sea nearby, bathe it in the sea; if not, douse it further with cold water. It has pleased some to cauterize the melikerides with bronze rather than iron instruments.
You also have a preparation of a plaster against melikerides, set out among the compound remedies near the end of this book.
Another.

'Side-swellings' (parapresmata) is another name for melikerides, and by some they are called 'hydatides' (watery cysts), or 'kynoposin' or 'sphyroi' as they are called. These must not be cauterized, for they are of a critical (turning-point) nature. There is also another

[lacuna] ...and it will be set right. Once it rises, it holds the thigh and the leg stretched out, and drags it a long way. This happens to it especially in winter; it is restored, by being exercised and made to walk about, to its natural state.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

The melikeris is a swelling that arises about the joints, wet and thick, in which, changing to the thickness and color of honey, it has also taken its name. It is treated with this remedy: four pounds of oil, one ounce each of ammoniac incense, litharge, and white-lead, half an ounce of burnt copper, eight ounces of verdigris; mix and use it. Anointing with the remedy warmer will disperse it more quickly.
By Hippocrates, for the same.

If a horse, or one of the other beasts of burden, has melikerides, bleed it about the knees, and apply a sponge with vinegar-water, mixing in honey. And if they persist, anoint. If they persist for a longer time, cauterize it at each knee, but not deeply, so that you do not undo the joint's fitting, yet not so lightly either that you leave gaps unconnected. Treat it, removing the bandages, as with the other cauterizations.
Another.
Two pounds of oil, two ounces of ammoniac salt, eight ounces of litharge, two ounces of burnt copper, two ounces of copper-scale, enough
soda-froth, three ounces each of frankincense-manna and white-lead; mix all these together and use it.
Another.
Three ounces of soda, dry oleander-leaves, old lard, and bitumen, three ounces of each.
Or one ounce each of ammoniac salt, litharge, refined litharge, and white-lead, two ounces of burnt copper, an equal amount of verdigris, and six ounces of oil; mix all these and use it.
Another.

If a horse has melikerides, you will treat it with adhesive plasters, and on the first day rub it with salt and oil, and on the following, douse it with hot water, anointing the hooves with goose-fat and butter.
Against varicose veins (kirsoi).

If varicose veins trouble the horse, you will treat it thus: open it with a scalpel and cauterize, and rub it with salt and oil for ten days. And if it is still troubled, draw blood from it, and it will be cured.
Another.

Sometimes an animal has varicose veins, and, when it rises from sleep, it drags its leg, as though it had been dislocated. Rub it down by hand, then, and make it walk about, and it will immediately be restored to proper order.
By Pelagonius, for the same.
Continually rub the feet with alum and unctuous ointment together with very sharp vinegar.
Another.
Two weights of rock-salt, one weight of orpiment, two weights of hellebore, an equal amount of roasted chalcitis; take it up with honey and use it.
Another: to make melikerides discharge without iron.
Burnt clustered acacia, verdigris, black hellebore, Judaean bitumen, red soda, burnt

blue vitriol, old lard, juice-oil from a red whetstone, ammoniac gum, chalcitis; pound and sift all the dry ingredients equally, together with the bitumen likewise sifted, the lard having been pounded beforehand, and add them to the liquid ingredients, mixing both together, and, making a plaster, spread it on linen, and wrap around it a small ring made of wool, and place a simple chest-wrap around it, over which place again a pad, both of what is called the 'child's' padding, and bind it thus. Let it remain bound, so that the horse cannot remove it. Undoing it every other day, use the remedy, until you find the place perforated like a sieve, and its contents strained out. And after this, dry it out with the 'barbara' plaster made of vinegar, oil, litharge, pitch, bitumen, and ammoniac gum.
A plaster, applied hot, against melikerides that have already discharged.
Four pounds of common oil, one pound of ammoniac gum, one pound each of litharge and burnt blue vitriol, six ounces of verdigris; mix in one ounce of white-lead, boil, and use it.
Another, by Helenus the horse-doctor: an emollient against melikerides.

Put a little oil into a pot, and, warming it, add six ounces of litharge and an equal amount of lard, and, straining it, add one pound of wax and one pound of resin, six ounces of cone-resin, one ounce of chalcitis, six ounces of melted misy, an equal amount of depilatory, four pounds of opopanax, four ounces of galbanum, a little less than half a pint of salt, six ounces of vinegar.
Another, a hot emollient, for the same.
Put oil into a pot, and, making it hot, add six ounces of litharge, one ounce of wax, six ounces of litharge-scum, six ounces of propolis; warm these in a small iron bowl, and apply to the knee.
Another emollient against fresh melikerides.

Half a pint of vinegar, six ounces of ammoniac salt, four ounces of ivy-berries, four ounces of crushed roasted-barley seed, six grains of dove-dung, two ounces of frankincense-manna, four ounces of quicklime-lye; put all these into a pot, first the vinegar, then, adding the ammoniac gum and the resin and the rest, boil. And when it is boiled, take it from the fire, and, spreading it onto linen, apply it, and bind it with a bandage, and undo it every five days, and douse with hot water. Then, warming the same remedy, apply it for five more days, and you will cure it.

Another: on the prognosis of a 'side-swelling' (parapresma). First, when it stands above the pastern-cushion, small swellings arise, the size of mustard-seeds or a little larger, joined one to another. This happens from a run, or a long journey, or overloading.
Another: the cure of a side-swelling. Take a lancet, pierce and cut into the vessel, then take oil and salt and grind them, then foment it and rub it with wax-ointment.

Preparation of pessaries against side-swellings. Three ounces of chalcitis, an equal amount of verdigris, four ounces of black fennel, four ounces of melted misy, three ounces of blue vitriol, three ounces each of black gall-nut, lees, and depilatory... [gap] ...enough flower,
enough Alexandrian cumin, add sharp vinegar, and, grinding it in a mortar and making pessaries, dry them and use them.
Another: to remove hydatid-cysts without iron.
By Tiberius.

Four drachms of oleander-leaves, six drachms of spurge, four drachms of dove-dung, an equal amount of cress-seed, two drachms of wild germander, three drachms of adarce; grind all these carefully, and mix in vinegar, and, working it up with lard, use it on the affected places.
Another, on a side-swelling.

Opening the vein above the pastern-cushion, let it bleed, and, chopping fresh soft wild-fig fruit fine, boil it in wine, and apply as a poultice with cow-dung. And if this does not work, lance the vein at the hock, and let about a cotyla's worth flow out, and grind roasted salt with oil and apply, mixing in crushed-vetch flour and a little honey.
By Hierocles, on 'prēsma' (swelling).

Swellings arise especially from a vigorous run, and the front fetlocks swell, so as to seem full of fluid. Lance the vein below the pastern-cushion, then, and douse it. And if this remedy does not help, shave the swollen place and score it, and, as it discharges its fluid, soak it with vinegar-water; on the following day, use the galbanum-emollient.
Remove the dung, and add ten ounces of Egyptian soda, and the tender parts of the Egyptian mulberry, or of its root... [lacuna]
By Hierocles.

If the hoof is pierced by a wooden splinter, or a bone, or a potsherd, one must remove the splinter, and, having first cleansed it, anoint it with the remedy made of verdigris or misy, or with another wound-remedy, and plug it with a sponge. On the following day, wash out the wound with unmixed wine, and anoint it with the remedy, until the abnormal swelling has gone down to nothing, then treat it with the dry dressing compounded with alum.
By Hierocles.

If an abscess arises from a jump, or a fall while rolling, or a blow, or a fall, grind quicklime thoroughly, and, pouring on wine, add an equal measure of oil. And when it reaches the consistency of a paste, anoint the swollen place, taking in also a little of the healthy tissue around it. Or knead the purest wheat-flour with vinegar, and pour on two weights of frankincense-manna and two eggs, and, making it the thickness of honey, anoint the swollen place, likewise taking in some of the healthy tissue.
By Hierocles.

Chop cypress-tips, and one pound of gall-nut, half a pound each of lard and wax, and, kneading about one pound of unripe-olive juice with vinegar, apply as a poultice. Apsyrtus says that one must first wipe it clean daily with its own urine, and sprinkle on black lime, until it is healed.
Against 'karides' (a hoof affliction).
By Hierocles.

When, from necessity, an animal has been cauterized, on the first day let the applied plugs be soaked with fine salt and oil. On the following days, let it be anointed with children's bath-oil-scrapings for seven days, twice a day, so that the scabs fall off, then let it be wiped clean with old wine and hot water mixed together. After the wiping, let it immediately be soaked with wine and oil, sprinkling in also vetch-flour. And if you cannot procure bath-oil-scrapings, grind wax, liquid pitch, pig-fat, salt, and oil together, and anoint with feathers.

And if, on the seventh day, the scabs have not fallen off from the ointment, there is danger that something internal has ruptured, and that it has fallen into inescapable danger. The best season for cauterizing is spring and summer.
Another, for the same.

One pound of wax, two ounces of propolis, two ounces of ammoniac gum, one ounce of unwashed wool-grease, two ounces of galbanum, two ounces of frankincense-manna, four ounces of mistletoe-glue, one ounce of soda-froth, two ounces of pepper.
Another.

One pound of wax, one ounce of propolis, two ounces of ammoniac gum, one ounce of unwashed wool-grease, two ounces of galbanum, four ounces of bitumen, two ounces of opopanax, two ounces of soda, one ounce of split alum, two ounces of pepper, two ounces of mistletoe-glue, one ounce of sulfur.
On figs (fig-warts) and ant-warts (myrmekiai).
By Apsyrtus.
