To Herodion of Alexandria, horse-doctor, greetings. As for the fig-warts, or so-called ant-warts, that arise in horses, mules, or donkeys, in whatever part of the body, but especially

on the extremities, one must not cauterize them, but cut them off, and scrape close with glass, and, grinding raw chalcitis in a mortar, bandage it on, and do this daily, and do not apply water, and it will become healthy. One must especially avoid cauterizing when it is located at the crown of the hoof; for such places scar over only with difficulty.

Apsyrtus advises against cauterizing the so-called fig-warts and ant-warts, wherever in the body they occur, but especially on the extremities; instead, cut them off and scrape close, then grind raw chalcitis and apply it, binding it on, and do this daily, not bringing water to the place, until it becomes healthy. He especially forbids cauterizing when it occurs at the crown of the hoof; for it scars over only with difficulty there.

It happens that, at the heel of the hind foot, right by the frog itself, a sore arises, which they call a 'sykē' (fig-sore). The horse is troubled by this, then, and goes lame and is in pain, and does not allow anyone to touch it. One must, then, treat this as quickly as possible with the cautery and other remedies. For, if it becomes chronic, in walking the hoof comes to be strained down onto the toe, and the horse becomes altogether lame. This happens to the donkey and mule, but not readily to the horse.
Another, against ant-warts.
One ounce of quicklime, one ounce of pounded litharge-scum, one pint of dripping lye, one ounce of frankincense, two ounces of lees, two ounces of
salt-lye, two ounces of verdigris, two ounces of vinegar.
Another.

Grind two ounces each of misy, blue vitriol, quicklime, and verdigris, and, having first cut out the wart and cauterized it, sprinkle this on. And if it is around the eye or eyelid, grind it with honey and anoint, having first removed the wart with a hair-ligature and applied small cauteries.
Another.

If ant-warts arise on the feet, take two ounces of chalcitis and one ounce of red ochre, two ounces of lees, and boil pomegranate-rind with vinegar, then also pound the pomegranate itself, and mix it in with these, and, straining it, apply it to a rag and pour it on. Use also the wound-remedy.
Another.
First cut it out, then apply honey and quicklime, and, pounding and sifting willow-bark, mix it in, and, anointing with it, you will cure it.
By Hierocles, for the same.

Having cut out the ant-warts, pour on sulfur, bitumen. Or burn dry colocynth, grind it, and sprinkle it on. Or burn the fern called 'pteris,' and pound and sift it, and do the same. Or boil goat's-beard root in water, and, grinding it, apply as a poultice. You also have other remedies against ant-warts written down among the compound preparations.
Another.

Two ounces each of soft alum, clustered cadmia, and misy, four ounces of chalcitis, two ounces of gum, enough gum-resin drippings; soak the gum in the drippings, add the rest, and, making troches, use them.
Another.
One ounce each of white quicklime, lees, dove-dung, and orpiment,

six ounces of chalcitis, enough gum-resin drippings; grind these and dissolve them in wine, and anoint the ant-warts, binding them with a hair or a fine sinew-thread. And when they fall off, sprinkle on this remedy once it has dried.
On neuritic horses (afflicted with a nerve/sinew ailment).
By Apsyrtus.

The neuritic horse suffers pain in the neck, and stretches out its head, and throws its muzzle upward. It is unable to open its mouth, and so it neither eats nor drinks. And, extending its member, it urinates little by little, and does nothing as regards its belly. It happens that, while walking, it staggers and falls onto its neck, because its internal sinews are drawn taut. Such a horse cannot live.
By Hierocles.

For those already seized by the neuritic affliction, no remedy can help at all. But it is good that the signs be recorded, so that no one, supposing the neuritic horse to have fallen into some other affliction, and being unable to cure it, should be condemned for it. The neuritic horse, then, stretches its neck taut, and extends its head, and is unable to raise its face or open its mouth, and so can neither eat nor drink. And, extending its genitals, it urinates little by little, and its belly does not move. It happens too that, while walking, it staggers and falls onto its neck, because its internal sinews are drawn extremely taut. For this reason, as I have said, a horse already seized by it could not live.
On wounds affecting the sinews.
By Apsyrtus.
Best for horses against wounds affecting the sinews: old olive-

lees, boiled down to a third - one cotyla; one cotyla of the pressed juice of boiled elm-root bark; half a cotyla of bull's gall; four staters of fine birthwort (or, if bull's gall is not available, that of a wild goat). Pour these together into a vessel and boil them in the open air. And when it is boiled, take a twig and let a drop fall onto a potsherd, and, if it sets, take it off promptly and use it.
Another, against sinew-wounds.

One pound of wax, eight ounces of oil, three ounces of verdigris, one pound of roasted grain, three ounces of frankincense-manna, enough vinegar; grind the manna together with the verdigris in sufficient vinegar and mix, and anoint.
Another, against pain of the sinews.

One pound of wax, one and a half pounds of storax, one pound of verdigris, one and a half pounds of propolis, one and a half pounds of white wax, one and a half pounds of poppy, four and a half pounds of bay-berries.
On lice and worms.
Wounds should be treated with pitch, oil, and lard, or with red ochre ground and sprinkled on. Quicklime, rubbed on while fresh, also helps, or likewise chamaeleon-root rubbed on does the same.
Another, by Hippocrates.

The affliction of worms is hard to cure, or rather incurable. These are the signs that appear in the suffering horse: it throws itself down on the ground, and rolls about, and whinnies. Take cabbage juice, then, and oil and soda, and drench through the

nostrils and the mouth. Or grind three ounces of litharge-scale and dried figs and four ounces of blue vitriol together, and add oil with vinegar, and, making large pessaries, as large as the nostrils can hold, insert them through them.
By Pelagonius, on lice and worms
that arise in the anus or in the belly.

Scatter unripe mulberries among the barley that the horse eats. Many also boil mulberry root in water, and douse the area around the belly and anus with it. And if it also causes a wound, they are treated with ironwort and leek-juice, mixed with salt and pitch and oil and old lard.
By Hierocles, on lice.

If lice arise in the mane, or over the whole body, one must grind fresh hemlock and anoint with it. Or chop cyclamen root and pour on oil and anoint together, and, after one day, wipe it clean with urine or a decoction of lupine-seeds, and, once wiped clean, anoint the lice-infested parts with pitch-oil.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

If lice arise on a horse or another beast of burden, one must cleanse the whole body, then chop cyclamen root and press out its juice, and, mixing it with oil, anoint. On the following day, wash it off with warm dripping lye, and anoint again.
Another.
Sprinkle sharp brine onto the barley and the fodder, and, by eating it, the horse will be cured.
Another.
If you wish to kill wild lice, if they are

internal, take about two cotylae of sandarach-juice and drench; and if external, take enough of the same sandarach with oil and anoint. Or anoint with hot olive-lees in the sun, and they will fall off.
On those bitten by a viper.

Apsyrtus to Julius Saturninus, decurion, greetings. You wrote to me asking what signs accompany one bitten by a viper. They are these: the body shivers, and the eyes swell, and the mouth and teeth are affected, and the hairs of the mane fall out, sometimes also of the tail, and discharges arise from the body with a foul smell. It is treated by drenching with thirty grains of white or black pepper, ground with wine, through the mouth, or with chopped thyme in wine, or with tordylium in wine, or with rose-oil in wine, or with rue ground in wine, or with the herb wormwood boiled. This affliction carries danger.
By Hierocles, for the same.

Some have run together the discussion of those bitten by a viper, or scorpions, or spiders, or shrews; but we shall speak of each clearly, one by one. When, then, a horse is bitten by a viper, a shivering runs through the body, and the eyes swell, and it grinds its teeth, and the hairs of the mane fall out, and eruptions arise from the body with an unpleasant smell. It is treated by drenching with thirty grains of white pepper, ground with wine, through the mouth, or with thyme in wine, or with the wormwood plant boiled in wine.
Some advise cutting the bite and cauterizing it,
then drenching. One must wipe the broken places clean with urine
and anoint them with a soft remedy.
Another, by Pelagonius, against bites
from a viper, a shrew, and a spider.
Earth from an ant-hill, drenched with wine, helps those who have been struck,
and rubbing the bites themselves with it also helps.
And if this ever happens to a horse on the road, where
the proper remedies cannot be found, take thirty grains of white pepper,
and, adding one pint of old wine, pour it
through a horn into the throat. Or give the herb thyme,
ground, with wine.
This too is said to be
suitable against all kinds of bites from venomous creatures: apply
asphodel root, ground with old wine, to the bites.
This too works: take swallow chicks and,
cutting them open, apply them to the wound. And also the nest
of the swallow itself, ground with old wine, apply
to the struck places. Against bites from spiders and shrews, chop mallow and grind it carefully, and store it away for use.
On those stung by a scorpion. By Apsyrtus.

For one bitten by a scorpion, dragging of the legs follows, and lameness, and refusal to eat, and a flow of pale humor from the nostrils, and difficulty rising and being roused likewise. It is treated as written above for those bitten by a viper.
By Hierocles, for the same.

Those stung by a scorpion drag their feet and go lame, and do not eat, and pale humor flows from the nostrils, and they breathe with difficulty. They will, however, be treated in the same way as those bitten by a viper.

Apply pig dung as a poultice to the struck part, or pound nightshade, or spurge, or henbane, or linseed, or roasted alum, or soda-froth, or rock-salt; for any one of these, applied as a poultice, will help quickly.

Pierce the wound with a reed, or, burning that same reed, rub the animal with its ash. Or grind the wormwood plant with chamomile and mix with wine, and give to drink. Or do the same with the root of the plant 'prosopitis.' Or warm four grammes of fig-tree root with one pint of wine, and give through the nostrils. Or apply to the sting earth mixed with oil, vinegar, and laser-resin, or a swallow's crop, or the nest of the same chicks, ground. Or dissolve the ash of burnt reeds in wine and give to drink.
The spider kind readily breeds, in the same way as

cobwebs, in the fodder. If the horse, while eating, takes in and swallows their brood, it is in danger, and will die. It is treated by drenching with wine and pepper, or with thyme in wine, or with deer rennet together with wine. It will be recognized by these signs: it wastes away in body, and likewise eruptions arise from the body resembling boils, with a putrid smell, and the eyes swell, and the urine comes out web-like, and it takes food only with difficulty and in small amounts. Best of all, in the case of all bites from venomous creatures, is to burn through the struck place as soon as one becomes aware of it.
By Hierocles, for the same.

The spider kind breeds, in the same way as cobwebs, into bundles of fodder. If, then, the horse, while eating, eats their brood, or is even bitten by a spider, it is in danger. You will recognize it by the body becoming inflamed, and eruptions resembling boils arising, and the urine being web-like, and, further, by its not desiring food, but taking only a little with difficulty. Treat it, then, by drenching with pepper in wine, or with thyme, or with thick birthwort, or likewise with deer rennet. Some approve, if it has been bitten, cutting around the place or cauterizing it, then drenching.
Another, against bites from spiders.
Grind one ounce of pepper, half an ounce of pellitory, and one ounce of wild grape together with wine, and pour it through the throat.
By Hierocles, on beasts of burden bitten by spiders or vipers.
If one of the beasts of burden eats a spider, or is bitten by one, its genitals swell, so that it seems to urinate something web-like, and it sweats all over.
It is treated thus: if it has been bitten, cut around the place or cauterize it; if it has eaten the creature, drench it. Use also these treatments for the bite itself:

take birthwort and grind it with fragrant wine, and pour it in; likewise wild celery-seed, or, failing that, cultivated celery-seed, and grind bay-berries in two cotylae of wine, adding rose-oil, and pour it in through the mouth.
Stand it in a warm place, then lead it into a bath-house, and douse it with hot water.

Give it barley-gruel and tender bay-leaves as feed, and the best fodder, and give it warm water to drink, until it yields; let it also have walks, and cauterize, as has been said, and drench, until it becomes healthy.
And if it is bitten by a viper, black pus comes out from the bite, or runs from it.
And if the animal is female, treat it thus: cut the bite, cauterize it, and drench with the same remedies as for the spider-bite.
Wipe the broken parts clean, and anoint with the soft remedy.
Another: on buprestis-beetle or spider poisoning.

If a horse swallows a buprestis-beetle or a spider together with its fodder, its belly becomes distended with gas, and it becomes averse to food, and its whole body becomes stretched taut, and it passes dung more frequently, and it breathes in short breaths.
Treat it, then, thus: binding it, bend the head back, and open the veins above the nostrils, so that
the blood may flow out through the mouth, and drench with boiled cabbage, and give it to eat with fish-sauce and oil.
If a horse is bitten by a snake, one must first bleed it, and apply millet and wheat as a poultice twice a day, and do this twice daily for three days.
Another, for the same.
If a horse has a snake-bite, swelling occurs over
the whole body, and the eyes become bloodshot and swollen,
and the anus turns inside out, and the penis protrudes, and it becomes
quite chilled. Drench, then, with one pint of wine, and give it to eat
bay-leaves or wild asparagus, and anoint with wine-and-oil and boiled bay-berries.
Draw blood from the neck, then, of polemonia
and birthwort, six ounces of each, mix with one pint of wine, and
drench. And if it has been bitten by a viper, take from the viper's-bugloss
plant's root, and the root of polemonia, six ounces of each,
and, grinding each and mixing it with wine, pour it through the left
nostril.
On the bite of a shrew.
If a shrew bites, a hard swelling arises around
the place, and the horse groans at brief intervals. It is helped by pricking
the place and anointing it with cabbage ground with
vinegar, and likewise with wormwood, or with onions and vinegar, or with
garlic likewise, or with chaste-tree berries ground with vinegar. It is also said
that anointing with earth from a wheel-rut, kneaded with vinegar, is
beneficial. And if it happens that a pregnant female donkey is bitten by
a pregnant shrew, there is danger of death. For fever and refusal of food follow. Also burning cyclamen
and mixing the ash with vinegar does the same, and also wearing the shrew itself as an amulet.

If a shrew bites, the whole animal becomes distended with gas, and its eyes water, and fluid drips from the swelling and the belly, and it will not take food. Take, then, the dust that arises from the friction of wheels, soak it with sharp vinegar, and, pricking the bitten place, first anoint it with this mud. Some, among them Tarantinus, say one should pound garlic and apply it, and fumigate with deer-horn. Apsyrtus, indeed, says it is better, in the case of all bites from venomous creatures, to burn through the place as soon as one becomes aware of it. Stratonicus, for a shrew-bite,

advises scarifying especially the swollen parts, and soaking them with vinegar and salt. On the following day, having rinsed it with fresh water, knead Cimolian earth with vinegar and anoint, and treat the bite with children's bath-oil-scrapings, until it heals.

If any of the animals is bitten by a shrew, grind an oxybaphon of black cumin in fragrant wine, and give it through the nostrils. Apply dog dung as a poultice to the wound. This is also beneficial for humans.
It generally happens that the horse is bitten in the stable. For, once it has lain down, the shrew creeps in gently against its flanks, and, when the horse stirs meanwhile,

the shrew, disturbed, bites the underlying spot, from which a certain swelling results. You will treat this, then, thus: take an oxybaphon of ground black cumin, mix it with wine, and drench, or pound garlic, and mix in equal parts of salt and cumin, and, kneading them with wine, anoint; or knead earth from a wheel-rut with urine.

Or grind the shrew itself, and drench with one pint of wine. And if you do not have a shrew, knead it with potter's clay and anoint. Or boil celery-seed in wine and oil and drench. Or scarify the swollen place with a straight lancet. And if the inflammation becomes more extensive, cauterize around it in a circle with a rounded cautery, taking in also some of the surrounding area. Cauterize with straight cauteries, so that the humors may flow off.

And if the swollen place ulcerates more extensively, burn barley and grind it finely and sprinkle it on, first anointing with old lard. There will be no ulceration, unless a pregnant shrew has bitten.
Another, for the same, by Pelagonius.

By Pelagonius. The shrew treats the danger it brings about with its own body. For the animal itself, thrown into oil and drowned, once it has rotted and been ground, and applied to the bite, becomes the cause of healing. And if this cannot be found, grind cumin, and, adding a little liquid pitch and a little lard, so as to have the consistency of an emollient, apply it, and you will free the horse from danger. And before the inflammation dissolves, if it should produce pus, you would do well, if
you remove the outer skin with a scalpel, and cauterize the whole affected area, and thus apply liquid pitch with oil.

There is also a preventive remedy, so that a horse is not bitten by a shrew, namely this: catch the shrew itself, and plaster it round with gypsum, and, once it has hardened, bind it to the animal's neck. For thus animals will be kept unharmed from a shrew's bite.
Another, for the same.

The shrew makes bites large in proportion to its own size. And if it is small, acting more mildly, the treatment is also easier. Worst of all is the bite of a pregnant shrew. The difference in the bite is shown by the size of the inflammation. One must, then, help in this manner: grind garlic with soda, or, if soda cannot be found, rub the struck places with salt and cumin. And when the inflamed matter breaks open into a wound, then, having washed the wound clean, burn barley, and sprinkle on its ash, and do nothing else. For if you use another remedy, you will only increase the severity of the wound further. Give also a preliminary drench prepared from dill, wheat-flour, a little cedar-tar, and one pint of wine.
By Hierocles, on the stingray.
If a sea-stingray strikes a horse, it becomes very dangerous. One must, then, apply the cautery, and stop the flow of blood, and drench through the mouth with the
stingray's own liver, ground in one cotyla of wine.
On those bitten by a rabid animal.
If a rabid dog bites someone, grind together six ounces each of goat dung, old salt-fish, and hyssop, and forty large walnuts, and apply.
On leeches.
By Apsyrtus.

To Bebius, decurion, greetings. I want you to know that, when watering the herds, one must especially watch out for leeches lurking in the water. For they attach themselves under the tongue and the lips. This is the lesser evil; for, laying the horse down, one can remove them. But when they pass down further, they cause the animal to waste away; and if there are many, it dies more quickly. For the one caught in the manger's water-trough, pour oil in through a horn; once touched by it, they fall off.
For the same, by Hierocles.

Leeches are wont to fall into the mouth of a horse while it drinks; one must open the mouth and remove them. And if several pass down further, toward the throat, it is in danger. One must, then, drench with water-and-oil and dislodge them. Others advise rubbing them with fine salt, or grinding thick birthwort in very sharp vinegar, making it the thickness of honey, and, adding oil, rubbing it wherever they are attached, drawing the tongue out of the mouth. It is fitting for those in charge of the herds to pay attention and watch out for leeches in the water, so that they are not swallowed by the horses in their drink, and, while the horses drink, become attached under the tongue and the lips.
If they notice they are in the mouth, it is necessary to throw the horse down and pick them out.
By Theomnestus.

If a horse or another beast of burden drinks a leech in water, blood-tinged water is discharged from its mouth, if the leech has attached itself to its tongue. One must, then, take note and remove it with a fig-leaf or a rough rag. And when one or more become lodged in the gullet or the throat, they suck out the animal's blood, and it wastes away. And whatever remedies you drench it with, you will accomplish nothing, for the animal will die. The only remedy that seems best to us is to drench with oil; for the oil, once it touches them, expels the leeches, and they die at once.
Against leeches stuck fast in the mouth.
Crush five bedbugs in the hand, and stick them to the mouth, and the leeches will immediately drop off. And if they are around the throat, place the bedbugs on a fire and fumigate with the smoke.
By Hippocrates.

Hippocrates says: if a horse or another beast of burden swallows a leech, or it goes up into the nostrils, and blood flows from that place, blow in salt or oil. Then push them out with flesh-forceps. Or burn them through with a cautery. Then burn bread, grind it finely, and, sprinkling it with wine, apply as a poultice.
On 'ornithia' (bird-droppings sickness).
By Apsyrtus.

It happens that birds breed in the mangers and pass liquid droppings there. If the horse takes this in, eating the dropping, and swallows it, it is troubled and endangered. These are the signs: it will excrete something thin and mucous. It is helped thus:
grind white bird-dung and one weight of lard together,
and mix in two choenixes of barley-groats, and, kneading it with wine, give it to eat, making little balls of it. Let the wine be dry and dark.
Another.
If a horse eats bird-dung, drench with five cyathi of celery-seed
with one pint of wine and half a pint of honey. And
Let it walk about, until its belly moves. And if
from the affliction some shivering and hair-standing-on-end appear in the horse as signs, do this:

mix enough bay-berries and half a pound of soda, one pint of vinegar and one pint of oil, and anoint in a warm place for three days. Or mix one ounce of sweet-flag, one ounce of dill, one spoonful of chopped and sifted all-heal root, in four ounces of wine and warm oil, and, warming it, drench.
And if you fail with this, in this case chop enough wild-fig leaves, and give them lukewarm, for the same number of days.
By Hierocles, for the same.
It happens, sometimes, that birds breed in the mangers and also pass droppings there, which becomes dangerous to a horse that eats it.
You will recognize this, if you see it passing mucous dung.
Grind, then, one weight of the white, firm bird-dung with lard,
mix in two choenixes of barley-groats, and, kneading it with wine, making
cakes, give it to eat. Let the wine be dark and dry.
By Eumelus, for the same.
Take about one ounce of older bird-dung, and, dissolving it
with fenugreek-flour, and mixing in two dates and good
wine, give it through the mouth. Or grind the inner part of a bird's gizzard together with the dung found in it, and give it with half a pint of wine to drink.
On wild cabbage.
By Apsyrtus.

Against those that have eaten wild cabbage in the fodder given, or in pasture, one must use this remedy: chop cultivated cabbage, pour on milk, and, pressing out its juice, holding the tongue, drench through the mouth; or mix water with the cabbage, or boil figs with water and mix it with the cabbage decoction. It is also said that one should grind sea-crabs and mix them with the cabbage juice. Give it for three days, until the animal excretes the cabbage. It will be recognized by these signs: it becomes bound up all over, and its hindquarters become paralyzed, and it cannot walk, but falls and rises again, until it excretes the cabbage.
By Hierocles, for the same.

If it eats wild cabbage in fodder or while grazing, it becomes bound up all over, and drags its hindquarters, and cannot walk, but is thrown down, until it excretes the cabbage. One must, then, chop cultivated cabbage, and, pouring milk over it, strain it into fragrant wine, then drench through the mouth. Or boil figs and mix them with the cabbage decoction, and drench likewise. Or grind sea-crabs and mix them with the cabbage juice, and drench twice a day, until it excretes it.
On 'myophonon' (mouse-bane, a poisonous plant).
By Hierocles.

If a horse grazes on what is called 'myophonon,' and then is seen to droop its head, and likewise its whole body, lance a vein at the temples, and drench with wild or cultivated celery-seed in wine, or pound rue and, pouring on old wine, drench.
On hemlock.
On caterpillars.
By Hierocles.

Sometimes, when horses roll about among caterpillars, or rub themselves against a tree infested with caterpillars, welts arise, and the skin swells and becomes hard, and the eyes become sunken. One must, then, take very sharp vinegar, half a mina of soda, and a quarter-portion of blue vitriol, and, grinding these, anoint the whole body, taking care that none gets into the eyes.
On shagginess (of the coat).
By Apsyrtus.

If a horse is shaggy in its coat, soak about half a choenix of white chickpeas, and, mixing in an equal amount of raisins, add them to the barley for thirty days, and it will grow a smooth coat. Giving more barley also achieves the same.
By Hierocles, for the same.
If a horse is shaggy in its coat, one must soak half a choenix of small chickpeas and mix in half that of raisins, and add them to the barley for thirty days, and it will grow a smooth coat. And when

it is bled, let it be anointed all over its body with its own blood, and let this remain for three days. On the third day, if it is combed with the currycomb used for grooming, it will have a smooth coat.
On the emergence of teeth.

Apsyrtus to Menecrates of Clazomenae, greetings. I wish you to know, in horses and other solid-hoofed animals, the emergence of the teeth and the progression of years. We have observed it thus: at thirty months, the foal first sheds the so-called middle incisors, two above and two below, which are the most important and the largest. It sheds the second pair at the beginning of the fourth year, within six months, and later one above and one below on each side. It seems also to grow its canine teeth at that time.

In another twelve months it completes its full set. Having completed five years and, entering the sixth, completed that year, it will have all its teeth level, and it is no longer easy to determine the remaining years by them. It is said, however, that when the teeth appear to protrude, and the eyebrows are also gray, and the area beneath the eyebrows and the eyes are more hollow, it has been observed by all that the horse is then in its sixteenth year.

From the completion of its set, the soft-hoofed horse is in its prime for another eight years, the hard-hoofed for ten. Know that, if you work it more than this time, it becomes exhausted and cannot endure it. For the pastern-joints of the forefeet, called the 'mesokynia,' become loosened at the ankles,

and it can neither walk nor stand, but throws itself down. The hard-hoofed horse lives, from birth to old age, twenty-eight or twenty-nine years, but does not easily complete thirty; the soft-hoofed, twenty-four.

Some shed their teeth, from the first to the second, at an interval of eight months, and, having shed the last ones, wait the same interval. In the earliest period, no horse that is shedding its first teeth exceeds or falls behind another, but in the rest, the same does not hold for all, nor do they keep the same interval, but the second teeth catch up with the first, and the last with the second. We have found that those shedding their first teeth shed, at the same time, the front molars, one above and one below on each side, the first ones,

and change the attachments related to them. And when, from the completion of the set, another three years have passed, the tooth cracks and becomes rounded and triangular, and it is then especially that a flux settles into the mouths of horses.

It has, in front, eight teeth above and eight below, including the canines, and molars, on one jaw, six above and six below, and likewise on the other. In all, it has forty teeth, apart from the attachments; the donkey and mule have thirty-six, including the attachments.
By Tiberius, a repellent remedy against fluxed teeth, also useful for humans.
One ounce of roasted pennyroyal, one ounce each of Illyrian iris and roasted
rock-salt, a third of an ounce of burnt cuttlefish-bone, three ounces of burnt whelk-shell, one gramme each of pepper and myrrh.
An astringent for the teeth, so that it holds the socket for one year and six months.

Three ounces of bramble-tips, three ounces of unripe grape, one ounce each of pomegranate and split alum, one ounce each of soreus, verdigris, and misy, three ounces of Alexandrian thistle. Grind these and boil them in vinegar, until reduced to a quarter. And when the animal is about to shed its first teeth, dip a small sponge into it and apply it to the gums, inside and outside, three times a month. For if the teeth already hang loose, so as to be about to fall out, press them with the fingers and astringe them with the remedy, and it will hold for the aforesaid time.
On how one must cauterize, and when.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Rufus Octavius, greetings. Since you are earnest in every part of horse-medicine, and ask in what manner one must cauterize, we shall show you, so that it may be clear both to those experienced in the work and to laymen. For fever, one must apply the cautery from the head, along both sides of the mane-ridge, in long lines, placing, alongside the mane, alternating upright, V-shaped burns down to the point where the shoulders emerge. For, since this region governs the body and is not overcome by the affliction, the animal will not die. And for those with opisthotonos, one must cauterize the same places thus, drawing off

the affliction in the opposite direction. We shall cauterize the horse with kidney trouble at the junction of the hips and the bladder, with upright burns, not more than twenty-four, half on each side of the spine, making three rows, spaced three fingers' breadth apart. We shall cauterize side-swellings near the hollow of the knee, if they are fresh and soft, but no longer once they have formed a hard callus.

And when, from travel and burdens, a flux settles into the knee, or it is in pain from a blow and goes lame chronically, or, having slipped and fallen, suffers a separation of the bones, or the fetlocks come to ache from travel and burdens, and the sinews and vessels in them swell, and from this a 'parasphyron' results, this too must be cauterized. But those in which fluxes settle into the fetlocks, which are called side-swellings, or melikerides, or hydatides, or into the knees, must not be cauterized. Likewise, sprains in the feet must not be cauterized.

For it happens that the pastern-joint becomes locked, when the cauteries are applied over the pastern-cushion and its point of attachment. This is a mistake that those who do it make. For the other hoof cannot come down properly, and the horse becomes lame.
'Excess growths' is the name given to what in Latin they call 'phalcinina.' These are eruptions in the body resembling boils, but larger, and they suppurate and burst open spontaneously.
These too must not be cauterized. For it is an outpouring of a hard, arthritic humor, which must be drawn out.
But if they are cauterized around,

it necessarily results in a narrowing of the outlet. For it happens that the matter shifts to another part of the body, especially to the joints, and produces swelling and lameness. They must be treated by dousing with hot water and anointing with the fatty ointment.

Cauterization wounds are treated thus: on the first day, one must soak the applied plugs with fine salt and oil, dipping them in with feathers, and on the following days with children's bath-oil-scrapings, twice a day, for up to seven days, so that the scabs fall off. Then wipe it clean with old wine and hot water mixed together, and, after wiping, soak it with wine and oil, and sprinkle on vetch-flour; on the following days use hot water twice a day, and the vetch-flour likewise. And if there is no bath-oil-scrapings, one must use this compound instead: mix wax, liquid pitch, pig-fat, salt, and oil, and grind them together, and anoint with feathers. For the horse with kidney trouble, if, on the seventh day, the scabs do not fall off from the ointment, know that something internal has ruptured, and that it cannot live, though it may linger on for a while. The best season for cauterizing is spring and summer.
By Theomnestus, on cauteries.
As for side-swellings, or so-called melikerides, which arise in the hind legs, which ones must be cauterized, and when?
We shall say that we cauterize them when they are fresh; but once they have formed a hard callus, we shall bleed instead. As for fetlocks and knees, and whatever
parts are around the sinews, we shall cauterize sparingly; but not too deeply,
since, by cauterizing, we shall lame the sinews. And when, from running
and traveling, the knees become wrinkled and bent from blows,
and are painful, and it goes lame chronically, or
it falls while traveling, and a separation of the bones occurs, we shall
cauterize down to the hide. Pains also arise around the fetlocks
to the beasts of burden from long journeys or burdens, and it
happens that their sinews are in pain and their vessels swell,
and the fetlocks become larger than natural, especially
as time goes on. Such animals are called 'parasphyra.'
These, then, must be cauterized sparingly, with straight cauteries.
But those into whose fetlocks or knees fluxes settle, and
which produce side-swellings, or melikerides, which some call hydatides,
these must not be cauterized. Nor, indeed, the sprains near the hoof-wall;
for the hoof-wall will fall off, and another will not grow, and
the animal will become useless. Nor, indeed, must one cauterize the swellings that arise
over the whole body, resembling boils. For it is
an outpouring of a hard humor, and, being sealed up by the cauteries, it turns
back inward, and harms the animal. And the hydatid-cysts in the joints
must not be cauterized.
As for the scars
resulting from the cauteries, we shall treat them by dousing with hot water, then
softening them and anointing with the fatty ointment. As for the burns themselves,
we shall treat them, on the first day, with fine salt, well ground
with oil, applying the anointing with feathers. On the
following

days, we shall anoint likewise with feathers, using a compound remedy made from wax, liquid pitch, pig-fat, salt, and oil, made to the consistency of bath-oil-scrapings. And when, after seven days, the scabs fall off, wash it clean with warm water-and-oil.

After the wiping, soak it with wine and oil, and sprinkle on vetch-flour made into flour, and, on the following day, wash it with hot water twice a day, and use the fat-based remedy, as described above. As for the kidney-trouble horse cauterized at the hips, if the scabs do not fall off within seven days, know that this one is in a poor state, and that something internal has ruptured, or the kidneys have been torn away.
Another caustic poultice.

Knead one part of fresh quicklime and an equal part of burnt wine-lees with mastic-tree lye, or lye from bean-straw, or from olive-pits, and use this fresh. Or grind fresh caper and apply. Or grind mullein leaves, and dissolve them with fig-sap and vinegar. Or one drachm of fresh quicklime and three drachms of soda-froth, and two weights of burnt sour lees, boiled in sharp lye, use it.
Another caustic, for lamenesses.

For swellings, hardenings, or fresh melikerides in the joints, or anywhere else, arising from a blow or some other cause, or even spontaneously, this is the treatment: eight staters of bitumen, four staters of Colophonian resin, four staters of dry pitch, six staters of wax, one stater of galbanum, one stater of opopanax, one stater of quicklime;
warm all these together to a heat the hand can bear, and anoint.
Another caustic, against pains of the sinews.
Put in equal parts galbanum, storax, bdellium, frankincense-meal, Brittany pitch, and bitumen, and, grinding the dry ingredients and mixing them with the liquid ones, use it.
Another.
One ounce of orpiment, six ounces of quicklime; grind each separately and mix, and use it.
Another.
Boil together, in equal weight, Colophonian resin, Judaean bitumen, unfired sulfur, fresh pitch, and wax with goat-fat, and use it.
Another caustic, for sores.

Two weights of blue vitriol, half an ounce of split alum, one ounce of chalcitis, six ounces of scraped verdigris. Pound and grind these with very sharp white vinegar, and boil them together in a bronze vessel, until it boils once, and grind again, adding in a weight of myrrh. Then store it, and use it with vinegar.
Another caustic emollient.
Two ounces of propolis, one ounce of galbanum, three ounces of bdellium, one and a half pounds of resin, three ounces of bitumen, one pound of Brittany pitch, one pound of ammoniac gum.
Against pain of the hip.
Use anointings for eight days. And if necessity presses, bleed, and use this remedy: four ounces each of spurge and common salt, four grammes of liquid pitch, boil together and use it.
Another: Apsyrtus' caustic against hip-ailments.
Galbanum, opopanax, deer-marrow, turpentine, ammoniac gum, bdellium, propolis, saffron-dregs, vinegar, dry
pitch, liquid pitch, Judaean bitumen, henna-oil, foam of resin, that is, its exudation, bull-fat, wax, two pounds of each.
One pound of chalcitis, six ounces each of honey and aloe, one pint of vinegar, one pound each of sheep-lard and wax, six ounces of roses.
Another caustic, against pains of the sinews.
Two pounds of storax, one pound each of galbanum, bdellium, propolis, Colophonian resin, unwashed wool-grease, ammoniac incense, dry pitch, and bay-berries, six ounces each of bitumen and vinegar.
Another: composition of a caustic.

Five pounds of wax, four pounds of Attic propolis, four pounds of ammoniac gum, one pound of galbanum, four pounds of poppy-juice, four pounds of foam of opopanax, one pound of Judaean bitumen, ten pounds of Brittany pitch, two pounds of marsh-mallow, four pounds of pine-resin, four pounds of roasted resin, two pounds of storax, four pounds of bdellium, one pound of deer-marrow, six ounces of bull-fat, two pounds of poppy-juice, twelve pounds of live sulfur, two cotylae of honey, four cotylae of old wine, one ounce of ground chamomile. Grind these into one, and, putting them into a bronze vessel, use for all fresh sores.
Another caustic ointment. By Hierocles.

One pound each of resin-drippings, roasted resin, Judaean bitumen, pitch, wax, and mistletoe-glue, six ounces of ammoniac gum, four ounces of frankincense, two ounces of galbanum, two ounces of opopanax. Melt the meltable ingredients,

add the opopanax, already ground beforehand, and, putting it into a small bowl and stirring with a spatula, anoint. And if it becomes too hard, add dissolved old lard and enough ammoniac gum. It also works well without the mistletoe-glue. And if there is heat, so that the ointment does not dissolve, add six ounces of ship-scrapings, and thus anoint. And if there are no ship-scrapings, use four ounces of old tow. This is the best of the caustic ointments.
Another caustic ointment.
Six ounces each of Judaean bitumen and split alum, one pound of old lard, three ounces of litharge, one ounce each of galbanum and opopanax, one pint of squill-vinegar, half a pint of oil.
Another, a hot caustic, by Pelagonius.

One pound of litharge, three ounces of soda, three ounces of ammoniac gum, six ounces of Cyprian copper-scale, six ounces of roasted resin, one pound of wax, three ounces of burnt copper, six ounces of white-lead, one pint of oil.
A caustic for the shoulders, joints, and hips,
of Hemeritus.

Six ounces of galbanum, four ounces of ammoniac gum, five grammes of Brittany pitch, four ounces of bitumen, two ounces of wormwood, two ounces each of bdellium, poppy-seed, propolis, frankincense-meal, bay-berries, and Colophonian resin, five ounces of dittany, five ounces of stomach-resin, two pounds of wax.
Another.
One pound of wax, one pound of bitumen, one pound of turpentine-resin, six ounces of ammoniac gum, one ounce of bdellium, one ounce of

unwashed wool-grease, three ounces of galbanum, three ounces of storax, one ounce of frankincense-manna, three ounces of split alum, four ounces of vinegar, one ounce of walnut-oil, one ounce of old oil, one ounce of soda, two ounces of pepper, two ounces of mistletoe-glue, one ounce of parsley, two ounces of propolis.
Another.

One pound of wax, six ounces of roasted resin, three ounces of ammoniac gum, three ounces of hemlock-seed, one ounce of bdellium, one ounce of galbanum, six ounces of Judaean bitumen, six ounces of old lard, three cyathi of wine.
Another.

One Italian pint of squill-vinegar, one pint of Brittany pitch, one pint of wax, two ounces of red ochre, one pint of roasted resin, half an Italian pint of fine flour-dust. Warm the vinegar with the pitch, and, when it has boiled well, add the rest gently and anoint. And after this, pound hemp and make wicks, and apply them, binding the place.
Preparation of a cautery-iron.
Boil beets in water, and mix their juice with soda and half a pint of oil, and cauterize.
How one must give green fodder (grastis).

Apsyrtus to Orion Marcellus, greetings. You wrote to me asking, in what manner one must give green fodder to horses? For this is the most necessary and primary treatment of the year. We shall stand the horse apart and offer it green fodder, offering nothing else of what feeds it. Best is wheat-fodder; if not, barley-fodder, which we shall give for up to five days, and after this double that number of days again (it is better still, if it
is sown near the sea; and if not, we shall use what is at hand),
and adding a half-choenix of barley each day.
And when we reach the appointed amount, we shall continue giving the customary ration, not letting green fodder run short, for as long a time as there may be.

And after the first five days, we shall lead it out and wash it, so that it also swims. Then, having scraped off all the moisture, one must blow in wine and oil, and rub with the hands against the grain of the hair, until the skin has no dampness left, and we shall offer the rest, as described above, along with the barley. And if it ever happens that the fodder falls short, so that it is not given equally, five out of the ten days. We shall also stand it and offer fodder at the month's end, measuring the five days up to the thirtieth, so that on the new moon we may begin
to give the rest with the barley up to the tenth of the month.

It is necessary, while offering the green fodder, to bleed the horse, cutting the veins in the chest and the palate, so that the pre-existing blood from the dry season, and the humors, may find an outlet, and thus new blood may be gathered into clean veins. For a horse dieted in this way does not readily fall into illnesses, and endures hardships.

This too is beneficial: offer salt to the horse while it is on green fodder, so that a mouth-inflammation, which some call 'aphtha,' does not occur. Never graze a horse in the open air if it has 'malis' (glanders); for the affliction easily runs beneath the hide, and becomes

a mange, from which madness also results in the heat. Such a horse must, then, be offered green fodder while standing under shelter. Best of all is to purge it beforehand with wild cucumber and soda before putting it on green fodder.

By Diocles, addressing some most esteemed king, Antigonus I think, healthful precepts, by using which one will win approval. It is well, then, for us too to say how one must give green fodder to horses in the spring season, offering them fresh grass. For, being well dieted, they will not easily fall into illnesses.
When the season of spring grass arrives, make the horse graze on wild grass from it for one day, then, on the following day, blow into its nostrils

an insufflation compounded of cockle-seed, leaf, costus, iris, and pepper, and immediately release it to pasture for about two or even three days, so that, by bending down after the insufflation, it may expel through its nostrils all the fluid lodged in its head.

And after grazing for three days, bring it into the stable, and offer wild grass for four days. Offer also the green fodder, best of all wheat-fodder, or, if not, barley-fodder, for five days. And after this, bleed the horse, and, taking the blood, mix it with soda, vinegar, oil, and eggs, and thus anoint the animal all over. And, standing it in the sun until the whole anointment has dried, use the green fodder, best of all, as we have said,

wheat-fodder, or, if you lack this, barley-fodder, for five days. And when the days are completed, lead it out of the stable, wash the horse, and wipe it with towels, so that all the moisture is wiped away. Then, having stood the animal thus, offer the green fodder for a certain number of days, best of all, if possible, fourteen, but at least no fewer than seven or nine, so that it becomes as fat as possible.
It is useful, while it is on green fodder, to offer it salt, so that the so-called 'aphtha' does not arise in its mouth.

Hence some have said it is better for the fodder to be sown in coastal areas. And if it happens, at this time, that the horse is afflicted with, or is being tested for, 'malis,' do not graze it in the open air. For the affliction easily runs beneath the hide, and mange results in due course, sometimes from the heat, and the animal turns to madness. One must, then, offer it the green fodder under shelter, having first purged it with wild cucumber and soda.
The treatise, then, has an end. We have appended compounded remedies and helps to it, so that it may be possible for everyone to know how each of these is prepared.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

graze it on fresh grass for one day first, then, on the following day, blow into its nostrils a dry, nose-clearing remedy, whose composition is this: one ounce each of cockle-seed, pepper, pennyroyal, and marjoram, half an ounce each of leaf, iris, costus, and the finest possible wild-cucumber root; pound all these and sift through a fine sieve, and blow it through a small reed into the nostrils, and, suspending the head thus for about half an hour, let it graze for three more days, so that all the phlegm-like fluid gathered in the brain from the winter may drain down, by the lowering of the head while grazing, and be discharged. For thus neither glanders, nor swollen tonsils, nor scrofulous swellings will arise in the animals.

And after this, lead it back to the stable again, and offer wild grass for five days. On the following day, begin giving the green fodder, better wheat-fodder, or, if not, barley-fodder, for five days. And thus bleed it, and, having caught all the blood, mix into it oil, vinegar, and soda, and anoint the animals against the grain of the hair from head to feet, and, rubbing them down carefully, stand them in the sun, so that they dry. Then bring them into the stable, and offer the green fodder for another five days, without currying them. On the sixth day, lead them out of the manger and wash them, and wipe them with rough towels as thoroughly as possible, so that all the moisture is drawn off from them. And stand them again in the manger, and offer green fodder for fourteen days, and you will have them fat, healthy, and fine. Those on green fodder must be given salt continually, on some

tray or board, so that they may take as much as they wish without compulsion. Let this be done after drinking. And let someone rub their whole mouth with the hand and salt; for, once this is done, the affliction of aphtha, which is an ulceration of the mouth, will not befall them.
On overeating and indigestion (raw/undigested food).

Apsyrtus to Papias, horse-doctor of Antioch, greetings. Many remedies have been written for overeating and indigestion. Best of all is bloodletting from the elbows and forelegs. For, the constitution of the animal being hot, it quickly draws off the indigestion from the food. For this reason one must draw blood, as written above. For it happens that, from this affliction, the horse passes into fever, and it is hard to help.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

Overeating together with indigestion is an acute affliction. This happens when the animals get hold of fresh grain, which, not yet having the digestive quality that comes with time, is wont to harm the animals, swelling and filling their bellies with its freshness, and often bursting them. One must, then, offer the animals lesser amounts of fresh grain, first soaking it in water, so that, by making it release its bulk, they leave the raw quality in the water, and the animals remain unharmed without danger and have good nourishment.
And if it ever happens, unintentionally or without the horse-keeper's knowledge, that the animal, as happens from grain-heaps or the threshing-floor itself, eats too much, one must treat it
with enemas and bloodlettings from the elbows and forelegs.
For it is those parts that the indigestion is wont to bind up first, and to seize the sinews within them.
By anticipating, then, and emptying this area, together with the drawing of blood, you will also remove the harm from the part that would otherwise suffer.
On castration.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Eudoxus of Tomis, greetings. It is useful for you, as a horse-keeper, to know at what seasons one must castrate horses, and in what manner. The best season for the cutting of the testicles is spring and autumn; we have also cut in summer, and done no harm.

One must cut thus: laying the horse down and securing its feet, take up the testicles evenly, and bind them with the 'ear-clamp,' and cut only the surrounding hide, as much as is sufficient, through which they will be brought out.
As you cut, you will apply linen or hempen loops, two on each side.
And then cut the membranes, then press them out thus, and cut off the suspensory cord with the cautery next to the testicle itself, applying it from behind, not in front.
Let your cautery be as fiery as possible, so that you remove it in one stroke; if not, in a second, for applying it more than that causes inflammation.

And, making tufts of rag and wool soaked in pitch-oil, insert them, and tie the loops, and, on the third day, remove it, undoing the dressings, and anoint underneath with pitch-oil, dipping it in with feathers.
And do this until it scars over, anointing
daily. On the day you operate, withhold all feed. On the following day, you will give water gradually and then feed.
Let it walk about in the cooler hours, but let it stand still in the heat. This is how you will treat it while it is in the stable.
And if you cut it while in a herd, cut it with the cautery, as written above, and anoint underneath with pitch-oil, and release it to pasture.
Let the season for this alone be spring.
And if inflammation occurs in the one kept in the stable, use Cimolian earth mixed with vinegar as an ointment.
One must not castrate those with only one testicle; for they are especially prone to accidents and are in danger during the operation.
And if, on rising after the operation, it whinnies, it does not easily survive.
It is said that a horse castrated after shedding its second teeth does not change its remaining teeth, nor does it grow large canine teeth.
In foals still of that age, the testicles cannot be seen.
One must know that gelded horses do not fall into glanders, nor are they troubled by a flux in the legs, nor do they develop scrofulous swellings.
By Hierocles, for the same.
As for how one must castrate a horse, Apsyrtus teaches sufficiently.

This much, however, is worth saying here: that the season of spring and of autumn are suitable for the excision of the testicles, and likewise one must not castrate those with a single testicle, since the operation is dangerous.
And if, after being castrated, it rises and whinnies, it is a sign that it does not easily survive.
They say, indeed, that a horse castrated after shedding its second teeth does not
change its remaining teeth, nor grow large canine teeth.
On the castration of a donkey.
One must castrate a two-year-old donkey thus: bind the testicles with a cord, and, securing it, cut obliquely. And, so that inflammation does not follow, cut it off with the cautery.
On 'karydosis' (walnut-castration technique), by Apsyrtus.

If you wish to 'karydose' an animal, in the month of May, when the north wind is blowing, dig a pit, and, hobbling the animal, and laying it on its back, so that it cannot rise, bind the testicles. Then, taking a sharp iron, quickly cut through the skin. And when the testicles come out through it, excise them with precision, so as not to take up their roots. Then fill the wound with salt, and raise the animal up, and let it be, so that it does not swell greatly. And on the following day, when you see that no blood comes out from it, undo it, and, taking pitch and oil, anoint the loins, the head, and its nostrils well. And do not let it walk about much, until it heals; let it stand in a warm place. And anoint its whole body with wine mixed with frankincense and manna, and cover it with a blanket. And if it bleeds, mix one ounce of ammoniac gum and one cyathus of horehound-juice with honey, and anoint.
On a bruise (of the hoof).

Apsyrtus to Damas of Laodicea, companion, greetings. I wish you to know: when, coming from the road, the horse steps only on the tip of the toe with its hind foot, and its hoof is hot, it has a bruise. One must, then, immediately scrape the foot at the

tip of the toe, near the hoof, and you will find fluid, and it will quickly become healthy. Sometimes, however, a bruise happens to have formed likewise in the same place, without the horse going lame. Such a horse, then, suppurates while standing. And then it is easily recognized that it has fluid, and one must open it at the same place. In the forefeet, it is not found quickly. Therefore, apply fresh cow-dung, boiled up with marjoram in vinegar and oil, repeatedly to the foot, or barley-groats boiled up in vinegar. Or pound figs and salt and apply as a poultice, or boil chaste-tree berries in vinegar and grind them, for this disperses the fluids, and opens a way for its discharge, both toward the burst opening and toward the lower perforations of the foot.

And when it bursts upward, one must melt lard and resin together, and put it into the burst opening and the lower perforations, or use the emollient compounded for sprains, and the hoof will descend more quickly. In such cases, do not prick the vein at the crown of the hoof; for from this mistake results 'marmarosis.' And if it ever happens that bruises occur, not in one foot, but in several, or even all, and the horse lies down and dozes, and neither eats nor drinks, but sleeps, it is lethargic. One must drench it through both nostrils with a cotyla of mild vinegar-water, and anoint the head with fresh fox's blood, and castoreum is said to do the same.
Bruises happen especially to beasts of burden and pack-carriers, that is, mules and donkeys, from which bruises the
occur more easily in the hooves of horses.

If you notice a bruise has occurred - and it is recognized both by the affected hoof being hotter, and by the horse stepping on the tip of the toe of the foot that pains it - boil barley, wrap it around and bind it on, then, pouring hot water onto the barley, foment for a long time, twice or even three times. And, above all, from extensive fomenting, the bruise will be dispersed. And if this does not happen, it will at any rate be brought to a head.

Or boil barley-flour in mixed wine and apply it, and add dove-dung as a poultice. And if this happens and it comes to a head, open it as is customary at the place where the bruise occurs, so that all the fluid may come out. And thus, having anointed with the remedy compounded of blue vitriol, plug the scraped place with a sponge, and do this, until it is healed. Or, if you cannot procure this remedy, take a wick and soak it in vinegar-oil, and apply it to the opened place. And do this, until it is healed.

And if it happens that the bruise bursts upward, that is, near the growth-point of the hoof, which happens especially to hard-hoofed animals, at first use the vinegar-oil and the wick. And if the pain, as far as possible, ceases, use the hoof-ointment applied over the whole hoof, compounded from lizards, for the strengthening of the hoof, and thus you will drive out what seems to have caused

the bursting. This is the remedy: into a new pot, put three pints of oil, and put in fresh green lizards, about two or even three, and, covering the pot, boil it, so that the lizards are thoroughly cooked in the oil. And after this, remove their bones, and add in six ounces of ground bitumen and half a pint of liquid pitch and two pounds of old pig-fat; boil all these together well, and use it, anointing the hoof. This will make the foot of the animal firmer, as far as possible, and harder.
For never letting an animal develop a bruise.
When the animal comes in from green fodder, take a date, remove its pit, and fill the date with white-lead, and give it through the mouth, sending it off healthy. Do this from time to time.
By Hippocrates, for the same.

If a bruise occurs inside the foot, you will treat the horse thus: scrape around the hoof, and apply as a poultice barley boiled in water. Or knead hot bran and mix in a little old dung, and apply as a poultice. And if the little bone in the frog becomes visible, use honey and vinegar with a wick as a plug for some days. Then apply an astringent: grind cypress-leaves with vinegar, or likewise apply tamarisk-leaves. Or boil pomegranate-rind husks in vinegar and grind and apply, or pound them dry and sprinkle on. Or use a portion of blue vitriol or pounded gall-nuts, doing the same, first washing the place with vinegar.
Another, by Pelagonius.

If the bruise has already been opened, mix grains of salt with vinegar and apply to the opened place at the toe. Warm the toe also with hot bran. And after three days, if the humor stops flowing, mix split alum with red ochre and vinegar, and store it. And when the heat has stopped, drain off pig-fat through the opened place. And when it no longer goes lame, undo it and seal with bitumen.
Another.

If the bruise has pus, scrape the whole hoof deeply, and, having opened the place well, douse it with vinegar-water, and treat the wound with the liquid remedy, and, having melted goat- and sheep-fat together, anoint with a sponge-on-a-stick, and place dry horse-dung on top and bind it. For it will do well.
On madness and rabies.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Gaius, horse-doctor of Alexandria, greetings. You wrote to me asking what remedies one must use against those that go mad and become rabid. They are helped by being drenched through the nostrils with four cotylae of dry, dark wine, being restrained with a rope and a halter. Or by boiling wild-cucumber root in two cotylae of wine and mixing in soda, and drenching. And by boiling black hellebore once in vinegar, and anointing the whole body with it, especially the head, and by using more vigorous rubbing, and exercising it more, and by drawing blood from the legs and forelegs. One must not offer them barley, until they become calm again.

It is also said that they must stand at rest, in a dark place; but we, doing this, found them rather more agitated and dying. The only remedy that has real power, whenever one perceives it beginning to become excited, is to lay it down and castrate it; for it stops its madness this way. This affliction happens to it either from excessive heat, or from an excessive quantity of vetch fed, or from an inflow of blood to the meninges, or from bile leaking into the blood-carrying veins, or from the poor quality of water.

The affliction of madness and rabies happens to horses especially either from excessive heat, or from an excessive quantity of vetch fed, or when more blood has been carried to the meninges, or from bile leaking into the blood-carrying veins, or from the poor quality of water. It whinnies, then, inopportunely and bites, and runs at people too. They are helped by being drenched through the nostrils with four cotylae of dry, dark wine, and restrained securely with a rope, or with wild-cucumber root boiled in two cotylae of wine, mixed with soda, or with rue pounded together with mint.

Let them be anointed all over the body with black hellebore boiled once in vinegar, especially the head, using more vigorous rubbing. Let them be exercised more, and let blood be drawn from the legs and forelegs. Do not offer barley, until they become calm.
Some say that they must be made to stand in a darker, quieter place, which Apsyrtus says does not help; that,
above all, he praises: that, whenever one perceives the horse beginning to go mad, one should lay it down and castrate it; for thus it stops its madness.
Another.

The horse has its eyes more hollow, and its nostrils more upright, and its ears upright. If, then, it begins to bite, treat it thus: draw blood from its legs and forelegs, and on that same day let it remain without food; on the following day give it a little, and, after three days, give it, while fasting, one ounce of hemlock mixed with water.
By Eumelus, for the same.

The animal, often - it is recognized thus: it gnaws at the manger, chews on itself with bites, attacks people, moves its ears continually, has fixed, gleaming eyes, and also sends forth froth. Bind this one carefully, and take blood from the legs and the spine, and rub the body with this same blood mixed with wine, and cauterize the belly and the temples with many small cautery-pricks. And if it is a stallion, geld it. And keep it shut up in a darker place, until it develops an appetite for food. And gradually, once it has become gentle, you will treat it thus: drench through the mouth with an oxybaphon of ground hemlock-seed in half a pint of water. Also loosen its belly, and anoint the head with hot vinegar mixed with ground black hellebore, and cover it with sheepskins. Then grind rue, and likewise anoint its head with it, and let it stand in a
warm place.
Another.
Another, by Hippocrates.

These signs accompany a rabid horse: the eyes protrude, bloodshot, and the veins stand out prominently, and the body [lacuna], and it refuses food and is in distress. One must treat it thus: cover its face with a cloth, so that it cannot see those approaching, and, tying the middle of its neck, open the broad veins, and let it bleed, until it faints. Then, having tied off the neck and stanched the blood, make it stand in a dark place, and let it rest, with neither noise nor disturbance occurring there. In the evening, give it a jugful of water to drink, and likewise on the following day, reducing both feed and drink for up to three days, then give the customary amounts.
Another.
Another, by Pelagonius.

Before all else, such a horse ought to stand in a darker place, and be fed gentler food, and be treated with this preliminary drench: a bundle of fresh celery, ground, four ounces of good honey, one cyathus of ground cardamom, two cyathi of white wine; grind all these with the wine and pour it down the throat. And if it is not cured this way, singe the head lightly, and anoint it with warm ointments, as we said for those with opisthotonos. Anoint the eyes too with an eye-salve.
Another.
Another.

First bleed it from the temples, then offer a drink of celery-seed, spikenard, Macedonian parsley, lettuce-seed, and poppy-seed, mixed in equal parts with honey-water, for five days. Cover its head with a woolen cloth, anointed with oil.
Another.
Dissolve cleaned bay-berries in oil, and, adding hot wine, pour it in through the nostrils.
Another.

Its gaze is fierce and bright, the veins that are reddish against the white of the eye stand out, and it turns this frequently, and its jaws move, and it bites itself, whether standing or rolling about, and it runs at whoever stands nearby to bite, and it sweats. Draw off, then, about six cotylae of blood from the legs of such a horse, and bind up the wound, and offer it nothing, so that the blood does not flow. And when the sun sets, bring it about a choenix of raw vetch, pouring on about four cotylae of lukewarm water. Offer nothing else. On the second day, best of all soft fodder, or, if not, about two bundles of dry fodder, and an equal drink of raw vetch. Then let it walk about a little, wrapped in a blanket. Then let it stand under shelter, and one must offer more fodder, but less drink, and offer the barley sparingly and little by little, so that it does not fall into the same affliction again. And salt its mouth, and let it walk about, and, if it does not settle down, then also castrate it, and close off the veins of the testicles,
pouring on pitch and salt and oil, and sprinkling on ash, then foment daily, and you will cure it.
On mismatched pairs, and those suited to the yoke.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Apollophanes, friend, greetings. It is useful for you, as a horse-keeper earnestly concerned with the composition of mismatched teams, to know, from bodily signs, which animals are well-suited for yoking together. They must, then, have a broad chest, likewise a broad neck, nostrils drawn back, shoulders set rather high, straight forelegs with the pastern-joints in them not overly large, feet not turned outward, a belly not small, and a back not humped. For from such animals one will find ones capable and vigorous in their work.
On flux (rheum) in the head.
On flux (rheum) in the head.
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Pasicrates, horse-doctor of Alexandria, greetings. I wish you to know that, when a flux arises in the head, if a discharge occurs spontaneously, or while the horse is being exercised, no harm results. But if not, it becomes suppurative and catarrhal. These are the signs: from its nostril flows a thick, white discharge, with a putrid smell, and, though eager to cough, it cannot, and it wastes away, having no appetite, and, when rolling about, does not turn itself all the way over, nor does it shake its head. For it feels heavy, and its veins in the head are swollen, and likewise in the face. It is treated by exercise, a moderate canter-run, and dousing the head
with hot water, and fumigating the mouth and nostrils over coals with bay-fruit, and rubbing the body, excluding the head, so that the pores are not sealed shut.

One must use purgative drenches, especially birthwort through the nostrils with wine, or likewise soda with water, or two weights of soft alum and an equal amount of salt with a cotyla of wine, drenched. And if, with these, the pus does not break open, use also this compound: bull's blood, or, failing that, that of a young ox, two oxybapha, and one oxybaphon of frankincense, and half an oxybaphon of salt; grind each of these separately, and again together, pour on very sharp vinegar, grind, and dry in the sun. And when it sets, shape it into troches the size of a walnut, and, once dried, store them, and drench with one of these into the mouth daily, grinding it in vinegar. And if the horse is weak, grind it in wine instead. Before giving the remedies, wash it with plenty of hot water. After this, fumigate it, and open its mouth. And when it has drawn in the smoke, one must hold the mouth shut.
Another, by Eumelus, against pain of the head.

These will be the signs for a horse suffering pain in the head: its eyes become inflamed, it discharges fluid through the mouth. One must, then, douse its head with hot water, and use gentle rest. Also draw blood from the eyebrows, and grind clover-leaves and give them to drink. And if it holds its eyes stretched wide, you will need to draw blood

from the neck and the skull. Then take three ounces of salt, dissolve it in water, and drench. And if you do not have this, take earthworms and about two pints of old urine, and, grinding them together, pour it in through the left nostril.
Another, for the same. By Eumelus.

Watering eyes and twisted, that is, bent-down ears, and a head drooping downward, indicate pain of the head. One must, then, treat it thus: open the vein below the eye, and foment the mouth with hot water, and make it abstain from food, and on the following day use green fodder and lukewarm water. On the third day, make it eat barley with vetch-fodder, and let it be watered little by little, so that it recovers its natural health by gradual stages.
Another, for the same.

Two ounces of castoreum, six ounces of bay-berries, two ounces each of soda, Brittany pitch, and frankincense-manna, six ounces of old oil, six ounces of bitter almonds; grind and mix these, and, first washing with urine, anoint.
Another, for clearing the head.
Half a pint of fish-sauce, poured in through the nostrils, clears the head.
Another: a fomentation against headaches of horses.

Soak twelve staters of white-lead a night and a day in water, in a new vessel, and, straining off the water, grind the white-lead in a mortar, so that it becomes as fine as possible. Then, mixing in wax, grind it thoroughly, and, when it becomes very fine, mix in a shell's-measure of honey, and, grinding these together, take oil into
the hand, and apply it to the temples of the horses and the anus. This also works on humans, against every kind of fatigue. Let the wax-salve be five staters.
Another, against catarrh.

If blood rushes into the head from riding or some other exertion, these are the signs: the ears are upright and cold, and the eyes discharge fluid through the nostrils, and the mouth is cold inside. One must, then, douse the head with hot water, covering the head with blankets, and fumigate with dry alum. Give it also wheat soaked in wine to eat. And if it is not helped, draw blood from the mouth or the neck.
By Apsyrtus, on 'katakrania' (a head-heaviness ailment).

The signs of 'katakrania' are these: it droops its ears, and its head feels heavy, and it cannot eat. It is treated thus: pound and sift black hellebore, grind it with wine, oil, and soda, and anoint the head and the inside of the nostrils and ears, using the remedy warm. Or take twenty bay-berries, and a handful of the tender tips of bay-leaves, and an equal amount of pomegranate-rind, about three beans'-weight of myrrh, and about two beans'-weight of Cyrenaic laser-sap; grind these fine, and, dissolving them in four cotylae of fragrant dark wine, pour it into the right nostril. Also draw blood from the nostrils. Barley-gruel, well boiled and poured in through the mouth, is also suitable.
By Eumelus, against pain of the head.

Pain of the head, which some call 'katakranion,' arises when the animal does not digest its feed at the proper time. One must, then, draw blood from the temples of such a horse, until the causes of the illness are dispersed. And, once clean blood flows, one must quickly stop it, and foment in this manner: boil very fine chaff in sharp vinegar and oil, if it is summer; but if winter, boil it in wine and oil, and use the decoction of these. Or mix one ounce each of black hellebore and soda with an equal amount of wine and oil,
and, grinding all these together and warming them, anoint the head; for by these means the ailment will easily be brought to resolution.
By Theomnestus: recognition and cure of headache.

The horse with a headache always looks downward, and cannot raise its head; a mist always seems to surround it, and its eyes water, and it takes nothing, and it half-closes its eyes and raises them only with difficulty, if it does so at all; and, remaining continually in the same posture, it takes no food either.

One must, then, treat it thus: opening its mouth, draw blood from the palate, using not a pointed but a broad lancet. Give it also these diuretic drenches: one pound of celery-seed, eight ounces of parsley, four pints of boiled leek-juice,

one Italian pint of wine-and-oil; mix these and drench through the mouth. And, having made it walk gently, let it rest for a while. Then let it be cooled in water, just like a horse foundered on barley. And if
it develops diarrhea, it stops the illness, but often its eyesight becomes clouded. Let it be anointed with honey and fennel-juice, and this too will be healed very quickly.

Watering eyes, drooping ears, a neck bowed down toward the ground, and altered vision indicate pains of the head. But, even though the animal is in this state, one must draw blood from the mouth, and give a drench able to loosen the belly. This regimen is the same as for horses foundered on barley. Know that, if the belly is checked quickly and the eyes develop a white film, the animal will suffer no further harm. But treat its eyes nonetheless.

Before all else, one must clear the head of the animal in this manner: boil spurge, centaury, and frankincense-meal for a long time in a pot with wine, and, in the warm sun, pour it in through the nostrils. And shortly after, drop a little rose-oil mixed with old oil and soda-froth into the ear.

Drop a little very sharp vinegar mixed with old oil and soda-froth into the ear. Or boil the creatures called wood-lice with butter and one small bundle of rue in oil, and, once it is lukewarm, pour it into the ear. Or put bird-fat mixed with nard into the ear.
If the animal suffers in its brain, one must manage it carefully, so that it does not fall into danger too quickly. These are the
signs of such a disorder: the animal walks sideways,
stumbles with its feet, trips continually, and its legs
become drawn together. Such an animal, then, must be put to work under the yoke, so that,
through sweat and exertion, all the affliction is driven off. And so that,
after the exertion, it may be better managed, use this method:
chop twenty bay-berries and one pound of soda finely,
and one small bundle of fresh rue with vinegar and oil
of bay, warming it, anoint the head between the ears,
and with a woolen cloth soaked in this remedy
bind the head.
Another.
Mix barley-flour with resin and apply. Use also
these preliminary drenches: chop seven river-crabs,
and mix with one pint of goat's milk and one cyathus of oil,
and, straining it cleanly, give it through the mouth. And if
these are not available, three cyathi of honey-water and
one obol of white pepper, two grammes of saffron, ground together in wine, give through
the mouth.
Another, for clearing the head.
Take a mandrake apple, and, cutting it into many pieces,
roast it in the sun or an oven, then, pounding and sifting it,
clear the head with this.
Another, against fullness (congestion) of the head.
If an animal has its head congested or chilled, one must
bleed it, either from the temples or the mouth,
then mix two parts of Cretan clay and old acacia with dry
wine, and, boiling it, apply it hot to the head.
Another, against heaviness of the head.

If a great deal of humor is discharged through the nostrils, you will treat it with this preliminary drench: grind one oxybaphon of mustard cleanly with an equal amount of honey, and give a preliminary drench from this with half a pint of wine daily for nine days.
Another: an ointment for the head.
Mix rose-oil and castoreum, bitter almonds, and fresh rue with vinegar, and use it.
Another, against pain of the head.

As many animals as become congested from acute illnesses must be purged. For it is necessary to forestall such cases, lest they fall into the disease of glanders, or become suppurative, which are hard to treat. Use, then, this regimen: mix two eggs, twenty grains of pepper, and one ounce of honey together, and drench through a horn. Then bend its head down to its feet, and let it remain so for half an hour, until the humors discharge. Then apply the heating fatigue-relieving liniment, to loosen it, then blow the best wine into the nostrils and make it walk about.
On recognizing good-footed and soft-footed horses.
By Apsyrtus.

Master Gallus, having distinguished, among horses, which signs belong to temperament and which to the body, I shall show you what is the first principle in the constitution of the animal. As for which are good-footed or soft-footed, and bad or good, they will be recognized thus: those with a white hoof and long frogs are soft and bad. And those with a dry, brittle, and white hoof

are soft and bad. And if it is hollow underneath, and has a small frog, they are good and good-footed. Long hooves with a small frog are good-footed and good; but if the frog is long, they are bad and useless. Flat, board-like hooves with a long frog are soft and bad; but if the frog is small, they are good.

Those with a black hoof are good-footed, but bad in quality. Those with a white hoof having black bands in it are good-footed and good. Those with a round hoof, tawny at the wall, are soft and bad. Those grown fused underneath, with small frogs, are good-footed and good. Those splayed outward on the inner side are good-footed, but bad in quality. Those with a square hoof, not high, but black, with a small frog, are good-footed. And those with a rounded, hollow, black hoof underneath are good and good-footed. Those tawny, long, and not broad but oblong, are good. Those with a black, oblong hoof are bad.

Those grown fused with a small frog are soft and bad. Those splayed outward on the outer side are soft, but not bad. Those with the hoof set low behind are soft, and they tread on the frog. Those with a black hoof having a white band in it are good and more good-footed than those with a white hoof and black bands. And those with a projecting crown of the hoof and a somewhat long hoof are good-footed, but bad. And those with a broad, shell-like hoof, and a small frog, are good-footed,

but bad. And those with a broad hoof at the toe, and bloodshot, are soft and prone to continual sores.
