And these too are good and good-footed, as written above: those with a hollow underneath and a thick hoof-wall, making a noise on it when walking. They are, however, poor at running and lack spirit for riding, though they are good-natured from birth up to the completion of their teeth; for the rest of the time they are bad, being prone to bite.

As for colors, generally worse than others are also those with white on a foot or leg, and those with a white forehead, and those with a white muzzle, especially chestnut-colored horses, when they have any of these.
Another: Apsyrtus' treatment of soft-footed horses.

Apsyrtus to Marcus Marius, decurion, greetings. You wrote to me asking what remedy one must use for the soft-footed horse. It is hard to correct, because it exists naturally so, and further because the wearing-down from the day's travel does not grow back during the night's standing, to the extent it is worn away. And it is always overheated and gets sores and develops bruises continually. It is improved, so as to be better for use, by fomenting the feet with cypress boiled in water, or likewise with bramble, or we do the same with boiled wormwood. Vinegar-brine
is also beneficial, and anointing the hooves with oil in winter, in summer with lard after fomenting. Much has been said by many about cauterizing. Best of all is to pour on bitumen, using a torch

to apply it. And if the hard-hoofed horse wears itself down, let it be bled from the pastern-veins, so that, becoming inflamed, it does not suffer a rupture at the crown. Pricking there is inadvisable, for it damages the hoof.
Another, by Eumelus, against worn-down feet.

If an animal wears down its foot, it is fitting to foment with hot water, and anoint with lard, and place it on a heated potsherd, until it bears it gently. After this, use ground garlic and sulfur, cauterizing with a heated iron for three days. This helps cattle too.
By Theomnestus, for the same.

An animal that has worn down its foot from travel, if then neglected, develops a fever, and, once feverish, quickly dies, unless it is helped in time. One must, then, douse the feet with hot water, in which marsh-mallow root, which some call wild mallow, has been boiled together, until the hoof becomes softer. Then scrape the affected hooves, and expose the bruised areas deeply, then have ready cord and rough rags, and apply garlic and old lard as a poultice, separately at first and then together, and bind up the hooves.

And if it becomes inflamed, let it be bled from the pastern-veins, and let it stand in a warm place, and, in winter, let a fire be kept burning nearby, and let dry dung be strewn beneath it, so that it does not suffer in its feet by stepping on hard ground. And when it remains free of inflammation, let it be treated from early morning for nine days, and let it stand indoors on dung, and there let its
drink be brought to it, so that its hoof is not worn down by walking, but grows, nourished by the filth of the dung.
On the growth of the hoof.
Pound old lard, garlic, bitumen, and unfired sulfur with pitch-oil, and anoint the coronet, and trim it round. Let the horse stand in a dry place.
For hardening the hoof.
Make wax, unfired sulfur, resin, pitch-oil, and lard into one, and use it carefully.
Another.

Take a resinous pine-torch, and, splitting it and inserting lard into it, light it, and, turning the hooves upward, let the dripping fall onto all the parts beneath the hooves. Do this for three days, and let it not touch water, nor stand in a wet place. And after six or seven days, do the same again.
Another.

Grind two parts of ivy-seed and one of round alum, [gap] apply to the hooves, until it can bear it. And after this, grind garlic and bitumen together, and, placing them on a heated flat iron, cauterize with them for three days. This is also suitable for cattle.
Another.

Make a shoe-poultice from liquid pitch and lard, and apply it hot, having first carefully cleaned the hoof. Then sprinkle pounded ivy-seed onto the hoof, so as to fill it entirely, and, having shod it, undo it after the third day. Doing this a third time, you will cure it.
By Pelagonius, for the growth of hooves.
Three heads of garlic, a bundle of rue, six ounces of pounded alum, two pounds of old lard, a handful of donkey dung; mix all these together and, taking it up, use it daily.
Another.
Boil broad beans in water, grind them with honey, and, spreading it onto a rag, apply, and you will cure it.
A remedy for the same.
Douse the hoof with hot vinegar, and after this rub it with horehound mixed with old lard and wild wormwood.
Preparation of a sole-plaster.

One ounce of galbanum, one and a half ounces of castoreum, half an ounce of adarce, an equal amount of roasted resin, two ounces of liquid resin, two ounces of Alexandrian gall-nut, one and a half ounces of Judaean bitumen, one ounce of chalcitis, one ounce of pitch, one ounce of lard, six ounces of vinegar, two pounds of wax, one and a half pints of oil; mix both parts and use it.
On a horse sweating for no cause.
By Apsyrtus.

When it happens, with no suspicion present of heat or warmth, that a horse standing still sweats in some parts of the body, or all over, and gives off a vapor from itself, one must know that its bile has settled upon those parts, or has spread throughout generally; for this reason, one must drench such a horse with sweet wine.
On those injured by a hobble
or some other binding.
By Apsyrtus.

It happens that the pastern-joints are injured by a hobble, or some other binding from a strap or cord, and the hide comes off, and the sinews of the pastern-cushion become bare. There will, then, be danger

of death, if this has happened in both legs. One must, then, first astringe with wine or vinegar or vinegar-brine, then use fatty and gentle white plasters. Excellent for this is: one part white-lead, half a part ammoniac gum, enough myrtle-oil. Grind the ammoniac gum in water, then, and mix it with the white-lead, pouring in the myrtle-oil, and use it.
On those injured by cold.

For the horse injured by cold, it happens that it loses its appetite, and, because of this, wastes away, and, while eating, its lips do not move, and, while walking, it advances only a little at a time, and, raising its head, it groans, and cannot bend down. And, once laid down, it cannot stretch out flat, because its internal sinews are drawn taut, while the surface ones remain unaffected.

It is treated by drenching with thirty grains of pepper, ground in a cotyla of fragrant white wine, or likewise with boiled rue, or with sage, or with the wormwood plant in wine, or with hoary-leaved mullein, and by gradual exercise, a canter-run, as it appears to be making progress with its feed, and by more extensive rubbing against the grain of the hair. And, if the season is caught right and it is put out to pasture, it recovers and becomes healthy.
By Apsyrtus.
By Hierocles, against chilling of an animal.
Boil rue and mastic with a little oil and honey, and drench, adding pepper.
By Eumelus, against illness of horses from weakness
and heat and cold.

Illness generally overtakes the animal from weakness and heat, and the same happens in cold, or when, being pressed, it does not urinate, or if it drinks after sweating, or also if, from much idleness, it comes to much running and becomes overstrained.
Treat it, then, by putting oil into its throat, or likewise giving fat with wine. You will drive off chilling of an animal, if you rub its loins, kidneys, and head with hot oil or fat.
Another, for chilling.
Drench with warm pig's blood mixed with wine.
On sphakelismos (a wasting/gangrenous condition) and the sacred disease (epilepsy).
By Apsyrtus.

Apsyrtus to Tiberius Claudius Heraclides of Clazomenae, greetings. I wish you to know that sphakelismos occurs in horses, whose signs are these: it falls suddenly, and some of its joints go slack, while others become rigid, and there is a trembling of the whole body, and sometimes froth appears around the mouth. This is what, in humans, is called the sacred disease. We offer such a horse feed soaked in soda, and give it to drink. Purging by means of wild cucumber and soda over seven days is also fitting for it, and it will not recur continually.

It is also said that one should mix half a pint of sea-turtle's blood, an equal amount of vinegar, an equal amount of wine, and one weight of Cyrenaic laser-sap, and pour it into the nostrils. It is also beneficial to anoint it all over with soda and oil mixed with vinegar, with vigorous rubbing.
On those that tread on the toe.
By Apsyrtus.

As for those that tread on the toe, or are naturally uneven-footed, or have become so in one hoof from some cause, and those whose hind pastern-joints are bent inward, so that they touch the ground, and drag their hooves, these are lame, and weak in the loins, and inferior in running.
On a flux of sores
and against those struck by a boar.

For fluxed sores, one must not use warm treatment, but cold, in both summer and winter. For it easily happens, in hunting, that a horse takes a wound from a wild boar on the inner part of the hock, at the hollow of the knee, or the inner thigh, and the sore becomes fluxed and swells. One must apply the cold to this, and treat it by anointing with the remedy made from blue vitriol, or by burning a dog's head, minus the tongue, and grinding it, and applying it as a poultice.
On choking from indigestion.
By Apsyrtus.

If it ever happens that a horse, having just eaten and full of feed, runs, choking easily results. It is helped by being drenched through the nostrils with a cotyla of fragrant white wine mixed with one weight of soda, or with a three-obol weight of cumin and an equal amount of galbanum ground with wine, or with bay-berries in wine. Do not lead it into cold water, and give it warm drink, and use rubbing of the whole body with oil, preferably old.
Against strains in the groin.
By Apsyrtus.
If a strain occurs in the groin, the groin swells, and,

while walking, it is in pain. Such a horse should rest, and the groins should be fomented with plenty of hot water, and likewise fomented with sponges soaked in hot wine. Anoint the places too, grinding together goat-fat, wax-salve, roasted soda, and vinegar.
Against hardenings on the crown of the hoof, which are called 'pōroi' (calluses).

Apsyrtus to Postumius the Dacian, horseman, greetings. You wrote to me that your horse has developed, in its forefoot, on the inner part of the hoof at the growth of the crown, a large, hard swelling, and goes quite lame from it. Know, then, that this occurs spontaneously in the forefeet, not readily in the hind feet, and is called a 'pōros.' It is treated thus: pound fleabane and apply as a poultice, or likewise grind ivy-leaves, or knead vine-ash with vinegar and do the same. This too is good. Others use cypress,

chopped with vinegar; some use sumac. We ourselves have used this: grind salt with honey, so that it becomes like bath-oil-scrapings, and, cutting into the callus, spread it onto linen, and bind it on twice a day, first fomenting with hot water.

This happens especially to horses kept in herds. The callus becomes large, and the foot misshapen from lack of treatment, and it cannot walk, nor keep up with the others. Standing still, it does not graze, but is distressed, seeking out the herd, and throws itself down, and cannot be roused, and readily dies.
Such horses must not be grazed in marshy or watery places, but moved to where there is no moisture, but rather fine dust.
And if anyone can manage it methodically, he will treat it by anointing with salt and honey, using feathers, or likewise with pitch and salt.
Another: prognosis and cure of the pōros.
The area above the pastern-cushion is thick and rounded. Grind salt fine, then, and, pouring on honey, grind it, until it becomes like flour, then, warming it...
On how one must purge those in the herds.

Apsyrtus to Marcus, greetings. I wish you, as a horse-keeper, to know that we shall treat those in the herds thus: chopping wild-cucumber root fine and drying it in the sun, until it becomes dry, we chop it again, so that it becomes as fine as possible, and, mixing in an equal amount of ground soda, and mixing in salt, we give it to eat, excluding the pregnant mares; but we give it to those with foals still at foot, for the suckling foal will also be purged through her. We mix in the salt for the sake of persuading the animal to take the purge. It is better to mix in wheat-bran instead of salt. Let the purging take place in the month of Hyperberetaios or Dios, from the fifteenth, every other day, for five days. Do this three times, up to the new moon. Once this is done, mange does not occur, and the animals also escape the other illnesses.
Aphorisms on the appearance (conformation) of horses.
On the appearance of the horse, much has been well written by many; best of all
but best of all, among all writers, Simon and Xenophon, Athenian men, and, on horse-training, Xenophon alone surpasses the rest.
It is necessary, then, for you, as one earnestly engaged in horse-breeding, to know also their breeds.
The Parthian horses are large and of good size, spirited and noble in appearance, and outstandingly good in their feet.
The Median horses exceed others in size.
The Armenians and Cappadocians have the Parthian breed, but are rather heavier-headed.

The Spanish horses are large, well-proportioned in bodily habit, upright, well-headed, double-ridged in the back, well-articulated, not well-hipped, strong on journeys and not becoming thin in body, most courageous. [But they are poor at running and lack spirit for riding.]
They are also good-natured from birth up to the completion of their teeth; for the rest of the time they are bad and prone to bite.

The Greek horses are good-footed, of good size, well-headed, upright in the forequarters and well-proportioned, not well-hipped, but spirited and good runners; among all of Greece, the Thessalian horses excel.
The Epirote horses are bad-tempered and prone to bite.
The Thracian horses are ugly and ill-formed, wooden-bodied, low-shouldered, humped in the back, thin-necked, splay-footed, poor walkers, and likewise in running.
The Cyrenaic horses are of good size, with flanks drawn in and small, for which reason they are also good runners, good-footed, and longer-winded in riding.
The Istrian horses are good-footed, of good size, ugly in body, and unarticulated and hollow in the back, but good runners and vigorous.
The Sarmatian breed is not unpleasant, but well-proportioned

in its own kind, and a good runner, though plain; well-headed, well-necked, of good size, well-fleshed, and of moderate stature. The Argive horses are good-footed, but not well-hipped, well-headed, unarticulated and hollow in the back, of good size, and short.

As for the eagle-marked horses [gap] on the shoulders and the rump-bone, the Sarmatians take these as good; and they are also good runners among them, for which reason they use them in raids and wars. But those that have this mark on the hind parts, at the hips and the tail, are not good; indeed, they say it has been observed among them that one should not go to war on them; for a rider is easily lost from them, or falls into some difficulty.

As for those born among solid-hoofed animals that are snub-nosed and have a hare-lip or protruding teeth, one must not raise them, but, while still newborn, cast them off and remove them from the herd, knowing that they are freaks of nature and monstrosities; this happens especially among mismatched pairings. Those that have straight bones in their pastern-joints are very poor walkers, and, carrying a rider, jolt him about; they are called 'deer-footed.'

And those that, in the same place, have short, low bones, called 'dog-walkers,' these thrust their hooves inward toward the so-called pastern-cushions or fetlocks, and drag their feet, and go lame in them. Some also readily stumble on their hooves.
Good, too, are those with supple, easily-flexing knees in riding. For they are less prone to stumbling

and are without danger to the rider, and less prone to fatigue in their work than those with stiff ones, and resembling the so-called 'straight-limbed' or 'stake-legged' horses. And those with large flanks are weaker in strength and ill-shaped. In these, the rider is uncomfortable. Best of all are those whose withers rise higher than the shoulder-blade. For they are not only safe for riders, but also strongest in the shoulders of all others.

As for those naturally suspicious and overly timid, it is best not to own them, knowing that, carrying some of the baggage, they have sometimes thrown it off to their ruin. And this is the lesser evil; for, by easily stumbling, they have put the rider in a bad state. And the horse-kind has its suspicion plainly visible, so that the rider can hold on to safety; but the donkey-kind, and mismatched pairings, being suddenly startled, bring danger.
On the training of a war-horse, and on breaking in colts.

Apsyrtus to Getullius Severus, of the Seventh Legion, greetings. It is necessary for you, being an excellent cavalryman, to know about breaking in colts. When the colt has become two years old, they draw it from the herd and tame it, best daily, or, if not, every other day. And once it has become obedient and tame to the rider, they then begin to teach it, exercising it with gentle exercises, gradually increasing them, mostly up to the age of three. And from this age they use more vigorous exercise, training it and adding more
time, until it is within the sixth year; then one must not let up on the exercises and labors, knowing that it is going to be a war-horse and able to endure a long time in the works of war.

For the colt being exercised, let the ground not be too deep-soiled, especially at the beginning of its life. For it easily happens that, in the shins, the fibula-bones become dislocated, and thus the pastern-joints become flattened. And if this happens, the horse will be lame. It is not advantageous to bring a soft-footed horse to this training, and to go to war with it. For in engagements, such a horse does not easily escape from the enemy, because its feet hurt, and thus it happens that the rider is not saved. Likewise, horses that are aggressive toward others also cause harm.
On a sprain in the foot of solid-hoofed animals, and on the growth of the hoof, and on a place suitable for rolling.

When a sprain occurs in the pastern-joint, or so-called pastern-cushion, one must use this remedy: first draw blood from the pastern-joint, but do not prick the pastern-cushion, which they call the 'crown'; for beneath it lies a sinewy ligament connected to the vessel. Then, soaking a linen bandage in vinegar and oil, bind up the pastern-joint, and, tightening the pastern-cushion, thread the crossed bandage beneath the hoof, and soak it with vinegar-oil. And, tying up the sound foot to the knee, let the horse stand on the affected foot for three hours, and, undoing it, douse with

hot water, and rub with wax-salve, and apply as a poultice ground bulbs and salt, and do this for up to three days, and then use the emollient compounded for sprains; the dry form too is beneficial for these.

And when there is excessive growth in the hooves of the feet, one must not remove too much when paring, but, leaving intervals, do the same again. Otherwise, the growth of the hoof at the foot is harmed. For, in walking, it bends the hoof backward, being unaccustomed to the removal.

Best for leading solid-hoofed animals to roll is ground that is firm and earthy, level and free of stones or roughness; unsuitable are deep-soiled or grassy or dungy places. For these do not make the horse loose-limbed, nor promote dispersal in the body, but firm, solid ground is beneficial for them.
By Eumelus, for the same.
Take sour lees with warm ash and old lard, mix both together and spread as a poultice, store it adding also one egg, and use it when needed.
By Hippocrates, on a sprain.

The signs of a sprain are these: the foot does not remain steady at the joint, called the pastern-joint, but slips away, and the parts at the toe become unsteady. Treat it, then, by scraping around the hoof and binding on pine-resin and a sponge with vinegar for seven days. And if it does not recover, take a choenix of 'boukeron,' that is, fenugreek, and soak it in wine for three days. Then, pouring off the wine, pound the fenugreek, and,
putting it into a pot with honey, boil it, and thus apply as a poultice for six days. Old sprains must be cauterized in a lattice pattern.
Another.

One must diagnose the sprain, or dislocation, thus: squeeze the hoof with the hands; and if it is in great pain, the hoof has been wrenched. This happens continually to chariot-horses at the time of a race. You will treat it by drawing blood from the coronet, and dousing it with vinegar and salt and rubbing it in. Then, taking up wine-and-oil in wool, apply it at the joint of the hoof, dousing frequently with hot water, and applying the same treatment for twelve days.

And if this does not help, then, under pressing necessity, cut beneath the hoof with a scalpel, about twice the size of a coin. And if more hangs loose, cut down to the living flesh, taking care not to touch the bone. And if much blood flows, mix oil with vinegar and fine salt and the horse's own dung, and bind the joints together with the hoof using a linen cloth, and, after the third day, douse with hot water. And if excess flesh grows, use astringent or wound-remedies. Continually clean and trim the hoof around with a scalpel, so that it grows evenly on all sides, and use the un-boiled emollient, applying it gently. And if it is not healed even so, one must cauterize it.
Prognosis and cure of a sprain.

First, it walks on the tips of its toes, and its pastern-joint moves in a jerky way, and it drags the foot. Draw off, then, two cotylae of blood from the sprained hoof, and, blowing in wine and oil, rub it, and give it what is needed, and, taking wool, foment it, pouring on hot water. And when it has improved sufficiently, rub the sprain, and, taking dirty wool, blow in wine and oil and fine salt, wrap it around and bind it with a bandage, and bind it further with cords, and tighten it lightly, so that you do not cause inflammation or cut off some small vein, and apply this daily, except for the bloodletting. And if it becomes healthy this way, well; but if not, blow air onto its pastern-joint, and treat it as with the rest.
On the cure of leprosy (a skin disease).

Take much sharp lye, mix it with hot water, and wash, and let it dry. Then take a mina of unfired sulfur, an equal amount of blue vitriol, one drachm of laser-sap; pound these together, and make them fine, and take four cotylae of pitch, two pints of oil, one cotyla of sharp vinegar, mix these together, and add about an oxybaphon of the marked-out remedy. Then put it into the vinegar and the oil and warm it, and anoint, and let it stand in a soft, sheltered place. And when you have done this a third or fourth time, wash it off with lye and hot water. And if it is doing well enough, blow in wine and warm oil. But if not, anoint with the remedy and continue the rest of the treatment.
On staphylinos (a toxic plant, wild parsnip).

Staphylinos resembles the vertebra-plants found at home, but is larger. It grows everywhere in the fields, and moves along holding its tail raised. If the horse, while grazing, or by taking a mouthful of it brought in with the fodder, chews and swallows it, it vomits it up at once. For its breath is sharp, and its discharges are like those of a viper, and it swells all over with huge swellings. First, then, pour in the same infusion as for the others, then douse with plenty of hot water and foment and rub it. Then take sour lees, and chop flax fine and add it to the lees,

boil them together with water, and anoint the whole body, as much as it can bear, with the remedy, and let it stand in a warm, soft place, wrapped in a blanket, and let a fire be kept burning nearby continually. Let your morning anointment be like a potsherd's crust. Then, on the third day, wash it off again with plenty of hot water, and foment, and rub it again under shelter. Then anoint with soda. Do not be alarmed, if the lips especially and the eyes swell. For this happens, but it is treated promptly and heals.
On loss of appetite in horses and beasts of burden.

If a horse does not eat, without being held by any other affliction, or likewise some other beast of burden, let this be the sign: it holds its gullet raised, and its mouth is hot and full of phlegm. The treatment for this: draw off about a cotyla of blood from the third vertebra of the gullet, and, grinding salt with marjoram, rub the mouth, and let it drain off. Then flush with cold water. Do not give it anything to eat until the sixth hour.
On displacement of the bladder.

If a horse's bladder shifts from the anus, and it cannot urinate, and drags its hips, and also drags its hooves, there is no cure for this. But if a cyst-like growth occurs at the anus, or elsewhere in the body, one must remove it in this manner: take hold of it with flesh-forceps, and, drawing it out, cut it off, so as to make it as clean as possible. And when you have cut it off, take salt and oil, and, spreading it as a poultice, bind it up, and on the following day douse it with hot water, and, having rinsed away the blood, treat it with lycium, and apply a soft, dirty wool plug soaked in wine, and do this twice a day.
On cracked heels (rhagades).

Cracks occur behind the heels, arising from excess moisture or from a jump. One must treat them thus: take one pound of calf-fat, six ounces of rose-oil, boil these together, and add a little white-lead, and use it on such places.
For giving a horse a protective (hoof-growth).

If a horse, lacking such protection, goes lame, and hangs its head down, and is pricked from the hoof, do this: take the hoof, pare it, and scrape it down to the living part, and do not be afraid of the paring. For iron nourishes the hoof. Then take one pound of figs and six ounces of wax, chop these together and bind it on for three days, and do not undo it. Then use fomentation with wine-and-oil, and thus a protective growth will quickly form.
For every animal
that is sick or starving, use this regimen:

One pint of celery-seed, three drachms of linseed, two pints of fenugreek, three pounds of vetch, six ounces each of all-heal root, Illyrian iris, and savin; take these up with old lard and old wine, and, making small loaves, dry them in the shade, and give a walnut-sized amount, that is, a seventh of a drachm, with three ounces of honey. Grind it with one pint of old wine and drench for three days. Fumigating a dog's head beneath the horse's head also helps.
Treatment against 'pagoplexia' (frostbite/ice-strike).
By Theomnestus.

In the winter season, ice troubles horses and the other beasts of burden on journeys, as it happens, and the sons of physicians have called this affliction 'pagoplexia.' The fetlocks, then, swell, and become inflamed and cracked, together with the hooves. One must, then, treat them in this manner: douse first with hot water-and-oil, poured hot into a bowl, then wipe dry with rough rags, carefully binding the places with bandages, and, if they are very swollen, scarify them. Then apply as a poultice barley-flour boiled in very sharp vinegar,
until the swelling and the throbbing of the feet cease. For, if neglected, the animals often become useless.
On 'eileōdes' (an intestinal-obstruction/ileus-like colic).

'Eileōdes' occurs, when an animal is filled to satiety and does not digest it. It forms in the colon like a stone, and this is a very bad affliction. When, then, this affliction occurs, the horse throws itself down, and rouses itself repeatedly, and walks about, and throws itself down again, and
twists toward its spine and flanks, and groans from the tension. One must help such a horse thus: anoint
the hand and insert it into the anus, and remove the dung lying nearby, and gently rub the bladder, so that it urinates. For it is not, as they say, that the gut twists, but that the passage becomes
narrowed.

Drench, then, taking cabbage juice, one cotyla of oil, one cyathus of celery, and boiling it with one cotyla of wine. Anoint with warm wine and oil, and force it to stand, and give it an enema also through the anus with warm wine-and-oil, and let it walk about on rising and falling ground, so that the gases find a way to pass. For, once passage occurs, it will be relieved of the swelling. Then, putting chaff into a sack and soaking it with hot water, bind it beneath the flanks; for this reheats and removes the affliction. Give also

and eat, if it grows faint, oats or green fodder, or, sprinkling the dry fodder with water, water it sufficiently. The signs will be, for the one that survives: relaxed ears, labored and hot breathing, and movement of the belly; but for the one that does not survive: a prolapsed member, cold sweat at the flanks, shallow breathing, forelegs stretched out and cold, a rigid neck, and a cold nostril.
Another, for the same.

One must give an enema to those with 'eileōdes' using a decoction of beets, soda, and ground bdellium, and wash them and cover them with blankets, and keep a fire burning nearby. Give as feed, especially

green fodder or the softest hay. And if the troublesome excess matter does not clear, make the hand slippery with oil, insert it into the anus, and remove it. Drench also with beet-seed with six cotylae of wine and oil. And if this is not available, scrape the hooves of the forefeet, and, grinding them with three cotylae of wine, give through the nostrils.
On sycamine (mulberry) poisoning.

If a horse has eaten mulberry, take four parts of orpiment, one part quicklime, two parts ammoniac gum, one part aloe, enough honey; grind these together with the aforesaid ingredients, and, making a paste-like consistency, boil it over warm ash, stirring, until it becomes red-ochre in color. Use this lukewarm.
Another.
Take split orpiment and an equal amount of unslaked quicklime, put them into fish-sauce, and, making a paste, rub the place, and you will cure it.
On a fistula (syrinx).
By Hierocles.

If such an affliction is at the withers, or in some other place, cut open the affected part, and cauterize it, and treat it with the remedy compounded from quicklime, until the scab falls off. For, once the bad matter has fallen away, it fills in gradually. And if the affliction intensifies, use straight cauteries, and treat likewise with a caustic remedy, until it is healed.
Another, by Hippocrates.
When a horse has a fistula, mix blue vitriol with very sharp vinegar, and, drying it out, sprinkle it onto the place. Or grind wild cucumber thoroughly and knead it with spurge-sap, and insert it.
Another, by Apsyrtus.
Four ounces each of scraped verdigris, burnt copper, misy, and unripe-grape gall-nut, eight ounces of gum; mix all these together and use it.
On the preparation of drenches (enchymatismoi).
Proem, by Apsyrtus.

Master Celer, since our friendship demands the aid of remedies, I shall show you as many remedies for horses as we ourselves, and others, have tried. In writing these, we give credit to those from whom we received our starting point, and because we came to know the same things independently. And if they left anything out, we shall hand it down more reliably. Let me speak first, then, of purgative drenches.

Slaughter a suckling puppy, singe it, remove the entrails, and, having washed it, put it into a pot and boil it in water, so that only the little bones remain. And, mixing in a little honey with this, drench with two cotylae daily, for up to three days. And boiling a pig's ham and doing the same works too, or likewise a white cockerel. These things, then, were written by those before us. We ourselves have also used these:

boiling fine spurge in water, or hog's-fennel, or wormwood, or fine centaury, or likewise boiling birthwort root, or wild-cucumber root with soda, as written above, or roasted Egyptian colocynth-seed with its raw pulp. Let the quantity of water in these be two cotylae, and let it be drenched through the mouth daily, for up to seven days.
Best of these is wild cucumber with soda.
A simple drench: one pint of good wine, six ounces of good oil, six ounces of good honey, six eggs, enough water.
A warming drench: one pint of good wine, one ounce of pepper, one ounce of fresh rue, six ounces each of oil, tragacanth, and honey, six eggs.
A drench made from juices: one pint each of barley-gruel and fenugreek, a bundle of beets, four pounds each of dried figs, oil, and milk, a bundle of rue.
An aromatic drench: one ounce each of hyssop, parsley, saffron, white pepper, frankincense, common pepper, and myrrh, two ounces each of costus, tragacanth, and malabathrum, one ounce of rose-oil.
A summer drench: two sixths of an ounce of saffron, one ounce each of tragacanth, hyssop, marjoram, myrrh, frankincense, and sugar; soak these in rose-water and give it as a drink on the third day.
A drench for green fodder: three pints of Italian wine, one pint of oil, one pint of Italian honey, twelve eggs, one ounce of pepper; give to the animal's head for three days.

Composition of a warming and diuretic drench: two ounces of cassia, two ounces of costus, one ounce of spikenard, one pound of cyperus, six ounces of Cretan hyssop, six ounces of Pontic wormwood, one ounce of myrrh; boil these in water, and drench for three days. It also works against expelling internal parasites, and against tetanus, and against coughing, and for rousing the whole body. On the fourth day, give oil, so that it is thoroughly cleared out.

Composition of a drench against heat-exhaustion. If the horse comes in from the road, and its flank throbs, and it has no appetite for feed, and groans a great deal, apply, according to the season, reed-leaves, or fresh dog's-tooth grass, or lettuce sprinkled with vinegar, so as to cool it.

Then, soaking three ounces of tragacanth and one ounce of saffron in water from evening to the next morning, and one pint of pine-nuts, and grinding each separately, then mixing them together again, add one pint of sweet nut-wine or must-wine, and three ounces of purslane juice, and enough cold water. Drench for three days, offering the barley sparingly, and it will stop the illness. Use also two bloodlettings, one from the temples, the other from the neck.

Another. If you perceive that an animal has become 'apeptos' (has indigestion) - you will recognize it from these signs: its lips are swollen, and it is entirely covered with blister-like spots, and its tongue thickens, and its head becomes larger - you will help it thus: bleed it on the first day from the neck, and use green feed, if it is the season, or, failing that, lettuce or dog's-tooth grass or reed-leaves alone. On the second day, bleed it from the temples, and use the same feed. On the third day, drench it, if it is winter, with the aforesaid warming and diuretic drench; and if it is summer, with the cooling drench made of tragacanth and sweet wine.
A drench for feverish animals, to cool them: one ounce of vinegar, one ounce of rose-oil; mix both together and drench first with these, and, after a short interval, then mix in
three ounces of honey, three ounces of rose-oil, one pound of milk, one Italian half-pint of wine, and drench. Use the green feed that is in season.
A biting, warming drink: two ounces each of gentian, black pepper, white pepper, and hartwort.
A preliminary drench: two ounces of Pontic wormwood, three ounces of bitter lupine-seeds, three ounces of cress.

For sleep in an animal: about an obol's-weight of poppy-juice, dill taken up with three fingers, ground together into one, and, adding a cyathus of vinegar, give it to drink. And if you do not have poppy-juice, use the seed itself, three times the amount as of the juice, with one cotyla of wine.

A preliminary drench: six ounces of saffron, four ounces each of marjoram and hyssop, six ounces of melilot, four ounces each of costus, myrrh, aloe, and iris, six ounces of Cretan wormwood, four ounces of southernwood, six ounces of leaf, four ounces of licorice, six ounces of cassia, four ounces of cardamom, four ounces of spikenard, four ounces of birthwort, six ounces of aromatic reed, four ounces of cyperus, four ounces of knotgrass, four ounces of pepper, four pounds of tragacanth, three ounces of sarcocolla, three ounces of cardamom, three ounces of parsley, four ounces of sweet-flag, three ounces each of gentian, centaury, and opopanax, four ounces of betony, three ounces of storax-drops, two ounces of savin, three ounces of Celtic nard, an equal amount of castoreum, four ounces of leeks; pound and sift these, and, adding three cotylae of honey, two eggs, enough rose-oil, and one pint of wine, drench.
Another: three ounces of spikenard, four ounces of costus, four ounces of cardamom, three ounces of leaf, four ounces of agaric, six ounces of myrobalan, iris
give half a pint to the animal.

Hierocles' drench: one pint of honey, one bundle of leeks, one pint of unripe-olive oil, one bundle of dill, an equal amount of celery, one bundle of pennyroyal; boil all these together, then, making a broth from fine wheat-flour and mixing it in, use it.
A preliminary drench: boil barley-gruel together with goat-fat, and add fenugreek to these, boiling it in together, and drench the animal.
A spring drench: soak five eggs in very sharp vinegar from evening until morning, and give to the horse.

Another, for summer: nut-syrup, that is, boiled-down must, one spoonful of saffron soaked in wine, tragacanth soaked in lukewarm water, pine-nuts likewise soaked in wine, all ground; drench, holding the horse's tongue.

A restorative drench: three bundles of celery, three bundles each of cabbage and leeks, two pints of bay-berries, four pounds of pork, two ounces each of pepper and opopanax, nine pints of barley-gruel, one and a half pints of honey; boil the celery, leeks, and cabbage with the meat, the barley, and the bay-berries, then, adding the rest thus, drench.
A sleep-inducing remedy against ill-tempered animals: four ounces each of cardamom, bean-seed, and storax, two ounces of myrrh, six ounces of pepper.
Against those with vertigo: one ounce of long-onion seed,
one ounce of aloe, three ounces of white pepper, a quarter-portion of honey.
A troche: one ounce of hyssop, two ounces each of pellitory, fresh rue, saffron, and gum, three ounces of aloe-flower, a quarter-portion of honey.
Archelaus' troche: two ounces of myrrh, four ounces of southernwood, an equal amount of saffron, two ounces each of pellitory, fresh rue, marjoram, and hyssop, enough vinegar.

Another powder: one ounce of cassia, four ounces of Indian nard, one ounce each of saffron, costus, Illyrian iris, cardamom, parsley, hartwort, white pepper, horehound, centaury, all-heal, Pontic valerian, camel-thorn flower, and cardamom.

A fatigue-relieving liniment: one pound each of wax, ammoniac gum, bay-berries, roasted resin, oil, and resin-drops, two pounds of opopanax, two pounds of bdellium, four pounds of marjoram, six ounces of turpentine, one ounce of pepper, an equal amount of frankincense-manna, six ounces of henna-oil, two ounces of old wine.
Against sciatica: equal parts of spurge, Sardian orris, soda-froth, and unfermented-must perfume.

A decocted potion: a third of an ounce of saffron, an equal amount of myrrh, six ounces of aloe, half an ounce of costus; grind these the day before, and soak them in wine. And soak two ounces of tragacanth separately in water, and on the following day put it into a mortar, and grind, so that it dissolves, adding wine little by little, until it reaches nine Italian pints, pouring in also two pounds of honey. And when everything has been thoroughly ground and mixed together,
put it into a pot, warm it, and sprinkle on a little pepper, and, on the following day, give it to drink, warm in winter, cold in summer.

Another: two ounces each of hyssop, gentian, and opopanax, one ounce each of sagapenum, myrrh, dried figs, ginger, parsley, costus, and sweet-flag, two ounces of camel-thorn flower, one small bundle of rue, two ounces of celery-seed, six ounces of horehound, four ounces of Cretan carrot, two ounces each of all-heal and cassia, four ounces of quicklime, African celery.

By Pelagonius, on a dried-out hide. If the hide of some animal becomes dry, and, though fed, shows no improvement, which happens from excessive heat, it is treated thus: first anoint the whole body with rue-oil, then give the following preliminary drench, that is, one and a half ounces each of carrot, tragacanth, wild rue, and wild mint, an equal amount each of celery, melilot, and Pontic wormwood. Grind all these together and mix them, and, boiling them with hot water, administer.
The same author's preliminary drench and treatment against colic and against those harmed by rotten fodder.

Pelagonius to Lucius, greetings. The signs of colic are not familiar to everyone, since this affliction is not unlike other afflictions that arise internally. It differs from these only in this: that it has more continual and greater pains than cardiac ailments and those with twisting-colic. We have come to know the signs of these often by observing the following: first, while standing, it suddenly collapses, so that one might suppose it seized by epilepsy,

then, after a brief interval, pain immediately follows, and, throwing itself down, it lies there. And when it drinks cold water, it trembles and sweats and pants and is distressed. For such cases, then, one must help with this preliminary drench, as Celsus says:

A preliminary drench for colic: one ounce of Pontic rhubarb, one ounce of parsley, one ounce of fennel-seed, one ounce of black pepper, one ounce of horehound, one ounce of southernwood, one gramme of dill, one ounce of lovage, one ounce of centaury-seed, six ounces of ground-pine, four grammes of hemp-agrimony, one ounce of clean pennyroyal, one ounce of rue, one ounce of celery-seed, half a portion of ginger, two pounds of first-quality honey; pound and sift the dry ingredients, and take them up with the honey, and, when needed, use a hazelnut-sized amount with one pint of lukewarm water.

Another: four spoonfuls of honey, one ounce of frankincense-meal, five spoonfuls of vinegar, half a pint of old wine. Grind all these, divide into three portions, and give through the mouth over three days, and, covering it with a blanket, make it move about.
Another: hang caper-root bark [gap] in the smoke to dry, then, grinding it with wine and pepper, give it.

Another: for recognizing a horse harmed by (bad) fodder. First, its breath will be unsteady and continually throbbing, and its step unsteady. Bleed this one from the belly or the shoulders, and give a preliminary drench of boiled-down wine, and let it abstain from barley. Use also diuretic remedies.
Against lethargic horses. You indicated to me that your horses
are afflicted with a most severe illness. For you say that they lie down more continually and often fall asleep, and, on account of this, do not even take feed, but become very thin over time.

This affliction, then, is both very grave and requires much watchfulness, so that it does not occur. And if it does occur, it must be treated with the remedies set forth by us above. This kind of affliction those skilled in the medical art have called 'lethargy.'

You will treat it, then, in addition to what has been set forth, also in this manner: first, let it stand in a soft stable, with chaff or soft fodder sprinkled on the floor, and let it be prodded continually by hand, so that it does not fall asleep. It also helps for it to walk about more continually, and to have its four feet rubbed with vinegar and hot bran. Let it also be given a preliminary drink that includes wheat-bran and salt with vinegar-water, one pint.
Another. Pound the flower of the wormwood plant with oil and a little myrrh-oil, and give it through a horn.

Another preliminary drench against lethargic horses. Before all else, make the lethargic horses abstain from barley; let them eat one pint of dry broad beans, and let blood likewise be drawn from their vertebrae, and after this let them be drenched with this treatment: three ounces of Pontic rhubarb, five ounces of aromatic reed, five ounces of caper-root; pound and sift these with one pint of water, and drench about three spoonfuls. Let its drink be small in quantity and lukewarm itself. It must, however, be made to rise repeatedly, either by a human
voice or with a rod, so that, little by little,
through such care, the illness may be driven off.

Another preliminary drench, necessary at every season. Prepare a dry compound from the following ingredients, which is the most beneficial of all together: gentian, birthwort, myrrh, bay-berries, ivory-shavings, all in equal parts; when needed, give a preliminary drench against all kinds of afflictions in this manner: boil sharp-rush roots and horehound in wine, strain the wine, add a full spoonful of the aforesaid dry compound, and give a preliminary drench for three days.

And if the animals have a fever, boil the sharp-rush root in water, adding also celery and honey-water, which is found preferable, and thus, adding one spoonful of the dry compound, give a preliminary drench for three days. Against poisons, add more of the spoonful, and give it in one ounce of wine and half a pint of oil, for three days. Use it as a most powerful remedy.

A preliminary drench, called by the Romans 'coudrigarium.' One ounce of tragacanth, one ounce of parsley, six ounces of betony, one ounce of sarcocolla, one ounce each of cassia-tube and Illyrian iris, two bundles of hyssop, one ounce each of spurge, frankincense-manna, and gentian, one pound of 'perdikion' herb, one ounce of pepper, one ounce each of costus, melilot, opopanax, spikenard, camel-thorn flower, ammoniac gum, cinnamon, opopanax-root, rue-seed, and myrtle-berries, twenty-five small green pine-cones, two ounces of grains, one ounce of licorice. These,
pound and sift through a fine sieve, all of them, and store it, and, when needed, mix it with wine and give it.

Another preliminary drench, suitable at every season. One ounce each of costus, melilot, dry hyssop, Illyrian iris, birthwort, cave-myrrh, dragonwort, and spikenard; pound and sift all these, and make a dry compound. And in summer, adding also one ounce of saffron, an equal amount of tragacanth, enough honey, and six pints of wine, drench thus. In winter, mix in with all the aforesaid three ounces of ground pepper, and give it through a horn.
A binding drink: two ounces of myrrh, two ounces of tragacanth, two ounces of cumin, one ounce of saffron; give with lukewarm wine.

A summer preliminary drench: put one ounce of saffron into wine and three ounces of tragacanth into hot water, then, grinding it, add to these a leek-head and fresh celery, and, grinding it together again, add also a little lettuce-juice and goat's milk with rose-oil, four ounces of honey, one pint of boiled must, enough old wine. Then give through a horn for three days.

A preliminary drench for green fodder: one ounce of butter, one ounce of honey, one pound of old lard, twelve dates, one pint of raisins, ten bulbs, half a pint of crushed linseed, an equal amount of crushed fenugreek, enough Gallic garlic, one ounce of saffron, three ounces of tragacanth. Grind all these, mix with honey and eggs and oil and enough boiled must,
and give over three days.

A simple winter preliminary drench: one pint of old wine, six ounces of good oil, one ounce of pepper, ten ounces of fresh rue, six ounces of tragacanth, an equal amount of honey, as many eggs as you like, and enough boiled must.

A preliminary drench effective against everything: one pint of barley-gruel, an equal amount of fenugreek, one bundle of beets, twenty dried figs, two pounds of oil, one pint of donkey's milk; mix these and give as a preliminary drench continually.
A cooling preliminary drench: one pint of old wine, six pints of first-quality oil, as many grapes as you like, enough cold water.

A winter preliminary drench: one ounce each of saffron, costus, Macedonian parsley, myrrh, male frankincense, tragacanth, germander, betony, Alexandrian cumin, frankincense-manna, and pepper. Pound all these, and give one ounce to the animal with enough wine and oil. Mix in also barley-gruel juice, twenty dates, twenty-five dried figs, goat-fat, and a small puppy boiled in water. Mix all these together, and give through a horn.
Another cooling remedy: put one gramme of frankincense-manna with lukewarm white wine into the left nostril.

Another, warming: four ounces of Colophonian resin, two ounces of hyssop, one ounce of deer-marrow, half an ounce of opopanax, an equal amount of galbanum, six ounces of bay-oil, one pound of oil, an equal amount of mastic-oil. Mix these, put them in a bronze vessel, and boil over a gentle fire, take it up, and, once it has thickened,
use it, anointing the foreheads of the animals in winter.
This also works on humans who have suffered in the hips from prolonged cold.
Nothing so keeps the animals unharmed in the winter season as taking spiced wine through a horn continually.
Preparation of an extraordinary preliminary drench, effective for restoring animals, for every treatment of them, and for stopping coughing.
It is suitable at every season.

Ten ounces of tragacanth, three ounces of opopanax, two ounces of galbanum, eight ounces of Alexandrian gum, five ounces of melilot, an equal amount of dried roses, an equal amount of cassia, three ounces of Celtic nard, five ounces of marjoram, four ounces of balsam-fruit, three ounces of spikenard, five ounces of camel-thorn flower, five ounces of cardamom, four ounces of goat-fat, five ounces each of myrrh and bull-fat, three pints of fenugreek-flour, twenty dates soaked in wine, nine bulbs, one pound of first-quality honey, three pints of boiled must, twenty-five pints of old wine.
Soak and grind the galbanum, tragacanth, and opopanax in wine, and then boil the rest along with the other ingredients, until reduced to a third.
Add the boiled must and the wine in due proportion.
A summer preliminary drench.
One pint of clary-sage seed, an equal amount of parsley, one pint of myrtle-berries, one pint of Gallic hartwort, one pint of celery-seed, three ounces of camel-thorn flower.
Grind and strain these, and pour it into the throat with honey-water.
A preliminary drench against every pain.
Make a dry compound from old brick-dust, mixing in one ounce of turpentine-resin,
and give it in hot water, and use it as a proven remedy.
Grind the herb called 'herakleia,' that is, panakeia, with old wine, and give as before described.

A most useful compound: grind panakeia-root and wheat-flour in equal parts, and sift them, and take them up with old wine, and make troches. Then, making it more liquid, give this later as a preliminary drench. And if a wound is found internally, it will be healed.
On emollients (malagmata).

By Apsyrtus: the emollient made from bdellium. Nineteen staters of pitch, the same of wax, an equal amount of resin, two staters of galbanum, an equal amount of opopanax, one stater each of storax and bdellium; this same recipe is also a fatigue-relieving liniment. Mix these and use it. Dissolved with henna-oil, it works against chills in humans.
A sour emollient: twenty-four staters of dry pitch, twenty staters of wax, four staters of ammoniac gum, one stater of galbanum, two staters of frankincense-manna, one cotyla of sharp white vinegar;
boil in an earthenware vessel, adding half the vinegar.
And if it rises up, sprinkle on the rest.
The emollient we ourselves have used, preparing it also for humans.

Sixteen staters of wax; soak the wax in henna-oil, and, softening it in the sun and making it into leaves, likewise place it in the sun, until it has absorbed all the henna-oil - let there be two cyathi of it.

And, having first ground twenty-four staters of ammoniac gum thoroughly fine with enough sharp white vinegar, so that it does not become too liquid, with two ounces of galbanum, two ounces of opopanax, two ounces of salt-flower, then we add the wax, and, grinding it together so as to mix, we use it thus.
An emollient made from fat and wax.

Sixteen staters of wax, an equal amount of deer- or beef-kidney-fat or goat-fat, one stater of frankincense-manna, two staters of Colophonian resin, two weights of galbanum, one cyathus of oil; put all these into a pan, and, pouring them together into one, boil.
And when it has melted together, remove it promptly.
Add the frankincense-manna and the galbanum last of all.
A softening remedy.
Twenty-four staters of lard, an equal amount of Colophonian resin, sixteen staters of wax.

A fatty composition of a fatigue-relieving liniment. By Apsyrtus. Two staters of white-lead and an equal amount of litharge; put the litharge into a mortar and soak it a night and a day in water in a new vessel, and, straining off the water, grind the white-lead in a mortar as finely as possible.
Then, making a wax-salve, mix it in and grind it all day.
And when it becomes smooth, mix in honey,

a shell's-measure, and, grinding it together, use it thus. And, taking oil into the hand, apply it to the temples of the horse and the anus. Likewise it also works on a human against all fatigue. Let the wax-salve be six staters. Composition of an emollient: one pound each of wax, roasted resin, ammoniac gum, hemlock, salt-flower, and bull-fat, two pounds of resin-drippings, six ounces of opopanax, two ounces of myrrh, two ounces of galbanum, an equal amount of frankincense. And if you wish it to be more binding, or an adhesive plaster, remove the bull-fat from it, and add one pound of Judaean bitumen and two cotylae of vinegar. An emollient for the thigh: one pound of wax, six ounces of turpentine, six ounces each of Colophonian resin, pine-resin, and pitch, one ounce each of opopanax, galbanum, ammoniac gum, sagapenum, bdellium, frankincense, and saffron. A golden-colored emollient: one ounce each of opopanax, salt-flower, ammoniac gum, sagapenum, and galbanum, six ounces each of Colophonian resin, turpentine, roasted resin, frankincense, and wax. An emollient against gas-swellings of the joints: nine ounces each of Judaean bitumen and wax, two ounces of dry pitch, six ounces each of roasted resin and frankincense, four pounds of Cyprian copper-scale, three and a half pounds of oil. An emollient against 'marmarosis' and inflammations: four pounds each of litharge, bay-oil, and white-lead, two pounds each of turpentine, Colophonian resin, storax, Illyrian iris, propolis, and Judaean bitumen, one pound of galbanum,
six ounces of Cretan hyssop, two ounces of golden-colored misy.
six ounces of ammoniac gum.
An emollient against pains of the sinews and joints, and for relieving pains without cauterization.

Six ounces each of mint, millet, sulfur, turpentine, storax, bdellium, galbanum, and pitch; chop all these together, mix in four pints of wine, then boil again, and, while still hot, spread it and apply.
An adhesive plaster against calluses: three ounces of roasted resin, one pint of fine flour, one pint of vinegar.

The emollient called 'ambla moula.' Three ounces each of opopanax, bitumen, galbanum, sagapenum, and oak-mistletoe glue, half an ounce of salt-flower, two ounces of castoreum, one ounce each of unwashed wool-grease and ammoniac incense, one and a half ounces of male frankincense, four ounces of turpentine, three ounces of bdellium, two and a half ounces of storax, four ounces of propolis, two and a half ounces of pine-resin, six ounces of wax, one and a half pounds of Brittany pitch. Grind the opopanax carefully with the salt-flower, and, melting all the other ingredients, add the ground ones.

Archedemus the horse-breeder's preparation: an emollient for colts. Three pounds of resin-drippings, one and a half pounds each of wax and propolis, one pound each of pine-resin and turpentine, six ounces each of oak-mistletoe glue, galbanum, salt-flower, and comfrey, three ounces each of castoreum and hemp-agrimony, two ounces of spurge, six ounces of melilot.
Another emollient: two ounces each of bitumen and ammoniac gum, one ounce each of myrrh and galbanum, six ounces each of spurge, castoreum, opopanax, and reed-adarce, three ounces of the
drippings from ships' coatings, six ounces of Colophonian resin, two pounds of wax.

Another emollient, made with figs: one pound each of African fig, galbanum, Brittany pitch, sulfur, and soda; grind these into one, and, mixing them with the pitch and the galbanum, use it, until it stops the pain. Then apply the raw emollient.

A raw emollient against strength of the sinews, and for humans with gout. Take two pounds of wax, six pounds of unwashed wool-grease, put them into a mortar and pound, and, when they are well pounded, weigh out six ounces, and transfer to a mortar-bowl, and grind with a lead pestle, until, from the grinding, it becomes two ounces. Then add three pounds of honey, enough vinegar. Then take one pint of ground marble and six ounces of ammoniac gum, pound and sift them, and, adding one pint of cress, fry it in an earthenware pan, and after this take one pound of galbanum, grind it until it becomes soft, and then put everything together into the mortar, and, having pounded it, take the compound out of the mortar, and, adding three ounces of deer-marrow and six ounces of old oil, mix carefully, and make little balls, and, for a human, spread it onto linen and apply it, but for horses onto a rag.
Another emollient against joints: one pound each of galbanum, storax, opopanax, and frankincense-manna, six pounds of red ochre.
Another emollient, by Hippocrates: put in equal parts spurge-froth and pine-hemlock, and use it.
Preparation of the emollient made from bdellium: bdellium,

one ounce each of galbanum, ammoniac gum, bitumen, bull-glue, and Pontic resin, an equal amount of deer-marrow, six ounces of hemlock, two ounces of mastic, one ounce of frankincense, one ounce each of wax, opopanax, aloe, and myrrh.

Hierocles' gentle emollient: six ounces each of wax and propolis, four ounces each of frankincense, storax, burnt Cyprian copper, deer-marrow, and galbanum, one pound of Colophonian resin, one ounce of opopanax, one pound of old oil, one pound of litharge. Grind the litharge with the oil, put it into a pot, until it dissolves, then grind the opopanax in wine and mix it with the rest, and use it.

Another emollient: three ounces of ammoniac incense, one pound of dry pitch, six ounces of wax, four ounces of turpentine-resin, eight and a half ounces each of frankincense-manna and galbanum; grind the ammoniac gum and the frankincense-manna with vinegar, and sprinkle in the meltable ingredients.
Another: a lard plaster. Grind lard, wax, and Colophonian resin in equal parts, and use it.
Another emollient: one pint of oil, one pound of resin-drippings, six ounces each of opopanax, galbanum, turpentine-resin, and Judaean bitumen, one pound of Colophonian resin, half a pound of wax.

A tightening and thinning boiled emollient: four grammes of bitumen, one pound of wax, six ounces of resin, six ounces of hemlock; one must, at the very start of spring, dig up the root of the giant-fennel plant, and, chopping it, dry it, and mix it in and use it.
Preparation of an emollient: spurge, opopanax, cas-
toreum, and galbanum, two ounces of each, one ounce each of sagapenum and storax,
one pound of ammoniac incense, jujube, turpentine,

one and a half pounds; three pounds of resin-drippings, three ounces of propolis, five ounces of bdellium, three ounces of frankincense-manna, two pounds of wax, two pounds of roasted resin, six pounds of bitumen, one pound of mistletoe-glue.
Pelagonius' preparation of an emollient: three pounds each of wax, African resin, oil, and litharge; mix all these together, and use it.
Against a burn: boil apple-bark in water, and use it.

Another preparation of an ointment: six ounces of wax, four ounces of cleaned black jujube, one pound of dry pitch, four ounces of bay-berries, six ounces of roasted resin, one ounce of pepper, two ounces of laser-resin, two ounces of male frankincense, seven ounces of good oil, two ounces of henna-oil; boil all these together with cold water, and pour it out, so that it unites. And when it reaches the consistency of a wax-salve, take it up and use it.
A cooling adhesive plaster: six ounces each of saffron, frankincense-meal, red ochre, African snails, and African bulbs, half a pint of fine flour, enough vinegar.

An adhesive plaster for the joints and loins of horses: two grammes of fine flour, one ounce of frankincense-meal, the yolks of two eggs; make an adhesive plaster, and use it on the joints and the loins.
An emollient against pains of the sinews: one pound of wax, six ounces of deer-marrow, three ounces of myrrh, and two spoonfuls of its dry compound; mix these, boil, and use it.
Another: preparation of an emollient: six ounces of wax, one pound of litharge,
five pounds of oil, two pounds of resin, two ounces of ammoniac gum, two ounces of galbanum, two ounces of opopanax, two ounces of myrrh, two ounces of frankincense, enough wine.

Another: one and a half pounds each of galbanum, frankincense-meal, deer-marrow, wallflower, and turpentine-resin, one pound each of bull-fat, poppy-juice, and Illyrian iris, half an ounce of birthwort.
Another emollient: two pounds each of strained fat, turpentine-resin, and oil, four pounds of litharge, one ounce each of galbanum and verdigris.
Against pains of the sinews: one pound each of wax and wallflower, one and a half pounds each of storax, propolis, white wax, poppy, and bay-berries.

Another emollient: four pounds of wax, one pound each of opopanax, storax, bay-berries, goat-fat, resin, and poppy-seed, two ounces of galbanum, six ounces of Colophonian resin, six ounces of iris-oil.

An emollient against various afflictions and against bruised joints: three ounces of yellow wax, two pounds of galbanum, six ounces each of storax, Colophonian resin, and iris-oil, one pound each of wallflower, bay-berries, goat-fat, roasted resin, and poppy-seed, six ounces of iris-oil.
Another: two pounds of bull-fat, one pound each of wallflower, ammoniac gum, Illyrian iris, soda-froth, goose-fat, and deer-fat, five ounces of white pepper.
An emollient against those with pain in the shoulder-blades: two pounds each of litharge, galbanum, wallflower, and frankincense-manna,

one pound each of turpentine-resin, Colophonian resin, African opopanax, Attic propolis, Illyrian iris, Attic poppy-juice, and ammoniac gum, two and a half pounds of mistletoe-glue, one and a half pounds of cardamom, four pounds of bull-fat, three pounds of wax.
A hard emollient: half a pound of yellow wax, two pounds of Attic hyssop, one and a half pounds of poppy, six ounces each of storax, propolis, deer-marrow, and wallflower.

A Cretan emollient: one pound each of processed wax and ammoniac gum, six ounces each of dry pitch and Illyrian iris, one and a half pounds of resin, eleven ounces of galbanum, five ounces of turpentine, enough vinegar.
The emollient made with figs: two pounds of sweet figs, four ounces of soda; grind the figs carefully, add the soda, and grind. This is most useful.
The emollient made with lard: chop one pound of old lard, and, adding enough quicklime, store it for three days, and bind it on. This surpasses all other remedies and removes pains.
A three-drug emollient: one pound each of ammoniac gum and wax, enough vinegar.

Apsyrtus' emollient: one pound of wax, six ounces of ammoniac gum-drops, an equal amount of henna-oil, iris-oil, and bay-oil, three ounces of bull-fat, four ounces of deer-marrow, one and a half ounces of storax, one ounce of laser-resin, one ounce of galbanum, six ounces of turpentine-resin, six ounces of male frankincense, one ounce of black pepper, two ounces of opopanax.
Another emollient: one pound of wax, bdellium, ammo-
two ounces each of ammoniac incense and stomach-frankincense-manna, six ounces each of turpentine, galbanum, and opopanax, one pound of resin. Pound all these in a mortar, and use it.

Another: one pound each of wax and ammoniac gum, two ounces each of galbanum and turpentine, enough henna-oil; boil all these except the ammoniac gum. Grind this separately, add the rest, and, once boiled, let it cool in a mortar. Then knead it by hand, and use it.

A pounded emollient: three pounds of wax, two ounces of galbanum, four ounces of turpentine, three ounces of bull-fat, two ounces of unwashed wool-grease, three ounces of bdellium, six ounces of ammoniac gum, one and a half ounces of white pepper, one and a half ounces of soda-froth, two ounces of Illyrian iris, two ounces of goose-fat, two ounces of deer-marrow.

A hard emollient: five ounces of wax, three ounces of storax, six ounces of unwashed wool-grease, four ounces of opopanax, four ounces of bay-oil, an equal amount of poppy, three ounces of deer-marrow, two ounces of bdellium.
An emollient against the sinews: two ounces of galbanum, an equal amount of opopanax, bdellium, and oak-mistletoe glue, one ounce each of rush and turpentine-resin.
Another aromatic emollient: four ounces of litharge, two ounces of bdellium, three ounces of poppy, one ounce of bay-berries, half an ounce of opopanax, six ounces of bay-oil.

An emollient against slackness and pains of the joints and sinews: six ounces of mint-seed, six ounces each of turpentine-resin, storax, bdellium, galbanum, and dry pitch, half an ounce of honey; boil all these, add four eggs and enough wine. Then spread it onto linen and use it.
Against blows to the joints: three pounds each of ammoniac gum, pitch, bitumen, and galbanum, two pounds each of bdellium, turpentine, and propolis, one pound each of storax and mistletoe-glue.
A poultice against swellings of the hocks from a blow or any other cause: knead bitumen, wax, and vinegar, and sprinkle it on.
The recipe of Apollo of Colophon, against swellings in the joints: grind ammoniac incense thoroughly, mix it with vinegar, and, making a wax-salve, use it.

An adhesive plaster against all afflictions of the joints: six ounces of acacia, one pound of pitch, two pounds of Cimolian chalk, one pound of cow-dung; grind all these together and warm them, and apply. First douse with lukewarm seawater.

Eumelus, against pain of the palate: pain of the palate-vault is cured by blood drawn from that place, or by one ounce of male frankincense and one oxybaphon of celery-seed, ground and mixed with lukewarm water, and given through the nostrils. For the one suffering a great deal, one must cauterize the shoulder-blades on either side, near the ribs, with a lighter cautery, so as not to reach more than a finger's depth.
Hierocles, against pain of the knees: boil rue in oil and anoint.
Pelagonius, if the foot is struck by a wheel: grind a red bulb and frankincense-manna together and apply, and, after three days, untie it and anoint again with the same remedy. Then use an emollient.
Against swellings of the feet: two ounces of spurge, four ounces of common salt, four grammes of liquid pitch; boil all these together,
and apply to the swollen parts. And if the pain persists in the joints, along with bad humor, cow-dung applied as a poultice to the joints helps.

An adhesive plaster against the joints, legs, and hydatid-cysts: one pound each of galbanum, storax, poppy, bdellium, turpentine-resin, and red ochre, two pints of fine flour. Boil all these and unite them, and use against the aforesaid afflictions.

An adhesive plaster against the joints: six ounces each of saffron, frankincense-meal, and African red ochre, half a pint of fine flour, twenty ground African bulbs, six ounces of mint. Chop all these together and mix with vinegar, and use it.

Apsyrtus' plaster for the fetlocks: six ounces of cadmia, three ounces of black hellebore, three ounces each of copper-flower, Judaean bitumen, burnt copper, ammoniac salt, burnt blue vitriol, burnt lees, verdigris, and soda-froth, six ounces each of old lard and whetstone-oil.

Composition of a plaster made from herbs: two ounces each of galbanum, myrrh, aloe, chalk, verdigris, frankincense-manna, Attic propolis, ammoniac gum, and Bithynian resin, six ounces of white wax, two pounds of silver-drippings, two pounds of old oil, two ounces of birthwort, two ounces of horehound, three ounces of cedar-oil, two ounces of Brittany pitch, six ounces of cyperus, three ounces of kyphi-incense, three ounces each of centaury, Illyrian iris, clover-root, and wormwood, four ounces of soda-froth, four ounces of white pepper, an equal amount of bay-berries. Pound and sift all these aforesaid ingredients,

then put them into a mortar, and pound with old oil, until it becomes an emollient, and use it thus. In winter, add also wine and oil, and, warming it, anoint. Let the horse stand in a warm place, covered with blankets.
A plaster for quickly filling in scars: one pound each of wax, butter, and resin, two pounds of roses.
A wound-plaster preparation: grind equal parts of white-lead and litharge in the sun, and mix them with vinegar and rose-oil, and use it. And if there is no rose-oil, mix in plain oil alone.

Hierocles' preparation of plasters: put resin-drippings, wax, and roasted resin all together into a mortar and stir, then add a little white-lead, previously ground with water and oil, adding in the meltable ingredients at the same time. And if you wish it to be more porous, mix in a little opopanax dissolved in wine.

Another, simple: one pound of wax, four pounds of roasted resin, six ounces of turpentine-resin. Boil these up, take it off the fire, and add three ounces of ground Judaean bitumen, and let it dissolve. Then add two ounces of pounded and sifted ammoniac gum, and put it back on the fire, and, stirring with a spatula, sprinkle in two ounces of frankincense-manna and an equal amount of galbanum. Then, taking it off the fire again and adding two ounces of pre-ground opopanax, use it.
Another: one pound of litharge, two pounds of fresh strained bath-oil-scrapings, one ounce of turpentine-resin.
Another, made with bath-oil-scrapings: two pounds of bath-oil-scrapings, litharge or
one ounce of white-lead, three ounces of resin-drippings, three ounces of roasted resin.
Boil, then, the bath-oil-scrapings and the litharge, and, when it thickens, add the rest.
Another, the 'quince-colored' plaster: one pound of wax, one pound of pine-resin, two ounces of turpentine, three ounces of ammoniac gum, one ounce of galbanum, one ounce of opopanax.
The blood-plaster: one pound each of vinegar, litharge, and oil; boil all these together and use it.

A plaster against fractures: one pound each of litharge and vinegar, one and a half pounds of oil, three ounces of ammoniac gum, two ounces of wax, two ounces of resin, three ounces of turpentine, six ounces each of bitumen, pitch, and verdigris. Having first boiled the vinegar, the oil, and the litharge, when it is about to thicken, add the pitch, until it too dissolves, and, taking it from the fire, add the bitumen, without stirring it. And when it too has dissolved, add the rest and boil. Then, once it has thickened, take it from the fire and strain it into a mortar.
Another melting plaster, softening and relaxing: one drachm each of pitch, wax, and resin, four ounces of ammoniac gum, enough opopanax ground beforehand with vinegar.

Another, dry, effective against bleeding and against pockets, and drying and binding together: one pound of litharge, one pound of sharp vinegar, one pound of common oil, one ounce each of resin-drippings and verdigris. Boil the vinegar, the oil, and the litharge, until it begins to change, add the resin-drippings, and boil again, and, having ground
the verdigris separately in a mortar with vinegar, add it in, and use it.

Another gentle plaster: one pound of litharge, an equal amount of oil, three pounds of ammoniac gum, three ounces of wax; boil the oil and the litharge. Then, when it is about to thicken, add the ammoniac gum and the wax.

Another 'quince-colored' golden plaster, effective for the sinews, the joints, and against chilling. It works well when dissolved with iris-oil or henna-oil, applied to a sore spot from exertion. Six ounces each of wax and roasted resin, half an ounce each of turpentine-resin and opopanax, an equal amount of galbanum and cave-myrrh, one ounce of ammoniac gum, an equal amount of frankincense, one ounce of bull-fat, three ounces of salt-flower; melt the meltable ingredients on one side, and on the other grind the opopanax in wine together with the myrrh and the salt-flower and the frankincense, until they mix, and, taking up everything together, use it.
Another strengthening plaster, called the sole-plaster: equal parts of cedar-oil and bitumen; boil each separately and anoint the tender place.

Another dissolved, fatty plaster: six ounces of litharge, one pound of white-lead, one pint of Italian vinegar, four ounces of iris-oil; grind the litharge and the white-lead, and add part of the vinegar with oil and wine, and, setting aside the pestle, grind by hand, until it reaches the thickness of bath-oil-scrapings, and use it thus. This also works against abrasions and gentle sores.
A dissolved white plaster, effective against fluxes, burns, abrasions, and spontaneously-arising sores: one pound each of litharge and white-lead,
enough common oil, enough vinegar.
Another: one pound each of red-lead and white-lead, six ounces of litharge, enough rose-oil, enough sharp vinegar.
Another: six ounces of red-lead, an equal amount of white-lead and rose-oil.
A fatty, dissolved, astringent plaster: six ounces of litharge, one pound of white-lead, one Italian pint of old wine, one Italian pint of common oil, four ounces of myrtle-oil.
A fatty plaster, effective against burns: six ounces of white-lead, an equal amount of red-lead, the whites of ten eggs, enough rose-oil, likewise enough nightshade-juice.

Pelagonius' green plaster: one pound of wax, two and a half pounds of myrtle-oil, two ounces of goose-fat, two ounces of unwashed wool-grease, three ounces each of verdigris and galbanum, two ounces of turpentine-resin, enough frankincense-meal; boil all these in a bronze vessel, and, taking it up, use it.
Another preparation of a plaster: two pounds each of soda, burnt copper, and lard, three pounds of Judaean bitumen, one pound each of blue vitriol and silphium.

Preparation of a remedy: one pound each of dry pitch, pine-resin, Brittany pitch, and opopanax, one ounce each of galbanum, propolis, unfired sulfur, frankincense-manna, saffron, ammoniac gum-drops, cave-myrrh, and storax, six ounces of Judaean bitumen, six ounces of wax, two ounces of deer-marrow, one ounce each of Colophonian resin and all-heal root; boil all these together over a gentler fire, and use it when the occasion presses.
Another plaster: verdigris, burnt copper, burnt
soda, ammoniac salt, lees, black hellebore, six ounces of each, one pound of lard, six ounces each of galbanum and wax.
Another composition of a plaster: cadmia, Judaean bitumen, burnt copper, blue vitriol, soda, and lard.
Another gentle, relaxing ointment: three pints of wine-lees or of boiled must, enough marjoram, bay-berries, linseed, sea-soda, willow-seed, and oil.
Apsyrtus, against 'ozainai' (foul-smelling sores): three ounces of mistletoe-glue, one and a half pounds of alum, six ounces of ironwort, enough vinegar.
By Hierocles, for the same. Wash out, in a vessel, the broom used to sweep the oven, and collect the water, and anoint in the sun, having first washed the place and wiped it clean with vinegar.

By Eumelus, for the same. Soak plump dried figs in squill-vinegar for four days. Then take them and grind them, so that their seeds are thoroughly ground in. Add also the white part of onions in due proportion. Then mix in cleaned salt-fish flesh, apart from the bones and the skin, and, grinding everything carefully and making a poultice, spread it onto a rag and bind it on the feet, in this manner: first rub vigorously with a coarse-woven rag and wipe clean with vinegar, and thus apply the plaster for two days. Let the animal being treated remain motionless, so that it eats and drinks in the stable. And, undoing it after the third day, you will find it healed.
Pelagonius, for the same. Chop writing-ink, gall-nuts, and alum in equal parts with lard, mix in apple-bark and enough vinegar, salt, and soda, and apply.

Another: chop figs and mustard, add vinegar with liquid alum, and apply. And on the third day, undoing it, if you do not perceive it helped, renew the remedy, and again undo it after three days, and, when it has improved, wash the joints with wine and release the horse untied.
Another: boil opopanax together with barley-flour, so that it becomes plaster-like, and apply.
On what 'raw solution' is: 'raw solution' is a mixture of fenugreek, linseed, and barley-flour in equal parts.

The 'coudrigarium' powder: one ounce each of cardamom, cinnamon, garlic-mustard, celery-seed, and birthwort, six ounces each of saffron, camel-thorn flower, and roses, one pound of Illyrian iris, nine ounces of wild ginger, one pint each of parsley and anise, two pounds of saffron-dregs, three ounces each of Pontic rhubarb, cassia, male frankincense, and calamint, four ounces each of spikenard, Celtic nard, black pepper, costus, all-heal, long pepper, and white pepper.
The 'coudrigarium' ointment: two pounds each of bull-fat, goat-fat, and deer-fat, one pound each of goose-fat, Tyrrhenian wax, and turpentine-resin, one pint of old oil.
A warming ointment: one pound each of wax, pine-resin, and turpentine-resin, two pounds of lard, one ounce each of galbanum, soda, unfired sulfur, bay-berries, and cyperus;
rub it onto the animals' foreheads and kidneys.

Apsyrtus' ointment against chilling of the sinews: one ounce of wax, four ounces of turpentine-resin, two ounces each of opopanax and deer-marrow, three ounces of storax-oil, one ounce of henna-oil; boil all these together into one, and use it on the chilled places, in winter in a warm place, in summer in the open air.

An ointment for weakened shoulders, loins, and hips, rousing and dispersing the weakness, and it also treats tetanic conditions: one pint each of bay-berries and marjoram, three ounces of unfired sulfur, one pound each of soda, clean frankincense-manna, and pine-resin, three ounces of Ethiopian cumin, three ounces of common oil, three pints of good wine; boil this, until it becomes like bath-oil-scrapings, store it in a vessel, and, warming it slightly when needed, use it.

A fomentation of Apsyrtus' ointment against those with opisthotonos: one pint each of bay-berries and cumin, three ounces each of unfired sulfur and galbanum, one pound of turpentine-resin, three pints of oil; boil these together, and anoint the whole animal. Use dry vine-shoots as feed.
The same author's fomentation for ligaments: wax,
one pound each of pitch and roasted resin, one ounce of opopanax,
one pint of oil. When these have melted, strain them, and, while still hot,
add vinegar, and knead, and use.
A relaxing joint-ointment: six ounces of wax, three ounces of propolis,
one ounce of opopanax, one ounce of galbanum, half an ounce of castoreum,
six ounces of bull-fat, four ounces of resin-drippings, four ounces of dry pine-resin,
